Interview questions

0 Questions

NTA2026A00001 is a business-facing reference number, not usually the database primary key. Break it into: NTA (organisation/product prefix), 2026 (year), A (branch/type), and 00001 (running number). Keep a normal technical primary key such as Long or UUID as well, and add a unique constraint to the business id.

Best choice for most Spring Boot applications

Generate the counter in the database and format the final string in the application. A database sequence or an atomic counter update is safe when several requests, pods, or service instances create records at the same time. Generating the counter only in application memory is unsafe: each instance can produce the same number after a restart or during concurrent traffic.

ApproachUse it whenImportant point
Database sequence + application formattingMost monoliths and Spring Boot APIsRecommended: simple, fast, and safe across instances.
Database stored procedure/functionThe database owns all business-number rulesStrong central control, but more database-specific logic.
Application counterOnly one instance and no concurrency, which is rare in productionDo not use for scalable production systems.
Snowflake/ULID/UUIDDistributed services needing IDs without a database callGood technical ID; usually not a short sequential business number.
PostgreSQL: use a sequence
CREATE SEQUENCE nta_reference_sequence START WITH 1 INCREMENT BY 1;

CREATE TABLE applications (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    application_number VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    applicant_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);
@Repository
public class ReferenceSequenceRepository {
    private final JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate;

    public ReferenceSequenceRepository(JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate) {
        this.jdbcTemplate = jdbcTemplate;
    }

    public long nextValue() {
        return jdbcTemplate.queryForObject(
                "SELECT nextval('nta_reference_sequence')",
                Long.class
        );
    }
}

@Service
public class ApplicationNumberService {
    private final ReferenceSequenceRepository sequenceRepository;

    public ApplicationNumberService(ReferenceSequenceRepository sequenceRepository) {
        this.sequenceRepository = sequenceRepository;
    }

    public String nextApplicationNumber() {
        long sequenceValue = sequenceRepository.nextValue();
        int year = Year.now().getValue();

        return "NTA" + year + "A" + String.format("%05d", sequenceValue);
    }
}

The first call returns NTA2026A00001, then NTA2026A00002. A database sequence is atomic, so two simultaneous requests receive different values. Gaps are normal: a transaction can obtain a number and later roll back, but the sequence value is not returned. Never promise gap-free IDs unless the business and database design explicitly require it.

If the number must restart every year

Do not reset one global sequence in a live application: concurrent requests around New Year can race. Instead maintain one counter row per business scope, for example (prefix, year, branch). The database increments that one row atomically. 

CREATE TABLE business_id_counter (
    prefix VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,
    id_year INTEGER NOT NULL,
    branch_code VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,
    last_value BIGINT NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (prefix, id_year, branch_code)
);

In PostgreSQL, an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE ... RETURNING last_value statement can create or increment the counter in one atomic operation. For MySQL, use a transaction with a row lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) or a stored procedure. Then build NTA + year + branch + zero-padded value in Java.

Save it with a unique database constraint
@Entity
@Table(name = "applications",
       uniqueConstraints = @UniqueConstraint(name = "uk_application_number",
                                             columnNames = "application_number"))
public class Application {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(name = "application_number", nullable = false, updatable = false)
    private String applicationNumber;
}

Interview answer: For readable sequential IDs, I keep a separate technical primary key and generate the sequence atomically in the database. The Spring Boot service formats it as NTA2026A00001, and a unique constraint protects the final value. For yearly or branch-wise counters, I use one locked/atomic counter per scope instead of resetting a global sequence.

In your example, main() does not call join(), and that is completely valid. The main thread can finish, but the JVM does not exit while any non-daemon thread is still running. Threads created with new Thread(...) are non-daemon by default, so Thread-1, Thread-2, and Thread-3 keep the application alive until they complete. 

main thread starts t1, t2, t3
        |
        +-- main() reaches its end and stops
        |
        +-- JVM remains alive because t1, t2, and t3 are non-daemon threads
        |
        +-- workers finish printing numbers
        |
        +-- JVM exits
What does join() do?

t1.join() makes the current thread wait until t1 terminates. It does not make the worker thread run differently and it is not required to prevent JVM shutdown in this case. Use it when the current thread has work that must happen after the worker threads finish, such as printing a final result, closing a resource, or running an assertion in a test.

Example: print a completion message only after all workers finish
public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
    NumberPrinter2 printer = new NumberPrinter2();

    Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> printer.print(0), "Thread-1");
    Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> printer.print(1), "Thread-2");
    Thread t3 = new Thread(() -> printer.print(2), "Thread-3");

    t1.start();
    t2.start();
    t3.start();

    t1.join();
    t2.join();
    t3.join();

    System.out.println("All number-printing threads finished.");
}

Without the three join() calls, the completion message could print immediately, before any number or before all numbers. With them, the main thread waits for all three workers in sequence. The total wait still ends only when every thread has completed.

Important daemon-thread difference

If you call t1.setDaemon(true) before t1.start(), that thread no longer keeps the JVM alive. Once only daemon threads remain, the JVM may exit immediately. Do not use daemon threads for work that must reliably finish, such as saving data or completing a payment.

Interview answer: join() is not needed just to keep the JVM alive; active non-daemon threads already do that. Use join() when one thread must wait for another thread's result or completion.

The goal is to share one counter and give each thread one turn in a fixed round-robin order. For three threads: Thread-1 prints 1, 4, 7...; Thread-2 prints 2, 5, 8...; and Thread-3 prints 3, 6, 9.... The shared NumberPrinter object is also the monitor used by synchronized, wait(), and notifyAll().

Your three-thread solution
package com.continuous.p2026;

public class NumberPrinter2 {

    private int number = 1;
    private final int max = 20;

    public synchronized void print(int threadId) {
        while (number <= max) {
            while ((number - 1) % 3 != threadId && number <= max) {
                try {
                    wait();
                } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                    return;
                }
            }

            if (number <= max) {
                System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " : " + number);
                number++;
                notifyAll();
            }
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        NumberPrinter2 printer = new NumberPrinter2();

        Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> printer.print(0), "Thread-1");
        Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> printer.print(1), "Thread-2");
        Thread t3 = new Thread(() -> printer.print(2), "Thread-3");

        t1.start();
        t2.start();
        t3.start();
    }
}
How each important line works
CodeReason
private int number = 1One shared counter. It is accessed only while holding the object's monitor.
synchronized void print(...)Only one thread can check, print, and increment at a time. It also allows wait() and notifyAll().
(number - 1) % 3Maps 1 to thread id 0, 2 to id 1, 3 to id 2, then repeats: 4 maps to id 0.
while (notMyTurn)The thread releases the lock and waits. Use while, not if, because it can wake spuriously or another thread can run first.
wait()Places the current thread in this monitor's wait set and releases the monitor so the correct thread can continue.
Thread.currentThread().interrupt()Restores the interrupt flag because wait() clears it before throwing InterruptedException.
number++Moves the turn to the next thread.
notifyAll()Wakes all waiters; only the thread whose modulo matches the new number proceeds.
Why notifyAll() instead of notify()?

With three or more threads, notify() may wake the wrong thread. That thread sees it is not its turn and waits again, while the correct thread can remain asleep forever. notifyAll() lets every waiting thread re-check the turn condition safely.

For 4 threads or any N threads

Replace the fixed 3 with a configurable thread count. Give threads ids from 0 through threadCount - 1. The rule remains (number - 1) % threadCount == threadId. 

public class OrderedNumberPrinter {
    private int number = 1;
    private final int max;
    private final int threadCount;

    public OrderedNumberPrinter(int max, int threadCount) {
        this.max = max;
        this.threadCount = threadCount;
    }

    public synchronized void print(int threadId) {
        while (number <= max) {
            while (number <= max && (number - 1) % threadCount != threadId) {
                try {
                    wait();
                } catch (InterruptedException exception) {
                    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                    return;
                }
            }

            if (number <= max) {
                System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " : " + number++);
                notifyAll();
            }
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int threadCount = 4;
        OrderedNumberPrinter printer = new OrderedNumberPrinter(20, threadCount);

        for (int threadId = 0; threadId < threadCount; threadId++) {
            int id = threadId; // Lambda captures an effectively final value.
            new Thread(() -> printer.print(id), "Thread-" + (id + 1)).start();
        }
    }
}

For four threads, the output ownership is: thread id 0 prints 1, 5, 9...; id 1 prints 2, 6, 10...; id 2 prints 3, 7, 11...; id 3 prints 4, 8, 12.... If max is not divisible by the thread count, the last few threads simply have fewer turns.

Interview answer: Use one shared monitor, protect the counter with synchronized, calculate the owner with modulo, wait in a while loop until it is that thread's turn, then increment and call notifyAll().

Both methods are defined on Object and are used for threads waiting on the same object's monitor. They must be called while the current thread owns that monitor, usually inside a synchronized block. Otherwise Java throws IllegalMonitorStateException.

MethodWhat it does
notify()Moves one arbitrary waiting thread from that monitor's wait set to the entry set.
notifyAll()Moves every waiting thread from that monitor's wait set to the entry set.

A notified thread does not run immediately. It first has to compete again to acquire the same monitor after the notifying thread leaves the synchronized block. It then returns from wait() and must re-check its condition.

Which thread does notify() wake?

If several threads called wait() on the same object, notify() selects one arbitrary thread. Java does not promise FIFO order, priority order, fairness, or a predictable selection rule. The exact choice is JVM and operating-system scheduling dependent, so code must never rely on a particular waiting thread being chosen.

Real-world producer/consumer example
class TaskQueue {
    private final Queue<String> tasks = new ArrayDeque<>();

    public synchronized void put(String task) {
        tasks.add(task);
        notifyAll(); // Several consumers may be waiting for work.
    }

    public synchronized String take() throws InterruptedException {
        while (tasks.isEmpty()) { // Use while, never if.
            wait();
        }
        return tasks.remove();
    }
}

notifyAll() is safer when different kinds of threads wait on the same monitor, such as producers waiting for space and consumers waiting for data. With notify(), Java may wake a thread whose condition is still false; the thread waits again while a thread that could proceed remains asleep. notifyAll() wakes everyone, and the while condition lets only eligible threads continue.

When can notify() be used?

Use it only when you can prove that all waiting threads are interchangeable and waking one is always sufficient. Otherwise prefer notifyAll(), or use higher-level concurrency utilities such as BlockingQueue, CountDownLatch, Semaphore, or ReentrantLock with separate Condition objects.

Interview answer: notify() wakes one arbitrary waiter; notifyAll() wakes all waiters. Neither method transfers the lock immediately, and every awakened thread must re-check its condition in a while loop.

No. A restart is not normally required to make a production application fast. A restart clears the process state and can temporarily hide symptoms such as a memory leak, stuck threads, exhausted connection pools, corrupted local cache, or excessive garbage collection. It does not fix the underlying cause.

Real-world example

Suppose a Spring Boot service slowly becomes slower because a code path never closes database connections. After the pool is exhausted, requests wait and time out. Restarting creates a fresh pool, so the service appears fast again for a while. The leak remains, and the same failure returns later. 

Temporary restart effect:
connection pool exhausted -> restart -> fresh pool -> requests recover

Correct fix:
find leaked connections -> close them with try-with-resources / framework management
-> add pool metrics and alerts -> deploy the fix
What should happen first?
  1. Check request latency, throughput, error rate, CPU, heap, garbage-collection pauses, thread count, and database connection-pool usage.
  2. Inspect logs, distributed traces, thread dumps, heap dumps, slow queries, and dependency health.
  3. Identify whether the bottleneck is application code, JVM memory, database, downstream service, network, or insufficient capacity.
  4. Mitigate safely with scaling, traffic reduction, cache refresh, circuit breaking, or a controlled restart if necessary.
  5. Fix the root cause, load-test the change, and monitor after deployment.
When can a restart be justified?
  • A process is deadlocked, corrupted, unresponsive, or has exhausted a non-recoverable resource.
  • A known memory leak or native-library issue requires temporary recovery while the permanent fix is prepared.
  • Configuration, certificates, native libraries, or a deployed code change requires process reinitialization.
  • A controlled rolling deployment is replacing old instances with a new version.
  • An operational runbook explicitly defines the restart as a safe, measured mitigation.
How production restarts safely

In a highly available system, we do not normally stop every instance together. A load balancer or orchestrator removes one instance from traffic, waits for it to finish active requests, starts or replaces it, checks readiness, and then returns it to service. The process repeats instance by instance. 

Load balancer
  |-> instance-1: drain requests -> graceful shutdown -> restart -> readiness check -> traffic restored
  |-> instance-2: continues serving
  |-> instance-3: continues serving

Result: capacity remains available during the rolling restart.
Liveness versus readiness
  • Liveness check: asks whether the process is alive. A failed liveness check may cause the platform to restart it.
  • Readiness check: asks whether the instance is ready to receive traffic. A failed readiness check should remove it from traffic without necessarily restarting it.

A readiness check should verify only what is necessary to serve requests. Making it depend on every optional downstream service can remove healthy instances unnecessarily.

Why a freshly restarted service may seem faster
  • Heap usage and old temporary objects are gone, so garbage collection may reduce temporarily.
  • Thread pools and connection pools start with available capacity.
  • Local caches are empty and then repopulate, although cold caches can initially make performance worse.
  • Queues, buffers, and leaked resources are cleared.
  • JIT compilation and class loading start again, so restart can also temporarily make the service slower during warm-up.
Better alternatives to restarting
  • Scale out more instances or scale up resources when demand exceeds capacity.
  • Tune slow SQL, indexes, connection pools, thread pools, JVM memory, and garbage collection based on measurements.
  • Use cache eviction or refresh controls when a cache is the specific problem.
  • Use circuit breakers and timeouts when a downstream dependency is slow.
  • Use graceful rolling restarts only as a controlled operational action, not as an automatic performance fix.
Interview-ready answer

"A production restart is not mandatory for fast service. It can temporarily clear leaked resources or unhealthy process state, but recurring slowness means we must find the root cause using metrics, logs, traces, thread dumps, heap analysis, and database monitoring. If a restart is needed, we use graceful shutdown, readiness checks, connection draining, and a rolling strategy so other instances continue serving traffic."

2-Phase Commit tries to make several participants commit one distributed transaction atomically. Saga breaks a business transaction into local transactions and uses compensating actions when a later step fails. 2PC targets strong atomicity; Saga targets availability, loose coupling, and eventual consistency.

Real-world example: placing an order

A checkout needs to create an order, reserve inventory, and charge payment. These operations belong to separate services and often separate databases.

How 2PC works
Coordinator -> Prepare?
                |-> Order database: ready
                |-> Inventory database: ready
                |-> Payment database: ready

Coordinator -> Commit
                |-> Order database: commit
                |-> Inventory database: commit
                |-> Payment database: commit
  1. Prepare phase: the coordinator asks every participant to validate the operation and reserve required resources. Each replies yes or no.
  2. Commit phase: if every participant says yes, the coordinator sends commit. If any participant says no, it sends rollback.

Participants usually keep locks or prepared transaction state between phases. If the coordinator fails after prepare but before the final decision, participants may wait, which is why 2PC can be blocking and expensive.

How Saga works

Each service commits its own local transaction. If a later step fails, the workflow runs a compensating action rather than asking every database to perform a global rollback. 

1. Order service: create order = PENDING
2. Inventory service: reserve stock = SUCCESS
3. Payment service: charge card = FAILED
4. Inventory service: release stock (compensation)
5. Order service: mark order = CANCELLED

A compensation is a new business operation, not a technical undo. For example, a successful payment may be refunded, and a shipped item may require a return instead of a database rollback.

Saga implementation styles
Style How it works Example
Choreography Services publish events and react to events without a central coordinator. OrderCreated -> inventory reserves -> InventoryReserved -> payment charges.
Orchestration A saga orchestrator sends commands, tracks state, and invokes compensations. Order orchestrator calls inventory, then payment, then confirms or cancels the order.
Comparison
Aspect 2PC Saga
Consistency Strong atomic commit when all participants and coordinator cooperate. Eventual consistency with explicit business compensations.
Failure behavior Can block while participants wait for the coordinator's decision. Continues through retries and compensating actions.
Performance Higher latency and resource locking across participants. Usually better availability and throughput, but more workflow messages.
Coupling Participants need distributed-transaction support and coordinator integration. Services communicate through commands/events and local transactions.
Rollback Technical rollback before the global commit. Business compensation after a local commit.
Complexity Infrastructure and blocking/failure recovery are difficult. Application workflow, retries, ordering, idempotency, and compensation are difficult.
When to use 2PC
  • Participants are trusted and support a compatible distributed transaction protocol.
  • Strong atomicity is more important than availability and latency.
  • The transaction is short-lived and the number of participants is small.
  • Examples include tightly controlled enterprise systems where two resource managers must commit together.
When to use Saga
  • Services own separate databases and should remain independently deployable.
  • The workflow may be long-running, such as payment, shipment, and approval.
  • Temporary inconsistency is acceptable if the final business state is correct.
  • High availability and throughput matter more than a single global database transaction.
  • Each step has a safe, well-defined, idempotent compensation.
Important Saga safeguards
  • Persist saga state so the workflow can resume after a service restart.
  • Use an outbox pattern so a database change and its event publication are reliable together.
  • Make commands and compensations idempotent because messages can be retried or delivered more than once.
  • Use timeouts, retry limits, dead-letter handling, and observability with a correlation or saga ID.
  • Design for duplicate, delayed, and out-of-order events.
Interview-ready answer

"2PC uses a coordinator and prepare/commit phases to make multiple participants commit atomically, but it can block, hold locks, and reduce availability. A Saga uses local transactions connected by events or an orchestrator; if a later step fails, compensating business actions undo the earlier effects. I prefer Saga for independent microservices and long-running workflows, and 2PC only when strong atomicity is essential, participants support it, and the transaction is small and tightly controlled."

A sharding router is the component that decides which database shard should receive a request. It reads the shard key, applies the configured routing rule, selects the correct shard endpoint, and forwards the query. It is not normally a copy of the business data; it manages routing metadata and database connections.

Real-world request flow
POST /orders, customer_id = 202
        |
        v
Sharding router
  1. Validate customer_id
  2. hash(202) -> virtual bucket 17
  3. bucket 17 -> shard-2
  4. write to shard-2 leader
        |
        v
shard-2 leader -> replicated followers
Main responsibilities
  • Extract and validate the shard key, such as customer_id or tenant_id.
  • Use range, hash, directory, geographic, or virtual-bucket mapping to identify the shard.
  • Route writes to the shard leader and reads to a suitable replica when consistency allows it.
  • Maintain or refresh a versioned shard map from a central catalog.
  • Manage connection pools, health checks, timeouts, and leader failover.
  • Reject unsafe cross-shard transactions or execute scatter-gather queries when explicitly supported.
  • Expose routing metrics such as per-shard latency, traffic, errors, and connection usage.
How the router finds the shard
Routing rule Example
Range customer_id 1-1,000,000 -> shard-1
Hash hash(customer_id) -> bucket 17 -> shard-2
Directory tenant-acme -> shard-3 from a shard catalog
Geographic region = EU -> eu-shard-group
Types of sharding routers
  • Application-side router: the service selects a DataSource or connection pool. It offers control but requires shared routing code and configuration in every service.
  • Database proxy router: applications connect to a proxy, which routes requests to shards. This keeps application code simpler but adds an infrastructure dependency and proxy capacity planning.
  • Database-native router: a distributed database or managed service owns the partition map and routing. It reduces custom operations, but ties the design to that product's capabilities.
  • Sharding library: a library integrates routing, SQL rewriting, and scatter-gather into the application. It can speed adoption but needs careful compatibility testing.
Central shard catalog
shard-map version = 42

bucket 0-15   -> shard-1 -> leader db1-writer -> replicas db1-r1, db1-r2
bucket 16-31  -> shard-2 -> leader db2-writer -> replicas db2-r1, db2-r2
bucket 32-47  -> shard-3 -> leader db3-writer -> replicas db3-r1, db3-r2

The router loads this map from a strongly consistent catalog or control-plane service. It caches the map locally for speed, refreshes it when the version changes, and should fail closed or use a safe retry when its map is stale. During a shard move, the catalog can represent states such as JOINING, MIGRATING, and ACTIVE.

Spring Boot-style application router
public DataSource chooseDataSource(String customerId, boolean write) {
    String shardId = shardCatalog.findShard(customerId);
    return write
        ? leaderPools.get(shardId)
        : replicaSelector.chooseReadablePool(shardId);
}

public Order createOrder(Order order) {
    DataSource leader = chooseDataSource(order.customerId(), true);
    return orderRepository.insert(leader, order);
}

The repository should not independently calculate a different shard from the router. Keep routing logic in one well-tested component, and make the shard key available for every operation that should be targeted.

What if the shard key is missing?

The router cannot safely choose one shard. It may reject the request, query a known subset, or perform a scatter-gather query across all relevant shards. For example, WHERE customer_id = 202 is targeted, while WHERE age > 30 may need every shard if users are sharded by customer ID.

Router risks and safeguards
  • Use a stable and evenly distributed shard key to avoid hot shards.
  • Version shard maps and update them atomically during migrations.
  • Use bounded connection pools and per-shard timeouts so one unhealthy shard does not exhaust all resources.
  • Route read-after-write operations to the leader or use a consistency mechanism when replicas can lag.
  • Use idempotency keys because retries during failover or migration can repeat a write.
  • Do not blindly retry a transaction after an unknown result; first determine whether it committed.
Interview-ready answer

"A sharding router receives a request, extracts its shard key, consults a range or shard map, and forwards the query to the correct shard. It commonly routes writes to a leader and reads to replicas, while a central, versioned catalog manages ownership. The router can live in the application, a proxy, a sharding library, or the database platform. Its main challenges are stale metadata, hot shards, missing keys, failover, and cross-shard queries."

Replication copies data. Sharding divides data. Replicas contain the same logical dataset, while shards contain different portions of the dataset.

Aspect Replication Sharding
Data placement The same rows are copied to multiple nodes. Different rows or columns are placed on different nodes.
Main purpose High availability, disaster recovery, and read scaling. Scaling storage, writes, CPU, and total dataset size.
Write behavior Usually one leader receives the write and replicates it. Different shard leaders can receive writes for different keys.
Read behavior Reads can be distributed across replicas, subject to replication lag. The shard key routes a request to the shard that owns the data.
Failure handling A replica can be promoted if the leader fails. Only the affected shard's data is available elsewhere if that shard is also replicated.
Typical challenge Stale reads, lag, conflict handling, and failover. Cross-shard joins, transactions, routing, and rebalancing.
Real-world example
Replication:
orders database
  primary  -> all orders
  replica1 -> all orders
  replica2 -> all orders

Sharding:
shard-1 -> customers 1 to 1,000,000
shard-2 -> customers 1,000,001 to 2,000,000
shard-3 -> customers 2,000,001 to 3,000,000

If the application has many reads but a manageable dataset, add replicas. If one database cannot store or write the entire dataset fast enough, shard it. A large e-commerce system commonly uses both: each shard owns part of the orders and has its own leader and followers.

Easy memory trick

Replication = same data, more copies.
Sharding = different data, more partitions.

Interview-ready answer

"Replication duplicates the same data across nodes to improve availability and read capacity. Sharding partitions the data across nodes to scale storage and write throughput. Replication alone does not normally distribute all writes because one leader still handles them. For a large application, we shard by a stable key and replicate every shard for failover and read scaling."

Yes. Large production applications commonly use both. Sharding divides the complete dataset across multiple shard groups, while replication creates redundant copies inside each shard group. They solve different problems and complement each other.

Real-world order-service architecture
Complete orders dataset
        |
        +--> Shard 1: customer IDs 1-1,000,000
        |       +--> leader   (writes)
        |       +--> follower (read scaling / failover)
        |
        +--> Shard 2: customer IDs 1,000,001-2,000,000
        |       +--> leader   (writes)
        |       +--> follower (read scaling / failover)
        |
        +--> Shard 3: customer IDs 2,000,001-3,000,000
                +--> leader   (writes)
                +--> follower (read scaling / failover)
How one request flows
  • POST /orders uses customer_id to find the shard and writes to that shard's leader.
  • GET /orders is routed to a follower when slightly stale data is acceptable.
  • A read-after-write request is routed to the leader, or uses a consistency token, so it does not read stale follower data.
  • If a leader fails, a healthy follower can be promoted without moving the entire dataset.
Why use both?
Requirement Technique How it helps
Dataset is too large for one database Sharding Each shard stores only part of the data.
Write traffic is too high for one database Sharding Different shard leaders handle different keys.
Many read requests Replication Followers distribute read traffic within each shard.
Database node failure Replication A follower can be promoted for the affected shard.
Regional disaster or recovery Replication across zones or regions A second copy can support recovery or regional failover.
Spring Boot request-routing idea
String shardId = shardCatalog.findShard(customerId);
DataSource shardLeader = shardLeaders.get(shardId);

// Write to the leader of the selected shard.
orderRepository.insert(shardLeader, order);

// For an eventually consistent read, select a replica in that shard.
DataSource replica = replicaSelector.choose(shardId);
return orderRepository.findByCustomerId(replica, customerId);

In practice, a sharding library, database proxy, or managed database service may handle shard maps, connection pools, replica selection, health checks, and leader failover. The application still needs to understand consistency and transaction boundaries.

Important limitations
  • Replication does not remove the need for sharding when one leader cannot handle the total write load.
  • Replication lag can make follower reads stale.
  • Transactions across shards are difficult; prefer a single shard key for one business transaction.
  • Cross-shard joins and global sorting may require scatter-gather queries or a separate reporting store.
  • Each shard must be monitored and capacity-planned independently.
  • Adding a shard requires data rebalancing, while adding a replica usually requires synchronization and routing updates.
Interview-ready answer

"Yes. We shard the dataset to distribute storage and write load, then replicate each shard for read scaling, availability, and failover. The shard key selects a shard, and the leader or one of its followers handles the request depending on whether strong or eventual consistency is required. This is powerful, but it adds shard-routing, replication-lag, cross-shard transaction, and operational complexity."

A failover system keeps a standby component or alternate path ready so that traffic can move away from a failed component. It does not prevent the original failure; it reduces downtime by detecting the failure, promoting or selecting a healthy replacement, and redirecting requests.

Real-world example: order database

An e-commerce service has one database leader and two replicated followers. The leader accepts new orders. A health monitor checks connectivity and replication health. If the leader's machine loses power, the cluster manager confirms the failure, promotes a sufficiently up-to-date follower, and updates the database endpoint used by the application. 

Normal:
Order Service -> db-primary
                  |-> db-replica-1
                  |-> db-replica-2

After primary failure:
Order Service -> virtual database endpoint -> db-replica-1 (promoted leader)

The application should use a stable endpoint or service discovery name rather than a hard-coded server address. Requests interrupted during the switch are retried only when the operation is safe or protected by an idempotency key.

Failover sequence
  1. Detect: health checks, heartbeats, timeouts, or error-rate monitoring identify a suspected failure.
  2. Confirm: a quorum or fencing mechanism prevents two nodes from becoming leader at the same time.
  3. Promote: a standby, replica, or alternate service becomes active.
  4. Redirect: DNS, a load balancer, service discovery, or a virtual IP sends new requests to the replacement.
  5. Recover: the failed component is repaired, rejoined, and resynchronized before becoming a standby again.
Main failover models
Model How it works Example and trade-off
Active-passive One node serves traffic; a standby waits for promotion. Primary database plus replica. Simple and safe, but standby capacity may be underused.
Active-active Multiple nodes serve traffic simultaneously. Two application regions behind a load balancer. Better utilization, but conflicts and split-brain need handling.
Warm standby Replacement is running and partly synchronized, but does not serve normal traffic. Lower failover time than a cold backup with moderate cost.
Cold standby Replacement is started or restored only after failure. Low ongoing cost, but recovery takes longer.
Failover in microservices

A service can run multiple instances across availability zones. A load balancer removes unhealthy instances from rotation. For an external dependency, a client can use timeouts, limited retries, circuit breakers, and a fallback such as a cached response or queued command. 

Client -> Load Balancer -> service-instance-1 (unhealthy, removed)
                      |-> service-instance-2 (healthy)
                      |-> service-instance-3 (healthy)

Payment provider unavailable:
request -> timeout -> circuit opens -> queue payment for retry / return safe response
RTO and RPO
  • RTO (Recovery Time Objective): maximum acceptable time to restore service. Automatic promotion can reduce it.
  • RPO (Recovery Point Objective): maximum acceptable data loss. Synchronous replication can reduce loss, while asynchronous replication may have replication lag.

For example, an RTO of 30 seconds means failover should complete within 30 seconds. An RPO of zero means the business cannot lose acknowledged data, which usually requires stronger replication and may increase write latency.

Important failure risks
  • False failure detection: a slow network can make a healthy node look dead, so use sensible timeouts and quorum.
  • Split-brain: two nodes accept writes as leader; use fencing, leases, or consensus to allow only one leader.
  • Stale replica: promoting a lagging replica can lose recently acknowledged data.
  • Retry duplication: a client may retry after an unknown result; use idempotency keys for payments and orders.
  • Failback risk: do not immediately return traffic to the repaired node; resynchronize and test it first.
Interview-ready answer

"A failover system detects that an active component is unavailable and redirects traffic to a healthy standby or alternate instance. In a replicated database, a cluster manager promotes a suitable follower and updates a stable endpoint. Active-passive is simpler, while active-active improves utilization but needs conflict and split-brain protection. Failover improves availability, but timeouts, idempotency, replication lag, quorum, RTO, and RPO must all be designed explicitly."

A scatter-gather query is used when the router cannot identify one shard for a request. It scatters, or sends, the same query to multiple shards, then gathers the partial results and merges them into one response.

Example: find all users whose age is greater than 30

Assume users are sharded by user_id, but the query filters by age. Since age is not the shard key, users older than 30 may exist on every shard. 

Application / query router
        |
        | Scatter: send to every relevant shard
        +--> shard-1: SELECT * FROM users WHERE age > 30
        +--> shard-2: SELECT * FROM users WHERE age > 30
        +--> shard-3: SELECT * FROM users WHERE age > 30
        |
        | Gather: combine, sort, remove duplicates, and paginate
        v
One response containing all matching users
SQL executed on each shard
SELECT user_id, name, age
FROM users
WHERE age > 30;

Each shard returns only its local matches. The router concatenates the results for a simple query, or performs a distributed merge for operations such as ORDER BY, LIMIT, COUNT, SUM, and pagination.

How aggregation is gathered

For COUNT(*), each shard returns a partial count and the router adds them. For ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT 10, each shard can return its local top 10, and the router merges those sorted lists to calculate the global top 10. 

shard-1 count = 120
shard-2 count = 95
shard-3 count = 140

global count = 120 + 95 + 140 = 355
Why it can be expensive
  • One user request creates multiple database requests, so network traffic and connection usage increase.
  • Latency is often close to the slowest shard, not the fastest one.
  • Sorting, grouping, joining, and pagination require extra memory and CPU in the router.
  • A failure or timeout on one shard makes the global result incomplete unless partial results are allowed.
  • Large offsets can cause every shard to scan and return many unnecessary rows.
Spring Boot-style pseudocode
List<User> allUsers = new ArrayList<>();

for (DataSource shard : shardDataSources) {
    allUsers.addAll(jdbcTemplate(shard).query(
        "select user_id, name, age from users where age > ?",
        userRowMapper,
        30));
}

return allUsers.stream()
    .sorted(Comparator.comparing(User::getAge).reversed())
    .limit(10)
    .toList();

A production implementation normally runs the shard requests in parallel with bounded concurrency, pushes filtering and aggregation down to each shard, enforces timeouts, and records which shards succeeded or failed. It must also avoid unbounded result collection.

How to improve this query
  • Choose a shard key that matches the most common access pattern, when possible.
  • Add a local index on age so every shard can filter efficiently.
  • Create a global search index or read model in Elasticsearch/OpenSearch for frequent cross-shard searches.
  • Maintain a reporting database or materialized view for analytics instead of querying transactional shards.
  • Use a directory or secondary index that maps an age range to candidate shards, if the data and update model support it.
  • Use cursor-based pagination and a stable sort key rather than large offset pagination.
Scatter-gather versus targeted query
Query Routing behavior
WHERE user_id = 101 Targeted query: the shard key identifies one shard.
WHERE age > 30 Scatter-gather: age is not the shard key, so many shards may be queried.
WHERE region = 'EU' Potentially targeted if the shard key or catalog is geographic.
Interview-ready answer

"A scatter-gather query is a distributed query used when the shard key cannot identify one shard. For finding users with age greater than 30, the router sends the filter to every shard, gathers each shard's matches, and merges them into one response. It is simple but can be slow and expensive, so frequent cross-shard searches should use suitable indexing, a global search index, a reporting read model, or a better routing key."

A hot shard is a shard receiving a disproportionately high amount of traffic, reads, writes, CPU work, or storage growth compared with the other shards. The entire system can look healthy overall while requests routed to that one shard become slow, time out, or fail.

Real-world example

Suppose orders are range-sharded by customer_id. If a large retailer with millions of active users is assigned to shard-2, most checkout traffic may hit shard-2 while shard-1 and shard-3 remain idle. A time-based design has a similar problem when all current writes go to the newest date range. 

1-1,000,000       -> shard-1
1,000,001-2,000,000 -> shard-2  (large tenant and heavy traffic)
2,000,001-3,000,000 -> shard-3

Result: shard-2 is a hot shard even if the row counts look reasonable.
Does overflow automatically move to the next shard?

No. A database does not normally decide that a full range belongs on another shard. The shard router follows the configured mapping. If the key falls in the range assigned to shard-2, the request continues going to shard-2, even if that shard is near its storage or performance limit.

If the range is defined by a database constraint, an insert outside the allowed range may fail. If the routing catalog has no mapping for the new key, the application may return an error such as NO_SHARD_MAPPING. A new mapping must be created deliberately.

How range overflow is handled

The usual solution is to update the shard map before capacity is exhausted. For example, split the old range and move part of its data to a new shard. 

Before:
1-2,000,000 -> shard-2

After adding shard-4:
1-1,000,000       -> shard-2
1,000,001-2,000,000 -> shard-4
  1. Provision the new shard and create the same schema, indexes, and security settings.
  2. Copy the selected rows from the overloaded shard while capturing ongoing changes.
  3. Wait until the destination catches up and validate counts, checksums, and application behavior.
  4. Atomically update the routing catalog so new requests use the new ranges.
  5. Keep the old mapping for rollback until the migration is proven safe.
Common ways to prevent hot shards
  • Use a high-cardinality, evenly distributed key instead of a low-cardinality key such as status or country alone.
  • Use hash sharding or virtual buckets when traffic is not naturally range-based.
  • Use composite routing, such as tenant_id + hash(user_id), for very large tenants.
  • Split a large tenant into multiple buckets or give that tenant dedicated shards.
  • For time-series data, use time plus a hash bucket so the current period is distributed across several shards.
  • Monitor per-shard QPS, latency, CPU, disk, connection count, replication lag, and error rate.
Range sharding versus hash sharding
Situation Better approach Reason
Queries mostly use date ranges Range sharding with planned range splits Queries can target only the relevant shard.
Uniform point lookups by customer ID Hash sharding with virtual buckets Traffic and data are usually distributed more evenly.
One tenant is much larger than others Directory or composite sharding The large tenant can be moved or divided independently.
Important distinction

A range being logically exhausted, such as all customer IDs in its assigned interval being used, is different from a shard being physically full or operationally overloaded. In both cases, the routing metadata must be changed through a controlled split, migration, or new-range assignment. The system should alert and scale before an insert or request reaches the limit.

Interview-ready answer

"A hot shard is an unevenly loaded shard that becomes the bottleneck. In range sharding, overflow is not automatically sent to the next shard; the router follows its shard map, so an unmapped key can fail. We handle it by provisioning a shard, splitting or extending ranges, migrating data with change capture, atomically updating the catalog, and validating the cutover. Hashing with virtual buckets or composite keys helps prevent hot shards in the first place."

Sharding divides one logical database into smaller databases called shards. Each shard owns a portion of the data, and a router uses a shard key to send a request to the correct shard.

1. Horizontal sharding (row-based)

Every shard has the same table structure, but different rows. For example, an orders table can be split by customer: customers 1-1,000,000 go to shard-1 and customers 1,000,001-2,000,000 go to shard-2. 

shard-1.orders: customer_id = 101, 102, 103
shard-2.orders: customer_id = 201, 202, 203

Use when: the table has too many rows or the write traffic must be distributed.

2. Vertical sharding (column-based)

Columns or functional tables are split across databases. A customer service may keep identity data in one database and a document service may keep large profile documents in another. 

customer_core_db: customer_id, name, email
customer_profile_db: customer_id, photo, preferences, biography

Use when: some columns are large, sensitive, or accessed by a different service. The application joins the data, because a normal database join across shards may not be available.

3. Range-based sharding

A range of the shard key maps to one shard. For time-series events, January data can go to shard-1 and February data to shard-2. 

2026-01-01 to 2026-01-31 -> shard-1
2026-02-01 to 2026-02-28 -> shard-2

Advantages: efficient range queries and easy archival. Risk: the newest range can become a hot shard when most writes are for the current date.

4. Hash-based sharding

A hash function is applied to the shard key to distribute records. An e-commerce system might calculate hash(customer_id) and use the result to choose a bucket. 

customer_id 202 -> hash -> bucket 17 -> shard-2

Advantages: generally even distribution. Risk: range queries become difficult, and simple hash(key) % shardCount can move many records when a shard is added.

5. Directory-based sharding

A lookup service or catalog explicitly maps a tenant, customer, or key to a shard. A SaaS platform can place large tenants on dedicated shards. 

tenant-acme  -> shard-1
tenant-globex -> shard-3
tenant-small-7 -> shard-2

Advantages: flexible placement and easy tenant movement. Risk: the directory is critical infrastructure and must be highly available, cached, and versioned.

6. Geographic sharding

Data is placed according to geography. EU customers can be routed to EU shards, Indian customers to India shards, and US customers to US shards. 

region = EU     -> eu-shard-group
region = India  -> india-shard-group
region = US     -> us-shard-group

Use when: low regional latency, data residency, or regional failure isolation matters. Cross-region reporting and users who travel between regions need an explicit design.

7. Composite or hybrid sharding

Two or more strategies are combined. For example, first choose a region, then hash the customer ID inside that region. This prevents cross-region traffic while balancing customers within each region. 

India + hash(customer_id) -> India shard-1 or India shard-2
EU    + hash(customer_id) -> EU shard-1 or EU shard-2

Use when: the system needs both geographic isolation and even distribution within each region.

8. Consistent-hashing sharding

Shards and keys are placed on a logical hash ring, often using virtual nodes or virtual buckets. When a new shard is added, only the keys owned by the reassigned buckets need to move instead of remapping every key. 

key A -> virtual bucket 12 -> shard-1
key B -> virtual bucket 29 -> shard-2
New shard-3 takes buckets 12 and 29 from the existing owners.

Use when: nodes can be added or removed frequently. A catalog still records ownership, and data migration must be completed before changing ownership permanently.

Quick selection guide
Requirement Good starting choice
Many rows and customer-isolated requests Horizontal hash or directory sharding by customer/tenant ID
Time-based queries and easy archival Range sharding by timestamp, with a plan for hot current ranges
Regional latency or legal residency Geographic sharding, optionally combined with hashing
Frequent node expansion Hashing with virtual buckets or consistent hashing
Large or sensitive columns Vertical sharding, usually aligned with service ownership

In real production systems, sharding is commonly combined with replication: the shard key chooses the shard, and each shard has a leader plus replicas for availability and read scaling. The hardest decisions are choosing a stable, evenly distributed key, avoiding cross-shard transactions, and planning resharding before the current shards become full.

A sharded system chooses a shard key, such as customer_id or tenant_id, and applies a routing rule to it. The result identifies the shard that owns the record. The application, a database proxy, or the database cluster itself can perform this routing.

Basic routing flow
Incoming request
      |
      | customerId = 202
      v
Shard router: hash(202) -> virtual bucket 17 -> shard-2
      |
      v
Connection pool for shard-2 leader
      |
      v
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 202

The routing key must be present in the request or derivable from it. Queries without the shard key may need a scatter-gather operation across many shards, which is slower and should be avoided for hot paths.

Common routing methods
Method Example Important consideration
Range routing Customer IDs 1-1,000,000 -> shard-1 Easy range queries, but one range can become a hot shard.
Hash routing hash(customerId) -> bucket -> shard Usually balances load; use virtual buckets so new shards do not require moving everything.
Directory routing tenant-abc -> shard-3 in a catalog Flexible tenant movement, but the catalog must be highly available and consistent.
Geographic routing EU tenant -> EU shard group Useful for latency and data-residency requirements; cross-region requests need care.
Is there a central configuration?

Usually there is a central shard catalog or control-plane service. It stores the mapping, not the business data. A production catalog can be backed by a strongly consistent database or a system such as ZooKeeper, etcd, or a managed service. Services cache a read-only copy locally and refresh it when the catalog publishes a version change. The version prevents a stale router from silently using an old map. 

Shard catalog
----------------------------------------------------------------
mapVersion | bucket/range | shardId | leaderEndpoint | status
42         | bucket 0-15   | shard-1 | db1-writer     | ACTIVE
42         | bucket 16-31  | shard-2 | db2-writer     | ACTIVE

The application receives version 42 and routes using the matching map.
Application-side routing example

In a Spring Boot application, a routing component can select a connection pool from the catalog before calling the repository. In practice, teams often use a database proxy or a sharding library to avoid duplicating this logic in every service. 

String shardId = shardCatalog.findShardByCustomerId(customerId);
DataSource dataSource = dataSources.get(shardId);

// The repository runs using the selected shard's connection.
return jdbcTemplate(dataSource).query(
    "select * from orders where customer_id = ?", orderRowMapper, customerId);

A real router also validates the key, maintains one pool per shard, routes writes to the shard leader, optionally routes consistent reads to the leader, and retries only safe or idempotent operations.

What happens when we add a new shard?
  1. Provision: create the new database node, security rules, schema, monitoring, and replicas.
  2. Register: add it to the catalog as JOINING; do not send normal traffic yet.
  3. Choose data to move: with virtual buckets, assign selected buckets to the new shard. With range sharding, split a range.
  4. Copy and catch up: bulk-copy the selected rows, then replay changes from a change log or CDC stream until the destination catches up.
  5. Cut over: briefly coordinate writes or use a migration state machine, update the catalog atomically, and mark the new mapping ACTIVE.
  6. Clean up: verify counts, checksums, latency, and error rates, then delete old copies only after the rollback window expires.
Why virtual buckets are preferred

With hash(customerId) % 3, adding a fourth shard changes the result for many customers, so a large amount of data moves. With 1,024 virtual buckets, the router first maps a customer to a bucket and then maps buckets to physical shards. Adding shard-4 might move only selected buckets instead of remapping every customer. 

customer 202 -> hash -> bucket 17 -> shard-2
After expansion:
customer 202 -> hash -> bucket 17 -> shard-4

Only bucket 17 (and other deliberately migrated buckets) changes owner.
Operational safeguards
  • Use an atomic catalog update and include a map version in routing logs.
  • Make migration resumable, throttled, and observable so it does not overwhelm production traffic.
  • Use idempotency keys or unique business keys because retries can happen during migration or failover.
  • Keep a rollback mapping until the destination is verified; never remove the source immediately after cutover.
  • Ensure every important query includes the shard key, or explicitly accept the cost of scatter-gather.
Interview-ready answer

"The router uses a stable shard key and a routing algorithm or shard catalog to select the correct shard. The catalog is commonly managed centrally and cached by services with versioned refreshes. To add a shard, we provision it, register it, migrate selected ranges or virtual buckets, catch up changes, atomically update the mapping, validate the cutover, and keep rollback support. Virtual buckets make expansion much safer than simple modulo hashing."

Replication keeps copies of the same data on multiple database nodes. It mainly improves availability, disaster recovery, and read capacity. Sharding splits different parts of the data across multiple nodes. It mainly improves storage capacity and write or query throughput.

Simple real-world analogy

Replication is like making photocopies of the same library in different cities. Sharding is like dividing one huge library into specialist branches: one branch stores science books, another stores history books. Copies help when a branch is unavailable; division helps when one branch cannot hold or serve everything.

Replication versus sharding
Concern Replication Sharding
Data on each node Usually the same dataset Different subset of the dataset
Main benefit Availability and read scaling Write, storage, and large-dataset scaling
Typical problem solved Read traffic or node failure One database has reached CPU, disk, or write limits
Typical challenge Replication lag and failover consistency Cross-shard joins, transactions, and resharding
Why replication alone is not enough

If an orders database has 10 TB of data and one primary receives every write, adding read replicas can distribute reads but does not normally distribute writes. Every replica still needs a copy of the 10 TB, every write still has to be replicated, and the primary can remain the bottleneck. Sharding can partition orders by customer_id, so different shard leaders handle different writes and each shard stores only part of the data.

Replication strategies
Strategy How it works When to use
Leader-follower (primary-replica) One leader accepts writes and followers copy its change log. Reads can go to followers. Most applications needing simple writes, read scaling, and failover.
Multi-leader (multi-primary) More than one node accepts writes and changes are replicated between leaders. Multi-region writes or independently operating data centers; requires conflict resolution.
Leaderless / quorum Clients write to and read from several replicas. A quorum such as W + R > N helps overlap reads and writes. Highly available key-value workloads where eventual consistency is acceptable.
Synchronous The write is acknowledged only after required replicas confirm it. Strong durability or consistency; accepts higher latency and possible write unavailability.
Asynchronous The leader acknowledges first and followers catch up later. Low latency and high availability when a small data-loss window or stale reads is acceptable.

Replication may copy physical database pages, write-ahead logs, or logical row changes, depending on the database. In an asynchronous leader-follower setup, a follower can be behind the leader, so a user may not immediately see a newly created order if the next read is routed to a lagging follower.

Sharding strategies
Strategy Example routing key Strength and risk
Range-based customer_id 1-1,000,000 goes to shard A Good range queries; hot ranges and uneven growth are possible.
Hash-based hash(customer_id) % shardCount Usually distributes load evenly; range queries become expensive and resizing needs care.
Directory-based A routing table maps each tenant to a shard Flexible placement and tenant moves; routing metadata must be highly available.
Geographic India customers to an India shard, EU customers to an EU shard Lower regional latency and data residency support; cross-region queries are harder.
Combined order-service example

Assume an e-commerce system has millions of customers. A request first uses a stable shard key such as customer_id to select a shard. Each shard has one leader and two followers. The leader handles order writes, followers serve safe read-only queries, and a coordinator or database proxy routes requests. 

customer_id 101  --hash--> Shard 1 leader --replicates--> Shard 1 followers
customer_id 202  --hash--> Shard 2 leader --replicates--> Shard 2 followers

POST /orders       - route by customer_id to that shard's leader
GET /orders        - route to a follower when slightly stale data is acceptable
GET /orders/latest - route to leader when read-after-write consistency is required

This architecture uses both techniques: sharding distributes the total workload, while replication protects each shard and distributes its reads. If a shard leader fails, an eligible follower can be promoted. The application should use idempotency keys because a retry during failover could otherwise create a duplicate order.

How to choose
  • Choose replication when the dataset fits on one node but you need read scaling, high availability, or disaster recovery.
  • Choose sharding when one node cannot handle the data size, write rate, storage, or working set.
  • Choose both for very large systems: partition data into shards and replicate every shard.
  • Do not shard prematurely. Start with good indexes, query tuning, connection-pool sizing, caching, and read replicas where they solve the problem.
  • Choose a shard key with high cardinality and even distribution. Avoid a key that creates a hot shard, and plan resharding before capacity is exhausted.
Important interview conclusion

"Replication creates redundant copies of the same data for availability and read scaling. Sharding divides data across nodes for write, storage, and dataset scaling. Replication does not automatically distribute the write workload, so large systems commonly shard first and then replicate each shard. The correct choice depends on the bottleneck, consistency requirement, query pattern, failure model, and operational complexity."

System.out.println() is the most common way to print text to the console in Java. It is actually three parts working together.

Breakdown
  • System: a final Java class in java.lang that gives access to system resources.
  • out: a public static field of type PrintStream that points to the standard output stream.
  • println: a method on PrintStream that prints the value and then moves the cursor to a new line.
Simple example
System.out.println("Hello Java");
What about System.err.println()?

System.err.println() writes to the standard error stream instead of standard output. We usually use it for error messages, warnings, or logs that should stand out from normal output. 

System.out.println("Normal application message");
System.err.println("Something went wrong");
What happens internally

Java looks up System.out, which is usually connected to the console, and then println() writes the text followed by a newline character.

Real-world analogy

Think of System as the control panel, out as the speaker line, and println as the person speaking a message and then pausing for the next line.

Interview-ready answer

"System is a utility class, out is the standard output PrintStream, and println prints the value to the console with a new line. So System.out.println() means write this message to standard output."

Java is always pass by value. The important difference is what value is copied: a primitive value is copied directly, while an object reference value is copied. Java never passes the original variable itself by reference.

Primitive values

When a primitive is passed, the method receives an independent copy. Changing the parameter does not change the caller's variable. 

static void changeNumber(int number) {
    number = 99;
}

int value = 10;
changeNumber(value);
System.out.println(value); // 10
Objects: the reference value is copied

For an object, the copied value is a reference pointing to the same object. Therefore, changing a field through that reference affects the original object. However, assigning a completely new object to the method parameter does not change the caller's reference. 

class Address {
    String city;

    Address(String city) {
        this.city = city;
    }
}

class Person {
    String name;
    Address address;

    Person(String name, Address address) {
        this.name = name;
        this.address = address;
    }
}

static void updatePerson(Person person) {
    person.name = "Maya";                 // Mutates the shared object
    person.address.city = "Bengaluru";    // Mutates the shared nested object
    person = new Person("Ravi", new Address("Pune")); // Only changes local copy
}

Person person = new Person("Anu", new Address("Chennai"));
updatePerson(person);

System.out.println(person.name);         // Maya
System.out.println(person.address.city); // Bengaluru
System.out.println(person.name);         // Not Ravi: caller still has original object
What happens with nested objects?

Nested objects follow the same rule. The copied reference points to the original Person, and its address field points to the original Address. Mutating person.address.city is visible to the caller because both references share the same object graph. To prevent this, create a deep copy or use immutable objects.

Real-world analogy

Imagine giving someone a copy of your house key. Both keys open the same house, so changing the furniture is visible to both people. But replacing the key in their hand with a key to another house does not change the key you kept. The key is the copied reference; the house is the object.

Interview-ready answer

"Java is strictly pass-by-value. For primitives, the primitive value is copied. For objects, the reference value is copied, so both variables can point to the same object. Object field or nested-object mutations are visible to the caller, but reassigning the method parameter to a new object is not visible outside the method."

Creational patterns focus on object creation. They help us create objects in a flexible and reusable way instead of hardcoding new everywhere.

Patterns and when to use them
Pattern Real-world idea When to use
Singleton One shared control room Use when one shared instance should manage a global resource like config or cache.
Factory Method Ordering food from a menu Use when a subclass or factory decides which object to create.
Abstract Factory Buying a matching furniture set Use when you need families of related objects that should work together.
Builder Customizing a burger step by step Use when an object has many optional fields and construction should stay readable.
Prototype Photocopying a document Use when creating from an existing object is easier than building from scratch.
Simple memory trick
  • Singleton: only one.
  • Factory: create on demand.
  • Abstract Factory: create matching families.
  • Builder: build step by step.
  • Prototype: copy existing object.
Tiny example code for each pattern
Pattern Example code
Singleton AppConfig cfg = AppConfig.INSTANCE;
Factory Method Notification n = NotificationFactory.create("email");
Abstract Factory GUIFactory f = new WindowsFactory(); Button b = f.createButton();
Builder User u = User.builder().name("Asha").age(30).build();
Prototype Employee copy = original.clone();
Interview-ready answer

"Creational design patterns deal with object creation. Singleton gives one instance, Factory Method and Abstract Factory hide creation logic, Builder helps with complex construction, and Prototype creates a new object by copying an existing one."

Structural patterns focus on how classes and objects are connected. They help us build larger structures that are easier to extend and maintain.

Patterns and when to use them
Pattern Real-world idea When to use
Adapter Power plug converter Use when one class has the wrong interface and must fit into existing code.
Bridge Remote control and TV brand Use when abstraction and implementation should vary independently.
Composite Folder with files and subfolders Use when treating single objects and groups of objects the same way is helpful.
Decorator Adding toppings to a pizza Use when you want to add behavior without changing the original class.
Facade Hotel receptionist Use when you want one simple entry point to a complex subsystem.
Flyweight Shared chess piece model Use when many similar objects share common data and memory needs to be reduced.
Proxy Security guard / stand-in Use when you need access control, lazy loading, logging, or remote access.
Simple memory trick
  • Adapter: make incompatible things work together.
  • Bridge: separate what something does from how it does it.
  • Composite: tree structure.
  • Decorator: wrap and add features.
  • Facade: one simple front door.
  • Flyweight: share repeated data.
  • Proxy: control access through a middle layer.
Tiny example code for each pattern
Pattern Example code
Adapter PaymentProcessor p = new RazorpayAdapter(); p.pay(1000);
Bridge Remote r = new Remote(new SamsungTV()); r.toggle();
Composite folder.add(new FileItem("a.txt")); folder.print();
Decorator Coffee c = new MilkDecorator(new BasicCoffee());
Facade new TravelFacade().bookTrip();
Flyweight ChessPiece king = factory.getPiece("black", "king");
Proxy Image img = new ProxyImage("photo.jpg"); img.display();
Interview-ready answer

"Structural patterns are about how objects are composed. Adapter fixes interface mismatch, Decorator adds behavior, Facade simplifies a subsystem, Composite handles tree structures, Proxy controls access, Bridge separates abstraction from implementation, and Flyweight reduces memory for shared data."

Behavioral patterns focus on how objects communicate and share responsibility. They help define clean workflows and interactions.

Patterns and when to use them
Pattern Real-world idea When to use
Chain of Responsibility Customer support escalation chain Use when a request may pass through multiple handlers until one processes it.
Command Remote button Use when you want to turn a request into an object that can be queued or undone.
Interpreter Grammar translator Use when you need to evaluate expressions in a small language or rule set.
Iterator Book pages one by one Use when you want to traverse a collection without exposing its internals.
Mediator Air traffic controller Use when many objects communicate through a central coordinator.
Memento Save game snapshot Use when you need to capture and restore an object's previous state.
Observer News subscribers Use when many listeners should react automatically to a state change.
State Traffic light Use when behavior changes based on internal state.
Strategy Different payment methods Use when you want to swap algorithms at runtime.
Template Method Cooking recipe steps Use when the skeleton is fixed but some steps vary in subclasses.
Visitor Inspector visiting rooms Use when you want to add new operations to object structures without changing them.
Simple memory trick
  • Chain: request passes through handlers.
  • Command: request becomes an object.
  • Observer: publisher notifies subscribers.
  • Strategy: swap algorithms.
  • State: behavior depends on current state.
  • Template Method: fixed flow, variable steps.
  • Mediator: central coordinator.
  • Memento: store and restore state.
  • Iterator: traverse one item at a time.
  • Visitor: add operations without changing objects.
  • Interpreter: evaluate expressions.
Tiny example code for each pattern
Pattern Example code
Chain of Responsibility auth.setNext(logging); auth.handle(req);
Command button.setCommand(new LightOnCommand(light)); button.press();
Interpreter context.evaluate("5 + 3");
Iterator for (Iterator<String> it = list.iterator(); it.hasNext();) { it.next(); }
Mediator chat.send("hi");
Memento caretaker.save(editor.save());
Observer subject.attach(obs); subject.notifyObservers();
State order.setState(new ShippedState()); order.process();
Strategy payment.pay(new CardPayment());
Template Method new CsvImporter().importFile();
Visitor element.accept(new ExportVisitor());
Interview-ready answer

"Behavioral patterns are about object interaction and responsibility. Strategy swaps algorithms, Observer broadcasts changes, Command wraps an action as an object, Chain of Responsibility passes work along handlers, State changes behavior based on state, and Template Method defines a fixed workflow with customizable steps."

Collectors is a utility class used with Java Streams to convert, group, summarize, and transform stream results into useful collections or aggregated values.

Most used Collectors methods
Method When to use Example
toList() Collect stream items into a mutable list. names.stream().collect(Collectors.toList())
toSet() Remove duplicates and collect unique values. names.stream().collect(Collectors.toSet())
toUnmodifiableList() Return a read-only list. names.stream().collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableList())
toUnmodifiableSet() Return a read-only set. names.stream().collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableSet())
toCollection(Supplier) Collect into a specific collection type. names.stream().collect(Collectors.toCollection(LinkedList::new))
toMap(keyMapper, valueMapper) Convert stream items to a map. emps.stream().collect(Collectors.toMap(Employee::id, Employee::name))
toMap(..., mergeFn) Handle duplicate keys during map creation. toMap(Employee::dept, e -> 1, Integer::sum)
toConcurrentMap(...) Create a concurrent map in parallel stream use cases. emps.parallelStream().collect(Collectors.toConcurrentMap(Employee::id, e -> e))
joining() Concatenate strings. names.stream().collect(Collectors.joining(", "))
counting() Count the number of elements. items.stream().collect(Collectors.counting())
mapping(mapper, downstream) Transform values before downstream collection. groupingBy(dept, mapping(Employee::name, toList()))
filtering(predicate, downstream) Filter values before downstream collection. groupingBy(dept, filtering(e -> e.active(), toList()))
flatMapping(mapper, downstream) Flatten nested streams before collecting. groupingBy(dept, flatMapping(e -> e.tags().stream(), toSet()))
collectingAndThen(downstream, finisher) Apply a finishing step after collection. collectingAndThen(toList(), Collections::unmodifiableList)
minBy(comparator) Find the minimum element wrapped in Optional. employees.stream().collect(Collectors.minBy(Comparator.comparing(Employee::salary)))
maxBy(comparator) Find the maximum element wrapped in Optional. employees.stream().collect(Collectors.maxBy(Comparator.comparing(Employee::salary)))
reducing(...) Combine elements into one value using a reduction. nums.stream().collect(Collectors.reducing(0, Integer::sum))
groupingBy(classifier) Group items by key. emps.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::dept))
groupingBy(classifier, downstream) Group items and collect each group in another way. groupingBy(Employee::dept, counting())
groupingByConcurrent(...) Concurrent grouping for parallel streams. emps.parallelStream().collect(Collectors.groupingByConcurrent(Employee::dept))
partitioningBy(predicate) Split into true/false groups. emps.stream().collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(Employee::active))
partitioningBy(predicate, downstream) Split into true/false groups and apply downstream logic. partitioningBy(Employee::active, counting())
summingInt/Long/Double() Add numeric values. emps.stream().collect(Collectors.summingInt(Employee::age))
averagingInt/Long/Double() Compute average. emps.stream().collect(Collectors.averagingDouble(Employee::salary))
summarizingInt/Long/Double() Get count, sum, min, max, and average in one shot. emps.stream().collect(Collectors.summarizingDouble(Employee::salary))
teeing(c1, c2, merger) Run two collectors in parallel and merge the result. collect(teeing(counting(), averagingInt(Employee::age), Result::new))
Small stream examples
List<String> list = names.stream().collect(Collectors.toList());
Set<String> set = names.stream().collect(Collectors.toSet());
String joined = names.stream().collect(Collectors.joining(", "));
Map<Long, String> byId = emps.stream().collect(Collectors.toMap(Employee::id, Employee::name));
Map<String, List<Employee>> byDept = emps.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::dept));
Map<Boolean, List<Employee>> activeInactive = emps.stream().collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(Employee::active));
int totalAge = emps.stream().collect(Collectors.summingInt(Employee::age));
DoubleSummaryStatistics stats = emps.stream().collect(Collectors.summarizingDouble(Employee::salary));
Deep dive: toMap

toMap is used when each stream element should become one key-value pair. The upstream stream provides the elements, the key mapper decides the map key, and the value mapper decides the value. 

Map<Long, String> idToName =
    employees.stream()
             .collect(Collectors.toMap(Employee::id, Employee::name));

This works best when keys are unique. If two elements produce the same key, plain toMap throws IllegalStateException. 

// duplicate key problem
employees.stream()
         .collect(Collectors.toMap(Employee::dept, Employee::name)); // fails if dept repeats

When duplicates are possible, provide a merge function so you can decide how to combine values. 

Map<String, Integer> deptCount =
    employees.stream()
             .collect(Collectors.toMap(
                 Employee::dept,
                 e -> 1,
                 Integer::sum
             ));

In this example, duplicate department keys are merged by adding counts. You can also keep the first value, keep the last value, or combine values into a list depending on the requirement. 

Map<String, Employee> latestByDept =
    employees.stream()
             .collect(Collectors.toMap(
                 Employee::dept,
                 Function.identity(),
                 (oldVal, newVal) -> newVal
             ));
When to use toMap
  • When you want direct lookup by a unique key.
  • When you are converting a stream into a map for fast retrieval.
  • When you need explicit duplicate-key handling via a merge function.
  • When you want to transform each element into a structured key-value result.
Deep dive: groupingBy

groupingBy is used when you want to group stream elements by a classifier function. The upstream stream provides the data, the classifier decides the group key, and the downstream collector decides how each group is stored or summarized. 

Map<String, List<Employee>> byDept =
    employees.stream()
             .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::dept));

This gives one list per department. If you need counts instead of lists, add a downstream collector. 

Map<String, Long> deptCounts =
    employees.stream()
             .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                 Employee::dept,
                 Collectors.counting()
             ));

You can also do nested grouping or collect different data per group. 

Map<String, List<String>> deptNames =
    employees.stream()
             .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                 Employee::dept,
                 Collectors.mapping(Employee::name, Collectors.toList())
             ));

This is useful when you want the group key to stay the same, but you want a transformed result inside each group.

When to use groupingBy
  • When you need more than two groups.
  • When you want to aggregate data by category, department, status, or type.
  • When you want a downstream collector like counting, mapping, summing, or summarizing.
  • When grouping is more natural than direct key-value mapping.
Easy difference
  • toMap: one key to one value, usually direct lookup.
  • groupingBy: one key to many values or aggregated results.
More about partitioningBy

partitioningBy is a special collector that splits the stream into exactly two groups: true and false. The upstream is the original stream flowing into the collector, the predicate decides which side each element goes to, and the downstream collector processes each side after the split. 

Map<Boolean, List<Employee>> result =
    employees.stream()
             .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(Employee::active));

In this example, the upstream is employees.stream(). The predicate is Employee::active. Every employee that returns true goes into the true bucket, and the rest go into the false bucket.

Partitioning with downstream collector
Map<Boolean, Long> counts =
    employees.stream()
             .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(
                 Employee::active,
                 Collectors.counting()
             ));

Here, the downstream collector is counting(). So instead of storing the full list of employees on each side, we store only the count of active and inactive employees.

Easy way to remember
  • Upstream: the original stream of elements.
  • Predicate: decides true or false.
  • Downstream: what to do with each partition after splitting.
When to use partitioningBy
  • When you only need two buckets, like active/inactive or pass/fail.
