  • When boolean grouping is clearer than a full groupingBy.
  • When you want to summarize each side separately using a downstream collector.
How to choose quickly
  • Need a list or set: use toList() or toSet().
  • Need a map: use toMap() or toConcurrentMap().
  • Need grouping: use groupingBy().
  • Need true/false split: use partitioningBy().
  • Need counts or sums: use counting(), summing*, or summarizing*.
  • Need post-processing: use collectingAndThen().
  • Need multiple aggregations: use teeing().
Interview-ready answer

"Collectors is the Streams utility class for turning stream data into collections or aggregates. I use toList and toSet for simple collection, toMap for key-value results, groupingBy for grouping, partitioningBy for boolean split, counting and summarizing for metrics, and teeing when I need two aggregations at once."

Virtual Threads are lightweight Java threads managed by the JVM. They let you write simple blocking-style code while the JVM multiplexes many virtual threads onto a smaller number of carrier threads.

Easy mental model
  • Platform thread: a real OS-backed worker.
  • Virtual thread: a cheap task-like thread managed by Java.
  • Carrier thread: the platform thread that temporarily runs a virtual thread.
  • Mount/unmount: the virtual thread attaches to a carrier to run, then detaches when it can park.
How it works internally
  1. The JVM schedules virtual threads, not the OS directly.
  2. When a virtual thread runs, it is mounted on a carrier thread.
  3. If it blocks on a JVM-managed operation like sleep or many I/O waits, it can unmount and free the carrier.
  4. Later, the JVM remounts it on any available carrier and continues execution.
Real-world example

Imagine a food delivery platform handling 50,000 order-tracking requests. Most requests spend time waiting for database or API responses. With virtual threads, each request can have its own thread-like flow without needing 50,000 OS threads. 

try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
        int orderId = i;
        executor.submit(() -> {
            String status = trackOrder(orderId); // blocking call is fine
            System.out.println(Thread.currentThread() + " -> " + status);
        });
    }
}
Why they feel faster
  • They are cheaper to create than platform threads.
  • Blocked virtual threads do not monopolize OS threads for long.
  • You can keep imperative code instead of rewriting everything to reactive style.
Important internal terms
  • Carrier thread: the real thread doing the work at that moment.
  • Pinned virtual thread: a virtual thread that cannot unmount, often because of certain synchronized blocks or native blocking.
  • Parking: the virtual thread pauses and frees the carrier.
When to use
  • I/O-heavy services like web APIs, gateways, batch workers, and service orchestration.
  • When you want simple thread-per-request code but higher concurrency.
  • When the bottleneck is waiting, not raw CPU work.
When not to expect magic
  • They do not make CPU-bound work faster.
  • They do not remove database connection limits.
  • They do not automatically fix poorly synchronized code.
Interview-ready answer

"Virtual Threads are lightweight JVM-managed threads. They run on carrier threads, can unmount while waiting, and later remount on another carrier. They are best for high-concurrency blocking workloads, because they let us keep simple imperative code without creating one OS thread per request."

Future represents the result of an asynchronous computation that may not be available yet. You submit a task, get back a Future, and later ask it for the result.

Simple idea
  • Start a task in the background.
  • Get a handle to the result immediately.
  • Wait for the result later using get().
Real-world example

Imagine an e-commerce app that needs to fetch order details from a remote service while continuing with other work. A Future lets the app submit the call first and collect the response later. 

ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);
Future<String> future = executor.submit(() -> fetchOrderStatus(101));

System.out.println("Doing other work...");
String status = future.get(); // waits for completion
System.out.println("Status = " + status);
When to use
  • When you want simple async execution with a result.
  • When one background task needs to return a value or throw an exception.
  • When you do not need a complex async pipeline.
Disadvantages
  • get() blocks the caller thread.
  • It does not compose well for many async steps compared to CompletableFuture.
  • Cancellation and chaining are limited compared to newer async APIs.
  • If overused, it can still lead to thread blocking and poor scalability.
Better alternative for complex flows

If you need chaining, combining multiple tasks, or non-blocking style composition, CompletableFuture is usually a better choice than plain Future.

Interview-ready answer

"Future is a handle to an async task result. I use it when I want to submit work in the background and get the result later. Its drawback is that get() blocks, so it is less flexible than CompletableFuture for complex asynchronous workflows."

CompletableFuture is a more powerful async API than Future. It lets you start work asynchronously, chain multiple steps, combine multiple tasks, and handle success or failure in a clean way.

Why it is useful
  • You can chain async steps instead of blocking after each task.
  • You can combine multiple independent tasks.
  • You can handle errors and fallbacks in the same pipeline.
  • You can run tasks asynchronously with or without a custom executor.
Real-world example

Imagine a checkout page that needs user profile, cart summary, and pricing rules from different services. With CompletableFuture, you can fetch them in parallel, combine the results, and then build the response. 

CompletableFuture<String> userFuture =
        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchUser(10));

CompletableFuture<String> cartFuture =
        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchCart(10));

CompletableFuture<String> responseFuture =
        userFuture.thenCombine(cartFuture, (user, cart) -> user + " | " + cart)
                  .exceptionally(ex -> "fallback-response");

System.out.println(responseFuture.join());
Most important methods
Method Purpose
supplyAsync(Supplier) Starts an async task that returns a value.
runAsync(Runnable) Starts an async task that does not return a value.
thenApply(Function) Transforms the result synchronously.
thenApplyAsync(Function) Transforms the result asynchronously.
thenAccept(Consumer) Consumes the result without returning a new value.
thenRun(Runnable) Runs a follow-up action after completion, ignoring the result.
thenCompose(Function) Flattens nested futures when one async step returns another future.
thenCombine(other, BiFunction) Combines results of two independent futures.
thenAcceptBoth(other, BiConsumer) Consumes results from two futures together.
runAfterBoth(other, Runnable) Runs after both futures complete.
thenAcceptEither(other, Consumer) Runs when either future completes first.
runAfterEither(other, Runnable) Runs after whichever future completes first.
allOf(f1, f2, ...) Waits for all futures to complete.
anyOf(f1, f2, ...) Completes when any one future completes.
exceptionally(Function) Provides fallback logic when an exception occurs.
handle(BiFunction) Handles both success and failure in one place.
whenComplete(BiConsumer) Observes completion without changing the result.
complete(value) Manually completes the future with a value.
completeExceptionally(ex) Manually completes the future with an error.
orTimeout(time, unit) Fails the future if it takes too long.
completeOnTimeout(value, time, unit) Returns a fallback value if timeout happens.
join() Waits for completion and returns result without checked exception.
get() Waits for completion and throws checked exceptions.
Small code patterns
// transform
future.thenApply(String::toUpperCase);

// chain another async call
future.thenCompose(value -> fetchDetailsAsync(value));

// combine two independent results
userFuture.thenCombine(cartFuture, (u, c) -> u + c);

// error fallback
future.exceptionally(ex -> "default");

// observe success or failure
future.whenComplete((value, ex) -> System.out.println(value));

// wait for many tasks
CompletableFuture.allOf(f1, f2, f3).join();
When to use
  • When you want non-blocking async flow composition.
  • When you need to combine multiple service calls.
  • When you want clear error handling and fallbacks.
  • When you want to avoid manual thread management.
Limitations
  • It can become hard to read if you build very deep chains.
  • It still needs care with thread pools and blocking operations.
  • It is not automatically non-blocking if you call blocking code inside it.
Interview-ready answer

"CompletableFuture is an enhanced async API over Future. It supports chaining, combining, error handling, and manual completion. I use it when I need to coordinate multiple async tasks or build a clear async pipeline instead of blocking on get()."

OutOfMemoryError means the JVM could not allocate memory or other native resources it needed to continue. It is usually a symptom of too much data, too many objects, too many threads, or memory leakage.

Common OOM types
Type What it means Typical cause
Java heap space The JVM heap is full and cannot create more objects. Large collections, memory leaks, too many cached objects, unbounded buffering.
GC overhead limit exceeded GC is spending too much time collecting very little memory. Heap is under pressure and most objects are still alive.
Metaspace Class metadata storage is exhausted. Too many loaded classes, classloader leaks, dynamic proxy/class generation.
Direct buffer memory Off-heap direct memory is exhausted. Too many NIO buffers, Netty/direct byte buffers not released.
Unable to create new native thread The JVM cannot create more OS threads. Thread leak, huge thread pools, low OS limits, virtual memory pressure.
Requested array size exceeds VM limit An array requested is too large for the VM to handle. Attempting to allocate an extremely large array.
Real-world example

Imagine a shopping app that keeps adding every request into an in-memory list for reporting and never clears it. Over time, heap usage grows, garbage collection becomes frequent, and eventually the JVM can throw Java heap space. 

List<String> cache = new ArrayList<>();
while (true) {
    cache.add(UUID.randomUUID().toString()); // keeps growing forever
}
How to think about it
  • Heap OOM: too many live objects.
  • Metaspace OOM: too many classes or classloader leaks.
  • Direct memory OOM: off-heap/native buffers not freed fast enough.
  • Thread OOM: too many threads created.
How to reduce risk
  • Use bounded collections and caches.
  • Close buffers, streams, and resources properly.
  • Avoid thread leaks and oversized thread pools.
  • Monitor heap, metaspace, direct memory, and thread count.
  • Take heap dumps and analyze top retainers when memory grows unexpectedly.
Interview-ready answer

"OOM means the JVM ran out of a required memory or native resource. The common ones are Java heap space, GC overhead limit exceeded, Metaspace, Direct buffer memory, and unable to create new native thread. I usually look for leaks, unbounded caches, classloader issues, or too many threads."

A thread leak happens when threads keep getting created or kept alive without being properly stopped, reused, or released. Over time, this wastes memory and CPU and can eventually cause poor performance or Unable to create new native thread OOM errors.

Real-world example

Imagine a web app that creates a new thread for every request but never shuts it down. After thousands of requests, the app accumulates many active or waiting threads, and the server becomes slow or fails to create more threads. 

while (true) {
    new Thread(() -> {
        try {
            Thread.sleep(1000);
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    }).start();
}
Why it happens
  • Creating threads in a loop without using an executor service.
  • Not shutting down thread pools with shutdown() or shutdownNow().
  • Threads waiting forever on locks, I/O, or external systems.
  • Submitting tasks faster than the pool can handle them.
  • Using too many scheduled or background threads that are never cleaned up.
How to detect it
  • Thread count keeps increasing over time.
  • Thread dumps show many waiting or blocked threads.
  • CPU or memory usage slowly grows without coming back down.
  • Requests become slower because thread pools are exhausted.
How to prevent it
  • Use ExecutorService instead of creating raw threads.
  • Always shut down executors when they are no longer needed.
  • Use bounded queues and sensible pool sizes.
  • Set timeouts for blocking calls.
  • Close resources and avoid indefinite waits.
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10);
try {
    pool.submit(() -> doWork());
} finally {
    pool.shutdown();
}
Interview-ready answer

"A thread leak is when threads are created or retained without proper cleanup, so thread count keeps growing and the application slows down or fails to create new threads. I prevent it by using ExecutorService, shutting down pools, setting timeouts, and watching thread dumps and thread counts."

A thread-safe LRU cache stores only the most recently used entries and removes the least recently used entry when capacity is full. The key challenge is keeping both the cache contents and the access order correct when multiple threads read and write at the same time.

Best simple design
  • Use LinkedHashMap with access-order enabled.
  • Override removeEldestEntry to evict the oldest item.
  • Guard get and put with synchronization or a lock.
Thread-safe example
class LruCache<K, V> {
    private final int capacity;
    private final Map<K, V> map;

    public LruCache(int capacity) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.map = new LinkedHashMap<K, V>(capacity, 0.75f, true) {
            @Override
            protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) {
                return size() > LruCache.this.capacity;
            }
        };
    }

    public synchronized V get(K key) {
        return map.get(key);
    }

    public synchronized void put(K key, V value) {
        map.put(key, value);
    }

    public synchronized int size() {
        return map.size();
    }
}
How it works
  • get() moves the key to the most recent position because access-order is enabled.
  • put() adds or updates a value.
  • When size exceeds capacity, the eldest entry is evicted automatically.
  • synchronized keeps map updates and LRU order changes atomic.
Real-world example

A product catalog service can cache the last 1,000 product lookups. Frequently used items stay in the cache, and old ones are evicted automatically when new items come in.

Tradeoffs
  • Very simple and correct for moderate concurrency.
  • All access is serialized, so it can become a bottleneck under heavy traffic.
  • For very high throughput, you may shard the cache or use a specialized cache library.
Interview-ready answer

"I would implement a thread-safe LRU cache using a LinkedHashMap in access order, override removeEldestEntry for eviction, and synchronize get and put so the access order stays correct. It is simple and safe; if concurrency is very high, I would consider sharding or a cache library."

The cleanest solution is to group employees by department and then use a downstream collector like minBy to find the lowest salary employee in each group.

Best stream solution
Map<String, Optional<Employee>> lowestByDept =
    employees.stream()
             .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                 Employee::getDepartment,
                 Collectors.minBy(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary))
             ));

The result is a map where the key is the department and the value is the lowest-salary employee wrapped in Optional.

If you want the plain employee object
Map<String, Employee> lowestByDept =
    employees.stream()
             .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                 Employee::getDepartment,
                 Collectors.collectingAndThen(
                     Collectors.minBy(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary)),
                     Optional::get
                 )
             ));

Use this only when you know each department has at least one employee. Otherwise keep the Optional and handle empty groups safely.

Alternative approach with toMap
Map<String, Employee> lowestByDept =
    employees.stream()
             .collect(Collectors.toMap(
                 Employee::getDepartment,
                 Function.identity(),
                 (e1, e2) -> e1.getSalary() <= e2.getSalary() ? e1 : e2
             ));

This version is useful when you want a direct map and want to merge duplicates by keeping the lower salary employee.

Real-world example

An HR dashboard can show the lowest-paid employee in each department for budget analysis, like IT, Finance, Sales, and Support.

When to use which
  • groupingBy + minBy: best for readability and the most natural stream solution.
  • groupingBy + collectingAndThen: when you want the plain object instead of Optional.
  • toMap + merge function: when you want a direct map with custom conflict handling.
Interview-ready answer

"I would group employees by department and use Collectors.minBy with a salary comparator to find the lowest-paid employee in each department. If I want a direct Employee instead of Optional, I can wrap it with collectingAndThen or use toMap with a merge function."

The nth smallest number is the element that would appear at position n if the array were sorted in ascending order.

Brute force solution

Sort the array and return the element at index n - 1. This is the simplest approach and is easy to explain in interviews. 

public static int nthSmallestBruteForce(int[] arr, int n) {
    Arrays.sort(arr);
    return arr[n - 1];
}

Time complexity is O(m log m) for an array of size m.

Optimal solution

Use a max heap of size n. Keep only the n smallest elements seen so far. The heap top is the largest among those n smallest, which becomes the answer at the end. 

public static int nthSmallestOptimal(int[] arr, int n) {
    PriorityQueue<Integer> maxHeap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> b - a);

    for (int num : arr) {
        maxHeap.offer(num);
        if (maxHeap.size() > n) {
            maxHeap.poll();
        }
    }

    return maxHeap.peek();
}

Time complexity is O(m log n) and space complexity is O(n).

Real-world example

Suppose you want the third cheapest product price from a list of thousands of prices. Sorting works, but the heap approach keeps only the best n candidates in memory.

When to use which
  • Brute force: when simplicity matters and the input is not very large.
  • Heap optimal: when the array is large and you want better memory usage than full sorting.
Interview-ready answer

"For the nth smallest element, the brute force solution is to sort the array and return the n-1 index. The optimal solution is to maintain a max heap of size n, so the heap always keeps the n smallest elements seen so far and the root becomes the nth smallest."

The nth highest number is the element that would appear at position n if the array were sorted in descending order.

Brute force solution

Sort the array in reverse order and return the element at index n - 1. 

public static int nthHighestBruteForce(int[] arr, int n) {
    Integer[] boxed = Arrays.stream(arr).boxed().toArray(Integer[]::new);
    Arrays.sort(boxed, Collections.reverseOrder());
    return boxed[n - 1];
}

Time complexity is O(m log m) for an array of size m.

Optimal solution

Use a min heap of size n. Keep only the n largest elements seen so far. The heap top is the smallest among those n largest, which becomes the answer at the end. 

public static int nthHighestOptimal(int[] arr, int n) {
    PriorityQueue<Integer> minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>();

    for (int num : arr) {
        minHeap.offer(num);
        if (minHeap.size() > n) {
            minHeap.poll();
        }
    }

    return minHeap.peek();
}

Time complexity is O(m log n) and space complexity is O(n).

Real-world example

Suppose you want the third highest salary in a company. Sorting works, but the heap approach keeps only the top n candidates in memory.

When to use which
  • Brute force: when simplicity matters and the input is not very large.
  • Heap optimal: when the array is large and you want better memory usage than full sorting.
Interview-ready answer

"For the nth highest element, the brute force solution is to sort the array in descending order and return the n-1 index. The optimal solution is to maintain a min heap of size n, so the heap always keeps the n largest elements seen so far and the root becomes the nth highest."

Java 8 Streams improved the way we work with collections by making data processing more readable, declarative, and composable. Instead of writing long loops with mutable state, we can express the operation as a pipeline.

What Streams improved
  • More readable code: map, filter, reduce, and collect express intent clearly.
  • Less boilerplate: no manual iterator or temporary list handling.
  • Lazy evaluation: intermediate operations run only when needed.
  • Short-circuiting: operations like findFirst() and anyMatch() can stop early.
  • Parallel processing support: parallelStream() can use multiple threads.
  • Powerful collectors: grouping, partitioning, mapping, summarizing, and custom reductions.
  • Functional style: encourages stateless operations and fewer side effects.
Before Streams
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
for (Employee e : employees) {
    if (e.getSalary() > 50000) {
        names.add(e.getName().toUpperCase());
    }
}
With Streams
List<String> names = employees.stream()
    .filter(e -> e.getSalary() > 50000)
    .map(Employee::getName)
    .map(String::toUpperCase)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
Real-world example

Imagine filtering premium customers, transforming their names, and collecting the final list for an email campaign. Streams make that pipeline compact and easy to read.

Why Streams are better
  • They separate what you want from how to loop.
  • They reduce accidental mutation and side effects.
  • They fit naturally with grouping, partitioning, and aggregation tasks.
  • They work nicely with method references and lambdas.
Interview-ready answer

"Java 8 Streams improved collection processing by making it more declarative, readable, and composable. They introduced lazy pipelines, short-circuiting, collectors, and easier parallel processing, so we can replace verbose loops with cleaner stream operations."

A Collection is a data structure that stores elements. A Stream is a pipeline used to process those elements.

Key differences
  • Collection: stores data.
  • Stream: processes data.
  • Collection: can be traversed many times.
  • Stream: can be used only once.
  • Collection: is eager by nature.
  • Stream: is lazy until a terminal operation runs.
  • Collection: supports direct add/remove operations.
  • Stream: does not modify the source collection directly.
Simple example
List<String> names = List.of("Asha", "Ravi", "Meera");

// Collection stores values
for (String name : names) {
    System.out.println(name);
}

// Stream processes values
List<String> upper = names.stream()
    .map(String::toUpperCase)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
When to use what
  • Use Collection: when you need to store and manage data.
  • Use Stream: when you need to transform, filter, group, or aggregate data.
Interview-ready answer

"A Collection stores data, while a Stream processes data. Collections are reusable and eager, while Streams are lazy, single-use pipelines that help us perform operations like filter, map, reduce, and collect in a readable way."

Java 8 Streams are powerful, but they are not a replacement for every loop or every data-processing need.

Main limitations
  • Single use: a stream cannot be reused after a terminal operation.
  • Harder debugging: stream pipelines can be harder to step through than loops.
  • Side effects are risky: mutating external state can lead to bugs.
  • Not always faster: streams can be slower for very small or simple workloads.
  • Parallel pitfalls: parallel streams can hurt performance if the work is not CPU-bound.
  • Checked exceptions: standard stream lambdas do not handle checked exceptions naturally.
  • Readability limit: very deep pipelines can become difficult to read.
Example of a bad use case
// Hard to debug and may be slower than a simple loop for tiny data
List<String> result = names.stream()
    .filter(name -> name.length() > 2)
    .map(String::trim)
    .map(String::toUpperCase)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
When not to use streams
  • When a plain loop is simpler and clearer.
  • When you must mutate complex external state.
  • When you need fine-grained debugging or step-by-step control.
  • When the operation is very small and performance is not worth the abstraction.
Interview-ready answer

"Streams are excellent for declarative data processing, but they have limits: they are single-use, harder to debug, not always faster, and parallel streams can be tricky. I use them when they improve readability and processing clarity, not just because they are modern."

reduce() is a terminal operation used to combine many stream elements into one result. We use it when we want to aggregate values like sum, product, max, min, or a custom combined object.

Why we use reduce
  • To collapse a stream into a single value.
  • To perform custom aggregation beyond built-in collectors.
  • To express associative operations cleanly in a functional style.
The three overloads
Overload Use case
Optional<T> reduce(BinaryOperator<T> accumulator) Combine stream elements when there is no initial value.
T reduce(T identity, BinaryOperator<T> accumulator) Combine stream elements with a default starting value.
U reduce(U identity, BiFunction<U, ? super T, U> accumulator, BinaryOperator<U> combiner) Combine and transform into a different result type, especially useful in parallel streams.
Simple examples
List<Integer> nums = List.of(10, 20, 30, 40);

// 1. Without identity: returns Optional
Optional<Integer> sum1 = nums.stream()
    .reduce((a, b) -> a + b);

// 2. With identity: returns plain value
Integer sum2 = nums.stream()
    .reduce(0, Integer::sum);

// 3. With identity + accumulator + combiner
Integer sum3 = nums.stream()
    .reduce(0, Integer::sum, Integer::sum);
What does combiner mean?

The combiner is used mainly in parallel streams. If the stream is split into multiple parts, each part gets reduced separately, and then the combiner merges those partial results into one final result.

  • Accumulator: combines one existing partial result with the next stream element.
  • Combiner: combines two partial results produced by different threads.
Easy example
Integer sum = nums.parallelStream()
    .reduce(
        0,                 // identity
        Integer::sum,      // accumulator: partial + element
        Integer::sum       // combiner: partial + partial
    );

In this example, if one thread sums 10 + 20 and another sums 30 + 40, the combiner merges those two partial sums into the final value.

Another example: string join
String joined = Stream.of("Java", "Spring", "Boot")
    .parallel()
    .reduce(
        "",
        (a, b) -> a.isEmpty() ? b : a + ", " + b,
        (a, b) -> a.isEmpty() ? b : b.isEmpty() ? a : a + ", " + b
    );

Here the accumulator builds each partial string, and the combiner joins two partial strings together.

Real-world example

Imagine calculating the total cart amount from many line items. Reduce lets you fold all item prices into one final bill.

When to use reduce vs Collectors
  • Use reduce: when you want one final value from a stream.
  • Use Collectors: when you want grouping, mapping, partitioning, or collection-based results.
  • Use reduce carefully: only for associative operations where the order of grouping does not change the result.
Important note

The operation should ideally be associative and stateless. If you write a non-associative reduce, the result may behave unexpectedly, especially in parallel streams.

Interview-ready answer

"reduce() is a terminal stream operation used to combine all elements into one result, such as a sum or product. It has three overloads: one without identity that returns Optional, one with identity that returns a plain value, and one with identity plus combiner for parallel-friendly transformations."

These are terminal operations used to check whether stream elements satisfy a condition. They are very useful when you only need a yes/no answer.

Meaning of each method
  • allMatch: returns true if every element matches the predicate.
  • anyMatch: returns true if at least one element matches the predicate.
  • noneMatch: returns true if no elements match the predicate.
Simple example
List<Integer> nums = List.of(10, 20, 30, 40);

boolean allPositive = nums.stream().allMatch(n -> n > 0);
boolean anyGreaterThan25 = nums.stream().anyMatch(n -> n > 25);
boolean noneNegative = nums.stream().noneMatch(n -> n < 0);
Spring Security role example

Think of user roles like ROLE_USER, ROLE_ADMIN, and ROLE_AUDITOR. These methods help answer authorization-style questions quickly. 

Set<String> roles = Set.of("ROLE_USER", "ROLE_ADMIN");

boolean allAreAdmin = roles.stream().allMatch(role -> role.equals("ROLE_ADMIN"));
boolean hasAdmin = roles.stream().anyMatch(role -> role.equals("ROLE_ADMIN"));
boolean noGuestRole = roles.stream().noneMatch(role -> role.equals("ROLE_GUEST"));
How to remember
  • allMatch: everyone must satisfy the rule.
  • anyMatch: at least one must satisfy the rule.
  • noneMatch: nobody should satisfy the rule.
When to use
  • Validation checks like "are all inputs valid?"
  • Access checks like "does any role allow this action?"
  • Safety checks like "is there no forbidden value?"
Interview-ready answer

"allMatch checks that every element satisfies the condition, anyMatch checks whether at least one does, and noneMatch checks whether none do. They are useful for validation and authorization-style checks, like verifying roles in Spring Security."

Both are terminal operations that return one matching element wrapped in Optional. The difference is about ordering and parallel performance.

Meaning of each method
  • findFirst: returns the first matching element in encounter order.
  • findAny: returns any matching element, which may be faster in parallel streams.
Simple example
List<String> names = List.of("Asha", "Ravi", "Meera", "Raj");

Optional<String> first = names.stream()
    .filter(name -> name.startsWith("R"))
    .findFirst();

Optional<String> any = names.stream()
    .filter(name -> name.startsWith("R"))
    .findAny();
Spring Security style example

Imagine a user has multiple roles and you want to pick one matching role for a check. findFirst respects order, while findAny can return any acceptable match. 

List<String> roles = List.of("ROLE_USER", "ROLE_ADMIN", "ROLE_AUDITOR");

Optional<String> firstAdmin = roles.stream()
    .filter(role -> role.contains("ADMIN"))
    .findFirst();

Optional<String> anyAdmin = roles.parallelStream()
    .filter(role -> role.contains("ADMIN"))
    .findAny();
How to remember
  • findFirst: strict order, first match.
  • findAny: any match, better freedom for parallel execution.
When to use
  • Use findFirst when order matters.
  • Use findAny when you only need one match and parallel speed matters.
Interview-ready answer

"findFirst returns the first matching element in encounter order, while findAny can return any matching element and is often better for parallel streams. I use findFirst when order matters and findAny when I only need one match."

These are intermediate operations used for pagination, sampling, and trimming a stream.

Meaning of each method
  • limit(n): keeps only the first n elements.
  • skip(n): ignores the first n elements and keeps the rest.
Simple example
List<Integer> nums = List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6);

List<Integer> firstThree = nums.stream()
    .limit(3)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

List<Integer> afterSkippingTwo = nums.stream()
    .skip(2)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
Spring Security style example

Think of a list of roles or permissions. limit gives only the first few roles to inspect, and skip jumps past initial roles when paging through results. 

List<String> roles = List.of("ROLE_USER", "ROLE_ADMIN", "ROLE_AUDITOR", "ROLE_MANAGER");

List<String> firstTwoRoles = roles.stream()
    .limit(2)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

List<String> rolesAfterFirst = roles.stream()
    .skip(1)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
When to use
  • limit: when you want top N results or preview data.
  • skip: when you want pagination or to ignore already processed items.
  • Both together: for page-based retrieval like page 2, 3, 4 etc.
Interview-ready answer

"limit keeps the first n elements and skip ignores the first n elements. I use them for pagination, sampling, and top-N style queries."

distinct() removes duplicate elements from a stream by using equals() and hashCode().

Simple example
List<Integer> unique = List.of(1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3).stream()
    .distinct()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
Spring Security style example

If a user accidentally has duplicate roles, distinct() can clean them before further processing. 

List<String> roles = List.of("ROLE_USER", "ROLE_ADMIN", "ROLE_USER");
List<String> uniqueRoles = roles.stream()
    .distinct()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
When to use
  • When you need unique values only.
  • When duplicates should be removed before sorting, grouping, or collecting.
  • When you want a clean list of distinct permissions, tags, or IDs.
Interview-ready answer

"distinct removes duplicate stream elements using equals and hashCode. I use it when I want unique values, like distinct roles, tags, or ids."

sorted() orders stream elements naturally or using a custom comparator.

Simple example
List<Integer> sortedNumbers = List.of(5, 2, 9, 1, 7).stream()
    .sorted()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
Spring Security style example

If you have role names, you can sort them alphabetically before displaying or auditing them. 

List<String> roles = List.of("ROLE_USER", "ROLE_ADMIN", "ROLE_AUDITOR");
List<String> sortedRoles = roles.stream()
    .sorted()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
Custom sort example
List<Employee> sortedEmployees = employees.stream()
    .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getDepartment)
        .thenComparing(Employee::getSalary, Comparator.reverseOrder()))
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
When to use
  • When you need ordered output.
  • When you want to sort by natural order or custom business fields.
  • When you want to sort roles, names, salaries, or report rows.
Interview-ready answer

"sorted() orders stream elements using natural ordering or a comparator. I use it when the final output needs to be arranged, like sorting roles, employees, or numbers."

peek() is mainly used for debugging or observing elements as they move through a pipeline.

Simple example
List<Integer> result = List.of(1, 2, 3, 4).stream()
    .peek(n -> System.out.println("Before filter: " + n))
    .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0)
    .peek(n -> System.out.println("After filter: " + n))
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
Spring Security style example

You can use peek() to inspect roles as they move through a security validation pipeline. 

Set<String> roles = Set.of("ROLE_USER", "ROLE_ADMIN");

roles.stream()
    .peek(role -> System.out.println("Incoming role: " + role))
    .filter(role -> role.startsWith("ROLE_"))
    .peek(role -> System.out.println("Allowed role: " + role))
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
When to use
  • For debugging stream pipelines.
  • To log intermediate values without changing them.
  • Not for critical business logic or side effects.
Interview-ready answer

"peek() is a debugging helper that lets me inspect elements inside a stream pipeline without modifying them. I use it for logging or troubleshooting, not for business logic."

Both are terminal operations used to process each element in a stream. The difference is ordering, especially in parallel streams.

Meaning of each method
  • forEach: processes elements as they become available; order is not guaranteed in parallel streams.
  • forEachOrdered: processes elements in encounter order.
Simple example
List<String> names = List.of("Asha", "Ravi", "Meera", "Raj");

names.stream()
    .forEach(System.out::println);

names.stream()
    .forEachOrdered(System.out::println);
Parallel stream example

In a parallel stream, forEach() may print in any order, while forEachOrdered() preserves the original order. 

List<Integer> nums = List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5);

nums.parallelStream()
    .forEach(n -> System.out.print(n + " "));

nums.parallelStream()
    .forEachOrdered(n -> System.out.print(n + " "));
Spring Security style example

Imagine logging roles after authorization. Use forEachOrdered() when the display order matters, such as user, admin, auditor. Use forEach() when order does not matter. 

List<String> roles = List.of("ROLE_USER", "ROLE_ADMIN", "ROLE_AUDITOR");

roles.parallelStream()
    .forEach(role -> System.out.println("Audit: " + role));

roles.parallelStream()
    .forEachOrdered(role -> System.out.println("Display: " + role));
How to remember
  • forEach: faster freedom, no guaranteed order.
  • forEachOrdered: ordered output, may be a bit slower in parallel.
When to use
  • Use forEach when order does not matter and you want simpler iteration.
  • Use forEachOrdered when output order matters, especially after parallel streams.
Interview-ready answer

"forEach processes stream elements without guaranteeing order in parallel streams, while forEachOrdered preserves encounter order. I use forEach when order does not matter and forEachOrdered when the result must stay in sequence."

map() transforms each element into one output element. flatMap() transforms each element into a stream and then flattens all those streams into one stream.

Simple example
List<List<String>> nested = List.of(
    List.of("Java", "Spring"),
    List.of("Streams", "Collectors")
);

List<String> mapped = nested.stream()
    .map(list -> list.toString())
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

List<String> flattened = nested.stream()
    .flatMap(List::stream)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
Spring Security style example

If each user has multiple roles, map() gives you nested role lists, while flatMap() gives you one flat stream of all roles. 

List<User> users = getUsers();

List<List<String>> nestedRoles = users.stream()
    .map(User::getRoles)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

List<String> allRoles = users.stream()
    .flatMap(user -> user.getRoles().stream())
    .distinct()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
Easy way to remember
  • map: one input becomes one output.
  • flatMap: one input becomes many outputs, then flatten them.
When to use
  • Use map() for simple transformation.
  • Use flatMap() when each item contains nested lists, optional values, or sub-streams.
Interview-ready answer

"map transforms each element into one output, while flatMap transforms each element into a stream and then flattens the result. I use flatMap when the source contains nested collections, like users with multiple roles or orders with line items."

Employee Analytics and Collectors

Counting, averaging, grouping, and salary-report style questions.

Map<String, Long> genderCount =
    employees.stream()
             .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::getGender, Collectors.counting()));

Use groupingBy with counting() to count each gender.

Set<String> departments =
    employees.stream()
             .map(Employee::getDepartment)
             .collect(Collectors.toSet());

Use map and toSet() to get unique department names.

Map<String, Double> avgAgeByGender =
    employees.stream()
             .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                 Employee::getGender,
                 Collectors.averagingInt(Employee::getAge)
             ));

Use averagingInt() as downstream of groupingBy().

Employee highestPaid = employees.stream()
    .max(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary))
    .orElseThrow();

Use max() with a salary comparator.

List<String> names = employees.stream()
    .filter(e -> e.getYearOfJoining() > 2015)
    .map(Employee::getName)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

Filter first, then map names, then collect.

Map<String, Long> countByDept =
    employees.stream()
             .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment, Collectors.counting()));

Standard groupingBy + counting use case.

Map<String, Double> avgSalaryByDept =
    employees.stream()
             .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                 Employee::getDepartment,
                 Collectors.averagingDouble(Employee::getSalary)
             ));

Use averagingDouble() to compute average salary per department.

Map<String, Map<String, Long>> count =
    employees.stream()
             .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                 Employee::getDepartment,
                 Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::getGender, Collectors.counting())
             ));

Nested groupingBy gives department-wise gender counts.

Salary and Department Queries

These are the common expert-level grouping and salary questions.

Map<String, Optional<Employee>> highestByDept =
    employees.stream()
             .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                 Employee::getDepartment,
                 Collectors.maxBy(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary))
             ));

Use maxBy() as downstream collector.

Map<String, Employee> secondHighestByDept =
    employees.stream()
             .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                 Employee::getDepartment,
                 Collectors.collectingAndThen(
                     Collectors.toList(),
                     list -> list.stream()
                         .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary).reversed())
                         .skip(1)
                         .findFirst()
                         .orElse(null)
                 )
             ));

Sort within each department and skip the top one to get second highest.

List<Employee> sorted = employees.stream()
    .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getDepartment)
        .thenComparing(Employee::getSalary, Comparator.reverseOrder()))
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

Use chained comparators for department then salary.

int sum = numbers.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum();

mapToInt().sum() is the simplest and fastest answer.

double avg = numbers.stream()
    .map(n -> n * n)
    .filter(n -> n <= 100)
    .mapToInt(Integer::intValue)
    .average()
    .orElse(0);

Chain map, filter, and average().

new Random().ints(5, 1, 100)
    .sorted()
    .forEach(System.out::println);

Use Random.ints(), sort, then print with forEach.

StringJoiner joiner = new StringJoiner(", ", "[", "]");
joiner.add("Java").add("Spring").add("Streams");
String result = joiner.toString();

StringJoiner helps join strings with delimiter, prefix, and suffix.

String result = Stream.of("Java")
    .map(s -> "[ " + s + " ]")
    .findFirst()
    .orElse("");

For multiple strings, use StringJoiner with prefix and suffix.

Stream<String> s1 = Stream.of("A", "B");
Stream<String> s2 = Stream.of("C", "D");
List<String> merged = Stream.concat(s1, s2).collect(Collectors.toList());

Use Stream.concat() to append two streams of the same type.

Map<Boolean, List<Employee>> result =
    employees.stream().collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(Employee::isActive));

It splits a stream into exactly two groups: true and false.

String Problems

Character, word, and StringJoiner-style coding questions.

String s = "swiss";
Character ch = s.chars()
    .mapToObj(c -> (char) c)
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), LinkedHashMap::new, Collectors.counting()))
    .entrySet().stream()
    .filter(e -> e.getValue() == 1)
    .map(Map.Entry::getKey)
    .findFirst()
    .orElse(null);

Use an ordered map and pick the first character whose count is 1.

String s = "programming";
Character repeated = s.chars()
    .mapToObj(c -> (char) c)
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), LinkedHashMap::new, Collectors.counting()))
    .entrySet().stream()
    .filter(e -> e.getValue() > 1)
    .map(Map.Entry::getKey)
    .findFirst()
    .orElse(null);

Count characters in order and return the first one with frequency more than 1.

Map<String, Long> wordCount =
    words.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), Collectors.counting()));

Use groupingBy + counting for word frequencies.

Number Problems

Min, max, second highest, sum, and numeric transformation questions.

int max = numbers.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).max().orElseThrow();
int min = numbers.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).min().orElseThrow();

Use max() and min() on primitive streams.

Integer secondHighest = numbers.stream()
    .distinct()
    .sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder())
    .skip(1)
    .findFirst()
    .orElse(null);

Remove duplicates, sort descending, skip the first, and take the next one.

Employee minSalary = employees.stream()
    .min(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary))
    .orElseThrow();

Employee maxSalary = employees.stream()
    .max(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary))
    .orElseThrow();

Use min() and max() with a salary comparator.

Map<String, Optional<Employee>> maxByDept =
    employees.stream()
             .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                 Employee::getDepartment,
                 Collectors.maxBy(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary))
             ));

Use nested groupingBy with maxBy().

Map<String, List<Employee>> byDept =
    employees.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment));

Group employees by department to list who works where.

Map<String, Long> countByDept =
    employees.stream()
             .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment, Collectors.counting()));

This is the same pattern as department count with counting().

List<Integer> asc = numbers.stream()
    .sorted()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

List<Integer> desc = numbers.stream()
    .sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder())
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

Use sorted() for ascending and Comparator.reverseOrder() for descending.

How to remember it
  • SonarQube finds code issues before production.

  • JaCoCo provides coverage evidence.

Interview-ready answer

"SonarQube is a static analysis platform used to inspect code quality, security, and coverage. I use it with a quality profile, quality gate, and JaCoCo coverage in CI/CD so the build can fail when the code does not meet the team's standards."

Spring Boot is built to reduce Spring configuration. Internally, it starts the application, scans the classpath, applies auto-configuration, creates beans, starts the embedded server, and then runs the app.

Startup flow
  1. main() calls SpringApplication.run().
  2. SpringApplication prepares environment, listeners, and application context.
  3. Classpath scan finds @SpringBootApplication, components, and config classes.
  4. Auto-configuration applies beans based on classpath and properties.
  5. Bean creation and dependency injection happen inside the container.
  6. Embedded server such as Tomcat, Jetty, or Undertow starts if it is a web app.
  7. Application ready event is published and the app begins serving requests.
Key internal pieces
  • @SpringBootApplication: combines @Configuration, @ComponentScan, and @EnableAutoConfiguration.
  • Auto-configuration: creates beans conditionally using classpath, properties, and existing beans.
  • Starters: curated dependency bundles that simplify setup.
  • Embedded server: lets Boot run as a standalone jar without external deployment.
  • Actuator: exposes health, metrics, info, and other operational endpoints.
How auto-configuration works

Spring Boot uses conditional annotations such as @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, and @ConditionalOnProperty to decide what to create. If the needed library exists and no custom bean is already present, Boot wires the default bean. 

@SpringBootApplication
public class DemoApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(DemoApplication.class, args);
    }
}
Real-world example

If you add spring-boot-starter-web, Boot automatically configures Spring MVC, JSON support, an embedded Tomcat server, and common web infrastructure. If you add spring-boot-starter-data-jpa, Boot configures the JPA pieces too.

Why Boot is helpful
  • Less XML and manual configuration.
  • Opinionated defaults that speed up development.
  • Easier packaging and deployment as a self-contained jar.
  • Good support for observability, metrics, and health checks.
What usually happens during startup delays
  • Large component scans.
  • Many auto-configurations on the classpath.
  • Database initialization, schema checks, or cache warm-up.
  • Heavy bean initialization or startup listeners.
Interview-ready answer

"Spring Boot internally starts through SpringApplication, builds the context, applies auto-configuration based on classpath and properties, creates beans, and starts the embedded server. It uses conditional configuration and starters to reduce manual setup, which is why Boot is much faster to build and deploy than plain Spring."

The Spring Bean lifecycle is the order in which Spring creates, configures, initializes, uses, and destroys a bean. A simple way to remember it is: instantiate -> populate -> aware -> post-process -> initialize -> ready -> destroy.

Hierarchy of lifecycle phases
  1. Instantiate: Spring creates the object using constructor or factory method.
  2. Populate properties: Spring injects dependencies and values.
  3. Aware callbacks: Spring gives context like bean name, factory, or application context.
  4. BeanPostProcessor before init: custom hooks run before initialization callbacks.
  5. Initialization: @PostConstruct, afterPropertiesSet(), and custom init methods run.
  6. BeanPostProcessor after init: final post-processing, often used by proxies.
  7. Bean ready for use: application code can now use the bean.
  8. Destroy: @PreDestroy, destroy(), and custom destroy methods run for singleton beans.
What runs at each level
Stage Annotation / Interface / Class hook What it does
Instantiation Constructor, factory method, @Bean Creates the bean object.
Dependency injection @Autowired, @Value Injects dependencies and configuration values.
Aware callbacks BeanNameAware, BeanFactoryAware, ApplicationContextAware Injects container metadata into the bean.
Before initialization BeanPostProcessor#postProcessBeforeInitialization() Runs custom logic before init callbacks.
Initialization @PostConstruct, InitializingBean, custom initMethod Runs setup logic after dependencies are ready.
After initialization BeanPostProcessor#postProcessAfterInitialization() Often used to wrap the bean with AOP proxy logic.
Destruction @PreDestroy, DisposableBean, custom destroyMethod Runs cleanup logic before bean removal.
Simple flow diagram
Constructor
   -> Dependency Injection
   -> Aware interfaces
   -> BeanPostProcessor before init
   -> @PostConstruct / afterPropertiesSet / initMethod
   -> BeanPostProcessor after init
   -> Bean ready
   -> @PreDestroy / destroyMethod
Example bean
@Component
class PaymentService implements BeanNameAware, InitializingBean, DisposableBean {
    @PostConstruct
    public void postConstruct() {
        System.out.println("PostConstruct called");
    }

    @Override
    public void setBeanName(String name) {
        System.out.println("Bean name = " + name);
    }

    @Override
    public void afterPropertiesSet() {
        System.out.println("afterPropertiesSet called");
    }

    @PreDestroy
    public void preDestroy() {
        System.out.println("PreDestroy called");
    }

    @Override
    public void destroy() {
        System.out.println("destroy called");
    }
}

In practice, @PostConstruct is preferred for initialization, and @PreDestroy for cleanup, because they are cleaner than implementing framework interfaces directly. Interfaces like InitializingBean and DisposableBean still work, but they couple the class to Spring.

Important interview points
  • BeanPostProcessor is often where Spring adds proxy behavior.
  • @PreDestroy usually runs only for singleton beans managed by the container.
  • Prototype beans are created by Spring, but Spring does not fully manage their destroy phase.
  • @Bean(initMethod = "...", destroyMethod = "...") lets you define custom lifecycle methods.
Interview-ready answer

"Spring bean lifecycle starts with instantiation, then dependency injection, aware callbacks, init callbacks like @PostConstruct or afterPropertiesSet, then BeanPostProcessor hooks, and finally destruction callbacks like @PreDestroy. Annotations are cleaner, while interfaces like InitializingBean and DisposableBean are framework-coupled alternatives."

Happens-before is a Java Memory Model rule that defines visibility and ordering. If action A happens-before action B, then B is guaranteed to see the effects of A.

Why it matters
  • It prevents stale reads between threads.
  • It gives a clear rule for when one thread can safely rely on another thread's writes.
  • It is the reason volatile, synchronized, and thread start/join work for visibility.
Real-world example
class SharedState {
    private int data;
    private volatile boolean ready;

    public void writer() {
        data = 42;      // write data first
        ready = true;   // volatile write publishes it
    }

    public void reader() {
        if (ready) {    // volatile read creates happens-before edge
            System.out.println(data); // guaranteed to see 42
        }
    }
}

Here, the write to ready happens-before the read of ready, so the reader also sees the earlier write to data.

Common rules
  • Program order: actions in the same thread happen in code order.
  • Monitor lock: unlocking a monitor happens-before a later lock on the same monitor.
  • Volatile: a write to a volatile field happens-before a later read of that field.
  • Thread start/join: starting a thread and joining it also create happens-before edges.
Interview-ready answer

"Happens-before is the Java Memory Model guarantee that one thread's writes become visible to another thread in a predictable order. I use volatile, synchronized blocks, or thread start/join to create the visibility edge and avoid stale data bugs."

The Prototype design pattern is a creational pattern where a new object is created by copying an existing object instead of building it from scratch. In Spring prototype scope, Spring creates a new bean instance every time the bean is requested from the container.

Main difference
  • Prototype pattern: object cloning or copying is part of your domain design.
  • Spring prototype scope: bean lifecycle rule inside the Spring container.
  • Prototype pattern: you control how the copy is made.
  • Spring prototype scope: Spring returns a fresh instance, but it does not manage full destroy lifecycle like singleton beans.
Real-world analogy

Think of a restaurant menu card template. The prototype pattern is like copying an existing menu design and changing only the title. Spring prototype scope is like asking the kitchen for a fresh plate each time you place an order.

Prototype design pattern example
class Employee implements Cloneable {
    private String name;
    private String department;

    public Employee(String name, String department) {
        this.name = name;
        this.department = department;
    }

    @Override
    public Employee clone() {
        try {
            return (Employee) super.clone();
        } catch (CloneNotSupportedException e) {
            throw new RuntimeException(e);
        }
    }
}

Here, the clone is a copy of an existing object, so we reuse the original object structure instead of rebuilding it.

Does it copy data or create an empty object?

Usually it copies the existing object's state, so the new object starts with the same field values as the original. It is not an empty object by default. If the object contains nested objects, the result depends on whether you do a shallow copy or a deep copy.

  • Shallow copy: primitive values are copied, but referenced child objects are shared.
  • Deep copy: both the object and its nested objects are copied.
Employee original = new Employee("Asha", "IT");
Employee copy = original.clone(); // copy has same field values initially

So in interviews, the safe answer is: the Prototype pattern normally gives a copied object with the existing data, not an empty shell, unless the clone logic explicitly resets fields.

Spring prototype scope example
@Component
@Scope(ConfigurableBeanFactory.SCOPE_PROTOTYPE)
class RequestContextHolder {
    private UUID requestId = UUID.randomUUID();
}

Every time Spring injects or looks up this bean, it creates a new RequestContextHolder instance. That is useful for per-request state, temporary helpers, or objects that should not be shared.

Important note in Spring

A prototype bean is created every time it is requested, but Spring does not fully manage its destruction lifecycle the way it does for singleton beans. If the bean needs cleanup, you usually handle that yourself.

Interview-ready answer

"The Prototype design pattern means creating a new object by copying an existing one. Spring prototype scope means the container gives a fresh bean instance every time it is requested. They are related by name, but one is a design pattern and the other is a Spring lifecycle scope."

Shallow copy copies the top-level fields, but nested referenced objects are shared. Deep copy copies the top-level fields as well as all nested objects, so the copy is fully independent.

Simple example
class Address {
    String city;
    Address(String city) { this.city = city; }
}

class Employee {
    String name;
    Address address;

    Employee(String name, Address address) {
        this.name = name;
        this.address = address;
    }

    Employee shallowCopy() {
        return new Employee(this.name, this.address);
    }

    Employee deepCopy() {
        return new Employee(this.name, new Address(this.address.city));
    }
}

If you change address.city in the shallow copy, the original object also changes because both objects point to the same Address. In the deep copy, the original stays unchanged.

Real-world analogy
  • Shallow copy: photocopying a form but sharing the same attached folder.
  • Deep copy: photocopying the form and making a separate copy of the folder too.
Best way
  • Best overall: prefer immutable objects when possible, because then copying is usually unnecessary.
  • Use shallow copy: when nested objects are immutable or shared state is acceptable.
  • Use deep copy: when nested objects are mutable and changes must not affect the original.
  • In interviews: say that deep copy is safer for independent state, but immutability is often the cleanest design.
Interview-ready answer

"Shallow copy duplicates the outer object but shares nested references, while deep copy duplicates the nested objects too. The best approach is usually immutability if possible; otherwise use shallow copy for shared immutable data and deep copy when you need full independence."

CountDownLatch is a synchronization aid that lets one or more threads wait until a set of operations in other threads finishes. Think of it like a countdown gate: when the count reaches zero, waiting threads are released.

How it works
  • You create the latch with an initial count, for example new CountDownLatch(3).
  • Each worker thread calls countDown() when it finishes its task.
  • The waiting thread calls await() and blocks until the count becomes zero.
  • Once the count hits zero, all waiting threads continue.
Real-world example

Suppose a dashboard needs data from Orders, Payments, and Inventory services before rendering the page. We can start all three requests in parallel, and the UI aggregator waits until all responses arrive or a timeout happens. 

CountDownLatch latch = new CountDownLatch(3);
ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3);

executor.submit(() -> {
    try {
        loadOrders();
    } finally {
        latch.countDown();
    }
});

executor.submit(() -> {
    try {
        loadPayments();
    } finally {
        latch.countDown();
    }
});

executor.submit(() -> {
    try {
        loadInventory();
    } finally {
        latch.countDown();
    }
});

latch.await(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // wait until all three finish or timeout

In a backend system, the same pattern is useful for waiting until several startup checks finish, or for running parallel integration test steps and continuing only when all are ready.

Important methods
Method Purpose
CountDownLatch(int count) Creates the latch with the initial count.
await() Waits until the count reaches zero.
await(long timeout, TimeUnit unit) Waits up to a timeout instead of blocking forever.
countDown() Decreases the count by one.
getCount() Returns the current count value for monitoring or debugging.
Where it is commonly used
  • Waiting for multiple service calls in parallel.
  • Coordinating startup checks or warm-up tasks.
  • Test cases that must wait for a background operation to finish.
  • One-time synchronization where a group of workers must finish before continuing.
Interview-ready answer

"CountDownLatch is used when one or more threads need to wait until a fixed number of other tasks finish. Each task calls countDown when done, and the waiting thread calls await. I often use it for parallel service aggregation, startup coordination, and test synchronization."

CyclicBarrier is a synchronization aid that makes a fixed number of threads wait until all of them reach the same barrier point. Once the last thread arrives, all waiting threads are released together, and the barrier can be reused again in the next phase.

How it works
  • You create it with a number of parties, for example new CyclicBarrier(3).
  • Each thread calls await() when it reaches the checkpoint.
  • When the last thread arrives, the barrier opens and all threads continue.
  • It is reusable, so the same barrier can be used again for the next round.
Real-world example

Imagine three services in a batch analytics pipeline: Order Loader, Payment Loader, and Inventory Loader. Each service fetches data in parallel, but the aggregation phase should begin only after all three finish the current step. CyclicBarrier is a good fit because the workers can meet at the same checkpoint repeatedly for each batch. 

CyclicBarrier barrier = new CyclicBarrier(3, () ->
        System.out.println("All services reached the checkpoint, starting aggregation"));

ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3);

executor.submit(() -> {
    loadOrders();
    barrier.await();
    aggregateOrders();
});

executor.submit(() -> {
    loadPayments();
    barrier.await();
    aggregatePayments();
});

executor.submit(() -> {
    loadInventory();
    barrier.await();
    aggregateInventory();
});

In real systems, this is useful for phased batch jobs, parallel simulations, or workflows where a set of threads must synchronize at repeated checkpoints.

Important methods
Method Purpose
CyclicBarrier(int parties) Creates a barrier for the given number of threads.
CyclicBarrier(int parties, Runnable barrierAction) Runs a task once the last thread arrives at the barrier.
await() Waits until all parties arrive.
await(long timeout, TimeUnit unit) Waits with a timeout instead of blocking forever.
getNumberWaiting() Returns how many threads are waiting at the barrier.
getParties() Returns the total number of parties required to trip the barrier.
isBroken() Checks whether the barrier is broken because of timeout, interruption, or failure.
reset() Resets the barrier so it can be reused after failure or for a fresh cycle.
CountDownLatch vs CyclicBarrier
  • CountDownLatch: one-time waiting for others to finish.
  • CyclicBarrier: repeated waiting at a checkpoint, then reuse for the next phase.
Interview-ready answer

"CyclicBarrier is used when a fixed number of threads need to meet at a checkpoint before continuing, and the same barrier may be reused again for the next phase. I use CountDownLatch when one or more threads wait for tasks to finish, and CyclicBarrier when the workers must synchronize with each other."

Phaser is a flexible synchronization aid that works like a reusable barrier, but with dynamic registration and multiple phases. It is useful when the number of participating threads can change over time and the same workflow has several checkpoints.

How it works
  • Threads can register and deregister dynamically.
  • Each phase ends when all registered parties arrive.
  • The phaser advances to the next phase and can be reused repeatedly.
  • It is more flexible than CyclicBarrier when the participant count changes.
Real-world example

Imagine a multi-step data pipeline for a banking batch job. Step 1 loads customers, step 2 loads accounts, and step 3 loads transactions. Some partitions may be skipped if there is no data, and new worker threads may join dynamically for extra shards. A Phaser lets all active workers finish each phase before the next phase starts. 

Phaser phaser = new Phaser(1); // main thread registers itself

phaser.register(); // customer loader
executor.submit(() -> {
    loadCustomers();
    phaser.arriveAndDeregister();
});

phaser.register(); // account loader
executor.submit(() -> {
    loadAccounts();
    phaser.arriveAndDeregister();
});

phaser.register(); // transaction loader
executor.submit(() -> {
    loadTransactions();
    phaser.arriveAndDeregister();
});

phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance(); // wait for phase 0 to finish
processPhaseTwo();

phaser.arriveAndDeregister(); // main thread done

In real systems, Phaser is a strong fit for batch processing, simulations, recursive task splitting, or workflows where workers join and leave dynamically across phases.

Important methods
Method Purpose
Phaser() / Phaser(int parties) Creates a phaser with optional initial registered parties.
register() Registers a new party dynamically.
bulkRegister(int parties) Registers multiple parties at once.
arrive() Signals arrival at the current phase without waiting.
arriveAndAwaitAdvance() Signals arrival and waits for all parties to reach the phase.
arriveAndDeregister() Signals arrival and removes the party from future phases.
getPhase() Returns the current phase number.
getRegisteredParties() Returns how many parties are currently registered.
getArrivedParties() Returns how many registered parties have already arrived.
getUnarrivedParties() Returns how many parties are still expected for the current phase.
isTerminated() Checks whether the phaser has terminated.
forceTermination() Forces the phaser to terminate immediately.
Phaser vs CyclicBarrier vs CountDownLatch
  • CountDownLatch: one-time waiting for tasks to finish.
  • CyclicBarrier: reusable fixed-party checkpoint.
  • Phaser: reusable checkpoint with dynamic registration and multiple phases.
Interview-ready answer

"Phaser is a reusable synchronization aid for phased workflows where threads may join or leave dynamically. I use CountDownLatch for one-time waiting, CyclicBarrier for fixed-party checkpoints, and Phaser when the number of participants can change across multiple phases."

Semaphore is a concurrency control tool that limits how many threads can access a shared resource at the same time. You can think of it like a parking gate with a fixed number of available spots.

How it works
  • It is created with a number of permits, for example new Semaphore(3).
  • A thread calls acquire() to take a permit before using the resource.
  • When the thread is done, it calls release() to return the permit.
  • If no permits are available, other threads block or time out until one becomes free.
Real-world example

Suppose a payment gateway can safely process only 5 checkout requests at a time because the downstream third-party provider has a strict concurrency limit. A Semaphore can enforce that limit so extra requests wait instead of overwhelming the provider. 

private final Semaphore semaphore = new Semaphore(5);

public PaymentResponse processPayment(PaymentRequest request) throws InterruptedException {
    semaphore.acquire();
    try {
        return callExternalPaymentGateway(request);
    } finally {
        semaphore.release();
    }
}

In a backend system, Semaphore is also useful for limiting access to a database connection pool, protecting a rate-limited external API, or controlling how many batch jobs run in parallel.

Important methods
Method Purpose
Semaphore(int permits) Creates a semaphore with the given number of permits.
acquire() Blocks until a permit is available, then takes one.
acquire(int permits) Acquires multiple permits at once.
tryAcquire() Tries to take a permit immediately without blocking.
tryAcquire(long timeout, TimeUnit unit) Waits up to a timeout for a permit.
release() Returns one permit to the semaphore.
release(int permits) Returns multiple permits to the semaphore.
availablePermits() Shows how many permits are currently free.
drainPermits() Takes away all currently available permits.
hasQueuedThreads() Checks whether threads are waiting.
getQueueLength() Returns an estimate of the number of waiting threads.
isFair() Indicates whether the semaphore uses fair ordering.
Fair vs non-fair
  • Fair semaphore: grants permits roughly in FIFO order, which is more predictable.
  • Non-fair semaphore: can be faster but may let some threads barge ahead.
Interview-ready answer

"Semaphore is used to limit concurrent access to a shared resource by controlling permits. I use it to protect rate-limited APIs, cap batch job concurrency, or control access to scarce resources like a connection pool. Threads call acquire before the work and release after they finish."

The easiest way to remember them is by the job they do:

  • CountDownLatch: one-way countdown, wait until others finish.
  • CyclicBarrier: meeting point, all threads wait for each other at a checkpoint.
  • Phaser: reusable meeting point across multiple phases, with dynamic thread registration.
  • Semaphore: permit counter, limit how many threads can access something at once.
Quick comparison
Utility Main idea Reusable? Typical use
CountDownLatch Wait for a fixed number of completions No Wait for parallel tasks, startup checks, tests
CyclicBarrier All threads meet at a checkpoint Yes Parallel batch steps, simulations, phased work
Phaser Checkpoint per phase with dynamic parties Yes Multi-phase workflows, dynamic thread counts
Semaphore Limit concurrent access with permits Yes Rate limiting, pool protection, bounded concurrency
Easy memory trick
  • Latch = wait: count down until zero, then move.
  • Barrier = meet: everyone meets at the barrier together.
  • Phaser = stage: multiple stages or phases, dynamic parties.
  • Semaphore = seats: only a fixed number of threads get a seat.
Real-world analogy
  • CountDownLatch: waiting for 3 delivery trucks before opening the warehouse.
  • CyclicBarrier: a team standup where everyone starts the next task only after all arrive.
  • Phaser: a multi-round tournament where new players can join and leave between rounds.
  • Semaphore: 5 seats in a restaurant, so only 5 customers can sit at once.
Interview-ready answer

"I remember them as CountDownLatch = wait, CyclicBarrier = meet, Phaser = meet across phases, and Semaphore = limit permits. CountDownLatch is one-time, CyclicBarrier and Phaser are reusable, and Semaphore controls concurrency rather than synchronization at a checkpoint."

A simple approach is to share one counter and one lock. Two threads handle odd and even numbers, and the third thread can act as a coordinator or a third worker in the exercise.

Simple idea
  • One shared counter decides what should print next.
  • The odd thread prints only when the counter is odd.
  • The even thread prints only when the counter is even.
  • The third thread can coordinate the turns or print a label/sequence marker.
Very small example
class Printer {
    private int num = 1;
    private final int max = 10;
    private final Object lock = new Object();

    public void printOdd() {
        while (num <= max) {
            synchronized (lock) {
                if (num % 2 == 1) {
                    System.out.println("Odd: " + num++);
                    lock.notifyAll();
                } else {
                    try { lock.wait(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
                }
            }
        }
    }

    public void printEven() {
        while (num <= max) {
            synchronized (lock) {
                if (num % 2 == 0) {
                    System.out.println("Even: " + num++);
                    lock.notifyAll();
                } else {
                    try { lock.wait(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

If you want a strict 3-thread version, the third thread can be a coordinator that starts the sequence and waits for both workers to finish.

Interview-ready answer

"I would use one shared counter, one lock, and wait/notify coordination so the odd and even threads print only when it is their turn. A third thread can be used as a coordinator or a separate worker in the exercise."

The simplest approach is to share one counter and use a lock so threads take turns printing the next number. You can do this with 2 threads or 3 threads depending on the interview setup.

Simple idea
  • One shared counter starts at 1.
  • Each thread checks whether it is allowed to print the current number.
  • After printing, it increments the counter and wakes other threads.
  • Use wait() and notifyAll() to hand over the turn.
Example with 2 threads
class NumberPrinter {
    private int num = 1;
    private final int max = 10;
    private final Object lock = new Object();

    public void printNumbers() {
        while (num <= max) {
            synchronized (lock) {
                System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " -> " + num++);
                lock.notifyAll();
                if (num <= max) {
                    try { lock.wait(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
Example with 3 threads

A third thread can be a coordinator or just another worker that also prints the next available number when it gets the lock. The logic stays the same: one shared counter, one lock, and turn-based printing. 

Runnable task = () -> {
    while (true) {
        synchronized (lock) {
            if (num > 10) return;
            System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " -> " + num++);
            lock.notifyAll();
            try { if (num <= 10) lock.wait(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        }
    }
};
Where this is used
  • Interview problems about thread coordination.
  • Ordered output tasks.
  • Learning wait(), notify(), and notifyAll().
Interview-ready answer

"I would use one shared counter and a lock so the threads print numbers in order. Each thread waits for its turn, prints the next number, increments the counter, and notifies the others. The same pattern can work with 2 or 3 threads."

The simplest approach is to share one counter and use a lock so threads take turns printing the next number. You can do this with 2 threads or 3 threads depending on the interview setup.

Simple idea
  • One shared counter starts at 1.
  • Each thread checks whether it is allowed to print the current number.
  • After printing, it increments the counter and wakes other threads.
  • Use wait() and notifyAll() to hand over the turn.
Example with 2 threads
class NumberPrinter {
    private int num = 1;
    private final int max = 10;
    private final Object lock = new Object();

    public void printNumbers() {
        while (num <= max) {
            synchronized (lock) {
                System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " -> " + num++);
                lock.notifyAll();
                if (num <= max) {
                    try { lock.wait(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
Example with 3 threads

A third thread can be a coordinator or just another worker that also prints the next available number when it gets the lock. The logic stays the same: one shared counter, one lock, and turn-based printing. 

Runnable task = () -> {
    while (true) {
        synchronized (lock) {
            if (num > 10) return;
            System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " -> " + num++);
            lock.notifyAll();

        }

};
Where this is used
  • Interview problems about thread coordination.
  • Ordered output tasks.
  • Learning wait(), notify(), and notifyAll().
Interview-ready answer

"I would use one shared counter and a lock so the threads print numbers in order. Each thread waits for its turn, prints the next number, increments the counter, and notifies the others. The same pattern can work with 2 or 3 threads."

The Thread class gives you the basic life-cycle and control methods for running work in a separate thread. In interviews, the important part is knowing what each method does and when to use it safely.

Most important methods
Method Difference / purpose When to use
start() Creates a new thread and calls run() on that new thread. Use when you want actual concurrent execution.
run() Just a normal method unless called by start(). Override it to define thread work, but do not call it directly for concurrency.
sleep(ms) Pauses the current thread for a fixed time. Use for delay, backoff, or test waiting; it does not release locks.
join() Makes one thread wait for another thread to finish. Use when a parent thread needs a child thread to complete first.
interrupt() Requests a thread to stop waiting/blocking cooperatively. Use for cancellation or shutdown signals.
isInterrupted() Checks whether a thread has been interrupted without clearing the flag. Use when you want to inspect interruption state.
interrupted() Static method that checks and clears the interrupt flag of the current thread. Use carefully when handling interrupt status in loops or cleanup code.
yield() Hint to the scheduler that the current thread can pause briefly. Rarely needed in production; mostly for low-level coordination experiments.
currentThread() Returns the currently executing thread. Use for logging, interruption checks, or debugging.
setName() / getName() Sets or reads the thread name. Use for debugging and readable logs.
setPriority() / getPriority() Changes the priority hint given to the scheduler. Usually avoid relying on priority for business logic.
setDaemon() / isDaemon() Marks a thread as a background daemon thread. Use for background tasks that should not keep the JVM alive.
