isAlive() Checks whether a thread has started and has not yet terminated. Use for basic state checks, not for synchronization.
getState() Returns the current thread state like NEW, RUNNABLE, or WAITING. Use for diagnostics, thread dumps, and monitoring.
setUncaughtExceptionHandler() / getUncaughtExceptionHandler() Handles uncaught exceptions from a thread. Use to log or react to unexpected thread failures.
getId() Returns the thread identifier. Use for logging and troubleshooting.
getStackTrace() Returns the current stack trace of the thread. Use for debugging or diagnostics.
Important differences to remember
  • start() creates concurrency, run() does not.
  • sleep() pauses the current thread, but it does not release locks.
  • join() makes another thread wait for completion.
  • interrupt() is cooperative cancellation, not forced termination.
  • isInterrupted() checks the flag, while interrupted() also clears it.
Deprecated methods to avoid
  • stop() is unsafe because it can leave objects in inconsistent state.
  • suspend() and resume() are deprecated because they can cause deadlock.
Real-world example

In a background batch job, I would use start() to launch workers, join() to wait for them to finish, interrupt() to cancel them during shutdown, and setName() so logs clearly show which worker failed.

Easy memory trick
  • start = begin a new thread
  • run = the task body
  • sleep = pause self
  • join = wait for another thread
  • interrupt = ask politely to stop
  • name / priority / daemon = thread metadata
Interview-ready answer

"The most important Thread methods are start, run, sleep, join, interrupt, isInterrupted, currentThread, setName, setPriority, setDaemon, isAlive, and getState. I use start for concurrency, join for waiting, sleep for delay, interrupt for cooperative cancellation, and getState or setName mainly for diagnostics."

In Java, only a nested class can be static. A static nested class belongs to the outer class itself, not to any one instance of the outer class.

Main benefit
  • It does not need an outer class object to be created.
  • It does not keep an implicit reference to the outer class instance.
  • It uses less memory than a normal inner class because it is not tied to the outer object.
  • It improves clarity when the helper type logically belongs to the outer class but does not need its instance state.
Example
class Outer {
    static class Inner {
        void show() {
            System.out.println("Hello from static nested class");
        }
    }
}

Outer.Inner obj = new Outer.Inner();
obj.show();
When to use it
  • Builder classes inside an outer class.
  • Helper or DTO classes that are logically grouped with the outer class.
  • Utility code that does not need access to instance fields of the outer class.
  • When you want to avoid the memory overhead of holding an outer instance reference.
Static nested class vs inner class
Type Needs outer object? Key point
Static nested class No Independent helper, no outer instance reference.
Inner class Yes Automatically tied to the outer class object.
Real-world example

In builder patterns or config holder classes, a static nested class is useful because it keeps the related code grouped together without forcing the outer class object to exist.

Interview-ready answer

"A static nested class is used when the helper type belongs to the outer class logically but does not need the outer instance. It saves memory, avoids an implicit outer reference, and is useful for builders, DTO helpers, and utility-style nested classes."

Cache eviction is the process of removing entries from cache when memory is limited, data becomes stale, or the cache needs space for hotter items. Without eviction, the cache can grow forever and hurt performance or even cause outages.

Why eviction is needed
  • Cache memory is finite.
  • Older data may no longer be useful.
  • We want the cache to keep the most valuable keys.
  • Eviction prevents stale or low-value entries from wasting space.
Common eviction policies
Policy How it works Best use case
LRU Least Recently Used entries are removed first. General-purpose caches where recent data is likely to be reused.
LFU Least Frequently Used entries are removed first. Hot-key workloads where frequently accessed data should stay longer.
FIFO First In, First Out removes the oldest inserted entry. Simple caches where recency or frequency is not very important.
MRU Most Recently Used entries are removed first. Rare cases where the newest items are least likely to be reused.
TTL / time-based expiry Entries expire after a fixed time. Rates, tokens, sessions, config data, or any data that must refresh periodically.
Size-based eviction Evict when cache reaches max item count or memory limit. Protect memory in local caches like Caffeine or in-memory maps.
Real-world examples
  • Product detail cache: LRU is a good fit because the most recently viewed products are often requested again.
  • API rate-limit counters: TTL expiry works well because the count should reset after the window.
  • Currency exchange rates: short TTL or refresh-ahead prevents stale values.
  • Session cache: TTL is essential because sessions must expire naturally.
  • Hot analytics dashboard: LFU can help keep the most frequently queried metrics in cache.
Spring / Caffeine example
@Bean
public Cache<String, ProductDto> productCache() {
    return Caffeine.newBuilder()
            .maximumSize(10_000)
            .expireAfterWrite(Duration.ofMinutes(10))
            .recordStats()
            .build();
}

In Redis, a similar idea is usually implemented with TTL plus a maxmemory policy such as allkeys-lru or volatile-ttl. That way Redis decides which keys to evict when memory pressure rises.

Practical rule of thumb

If you want a simple and effective default, use LRU with TTL. If access frequency matters a lot, use LFU. If freshness is the main concern, use TTL-based expiry. For local application caches in Spring Boot, Caffeine is often a strong choice; for distributed shared caches, Redis eviction policies matter more.

Interview-ready answer

"Cache eviction is how we remove entries when the cache is full or data becomes stale. The common policies are LRU, LFU, FIFO, MRU, TTL-based expiry, and size-based eviction. I usually pick LRU plus TTL for general use, LFU for hot-key workloads, and short TTL for session or rate-limit data."

Deadlock happens when two threads wait on each other forever. A classic case is Thread-1 holding lockA and waiting for lockB, while Thread-2 holds lockB and waits for lockA.

How to identify it from a thread dump

Take a thread dump with jstack <pid> or by capturing a JVM dump from your tooling. In the dump, look for:

  • Threads stuck in BLOCKED state.
  • Lines saying waiting to lock or parking to wait for.
  • A cycle where Thread-1 owns one monitor and waits for another, while Thread-2 owns the second and waits for the first.
"Thread-1" BLOCKED
  waiting to lock monitor 0x00000001 (object A)
  owned by "Thread-2"

"Thread-2" BLOCKED
  waiting to lock monitor 0x00000002 (object B)
  owned by "Thread-1"

That lock cycle is the root cause. The important interview move is not just "there is deadlock", but "which locks are involved and in what order are they acquired?".

Example of the bug
class TransferService {
    private final Object lockA = new Object();
    private final Object lockB = new Object();

    void transferAB() {
        synchronized (lockA) {
            synchronized (lockB) {
                // do work
            }
        }
    }

    void transferBA() {
        synchronized (lockB) {
            synchronized (lockA) {
                // do work
            }
        }
    }
}

If one thread enters transferAB() and another enters transferBA(), they can deadlock because the lock order is inconsistent.

How to rewrite it

Use one of these fixes:

  • Always acquire locks in the same global order.
  • Use tryLock() with timeout and back off if the second lock is not available.
  • Reduce nested locking by using a single lock or a higher-level concurrent structure.
  • Prefer immutable data or lock-free/atomic designs where possible.
class TransferService {
    private final Object lockA = new Object();
    private final Object lockB = new Object();

    void transfer(Object first, Object second) {
        Object lock1 = first == lockA ? lockA : lockB;
        Object lock2 = first == lockA ? lockB : lockA;

        synchronized (lock1) {
            synchronized (lock2) {
                // do work with consistent lock ordering
            }
        }
    }
}

A better production fix is often to avoid nested locks entirely or move the update into a single atomic operation if the data structure supports it.

Interview-ready answer

"I would confirm the deadlock from a thread dump using jstack or a similar dump tool, find the two threads and the two monitors they are waiting on, and then fix the code by enforcing a single lock ordering, using tryLock with timeout, or removing the nested locking altogether."

2PC → strong consistency; slow, blocking. Saga → sequence of local transactions + compensating transactions. Used in payments, booking systems.

JVM internals means understanding how Java code is loaded, stored in memory, executed, and cleaned up. In interviews, a strong answer usually covers: class loading, runtime memory areas, execution engine, garbage collection, JIT compilation, JNI, and the full execution flow.

1. Big picture flow
.java source
   ↓
javac compiler
   ↓
.class bytecode
   ↓
Class Loader Subsystem
   ↓
Runtime Data Areas (Heap, Stack, Metaspace, PC Register, Native Stack)
   ↓
Execution Engine (Interpreter + JIT)
   ↓
Native Method Interface / Native Libraries if needed
   ↓
Program runs
   ↓
Garbage Collector cleans unused objects
2. What is JVM?

JVM stands for Java Virtual Machine. It is the runtime engine that executes Java bytecode. Because JVM exists on many operating systems, Java gets its “write once, run anywhere” behavior.

Real-world analogy: JVM is like a universal machine that understands Java bytecode and runs it correctly on Windows, Linux, or Mac.

3. Class Loader Subsystem

Class Loader loads .class files into memory when they are needed. 

Main steps:
1. Loading
2. Linking
   - Verification
   - Preparation
   - Resolution
3. Initialization
  • Loading: reads class bytecode into memory.
  • Verification: checks bytecode safety and format.
  • Preparation: allocates memory for static fields and default values.
  • Resolution: converts symbolic references into direct references.
  • Initialization: runs static blocks and assigns actual static values.

Real-world example: When Spring Boot starts, JVM loads your main class, controllers, services, entities, and framework classes as needed.

4. Types of class loaders
  • Bootstrap ClassLoader: loads core Java classes like java.lang, java.util.
  • Platform / Extension ClassLoader: loads platform-level libraries.
  • Application ClassLoader: loads your application classes from classpath.

Real-world analogy: Bootstrap is like the main foundation team, and Application ClassLoader loads your project code on top of that.

5. Runtime Data Areas inside JVM

JVM uses different memory areas for different responsibilities.

6. Heap Memory

Heap stores objects and instance data. It is shared by all threads.

  • Most objects created with new go to heap.
  • Garbage Collector mainly works here.
  • It is generally divided into Young Generation and Old Generation.
User user = new User(); // object typically goes into heap

Real-world analogy: Heap is like a common warehouse where application objects are stored.

7. Stack Memory

Each thread has its own JVM stack. It stores method call frames, local variables, partial results, and references. 

public int add(int a, int b) {
    int sum = a + b;
    return sum;
}

Here a, b, and sum are inside the current stack frame. If recursion is too deep, it can cause StackOverflowError.

8. Method Area / Metaspace

This area stores class metadata like class structure, method metadata, field metadata, static variable information, and runtime constant pool details.

  • In older JVM explanations, people say Method Area.
  • In modern HotSpot JVM, class metadata is mainly stored in Metaspace.

Real-world analogy: If heap is a warehouse for objects, Metaspace is the blueprint room that stores class designs.

9. Program Counter (PC) Register

Each thread has its own PC Register. It stores the address of the current JVM instruction being executed.

Simple meaning: It tells the JVM which instruction to execute next for that thread.

10. Native Method Stack

This is used when Java code calls native methods written in C/C++ or platform code.

Example: Some low-level JVM or OS interaction uses native code.

11. Execution Engine

After bytecode is loaded, the Execution Engine runs it.

  • Interpreter: reads bytecode line by line and executes it.
  • JIT Compiler: converts frequently used bytecode into native machine code for speed.
  • Garbage Collector: frees unused heap memory.
12. Interpreter vs JIT
Part How it works Benefit
Interpreter Executes bytecode instruction by instruction Fast startup
JIT Compiler Compiles hot code into native machine code Better runtime performance

Real-world example: A method called thousands of times in a payment API becomes “hot”, so JIT compiles it for faster execution.

13. Runtime Constant Pool

This is a per-class runtime structure that stores constants, string literals, symbolic references, and method/field references.

Simple meaning: It helps JVM resolve class, method, and field references while executing code.

14. Garbage Collector role

GC removes objects from heap when they are no longer reachable.

  • Young generation collections are usually fast.
  • Old generation collection is heavier.
  • Collectors like G1, ZGC, Shenandoah handle memory differently.

Real-world example: In a Spring Boot API, request DTOs, response objects, and temporary lists are created continuously and later cleaned by GC.

15. JNI and Native Libraries

JNI means Java Native Interface. It allows Java code to talk to native libraries written in C/C++.

Real-world example: Some high-performance drivers, OS integrations, or image processing libraries may use native code.

16. How method execution actually happens
public class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int result = add(10, 20);
        System.out.println(result);
    }

    static int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }
}
Flow:
1. JVM starts and loads Demo class
2. main method is called
3. main frame is created in stack
4. add() is called, so a new stack frame is created
5. values a and b are used, result is computed
6. frame returns result to main
7. object creation, if any, would happen in heap
8. unused objects later become GC candidates
17. Common JVM errors connected to internals
Error Reason
OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space Heap is full
StackOverflowError Too many nested method calls / recursion
OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace Too much class metadata loaded
NoClassDefFoundError / ClassNotFoundException Class loading issue
18. JVM Internals one simple diagram
                +----------------------+
                |   Class Loaders      |
                +----------+-----------+
                           |
                           v
                +----------------------+
                |  Runtime Data Areas  |
                |  Heap                |
                |  Stack               |
                |  Metaspace           |
                |  PC Register         |
                |  Native Method Stack |
                +----------+-----------+
                           |
                           v
                +----------------------+
                |   Execution Engine   |
                | Interpreter + JIT    |
                | GC                   |
                +----------+-----------+
                           |
                           v
                +----------------------+
                | JNI / Native Libs    |
                +----------------------+
19. Real-world interview answer

JVM first loads class bytecode using class loaders, stores class metadata in Metaspace, creates objects in heap, uses per-thread stacks for method execution, tracks current instruction using PC Register, and executes bytecode through interpreter and JIT compiler. Garbage Collector cleans unreachable heap objects, and JNI is used when Java interacts with native code.

20. Short one-liner

JVM Internals means understanding how Java classes are loaded, how memory is organized, how bytecode is executed, and how memory is cleaned automatically.

When a Java app becomes slow and memory grows over time, I first confirm whether the problem is a real leak or just high temporary allocation. Then I capture a heap dump and inspect what is retaining the objects.

How I analyze the heap dump
  • Take a heap dump with jmap, JDK tools, or your APM when memory is high.
  • Open it in Eclipse MAT, VisualVM, YourKit, or similar tooling.
  • Sort by retained size to find the objects holding the most memory alive.
  • Use the Dominator Tree to find the root object that keeps a large object graph reachable.
  • Check Path to GC Roots to understand why the objects cannot be collected.
Static collection leak pattern
public class CacheHolder {
    private static final Map<String, byte[]> CACHE = new HashMap<>();

    public static void put(String key, byte[] data) {
        CACHE.put(key, data);
    }
}

Because the collection is static, it lives as long as the class loader lives. If entries are never removed, the heap keeps growing. In a heap dump, MAT will often show the static map as the dominator retaining many large arrays or domain objects.

ThreadLocal leak pattern
private static final ThreadLocal<byte[]> BUFFER = new ThreadLocal<>();

public void handleRequest() {
    BUFFER.set(new byte[10 * 1024 * 1024]);
    try {
        // work
    } finally {
        BUFFER.remove();
    }
}

If remove() is forgotten in thread pools, the worker thread keeps the ThreadLocal value attached to the thread for a long time. The value may stay reachable even after the request is done.

What I look for in the dump
  • Large collections retained by a static field.
  • ThreadLocalMap entries whose keys are cleared but values remain reachable through pooled threads.
  • Repeated class-loader related retention if the app is redeployed often.
  • Large retained graphs from caches, listeners, or session maps that never evict data.
How I fix it
  • Add proper eviction, TTL, or size limits to caches.
  • Call ThreadLocal.remove() in a finally block or use request filters/interceptors to clean up.
  • Replace static accumulation with bounded caches or weak references when appropriate.
  • Verify the fix by repeating the same workload and comparing heap usage and retained size.
Interview-ready answer

"I would take a heap dump, use MAT to sort by retained size, inspect the dominator tree and GC roots, and then trace the retention path. Static collections usually appear as long-lived roots, while ThreadLocal leaks show up when pooled threads keep values because remove() was not called."

I choose G1 GC for most enterprise applications because it gives a good balance of throughput and predictable pauses. I choose ZGC when ultra-low pause times matter more than raw throughput, especially for large heaps and latency-sensitive services.

When to choose G1
  • General Spring Boot and enterprise services.
  • Need predictable but not extreme pause times.
  • Want a mature default collector with strong tuning support.
When to choose ZGC
  • Very large heaps.
  • Latency-sensitive services where long pauses are unacceptable.
  • Systems that care more about very short pauses than maximum throughput.
What happens during Stop-the-World

A Stop-the-World pause means the JVM temporarily pauses application threads so the GC can perform certain work safely. During this pause, worker threads stop running Java code while the GC marks, scans, updates references, or compacts memory depending on the collector and phase.

  • Threads are suspended at a safepoint.
  • GC may scan roots, mark live objects, and update references.
  • Some collectors also compact or evacuate objects to reduce fragmentation.
Practical difference

G1 still has small Stop-the-World phases, but it tries to keep them predictable. ZGC is designed to keep those pauses extremely short by doing much of the work concurrently with application threads.

Real-world example

For an order-management Spring Boot API with normal traffic, G1 is usually the safe default. For a trading or low-latency service where a long GC pause can break SLAs, ZGC is often the better choice if the JDK version and support fit the environment.

Interview-ready answer

"I choose G1 for balanced general-purpose enterprise workloads and ZGC when ultra-low pause times are the priority. Stop-the-World means the JVM pauses application threads at a safepoint so GC can safely mark, scan, and sometimes compact memory."

📌 Problem
Implement a simple in-memory rate limiter for N requests per second.
💡 Approach
  • Token bucket: refill tokens at fixed rate, consume per request

public class TokenBucket {

    private final int capacity;
    private final int refillPerSecond;
    private double tokens;
    private long lastRefillTimestamp;

    public TokenBucket(int capacity, int refillPerSecond) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.refillPerSecond = refillPerSecond;
        this.tokens = capacity;
        this.lastRefillTimestamp = System.nanoTime();
    }

    public synchronized boolean allowRequest() {
        refill();
        if (tokens >= 1) {
            tokens -= 1;
            return true;
        }
        return false;
    }

    private void refill() {
        long now = System.nanoTime();
        double seconds = (now - lastRefillTimestamp) / 1_000_000_000.0;
        double add = seconds * refillPerSecond;
        if (add > 0) {
            tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + add);
            lastRefillTimestamp = now;
        }
    }
}

📌 Problem
Implement producer-consumer using a bounded LinkedBlockingQueue. 
import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue;

public class ProducerConsumerDemo {

    private final BlockingQueue<Integer> queue = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(10);

    class Producer implements Runnable {
        @Override
        public void run() {
            int i = 0;
            try {
                while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
                    queue.put(i); // blocks when queue is full
                    System.out.println("Produced " + i);
                    i++;
                }
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            }
        }
    }

    class Consumer implements Runnable {
        @Override
        public void run() {
            try {
                while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
                    Integer val = queue.take(); // blocks when queue is empty
                    System.out.println("Consumed " + val);
                }
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            }
        }
    }
}

This is the preferred production solution because the queue handles locking, waiting, signaling, and capacity control for us. The bounded size prevents unbounded memory growth.

🔁 Follow-up: low-level wait/notifyAll version
import java.util.LinkedList;
import java.util.Queue;

public class ProducerConsumerWaitNotify {

    private final Queue<Integer> queue = new LinkedList<>();
    private final int capacity = 10;

    public void produce(int value) throws InterruptedException {
        synchronized (queue) {
            while (queue.size() == capacity) {
                queue.wait();
            }
            queue.offer(value);
            System.out.println("Produced " + value);
            queue.notifyAll();
        }
    }

    public int consume() throws InterruptedException {
        synchronized (queue) {
            while (queue.isEmpty()) {
                queue.wait();
            }
            int value = queue.poll();
            System.out.println("Consumed " + value);
            queue.notifyAll();
            return value;
        }
    }
}

In the low-level version, the shared queue object acts as the monitor. Producers wait when the queue is full, consumers wait when it is empty, and notifyAll() wakes waiting threads after every state change.

JMM defines how threads interact with memory: ✔ Happens-before relationships ✔ Visibility rules ✔ volatile guarantees ✔ atomicity vs non-atomic operations

volatile → guarantees visibility & ordering, NOT atomicity. i++ is not atomic even if variable is volatile. Use AtomicInteger for atomic operations.

Double-checked locking reduces synchronization overhead by checking the instance twice: once before locking and once after locking. The instance field must be volatile so all threads see the correctly initialized object and not a partially constructed one.

Thread-safe Singleton
public final class Singleton {
    private static volatile Singleton instance;

    private Singleton() {
        // heavy initialization if needed
    }

    public static Singleton getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) { // first check without locking
            synchronized (Singleton.class) {
                if (instance == null) { // second check with locking
                    instance = new Singleton();
                }
            }
        }
        return instance;
    }
}
Why volatile is important
  • Visibility: once one thread assigns the instance, other threads immediately see it.
  • Ordering: prevents instruction reordering from exposing a half-built object.
  • Safe publication: ensures the fully constructed singleton is published to all threads.

Without volatile, the JVM could reorder steps so the reference is assigned before the object is fully initialized. Another thread might then observe a non-null reference whose fields are still in an invalid default state.

Real-world example

A configuration manager or shared cache client is often created once and reused across the application. Double-checked locking gives lazy initialization without synchronizing every access after startup.

Interview-ready answer

"I use double-checked locking with a volatile instance field. The first null check avoids locking on every call, the synchronized block ensures only one thread creates the object, and volatile guarantees visibility and prevents publishing a partially constructed singleton."

The Java Memory Model (JMM) defines when one thread's writes become visible to another thread. The key idea is happens-before: if action A happens-before action B, then all memory writes done by A must be visible to B, and B must see them in the correct order.

Why this matters

Without happens-before, one thread may keep seeing stale data from CPU cache or compiler/JIT reordering. So even if a field is updated in one thread, another thread may not see the latest value unless there is a proper synchronization edge between them.

Common happens-before rules
  • Program order: inside one thread, earlier actions happen-before later actions.
  • Monitor lock: an unlock on a monitor happens-before a later lock on the same monitor.
  • volatile: a write to a volatile field happens-before a subsequent read of that same field.
  • Thread start: actions before Thread.start() happen-before the started thread runs.
  • Thread join: all actions in a thread happen-before another thread successfully returns from join().
  • Final fields: safe publication gives stronger guarantees for properly constructed immutable objects.
  • Transitivity: if A happens-before B and B happens-before C, then A happens-before C.
Simple visibility example
class SharedState {
    private int data = 0;
    private volatile boolean ready = false;

    void writer() {
        data = 42;     // 1
        ready = true;  // 2 volatile write
    }

    void reader() {
        if (ready) {   // 3 volatile read
            System.out.println(data); // guaranteed to print 42
        }
    }
}

Here, write data = 42 happens before the volatile write ready = true. That volatile write happens-before the reader's volatile read of ready. By transitivity, the reader also sees the earlier write to data. This is a classic safe-publication pattern.

Without happens-before
class BrokenState {
    private int data = 0;
    private boolean ready = false;
}

If ready is not volatile and there is no synchronization, the reader may see ready == true but still observe an old value of data, or it may never see the update at all. That is the visibility problem the JMM solves with happens-before rules.

How synchronized helps

A synchronized block also creates a happens-before edge. Unlocking the monitor flushes changes, and the next thread that locks the same monitor sees them. That is why synchronization solves both mutual exclusion and visibility.

Real-world example

Imagine a payment worker thread updates an in-memory status flag after calling a downstream service. Another thread polling that flag must either read a volatile field, use synchronized access, or use an atomic class; otherwise it may keep seeing stale status from its own cache.

Interview-ready answer

"Happens-before is the JMM rule that defines memory visibility and ordering between threads. If A happens-before B, then B is guaranteed to see A's writes. We create happens-before edges through synchronization, volatile, thread start/join, and transitivity. This is why volatile helps visibility and synchronized helps both visibility and atomicity around a critical section."

Two-Phase Commit (2PC) is a distributed transaction protocol that tries to make all participating services commit or roll back together. It gives strong consistency but is slow, blocking, and hard to operate at scale.

Saga breaks the work into local transactions. Each service commits its own change, and if a later step fails, the system runs compensating actions to undo earlier steps.

When to use
  • 2PC: rare in modern microservices; only when strong atomicity is absolutely required and the infrastructure supports it.
  • Saga: common in microservices for orders, payments, booking, and onboarding workflows.

Real-world example: in checkout, Order Service creates the order, Payment Service charges the card, and Inventory Service reserves stock. If payment fails, Saga can cancel the order and release stock.

Interview-ready answer: "2PC provides atomic commit across services but is heavy and fragile. Saga is usually the better microservices choice because each service commits locally and failures are handled by compensating actions."

In microservices, we usually avoid one global database transaction because it tightly couples services and becomes slow and fragile at scale. Instead, we usually choose between Two-Phase Commit (2PC) and the Saga Pattern, depending on how much atomicity we need and how much latency we can tolerate.

Two-Phase Commit vs Saga
Approach How it works Pros Cons
2PC Coordinator asks every service to prepare, then commit only if all agree. Strong atomicity across participants. Slow, blocking, hard to scale, fragile when a participant is down.
Saga Each service does a local transaction; failures are handled with compensating actions. Better scalability, loose coupling, fits microservices well. Only eventual consistency; compensation logic can be complex.
When I would use each one
  • 2PC: only in rare systems where strict atomic commit across participants is mandatory and the platform supports it.
  • Saga: the normal choice for order, payment, booking, onboarding, and workflow-based systems.
How Saga usually works
  • Step 1: Service A commits its own local transaction.
  • Step 2: Service A publishes an event or calls Service B.
  • Step 3: Service B commits its local transaction.
  • Step 4: If a later step fails, earlier services run compensation.
Real-world example

In an e-commerce checkout, the Order Service creates the order, the Payment Service charges the card, and the Inventory Service reserves stock. If inventory reservation fails after payment succeeds, the saga can trigger a compensating action to refund the payment and cancel the order.

Example flow
Order Service
  - create order
  - publish OrderCreated

Payment Service
  - charge card
  - publish PaymentSucceeded

Inventory Service
  - reserve stock
  - if fail -> publish InventoryFailed

Compensation
  - refund payment
  - cancel order
Spring style example
@Service
public class OrderSagaService {

    @Transactional
    public OrderResponse createOrder(CreateOrderRequest request) {
        Order order = orderRepository.save(Order.createPending(request));
        eventPublisher.publish(new OrderCreatedEvent(order.getId(), request.customerId()));
        return OrderResponse.from(order);
    }

    @Transactional
    public void handlePaymentFailed(PaymentFailedEvent event) {
        orderRepository.updateStatus(event.orderId(), OrderStatus.CANCELLED);
    }
}
Why 2PC is uncommon in microservices
  • It keeps locks and resources open while waiting for every participant.
  • A slow or failed service can block the whole transaction.
  • It does not fit well with independently deployable services.
  • Operationally, it is much harder to recover from coordinator or participant failures.
Interview-ready answer

"For microservices, I usually avoid 2PC because it is blocking and tightly couples services. I prefer Saga with local transactions and compensating actions, plus Outbox and idempotent consumers for reliable event delivery. 2PC is only for rare cases where strong atomic commit is non-negotiable."

Redis and Memcached are best for fast shared caching, but the hard part is not storing data, it is keeping cache behavior correct under load.

Key concerns
  • Cache invalidation: remove or refresh stale entries after writes.
  • Cache stampede: many threads miss the same hot key at once and overload the DB.
  • Cache penetration: repeated requests for missing keys hammer the database.
Typical fixes
  • Use TTL and explicit invalidation on updates.
  • Protect hot keys with locking, single-flight loading, or request coalescing.
  • Use negative caching for known-missing values.
  • Add rate limiting and fallback behavior for repeated misses.

Real-world example: product detail pages are cached in Redis, but if a popular product expires for everyone at once, a stampede can hit the DB unless we add jittered TTLs or a cache loader lock.

Interview-ready answer: "Redis and Memcached are effective for hot reads and session-like data. I use TTL, invalidation, single-flight loading, and negative caching to avoid stale data, stampedes, and repeated misses."

STAR is a simple format for answering behavioral interview questions clearly.

  • S - Situation: describe the context.
  • T - Task: explain your responsibility.
  • A - Action: describe what you did.
  • R - Result: explain the outcome with numbers if possible.

Real-world example: "The payment API was timing out (Situation). I had to reduce checkout failures (Task). I added timeouts, circuit breakers, and better logging (Action). Checkout latency dropped by 40% and failures fell sharply (Result)."

Interview-ready answer: "STAR is a structured way to answer behavioral questions with Situation, Task, Action, and Result so the story stays focused and measurable."

I balance it by protecting delivery speed while refactoring the parts that create the most risk or slow future work. I prefer small, safe improvements over big rewrites.

Practical approach
  • Deliver the feature behind tests and guardrails.
  • Refactor the hot spots that cause bugs, slow development, or deployment risk.
  • Use boy-scout changes: improve the code a little whenever touching it.
  • Reserve larger refactors for clear technical debt or high-value modules.

Real-world example: if a legacy payment class is hard to read, I would first add tests, extract helper methods, and isolate the risky logic rather than rewriting the entire module.

Interview-ready answer: "I keep feature delivery moving, but I refactor incrementally around the highest-risk or highest-change areas. That gives the business value now without letting the codebase decay further."

A strong answer should be honest, calm, and focused on learning. I would explain what failed, how I found it under pressure, and what permanent safeguards were added after the incident.

Good structure
  • What was the outage and business impact?
  • How did you detect and debug it?
  • What was the root cause?
  • What did you change afterward to prevent a repeat?

Real-world example: a bad config rollout caused 500 errors. I checked logs, metrics, and traces, rolled back quickly, then added validation, canary deploys, and an alert for the failing config path.

Interview-ready answer: "I would explain the outage honestly, show how I diagnosed it with logs and metrics, describe the rollback or fix, and then focus on the prevention steps such as validation, monitoring, and safer deployment gates."

The best answer shows respectful disagreement, data-driven discussion, and commitment to the team decision.

How to answer
  • State the disagreement clearly and professionally.
  • Explain what tradeoffs you raised and why.
  • Show how you used data, prototypes, or benchmarks.
  • End with the result and what you learned.

Real-world example: I pushed back on a synchronous design that would have hurt latency. I showed a small prototype, proposed an async event flow, and we agreed on a phased rollout.

Interview-ready answer: "I focus on the problem, not the person. I bring data, explain the tradeoffs, propose options, and support the final team decision once we align."

The biggest jump from Java 8 to Java 17 is not just language syntax. The real work is dealing with strong encapsulation, dependency compatibility, removed APIs, and framework upgrades.

Main migration challenges
  • Strong encapsulation: reflective access to JDK internals can fail with InaccessibleObjectException.
  • Internal API usage: old code may depend on sun.* or jdk.internal.* classes.
  • Removed components: Java EE modules, CORBA, Nashorn, Pack200, and some legacy APIs are no longer available.
  • Framework compatibility: Spring, Hibernate, Mockito, ByteBuddy, JAXB, and Jackson versions may need upgrades.
  • Build/tooling changes: Maven/Gradle plugins, test runners, and bytecode libraries often need newer versions.
  • GC and runtime behavior: defaults changed over time, so memory and startup behavior may differ from Java 8.
Why failures happen

Java 9 introduced the module system and later releases tightened access to JDK internals. Code that used reflection to touch private JDK fields or methods may work on Java 8 but break on Java 17 unless we refactor it or temporarily open packages. 

Field valueField = String.class.getDeclaredField("value");
valueField.setAccessible(true); // may fail on Java 17 without --add-opens
How I approach the migration
  • Run jdeps to find deprecated or internal JDK dependencies.
  • Upgrade third-party libraries before changing the runtime in production.
  • Fix reflective access instead of relying only on --add-opens as a permanent solution.
  • Move from old APIs such as JAX-B bundled in the JDK to explicit dependencies where needed.
  • Test startup, unit tests, integration tests, and production-like workloads before rollout.
Interview-ready answer

"Java 8 to 17 migration usually breaks because of strong encapsulation, removed JDK modules, and library incompatibilities. I first scan with jdeps, upgrade frameworks and plugins, fix reflection on JDK internals, and use --add-opens only as a temporary bridge during the migration."

For resilient microservices, I combine timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads, and fallback logic. The goal is to stop one failing dependency from taking down the whole system.

What the circuit breaker does
  • Closed: calls flow normally while the dependency is healthy.
  • Open: calls are rejected fast when failures cross the threshold.
  • Half-open: a few trial requests are allowed to see if the dependency recovered.
Spring Boot + Resilience4j example
@Service
public class PaymentClient {

    @CircuitBreaker(name = "paymentService", fallbackMethod = "paymentFallback")
    @Retry(name = "paymentService")
    public PaymentResponse callPayment(OrderRequest request) {
        return restTemplate.postForObject("/payments", request, PaymentResponse.class);
    }

    private PaymentResponse paymentFallback(OrderRequest request, Throwable ex) {
        return new PaymentResponse("DEGRADED", "Payment service unavailable");
    }
}
Interview-ready answer

"I design resilient service-to-service communication with timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, and bulkheads. With Resilience4j in Spring Boot, I protect downstream calls using @CircuitBreaker and fallback methods, so a slow dependency fails fast instead of causing cascading outages."

I would make the API stateless, accept data quickly, and push the heavy work to Kafka and downstream consumers. That keeps latency low even when millions of devices send telemetry concurrently.

High-level design
  • Devices call a Spring Boot ingestion API behind a load balancer or API gateway.
  • The API authenticates the device, validates the payload, and publishes the event to Kafka.
  • Partition Kafka topics by deviceId so ordering is preserved per device.
  • Consumer groups process events in parallel and persist them to time-series storage, object storage, or analytics systems.
Spring Boot producer example
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/telemetry")
public class TelemetryController {

    private final KafkaTemplate<String, TelemetryEvent> kafkaTemplate;

    public TelemetryController(KafkaTemplate<String, TelemetryEvent> kafkaTemplate) {
        this.kafkaTemplate = kafkaTemplate;
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<Void> ingest(@RequestBody TelemetryEvent event) {
        kafkaTemplate.send("telemetry-events", event.deviceId(), event);
        return ResponseEntity.accepted().build();
    }
}
Interview-ready answer

"For millions of IoT devices, I would use a stateless Spring Boot ingestion API, publish telemetry to Kafka, partition by deviceId, and scale consumers independently. That gives low latency at the edge, high throughput in the pipeline, and resilient asynchronous processing downstream."

The best cache strategy depends on whether your system reads more than it writes, how fresh the data must be, and whether the cache is local, distributed, or edge-based.

Common cache strategies
Strategy How it works Best use case
Cache-aside App checks cache first, then loads from DB and puts value in cache. Most common pattern for Spring apps, product catalog, user profile, reference data.
Read-through App asks cache, and cache loader fetches data from DB if missing. Simple lookup-heavy systems where cache library supports a loader.
Write-through Writes go to cache and DB together before the call returns. When read freshness matters and you want cache and DB to stay in sync immediately.
Write-behind / write-back Write lands in cache first, and DB is updated asynchronously later. High-write systems that can tolerate eventual consistency, like analytics or counters.
Refresh-ahead Cache refreshes hot keys before they expire. Very hot data such as rates, configs, and dashboards that should stay warm.
Near cache A small local cache sits in front of a distributed cache. Ultra-low latency reads in clustered systems.
CDN / edge cache Content is cached near users at the network edge. Images, CSS, JS, static files, and public API responses.
When I would use each one
  • Cache-aside: best default for most business services because it is simple and flexible.
  • Read-through: use when you want cache abstraction to hide DB loading logic.
  • Write-through: use when stale reads are risky, such as user settings or inventory-like data.
  • Write-behind: use when write speed matters more than immediate persistence.
  • Refresh-ahead: use when popular keys must stay warm and latency spikes are unacceptable.
  • Near cache: use in high-throughput clusters where network hops to Redis are still too expensive.
  • CDN cache: use for frontend assets or publicly cacheable responses.
Spring Cache-aside example
@Service
public class ProductService {

    @Cacheable(cacheNames = "products", key = "#productId")
    public ProductDto getProduct(Long productId) {
        return repository.findById(productId)
                .map(this::toDto)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new ProductNotFoundException(productId));
    }

    @CachePut(cacheNames = "products", key = "#result.id")
    public ProductDto updateProduct(ProductDto request) {
        Product saved = repository.save(toEntity(request));
        return toDto(saved);
    }

    @CacheEvict(cacheNames = "products", key = "#productId")
    public void deleteProduct(Long productId) {
        repository.deleteById(productId);
    }
}
Real-world examples
  • Product catalog: cache-aside works well because reads are frequent and updates are less frequent.
  • Currency exchange rates: refresh-ahead or short TTL avoids stale values.
  • User session: Redis cache or session store works well because reads must be fast.
  • Leaderboard or counters: write-behind can help if immediate persistence is not critical.
  • Static assets: CDN cache gives the biggest win for global users.
Interview-ready answer

"The most common strategy is cache-aside, where the app checks cache first and loads from the DB on a miss. I use write-through when freshness matters, write-behind when write throughput matters, and refresh-ahead or near cache for very hot data. For static content, CDN caching is the best fit."

Cache eviction is the process of removing entries from cache when memory is limited, data becomes stale, or the cache needs space for hotter items.

Why eviction is needed
  • Cache memory is finite.
  • Older data may no longer be useful.
  • We want the cache to keep the most valuable keys.
  • Eviction prevents stale or low-value entries from wasting space.
Common eviction policies
Policy How it works Best use case
LRU Least Recently Used entries are removed first. General-purpose caches where recent data is likely to be reused.
LFU Least Frequently Used entries are removed first. Hot-key workloads where frequently accessed data should stay longer.
FIFO First In, First Out removes the oldest inserted entry. Simple caches where recency or frequency is not very important.
MRU Most Recently Used entries are removed first. Rare cases where the newest items are least likely to be reused.
TTL / time-based expiry Entries expire after a fixed time. Rates, tokens, sessions, config data, or any data that must refresh periodically.
Size-based eviction Evict when cache reaches max item count or memory limit. Protect memory in local caches like Caffeine or in-memory maps.
Real-world examples
  • Product detail cache: LRU is a good fit because the most recently viewed products are often requested again.
  • API rate-limit counters: TTL expiry works well because the count should reset after the window.
  • Currency exchange rates: short TTL or refresh-ahead prevents stale values.
  • Session cache: TTL is essential because sessions must expire naturally.
  • Hot analytics dashboard: LFU can help keep the most frequently queried metrics in cache.
Spring / Caffeine example
@Bean
public Cache<String, ProductDto> productCache() {
    return Caffeine.newBuilder()
            .maximumSize(10_000)
            .expireAfterWrite(Duration.ofMinutes(10))
            .recordStats()
            .build();
}

In Redis, a similar idea is usually implemented with TTL plus a maxmemory policy such as allkeys-lru or volatile-ttl. That way Redis decides which keys to evict when memory pressure rises.

Practical rule of thumb

If you want a simple and effective default, use LRU with TTL. If access frequency matters a lot, use LFU. If freshness is the main concern, use TTL-based expiry. For local application caches in Spring Boot, Caffeine is often a strong choice; for distributed shared caches, Redis eviction policies matter more.

Interview-ready answer

"Cache eviction is how we remove entries when the cache is full or data becomes stale. The common policies are LRU, LFU, FIFO, MRU, TTL-based expiry, and size-based eviction. I usually pick LRU plus TTL for general use, LFU for hot-key workloads, and short TTL for session or rate-limit data."

Consider a food-delivery app calling POST /api/orders. The API cycle is the journey from a mobile or web request to a persisted order and the final HTTP response.

End-to-end request flow
Mobile/Web client
  -> DNS resolves api.company.com
  -> HTTPS/TLS and Load Balancer / API Gateway
  -> Spring Boot embedded server (Tomcat/Netty)
  -> Filters: request ID, CORS, logging, Spring Security
  -> DispatcherServlet -> Controller -> validation
  -> Service -> transaction -> Repository/Hibernate
  -> HikariCP connection pool -> database
  -> Response DTO -> JSON response, logs, metrics, trace
1. Client, DNS, gateway, and HTTPS

The client sends JSON, an access token, and optionally an idempotency key. DNS maps the domain to an endpoint. A load balancer distributes requests across healthy instances; an API gateway can route, rate-limit, validate tokens, and terminate TLS. HTTPS encrypts data while it travels. 

POST /api/orders HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer <JWT>
Idempotency-Key: 9350f611-7ffc-4f79-9fd3-58b8e95a8dc5
Content-Type: application/json

{"customerId":42,"restaurantId":9,"items":[{"productId":7,"quantity":2}]}
2. Server, filters, and security

Spring Boot starts embedded Tomcat by default. Filters can add a correlation ID to MDC, log the request, and apply CORS. Spring Security validates the JWT and stores the authenticated user and roles in SecurityContext. An invalid token returns 401; a valid user without the required role returns 403, before business logic runs.

3. DispatcherServlet, controller, and validation

DispatcherServlet is Spring MVC's front controller. It finds the controller, uses Jackson to map JSON into a DTO, and runs Bean Validation. Invalid JSON or required fields should fail with 400 Bad Request before calling the database. 

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/orders")
class OrderController {
  private final OrderService orderService;

  @PostMapping
  ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateOrderRequest request,
      @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt, @RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String key) {
    return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).body(orderService.create(request, jwt.getSubject(), key));
  }
}
4. Service layer and transaction

The service owns business rules: confirm the customer, calculate the amount, reserve stock, and create the order. @Transactional makes related database updates atomic: all commit together or roll back together. Keep it on a public service method, not normally in the controller. 

@Service
class OrderService {
  @Transactional
  public OrderResponse create(CreateOrderRequest request, String userId, String key) {
    Order existing = orderRepository.findByIdempotencyKey(key).orElse(null);
    if (existing != null) return OrderResponse.from(existing); // safe retry
    inventoryService.reserve(request.items());
    return OrderResponse.from(orderRepository.save(Order.create(request, userId, key)));
  }
}
5. Repository, database, and response

Spring Data calls Hibernate/JPA, which produces SQL. HikariCP borrows an existing JDBC connection rather than opening one per request. The database validates constraints and commits the transaction. The controller returns a response DTO, not a JPA entity, and Jackson serializes it to JSON.

@RestControllerAdvice maps expected failures to a consistent error body: use 201 for a created order, 400 for bad input, 404 for a missing resource, 409 for stock conflict, and 500 only for unexpected failures.

6. Logs, metrics, tracing, and microservice calls

Put a request or trace ID in every log. Micrometer exposes latency, error-rate, JVM, and connection-pool metrics to Prometheus and Grafana. OpenTelemetry creates spans through the gateway, order service, database, and payment service. Do not keep a database transaction open while waiting for slow payment or notification calls; use an event/outbox pattern when reliable asynchronous processing is needed.

Interview-ready answer

"A request reaches the gateway over HTTPS, then Spring Boot's server. Filters handle request IDs, logging, CORS, and security. DispatcherServlet routes to a controller, Jackson maps and validates the DTO, and the service applies business rules in a transaction. Hibernate uses a pooled connection to persist data. A response DTO becomes JSON, while controller advice, logs, metrics, and traces make both errors and performance observable end to end."

In a normal Spring MVC / Spring Boot application, Spring Security runs before DispatcherServlet. It is part of the servlet filter chain, so it can reject an unauthenticated or unauthorized request before a controller method is selected or executed.

Actual request order
Client request
  -> Tomcat / servlet container filter chain
  -> DelegatingFilterProxy
  -> Spring Security FilterChainProxy
  -> SecurityFilterChain
       -> CORS / CSRF checks (when enabled)
       -> JWT, session, or API-key authentication
       -> SecurityContext is populated
       -> URL/role authorization
  -> DispatcherServlet
  -> Controller
  -> Service
  -> Response travels back through filters
Real-world JWT example

For POST /api/orders, a JWT authentication filter reads the Authorization: Bearer <token> header. If the signature, expiry, or issuer is invalid, Spring Security returns 401 Unauthorized; the controller is never called. If the token is valid but the user lacks the required role, it returns 403 Forbidden before the controller.

Important exception: method security

@PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize, and @Secured are method-level security. They execute later, when Spring calls the protected controller or service method through a proxy. Therefore, URL authentication is before DispatcherServlet, while @PreAuthorize runs immediately before the annotated method body. 

@RestController
class OrderController {
  @PostMapping("/api/orders")
  @PreAuthorize("hasRole('CUSTOMER')")
  OrderResponse createOrder(@RequestBody CreateOrderRequest request) {
    return orderService.create(request);
  }
}

@Service
class RefundService {
  @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
  public void approveRefund(Long orderId) { /* only an admin reaches this body */ }
}
Interview-ready answer

"Spring Security is a filter-chain concern, so authentication and request-level authorization run before DispatcherServlet and before the controller. It validates the token and places the authenticated user in SecurityContext. Method-level checks such as @PreAuthorize are different: they run through a Spring AOP proxy just before the secured controller or service method executes."

These are three different ways to handle access. The simplest way to think about them is: Basic Auth sends credentials directly, OAuth 1 adds signed requests, and OAuth 2 uses tokens for delegated access.

Simple comparison
Type Simple meaning Real-world idea
Basic Auth Sends username and password on every request, usually encoded, not encrypted by itself. Showing your ID card every time you enter a room.
OAuth 1 Uses signed requests with tokens and secrets. Older and more complex. Signing every gate pass so nobody can tamper with it.
OAuth 2 Uses access tokens so one app can access another app's data without seeing the password. Giving a valet key that opens only specific doors for a limited time.
When to use
  • Basic Auth: for very simple internal APIs or testing, and usually only over HTTPS.
  • OAuth 1: mostly legacy systems now; rarely chosen for new projects.
  • OAuth 2: modern login and third-party access flows like Google login, API access, or delegated authorization.
Easy memory trick
  • Basic Auth: "I send my username and password."
  • OAuth 1: "I sign every request."
  • OAuth 2: "I use a token instead of sharing my password."
Spring Security angle

In Spring Boot, Basic Auth is quick to configure, but OAuth2 is what we usually use for modern authorization flows with login providers, authorization servers, or JWT-based resource servers.

Interview-ready answer

"Basic Auth sends username and password with each request, OAuth 1 is an older signed-request model, and OAuth 2 is the modern token-based approach for delegated access. In most Spring Boot systems today, OAuth 2 is the common choice, while Basic Auth is mostly for simple internal use."

This is the comparison most interviewers actually expect. The easy way to remember it is: Basic Auth sends the password, JWT carries identity in a signed token, and OAuth 2 is the authorization framework that usually issues those tokens.

Simple comparison
Type Simple meaning Real-world idea
Basic Auth Username and password are sent with every request. Showing your full ID and password every time.
JWT A signed token that carries claims like user name, roles, and expiry. A tamper-proof entry pass with your details printed on it.
OAuth 2 A framework for delegated authorization that often uses access tokens and refresh tokens. Giving limited access to a trusted helper without giving away your password.
How they relate
  • Basic Auth is a simple authentication mechanism.
  • JWT is a token format, not a full login framework by itself.
  • OAuth 2 is the authorization framework; it may use JWT as the access token format.
When to use
  • Basic Auth: quick internal tools, demos, or simple server-to-server checks over HTTPS.
  • JWT: stateless API authentication where the server does not want to store session data.
  • OAuth 2: login with Google/Facebook, delegated access, or enterprise identity flows.
Spring Boot angle

In Spring Boot, Basic Auth is the easiest to configure, JWT is common for stateless REST APIs, and OAuth2 is used when you want login/authorization to be managed by an authorization server like Keycloak, Okta, or Google.

Interview-ready answer

"Basic Auth sends username and password every time, JWT is a signed token that carries user identity and claims, and OAuth 2 is the authorization framework that issues tokens and enables delegated access. In modern Spring Boot apps, JWT is common for stateless APIs and OAuth 2 is used for full authorization flows."

This comparison is about where the login state lives. With Basic Auth, the password is sent each time. With JWT, the token itself carries the identity. With Session, the server stores the login state and the browser only keeps a session id.

Simple comparison
Type Simple meaning Real-world idea
Basic Auth User sends username and password with each request. Showing your full ID card every time you enter.
JWT User sends a signed token with each request. Carrying a sealed pass that proves who you are.
Session Server remembers the user after login and client sends only session id. Getting a wristband after check-in, while the venue keeps your details.
Main difference
  • Basic Auth: credentials travel every time.
  • JWT: stateless, token contains the identity claims.
  • Session: stateful, server keeps login data in memory or shared store like Redis.
When to use
  • Basic Auth: simple internal APIs, demos, or tooling.
  • JWT: stateless REST APIs, mobile apps, and microservices.
  • Session: classic web apps where server-side state is acceptable.
Spring Boot angle

In Spring Boot, session-based auth is common for browser apps, JWT is common for REST APIs, and Basic Auth is usually the quickest but least flexible option.

Interview-ready answer

"Basic Auth sends username and password every time, JWT is a stateless signed token that carries user claims, and Session authentication stores the login state on the server while the client keeps only a session id. For modern APIs, JWT is usually preferred; for browser apps, session-based auth is common."

Spring MVC uses DispatcherServlet as its front controller. At application startup, component scanning finds classes annotated with @Controller or @RestController. RequestMappingHandlerMapping scans their @RequestMapping, @GetMapping, @PostMapping, and similar annotations and builds an in-memory mapping registry from request conditions to Java methods.

What Spring matches
Incoming request: POST /api/orders/42?includeItems=true

Spring matches using:
  1. HTTP method       - POST
  2. URL path          - /api/orders/{id}
  3. params            - e.g. version=v2 or includeItems=true (if declared)
  4. headers           - e.g. X-API-Version: 2 (if declared)
  5. consumes          - request Content-Type, such as application/json
  6. produces          - requested Accept type, such as application/json
Example
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/orders")
class OrderController {

  @GetMapping("/{id}")
  OrderResponse get(@PathVariable Long id,
      @RequestParam(defaultValue = "false") boolean includeItems) {
    return orderService.get(id, includeItems);
  }

  @PostMapping(consumes = "application/json", produces = "application/json")
  ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateOrderRequest request) {
    return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).body(orderService.create(request));
  }
}

GET /api/orders/42?includeItems=true selects get(...) because its path and HTTP method match. POST /api/orders with JSON selects create(...). Once the method is selected, a HandlerAdapter resolves its arguments: @PathVariable from the path, @RequestParam from the query string, @RequestBody through Jackson, and @AuthenticationPrincipal from Spring Security.

What if no or multiple methods match?

If no path matches, Spring returns 404 Not Found. A matching path with the wrong HTTP method returns 405 Method Not Allowed. A wrong request content type returns 415 Unsupported Media Type; an unacceptable response type can return 406 Not Acceptable. Two exactly identical mappings normally fail application startup with an ambiguous mapping error. Spring prefers the more specific path, such as /orders/special, over a variable path such as /orders/{id}.

Interview-ready answer

"At startup, RequestMappingHandlerMapping scans controller annotations and registers each endpoint in a mapping table. For every request, DispatcherServlet asks that mapping to find the best handler using the URL, HTTP verb, headers, parameters, consumes, and produces conditions. HandlerAdapter then builds the method arguments and invokes the selected controller method."

A servlet filter wraps everything downstream of it. On the incoming path it runs before DispatcherServlet and the controller. After it calls chain.doFilter(...), it pauses while the rest of the chain and the controller run. When they finish, it resumes on the outgoing path. So yes: the response passes through filters in reverse order before it is sent to the client.

Two-way filter picture
Incoming request: Client -> Filter A -> Filter B -> Spring Security
                  -> DispatcherServlet -> Controller -> Service

Outgoing response: Service -> Controller -> DispatcherServlet -> Spring Security
                  -> Filter B -> Filter A -> Client
The key is chain.doFilter()
@Component
class RequestLoggingFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
  @Override
  protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest request,
      HttpServletResponse response, FilterChain chain)
      throws ServletException, IOException {
    long start = System.currentTimeMillis();
    log.info("Before controller: {} {}", request.getMethod(), request.getRequestURI());

    try {
      chain.doFilter(request, response); // next filter, then DispatcherServlet/controller
    } finally {
      log.info("After controller: status={}, time={}ms", response.getStatus(),
          System.currentTimeMillis() - start);
    }
  }
}

Code before chain.doFilter handles the incoming request; code after it handles the outgoing response. The finally block also runs if a later filter or controller throws an exception.

Can a filter stop the request?

Yes. A filter can write a response and not call chain.doFilter. A JWT filter may return 401, a rate-limit filter 429, or a maintenance filter 503. Then DispatcherServlet and the controller are never reached. Earlier filters still resume as the chain unwinds and can log the final response.

Filter order matters

Filters execute in ascending order on the request and descending order on the response. Configure an application filter with @Order or FilterRegistrationBean. Spring Security is a filter chain too, so place a custom filter after authentication when it needs the authenticated user.

Interview-ready answer

"Filters surround the controller call. Before chain.doFilter they process the request; after it they process the response in reverse order. A filter can short-circuit by not calling the chain, returning errors such as 401 or 429 before the controller executes."

Both can run before and after an API call, but they belong to different layers. A Filter is a Servlet API component and runs before DispatcherServlet. A Spring MVC HandlerInterceptor runs after Spring has selected the controller handler but before the controller method executes.

Position in the flow
Client
  -> Servlet Filter (works at HTTP/Servlet level)
  -> Spring Security filters
  -> DispatcherServlet
  -> HandlerMapping chooses controller method
  -> HandlerInterceptor.preHandle (knows the selected handler)
  -> Controller method
  -> HandlerInterceptor.postHandle / afterCompletion
  -> Servlet Filter resumes after chain.doFilter
  -> Client
Use a Filter when

You need low-level HTTP behavior for every request, including requests that do not reach a controller: CORS, request/response wrapping, correlation IDs, raw request logging, compression, security filter integration, rate limiting, or handling static files. A filter receives HttpServletRequest, HttpServletResponse, and FilterChain; it can alter headers/body wrappers or stop processing by not calling chain.doFilter. 

@Component
class TraceIdFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
  @Override
  protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest request,
      HttpServletResponse response, FilterChain chain) throws ServletException, IOException {
    String traceId = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
    MDC.put("traceId", traceId);
    response.setHeader("X-Trace-Id", traceId);
    try {
      chain.doFilter(request, response);
    } finally {
      MDC.remove("traceId");
    }
  }
}
Use an Interceptor when

You need Spring MVC knowledge, especially the chosen controller and method. Common examples are audit logging with the controller name, tenant checks, API version checks, or applying rules only to selected URL patterns. In preHandle, return false to stop the controller call. afterCompletion is best for cleanup and final exception-aware logging. 

@Component
class TenantInterceptor implements HandlerInterceptor {
  @Override
  public boolean preHandle(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response,
      Object handler) throws IOException {
    if (handler instanceof HandlerMethod method && request.getHeader("X-Tenant-Id") == null) {
      response.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_BAD_REQUEST, "X-Tenant-Id is required");
      return false;
    }
    return true;
  }
}

@Configuration
class WebConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
  private final TenantInterceptor tenantInterceptor;

  WebConfig(TenantInterceptor tenantInterceptor) {
    this.tenantInterceptor = tenantInterceptor;
  }

  public void addInterceptors(InterceptorRegistry registry) {
    registry.addInterceptor(tenantInterceptor).addPathPatterns("/api/**");
  }
}
Key differences and caution

Filters are servlet-container components and can run even when there is no mapped controller. Interceptors are Spring MVC components and normally apply only after a handler mapping succeeds. Interceptors can inspect the HandlerMethod; filters cannot. Prefer Spring Security's SecurityFilterChain for authentication and authorization rather than writing equivalent security logic in an interceptor. Also do not rely on postHandle to modify a final REST JSON body; use a filter or ResponseBodyAdvice if response-body transformation is required.

Interview-ready answer

"Use a filter for generic HTTP or servlet-level concerns that must wrap all traffic, such as CORS, trace IDs, and security filters. Use a HandlerInterceptor for Spring MVC concerns that need the selected controller method, such as tenant validation or controller audit logging. Filters are before DispatcherServlet; interceptors are between handler mapping and controller execution."

transient tells Java serialization to skip that field when the object is written to a stream. The field is not serialized. After deserialization, the field is restored to its default value for that type.

Default values after deserialization
  • int, long, double, etc. become 0 / 0.0.
  • boolean becomes false.
  • Object references become null.
Example
class User implements Serializable {
  private String username;
  private transient String password;
  private transient int loginCount;

  User(String username, String password, int loginCount) {
    this.username = username;
    this.password = password;
    this.loginCount = loginCount;
  }
}

If you serialize and then deserialize this object, username is restored, but password becomes null and loginCount becomes 0.

When to use it

Use transient for sensitive data like passwords, derived fields that can be recomputed, or temporary caches that should not be stored in the serialized form.

Important note

transient only affects Java object serialization. It does not automatically hide the field in JSON unless the JSON library is configured to respect it. For example, Jackson can be configured to include or ignore transient fields depending on its settings.

Interview-ready answer

"Transient fields are skipped during Java serialization. They are not serialized at all, and after deserialization they get default values like null, 0, or false depending on the type."

Deserialization happens on the incoming request, before the controller method runs: Spring converts JSON bytes into a Java DTO. Serialization happens on the outgoing response, after the controller returns: Spring converts a Java object into JSON bytes for the client. In Spring Boot, Jackson is normally the JSON library that performs both conversions.

Exact REST request flow
POST /api/orders
Content-Type: application/json
Body: {"customerId":42,"quantity":2}

Filters -> Spring Security -> DispatcherServlet
  -> HandlerMapping selects the controller method
  -> HttpMessageConverter (MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter)
  -> DESERIALIZATION: JSON request body -> CreateOrderRequest Java object
  -> @Valid validation
  -> Controller method and service run
  -> Controller returns OrderResponse Java object
  -> HttpMessageConverter
  -> SERIALIZATION: OrderResponse Java object -> JSON response body
  -> Filters resume -> client receives response
Example
record CreateOrderRequest(Long customerId, Integer quantity) {}
record OrderResponse(Long orderId, String status) {}

@RestController
class OrderController {
  @PostMapping(value = "/api/orders", consumes = "application/json",
      produces = "application/json")
  OrderResponse create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateOrderRequest request) {
    // request is already a Java object here: deserialization is complete.
    return new OrderResponse(101L, "CREATED");
    // Spring serializes this returned object to JSON after the method returns.
  }
}

For the request above, Jackson creates CreateOrderRequest(42L, 2). The response object becomes {"orderId":101,"status":"CREATED"} and is written to the HTTP response. The chosen converter depends on Content-Type for input and Accept / produces for output. JSON typically uses MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter.

What does not use JSON deserialization?

@PathVariable and @RequestParam are strings from the URL and are converted by Spring's conversion service, for example "42" to Long. HTML form fields often bind with @ModelAttribute. Neither is the same as Jackson reading a JSON request body.

Errors and customization

Invalid JSON, a wrong field type, or an unknown required format fails during deserialization, so the controller method is not called and Spring normally returns 400 Bad Request. Customize JSON field names, dates, ignored fields, and formatting with Jackson annotations such as @JsonProperty, @JsonFormat, and @JsonIgnore, or configure the shared ObjectMapper. Never serialize sensitive fields such as passwords or tokens.

Interview-ready answer

"For @RequestBody, deserialization happens before the controller method: Spring's HTTP message converter uses Jackson to turn JSON into a DTO. For @RestController or @ResponseBody, serialization happens after the method returns: the converter turns the returned Java object into JSON. Filters wrap the whole flow, so their after-chain code runs after serialization has written the response."

A stereotype annotation tells Spring what role a class plays. During component scanning, Spring finds these annotations and registers the class as a bean. The core stereotype is @Component; the common layer-specific stereotypes are specializations of it.

Core stereotypes
AnnotationTypical layerPurpose / extra behavior
@ComponentGenericAny Spring-managed bean with no more specific role.
@ServiceBusiness logicCommunicates service-layer intent; functionally behaves like @Component.
@RepositoryPersistence / DAOCommunicates data-access intent and enables persistence exception translation.
@ControllerSpring MVC webHandles web requests, normally returning a view name.
@RestControllerREST API web@Controller + @ResponseBody; returned objects become HTTP response bodies, usually JSON.
Related component annotations

@Configuration is also a component and declares @Bean methods. For global web error handling, use @ControllerAdvice; @RestControllerAdvice adds @ResponseBody. These are component-style annotations, but the five annotations above are the standard layer stereotypes usually expected in interviews.

What @Repository adds

Yes. @Repository is not only a naming convention. In addition to being detected as a bean, it marks a data-access class for persistence exception translation. Spring can convert technology-specific exceptions such as Hibernate's ConstraintViolationException or a JDBC SQLException into Spring's consistent unchecked DataAccessException hierarchy, for example DuplicateKeyException or DataIntegrityViolationException. 

@Repository
class CustomerRepository {
  // JPA/JDBC/Hibernate work happens here.
  // A database duplicate-key error can be exposed as DataIntegrityViolationException.
}

@Service
class CustomerService {
  void register(Customer customer) {
    try {
      customerRepository.save(customer);
    } catch (DataIntegrityViolationException ex) {
      throw new EmailAlreadyRegisteredException(customer.email());
    }
  }
}

The translator is supplied by Spring's persistence exception translation infrastructure. Spring Boot's JPA/JDBC auto-configuration normally provides the required setup. With Spring Data JPA, repository interfaces such as interface CustomerRepository extends JpaRepository<Customer, Long> are already discovered and proxied by Spring Data, so adding @Repository is usually not necessary.

Practical rule

Use the most specific annotation: @RestController for REST endpoints, @Service for use cases/business rules, @Repository for manual DAO classes, and @Component for supporting beans such as validators, mappers, schedulers, or listeners. The names also make architecture easier to read and allow framework tooling to understand intent.

Can we replace @RestController with @Component?

In practice, no. @RestController is a web stereotype that tells Spring MVC to expose request-handling methods and write return values directly to the HTTP response body. @Component only makes the class a Spring bean; it does not make it a REST endpoint. 

// Correct for REST endpoints
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/users")
class UserController {
  @GetMapping("/{id}")
  User getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
    return service.findById(id);
  }
}

// Not a replacement for REST endpoints
@Component
class UserControllerLikeBean {
  // Spring will manage it as a bean, but it will not act as a REST controller
}

If you want a web controller, use @RestController or @Controller plus @ResponseBody. Use @Component for helper beans that the controller calls, such as mappers, validators, or utility services.

Interview-ready answer

"@Component is the generic Spring bean stereotype. @Service, @Repository, @Controller, and @RestController are specialized roles. Most behave like @Component for bean discovery, but @Repository additionally participates in persistence exception translation, converting database-vendor exceptions into Spring DataAccessException types."

Dependency Injection (DI) means an object receives the collaborators it needs from outside instead of creating them with new. It is one result of Inversion of Control (IoC): Spring owns bean creation, finds dependencies, builds the object graph, and injects the required beans.

Without DI vs with DI
// Tightly coupled: difficult to replace or test.
class OrderService {
  private final PaymentClient paymentClient = new PaymentClient();
}

// Dependency is supplied by Spring (or directly by a unit test).
@Service
class OrderService {
  private final PaymentClient paymentClient;

  OrderService(PaymentClient paymentClient) {
    this.paymentClient = paymentClient;
  }
}
Three injection styles
StyleBest forRecommendation
Constructor injectionRequired dependenciesPreferred default.
Setter injectionOptional or changeable dependenciesUse sparingly and validate when needed.
Field injectionVery short demos onlyAvoid in production code.

Since Spring 4.3, when a class has exactly one constructor, @Autowired is optional. Spring automatically uses that constructor. With multiple constructors, mark the intended one with @Autowired.

Why constructor injection is better

It makes required dependencies explicit in the class API and lets them be final, so a bean cannot exist in a partially initialized state. Missing dependencies fail immediately during application startup. It is easy to unit-test without Spring because a test can pass a fake or mock directly. It also exposes circular dependencies early: A -> B -> A cannot be constructed and Spring reports the design problem instead of hiding it. 

@Service
class OrderService {
  private final OrderRepository orderRepository;
  private final PaymentClient paymentClient;

  OrderService(OrderRepository orderRepository, PaymentClient paymentClient) {
    this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
    this.paymentClient = paymentClient;
  }

  Order place(CreateOrderRequest request) {
    paymentClient.charge(request.total());
    return orderRepository.save(Order.from(request));
  }
}

// No Spring context is needed for this unit test.
