OrderService service = new OrderService(fakeRepository, fakePaymentClient);
Why field injection is discouraged

A field-injected class can be created with new but its dependencies stay null. Its required collaborators are hidden, fields cannot naturally be final, and unit tests often need reflection to set them. This is why constructor injection is clearer and safer.

When setter injection is useful

Use setter injection only when a dependency is truly optional or can change after construction, such as an optional notification integration. For lazy/optional resolution, Spring also provides ObjectProvider<T>. Do not use setter injection merely to avoid a circular dependency; redesign the responsibilities first.

Interview-ready answer

"Dependency Injection means Spring creates an object's dependencies and supplies them rather than the object creating them itself. Constructor injection is preferred for required dependencies because it makes the class immutable, explicit, fail-fast, and easy to unit-test. Setter injection suits real optional dependencies; field injection is generally avoided in production code."

A Spring Boot starter is a curated dependency bundle that pulls in the libraries usually needed for one feature area. For example, spring-boot-starter-web brings Spring MVC, embedded server support, validation, and Jackson-based JSON handling together in one dependency.

Why it exists

Without starters, we would manually pick and version many Spring jars and their transitive dependencies. Starters solve the "which dependencies do I need?" problem by giving a sensible default stack that works together.

How it helps
  • Reduces dependency setup time and version mismatch problems.
  • Gives a consistent, opinionated default for common use cases.
  • Works well with auto-configuration, so Spring Boot can wire beans based on what is on the classpath.
  • Makes project setup simpler for web, data, messaging, testing, security, and observability features.
Example
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>

This single dependency is enough for a typical REST API. It is much easier than assembling MVC, Jackson, validation, and embedded server dependencies by hand.

Real-world analogy

Think of a starter like a pre-packed toolkit. Instead of buying a hammer, nails, screwdriver, and screws one by one for every project, you get the common set ready to use.

Important note

A starter does not mean "magic". It mainly adds dependencies and lets Boot auto-configure defaults. You can still override the defaults or exclude parts you do not need.

Interview-ready answer

"A Spring Boot starter is an opinionated dependency bundle for a specific feature area. It exists to reduce dependency management, avoid version conflicts, and work with Boot auto-configuration so we can start building faster with sensible defaults."

I first find what part of startup is slow, then I remove or defer the expensive work. In Spring Boot, the delay usually comes from auto-configuration, component scanning, bean creation, database connections, remote calls in initialization code, or heavy startup logic in @PostConstruct and ApplicationRunner.

How to analyze it
  • Enable startup timing logs with ApplicationStartup or Spring Boot startup metrics.
  • Check logs around auto-configuration, bean creation, Flyway/Liquibase, JPA schema creation, and cache warm-up.
  • Use Actuator and metrics to see slow initialization paths and slow DB or HTTP dependencies.
  • Profile the JVM if needed to see which methods dominate startup time.
Typical root causes
  • Too many scanned packages or unnecessary auto-configurations.
  • Large object graphs created eagerly at startup.
  • JPA entity scanning, schema validation, and repository initialization.
  • Network calls, file reads, or cache loading during bean construction.
  • Heavy logging, secret fetching, or cloud config calls before the app becomes ready.
How to fix it
  • Reduce component scan scope and exclude unused auto-configurations.
  • Make non-essential beans lazy with @Lazy.
  • Move slow work out of constructors and @PostConstruct.
  • Defer cache warm-up or remote calls until after startup, or run them asynchronously.
  • Trim dependencies and avoid loading starters you do not need.
Example
@Lazy
@Service
class ReportService {
  ReportService() {
    // Avoid heavy work here
  }
}

If a startup task is necessary, keep it small and measurable. For example, use a health check or background warm-up instead of blocking the application from becoming ready.

Real-world example

In an order service, startup becomes slow when it connects to multiple databases, loads reference data, warms caches, and fetches remote configuration synchronously. A better approach is to keep the app booting fast, then load optional data asynchronously after it becomes healthy.

Interview-ready answer

"I analyze Spring Boot startup by identifying slow auto-config, bean creation, database initialization, and any work done in constructors or startup hooks. Then I reduce scanning, exclude unused configs, make beans lazy, and move expensive work out of startup so the app becomes ready faster."

SonarQube is a code quality and static analysis platform. It scans source code, tests, and build reports to find bugs, code smells, vulnerabilities, duplication, and coverage gaps. We use it because it catches quality problems early and gives teams a repeatable standard before code reaches production.

What is a quality gate?

A quality gate is a pass/fail rule set applied to the analysis result. For example, the gate may require no new critical issues, no new security vulnerabilities, and a minimum coverage threshold on new code. If the gate fails, the build should fail or at least block the merge/release.

Why SonarQube?
  • Finds bugs and smells before release.
  • Enforces consistent coding standards across teams.
  • Shows coverage, duplication, maintainability, reliability, and security trends.
  • Helps reviewers focus on important issues instead of style-only noise.
How it works internally
Developer commits code
  -> Jenkins builds and runs tests
  -> JaCoCo generates coverage report
  -> SonarScanner sends source code + test + coverage data to SonarQube server
  -> SonarQube computes analysis and applies the quality gate
  -> Jenkins waits for the result and fails the pipeline if the gate fails
Jenkins setup
  1. Install the SonarQube server or use SonarCloud.
  2. Install the SonarScanner plugin in Jenkins.
  3. Configure SonarQube server URL and token in Jenkins credentials/global tools.
  4. Run tests and generate JaCoCo reports before analysis.
  5. Invoke the scanner in the Jenkins pipeline.
  6. Wait for the quality gate result and stop the pipeline if it fails.
stage("SonarQube Analysis") {
    steps {
        withSonarQubeEnv("sonarqube-server") {
            sh "mvn clean verify sonar:sonar"
        }
    }
}

stage("Quality Gate") {
    steps {
        timeout(time: 10, unit: "MINUTES") {
            waitForQualityGate abortPipeline: true
        }
    }
}
JaCoCo and SonarQube

JaCoCo produces test coverage data. SonarQube reads that report and displays line, branch, and method coverage. This helps the quality gate enforce coverage on new code and gives developers a visible report inside SonarQube.

In Maven, the usual flow is to run mvn test or mvn verify with the JaCoCo plugin, then run sonar:sonar so SonarQube can import the coverage report.

Can we customize the rules?

Yes. We can use built-in rule sets, create custom quality profiles, activate or deactivate specific rules, and set different thresholds for different projects or branches. For example, one team may require stricter coverage or security rules on new code than another team.

  • Create or clone a Quality Profile for Java.
  • Enable or disable rules in that profile.
  • Adjust quality gate thresholds such as coverage or duplicated lines on new code.
  • Use project-level settings if a specific service needs a different policy.
Typical Sonar interview questions
  • SonarQube vs SonarCloud: SonarQube is usually self-hosted; SonarCloud is hosted.
  • Bug vs vulnerability vs code smell: bug is likely wrong behavior, vulnerability is a security risk, smell is maintainability debt.
  • New code vs overall code: quality gates often focus on new code so legacy issues do not block all delivery.
  • Does Sonar replace tests? No. It complements tests, it does not validate business behavior by itself.
  • What does the scanner do? It sends analysis metadata to the SonarQube server for computation and reporting.
Real-world example

In a Spring Boot payment service, SonarQube can flag an unhandled null check, duplicated logic in two controllers, a low-coverage exception branch, or a risky SQL string. The quality gate stops the release until the team fixes the issue or consciously adjusts the rule.

Interview-ready answer

"SonarQube is a static analysis platform that checks bugs, smells, security issues, and coverage. A quality gate is the pass/fail rule set applied to the analysis. In Jenkins, we run tests, generate JaCoCo coverage, run sonar analysis, wait for the quality gate, and fail the pipeline if it does not pass. Rules can be customized through quality profiles and project-specific settings."

Code coverage tells us how much of the application code is exercised by our tests. In a Spring Boot app, it helps us spot untested service logic, controller paths, exception branches, and edge cases. The most common tool is JaCoCo.

Why it matters
  • Shows which code paths are not touched by tests.
  • Helps prevent regressions in business logic.
  • Gives a quick signal in CI/CD about test quality.
  • Works well with unit tests and integration tests together.
How to use it
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.jacoco</groupId>
  <artifactId>jacoco-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>0.8.12</version>
  <executions>
    <execution>
      <goals>
        <goal>prepare-agent</goal>
      </goals>
    </execution>
    <execution>
      <id>report</id>
      <phase>test</phase>
      <goals>
        <goal>report</goal>
      </goals>
    </execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>

Run mvn test or mvn verify, then open the JaCoCo report to see covered and uncovered lines, branches, and methods.

Example focus areas

For a Spring Boot service, pay special attention to controller validations, service-layer business rules, exception handlers, repository interactions, and edge conditions like null input or empty responses.

Important caution

High coverage does not automatically mean good tests. A test can hit code without asserting behavior. We should use coverage as a metric, but still write meaningful assertions, boundary tests, and integration tests.

Interview-ready answer

"Code coverage shows how much of the Spring Boot code is exercised by tests. We usually measure it with JaCoCo in Maven or Gradle, review the report in CI, and use it to find untested paths. But coverage alone is not enough; the tests must also verify the correct behavior."

Spring Cloud OpenFeign is a declarative HTTP client. Instead of manually building HTTP requests with URLs, headers, JSON mapping, and response parsing, we declare a Java interface. Spring creates a proxy for it; calling an interface method makes the remote HTTP call.

Why use Feign?

In an order service, we may need the inventory service before accepting an order. With a low-level HTTP client, every service repeats boilerplate. Feign keeps the remote contract close to a Spring MVC controller signature, integrates with service discovery and load balancing, and centralizes timeouts, authentication headers, error decoding, logging, and resilience configuration. It improves readability, but the call is still a slow, fallible network call, not a local Java method call.

How to enable it
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-cloud-starter-openfeign</artifactId>
</dependency>
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableFeignClients
class OrderApplication {}

Keep the Spring Cloud BOM compatible with the application's Spring Boot version. In a multi-module project, @EnableFeignClients(basePackages = "...") can explicitly point to client packages.

Real-world client example
@FeignClient(name = "inventory-service", path = "/api/inventory")
interface InventoryClient {
  @PostMapping("/reservations")
  ReservationResponse reserve(@RequestBody ReserveStockRequest request);

  @GetMapping("/{productId}")
  InventoryResponse get(@PathVariable Long productId);
}

@Service
class OrderService {
  private final InventoryClient inventoryClient;

  OrderService(InventoryClient inventoryClient) {
    this.inventoryClient = inventoryClient;
  }

  @Transactional
  OrderResponse create(CreateOrderRequest request) {
    inventoryClient.reserve(new ReserveStockRequest(request.productId(), request.quantity()));
    return OrderResponse.from(orderRepository.save(Order.from(request)));
  }
}

If inventory-service is registered in Eureka, Consul, or another discovery source, the name is resolved to its available instances. Spring Cloud LoadBalancer chooses one instance for the request. For a fixed external API instead, configure url = "https://partner.example.com" on @FeignClient; then service discovery is not used.

How it works internally
OrderService calls inventoryClient.reserve(...)
  -> Spring-created Feign dynamic proxy intercepts the interface call
  -> Spring MVC annotations become HTTP method, path, headers, and body
  -> LoadBalancer resolves inventory-service to one instance (if discovery is used)
  -> Underlying HTTP client sends the request
  -> Response decoder/Jackson converts JSON to ReservationResponse
  -> Method returns the Java response object or throws an error
Does Feign do load balancing?

Yes, when you use a service name such as @FeignClient(name = "inventory-service") with Spring Cloud discovery and LoadBalancer on the classpath, Spring resolves the service name to one of the available instances and chooses a target instance for the call. If you use a fixed url = "https://partner.example.com", then discovery-based load balancing is not involved.

Can we customize Feign?

Yes. We can customize request headers, timeouts, retries, logging, encoding, decoding, and error handling. We can also switch the underlying HTTP client depending on what the project needs. 

@Configuration
class InventoryFeignConfig {

  @Bean
  RequestInterceptor requestInterceptor() {
    return template -> template.header("X-Client-Id", "order-service");
  }

  @Bean
  ErrorDecoder errorDecoder() {
    return new InventoryErrorDecoder();
  }

  @Bean
  Logger.Level feignLoggerLevel() {
    return Logger.Level.FULL;
  }
}

Common customizations include RequestInterceptor for auth/correlation headers, ErrorDecoder for mapping HTTP errors to domain exceptions, Retryer for retry policy, custom Encoder/Decoder for payload conversion, and per-client config for timeouts.

Timeouts, headers, and errors
spring:
  cloud:
    openfeign:
      client:
        config:
          inventory-service:
            connectTimeout: 1000
            readTimeout: 2000
            loggerLevel: basic

Always set short, business-appropriate connect and read timeouts. Use a RequestInterceptor to add headers such as a correlation ID or service token. Non-2xx responses normally become FeignException; use a custom ErrorDecoder to convert a 404 or 409 into a meaningful domain exception. 

@Bean
RequestInterceptor correlationId() {
  return template -> template.header("X-Trace-Id", MDC.get("traceId"));
}
Production cautions

Do not make long chains of synchronous Feign calls; one slow downstream service can exhaust request threads across the system. Use timeouts, bulkheads/circuit breakers where appropriate, and fallback only when a safe degraded response exists. Retry only idempotent operations or requests protected by an idempotency key. For important order/payment events, asynchronous messaging may be safer than a synchronous Feign call. Never keep a database transaction open while waiting on an unreliable remote service unless the trade-off is explicitly understood.

Interview-ready answer

"Feign is Spring Cloud's declarative HTTP client. We define an interface with Spring MVC annotations, and Spring creates a proxy that converts method calls into HTTP requests. We use it for readable service-to-service communication with discovery, load balancing, headers, timeouts, and error handling, while still treating every call as a remote failure point."

A NullPointerException happens when code dereferences a null reference, such as calling customer.getName() when customer is null. There is no single solution: design null out of normal flows, validate required input, and make genuinely optional values explicit.

Main techniques
TechniqueUse it forExample
Empty collectionsA result with zero itemsReturn List.of(), never null.
Constructor validationRequired dependency/valueObjects.requireNonNull(value).
Guard clauseNullable external inputReject/return before dereferencing.
OptionalGenuinely optional method resultfindById() returns Optional<User>.
Safe utility methodsEquality and collectionsObjects.equals(a, b), CollectionUtils.isEmpty(list).
Bean ValidationAPI/message input@NotNull, @NotBlank, @Valid.
Null Object/defaultA valid no-op behaviorNoOpNotifier instead of a null notifier.
Static analysisBefore runtimeIDE inspections and nullability annotations.
Required values: constructor injection and fail-fast validation
class PaymentService {
  private final PaymentGateway gateway;

  PaymentService(PaymentGateway gateway) {
    this.gateway = Objects.requireNonNull(gateway, "gateway is required");
  }
}

requireNonNull does not eliminate an error; it fails immediately with a useful message, instead of letting an unclear NPE occur later. Constructor injection also ensures required Spring beans are present when the application starts.

Optional values: Optional, defaults, and safe equality
String name = customerRepository.findById(id)
    .map(Customer::getName)
    .orElse("Guest");

boolean sameEmail = Objects.equals(left.email(), right.email());
boolean paid = "PAID".equals(order.status());
List<Order> orders = List.of(); // safe to iterate even when empty

Prefer Optional as a return type, not normally for entity/DTO fields or method parameters. Do not call optional.get() without checking. Use orElseThrow when the value is required for the next business step.

Validate at a Spring Boot boundary
record CreateOrderRequest(@NotNull Long productId,
    @NotNull @Positive Integer quantity, @NotBlank String deliveryAddress) {}

@PostMapping("/api/orders")
OrderResponse create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateOrderRequest request) {
  return orderService.create(request); // required fields have already been checked
}

Invalid API input returns 400 Bad Request before business logic runs. Use database NOT NULL constraints too for required persisted data. Apply this validation at all trust boundaries: HTTP APIs, message consumers, file imports, and configuration.

What not to do

Do not catch NullPointerException as normal control flow or silently default a value that is actually required. Decide the rule: required means reject/fail fast; optional means model it with Optional or a safe default; a no-result collection means return an empty collection. Modern Java has helpful NPE messages, but they help diagnosis rather than prevention.

Interview-ready answer

"I avoid NPE by not using null as a normal result: return empty collections, use constructor injection and requireNonNull for mandatory values, model optional return values with Optional, and validate DTOs at API boundaries. For comparisons I use Objects.equals or a constant on the left. The goal is to make nullability explicit rather than catch NPE later."

Java 8 introduced the java.time API, inspired by Joda-Time. It replaces the difficult parts of legacy java.util.Date, Calendar, and SimpleDateFormat with immutable, thread-safe, clear types that separate a date, time, instant, offset, and time zone.

Legacy API vs Java 8 API
Old API problemJava 8 improvement
Date is mutable and represents an instant despite its name.LocalDate, LocalTime, LocalDateTime, and Instant have explicit meanings.
Calendar is mutable, verbose, and has zero-based months.Readable factories such as LocalDate.of(2026, 8, 8); months use Month.AUGUST or 1-12.
SimpleDateFormat is not thread-safe.DateTimeFormatter is immutable and thread-safe.
Time zones are easy to miss or mix up.ZoneId, ZoneOffset, ZonedDateTime, and OffsetDateTime make zone/offset explicit.
Date arithmetic is error-prone.Fluent plus, minus, with, Period, and Duration operations.
Main classes
ClassUseExample
LocalDateDate without time/zoneBirthday, invoice due date.
LocalTimeTime without date/zoneShop opens at 09:00.
LocalDateTimeDate and time without zoneLocal appointment input; not ideal for a global event timestamp.
InstantOne point on the UTC timelineAudit timestamps, event time, database storage.
ZonedDateTimeDate/time plus region rulesMeeting at 09:00 in Asia/Kolkata, including daylight-saving rules where relevant.
OffsetDateTimeDate/time plus numeric offsetREST timestamp such as 2026-08-08T10:00:00+05:30.
DurationTime-based amount30 seconds, 2 hours.
PeriodDate-based amount2 years, 3 months, 5 days.
DateTimeFormatterParse and formatAPI or display format.
ZoneId / ClockZone rules / controllable current timeTimezone conversion and deterministic tests.
Most useful methods
LocalDate today = LocalDate.now();
LocalDate dueDate = LocalDate.of(2026, Month.AUGUST, 8);
LocalDate parsed = LocalDate.parse("2026-08-08");

LocalDate nextWeek = today.plusWeeks(1);
LocalDate previousMonth = today.minusMonths(1);
LocalDate monthEnd = today.with(TemporalAdjusters.lastDayOfMonth());
boolean overdue = dueDate.isBefore(today);
long days = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(today, dueDate);

Instant createdAt = Instant.now();
ZonedDateTime indiaTime = createdAt.atZone(ZoneId.of("Asia/Kolkata"));
Instant sameMoment = indiaTime.toInstant();

Duration timeout = Duration.ofSeconds(30);
Period subscription = Period.ofMonths(1);
DateTimeFormatter formatter = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd-MM-uuuu HH:mm");
String display = indiaTime.format(formatter);

Common static factories are now(), of(...), parse(...), and from(...). Common instance operations are plus..., minus..., with(...), atZone(...), toInstant(), format(...), isBefore(...), isAfter(...), and until(...). Each operation returns a new value; it never changes the original object.

Why it is safe in multi-threaded applications

Most java.time value types, including LocalDate, Instant, ZonedDateTime, and DateTimeFormatter, are immutable. Two threads can safely share one formatter or date-time instance because no method changes its internal state. The old SimpleDateFormat mutates internal calendar/parse state, so sharing one instance between request threads can produce wrong dates or parsing exceptions. 

// Safe as a shared static field: DateTimeFormatter is immutable.
private static final DateTimeFormatter API_FORMAT =
    DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("uuuu-MM-dd HH:mm:ss");

String value = LocalDateTime.now().format(API_FORMAT);
Practical rules

Store an Instant (or UTC timestamp) for events that occur at one global moment, then convert to a user's ZoneId for display. Use LocalDate for date-only business rules such as birthdays. Avoid using LocalDateTime for a globally meaningful timestamp unless the zone is separately known. Inject a Clock into business services so tests can use a fixed time. 

class SubscriptionService {
  private final Clock clock;
  SubscriptionService(Clock clock) { this.clock = clock; }
  boolean expired(LocalDate expiryDate) { return expiryDate.isBefore(LocalDate.now(clock)); }
}
Interview-ready answer

"Java 8 introduced java.time to replace mutable, confusing legacy date APIs. It provides clear types for date, time, instant, zones, durations, and formatting, plus fluent immutable arithmetic. Its key concurrency benefit is that java.time classes and DateTimeFormatter are immutable and thread-safe, unlike Calendar and SimpleDateFormat."

SQL databases model related data in tables and use SQL, joins, constraints, and transactions. NoSQL is a family of non-relational databases optimized for specific access patterns such as flexible documents, ultra-fast key lookups, distributed writes, or graph traversal. The right choice comes from data shape, consistency rules, queries, scale, and operational needs, not from which database is more popular.

How to decide
QuestionPrefer SQLPrefer NoSQL
Data relationshipMany related entities and joins: order, payment, invoice, customer.Aggregate/document-shaped data, graph relationships, or simple key lookups.
ConsistencyStrict multi-row transactional correctness and constraints are central.Per-record/document consistency or eventual consistency is acceptable for the chosen use case.
SchemaStable, structured schema with governance and reporting.Rapidly changing or heterogeneous attributes, such as product specifications.
Query patternAd hoc reports, joins, aggregates, relational filters.Known high-volume access patterns designed around keys, partitions, documents, or graph edges.
ScaleVertical scale plus replicas/partitioning is enough.Very high write/read throughput or natural horizontal partitioning is required.
Four main NoSQL types
TypeExamplesBest fit
DocumentMongoDB, CouchbaseJSON-like aggregates: product catalog, content, user profiles.
Key-valueRedis, DynamoDBCache, sessions, rate limits, feature flags, simple high-speed lookup.
Wide-columnCassandra, HBaseHuge write-heavy, time-series/event data with known partition-key queries.
GraphNeo4j, Amazon NeptuneRelationship traversal: fraud rings, social connections, recommendations.
Real e-commerce example: use both
Checkout and payments       -> PostgreSQL/MySQL
  Reason: ACID transaction, foreign keys, audit, stock/order/payment consistency

Product catalog             -> MongoDB
  Reason: each product has different JSON attributes (size, RAM, color, warranty)

Login sessions and cart cache -> Redis
  Reason: millisecond key lookup, TTL, atomic counters/rate limits

Clickstream / IoT events    -> Cassandra or a streaming store
  Reason: very high append rate and time/partition-based queries

Customer recommendation graph -> Neo4j
  Reason: efficiently traverse customer -> viewed -> product relationships

This is called polyglot persistence. The checkout system should not move to a document database merely because the catalog uses one. A product's flexible description and an order's payment integrity have different requirements.

Advantages of NoSQL

NoSQL can give flexible schema evolution, natural storage for nested JSON, low-latency key access, horizontal scale-out, high write throughput, and models tailored to the query. It can reduce costly joins by storing an aggregate together. The trade-off is that denormalization can duplicate data and shifts consistency, integrity, and query design responsibility to the application and database-specific model. NoSQL does not automatically mean "no transactions" or "eventual consistency": capabilities differ by product; for example, many document databases support transactions, but with different trade-offs.

Spring Boot implementation: MongoDB catalog
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-mongodb</artifactId>
</dependency>
spring:
  data:
    mongodb:
      uri: mongodb://localhost:27017/catalog
@Document("products")
record Product(@Id String id, String name, BigDecimal price,
    Map<String, Object> attributes) {}

interface ProductRepository extends MongoRepository<Product, String> {
  List<Product> findByNameContainingIgnoreCase(String name);
}

@Service
class CatalogService {
  private final ProductRepository products;
  CatalogService(ProductRepository products) { this.products = products; }
  Product save(Product product) { return products.save(product); }
}

Mongo stores a product as one document, so a laptop can have RAM and CPU fields while a shirt has size and fabric fields. Index the exact fields your application queries, such as category, brand, or attributes.ram; a flexible schema without indexes will still be slow.

Implementation cautions

Start from access patterns and design keys, partitions, and indexes before choosing a NoSQL database. Avoid unbounded documents, hot partition keys, and cross-service distributed transactions. Keep a clear source of truth, design idempotent writes, back up and monitor the database, and use SQL for reporting and relational integrity when those are primary needs. Redis is usually a cache/session store, not a replacement for an order system of record.

Interview-ready answer

"I choose SQL when relationships, joins, constraints, and strong transactional consistency drive the use case, such as payments and orders. I choose a NoSQL type based on the access pattern: MongoDB for flexible documents, Redis for cache/session lookup, Cassandra for high-volume partitioned writes, and Neo4j for graph traversal. In real systems we commonly use both, with each database owning the data it is best suited to manage."

Normalization organizes relational data into related tables to reduce duplicate data and avoid insert, update, and delete anomalies. Denormalization deliberately adds selected duplicate or precomputed data to make important reads faster and simpler. Normalize first for correctness; denormalize later only for a measured read/performance need.

Why normalization matters
Bad single table
order_id | customer_name | customer_email | product_name | product_price | quantity
101      | Ravi          | ravi@mail.com  | Laptop       | 70000         | 1
102      | Ravi          | ravi@mail.com  | Mouse        | 1000          | 2

If Ravi changes email, every past and future order row must be updated.
Missing one row creates inconsistent data: this is an update anomaly.

A normalized design separates this into customers, orders, products, and order_items, linked with primary and foreign keys.

Normal forms in simple terms
FormSimple ruleExample fix
1NFEach column has one atomic value; no repeating groups.Do not store "Laptop, Mouse" in one order column. Store each item as a separate order_items row.
2NFBe in 1NF, and every non-key column depends on the whole primary key.In order_items(order_id, product_id), product name depends only on product_id, so move it to products.
3NFBe in 2NF, and non-key columns must not depend on another non-key column.Move customer_zip -> city out if city is determined by zip, not directly by customer ID.
BCNFEvery determinant must be a candidate key.Use when 3NF still allows a dependency that can cause redundancy in special multi-candidate-key cases.
4NFRemove independent multi-valued facts.A student with many hobbies and languages needs separate tables; otherwise combinations multiply unnecessarily.
5NFRemove rare join dependencies that cannot be reconstructed safely from smaller tables.Mainly used in complex relationship models; uncommon in normal application tables.

In most application interviews and day-to-day schemas, understanding 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF well is enough. BCNF and higher forms are more specialized refinements.

Normalized order schema
CREATE TABLE customers (
  customer_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  email VARCHAR(150) NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
  created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(order_id),
  product_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES products(product_id),
  quantity INT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);
What is denormalization?

Denormalization intentionally copies a value or stores an aggregate so a frequent read avoids expensive joins or calculations. Examples include order_total in orders, customer_name_snapshot on an invoice, a precomputed daily-sales table, a search index, a materialized view, or a read model built from events. 

-- Deliberately duplicated read/snapshot fields
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN customer_name_snapshot VARCHAR(100);
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN order_total DECIMAL(12,2);

-- Reads the order history page without joining and summing every item each time.
SELECT order_id, customer_name_snapshot, order_total, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = :customerId
ORDER BY created_at DESC;

The snapshot is often correct for invoices: if Ravi later changes his profile name, historical invoices should still show the name at the time of purchase. This is a valid business reason for duplication, not an accidental design flaw.

When denormalization is used most

Use it most often in read-heavy systems: dashboards, reporting, analytics/data warehouses, catalog/search pages, feeds, and high-traffic APIs where profiling shows joins or aggregates are the bottleneck. It is also common for historical snapshots and CQRS read models. Keep the normalized transactional schema as the source of truth, then refresh denormalized data with application logic, database triggers only when carefully controlled, batch jobs, materialized-view refreshes, or events.

Trade-offs and rule of thumb

Denormalization improves read speed but increases storage, write cost, and the risk of stale or inconsistent copies. Every duplicate field needs a clear ownership and update strategy. Do not denormalize only to avoid learning joins; first add the correct indexes, inspect the query plan, and measure. For write-heavy payment/inventory data, favor normalization and integrity. For a slow, repeatedly-read dashboard, a denormalized summary is often the right solution.

Interview-ready answer

"Normalization reduces redundancy and anomalies by splitting data into correctly related tables. 1NF makes values atomic, 2NF removes partial dependency, and 3NF removes transitive dependency. I use denormalization selectively for measured read-heavy needs such as dashboards, reports, search, and historical snapshots, while keeping a normalized source of truth and a clear synchronization strategy."

The correct answer is: it depends on the database. TRUNCATE removes all rows very quickly while keeping the table structure, but databases implement its transaction behavior differently. Never assume it is reversible without checking the database you are using.

Rollback behavior by database
DatabaseCan TRUNCATE roll back?Why
PostgreSQLYes, inside an uncommitted transaction.TRUNCATE is transactional DDL in PostgreSQL.
SQL ServerYes, inside an explicit transaction.The operation is logged sufficiently for transaction rollback.
MySQLUsually no.TRUNCATE is DDL and causes an implicit commit; it cannot be undone with ROLLBACK.
OracleNo.TRUNCATE is DDL and commits implicitly, so rollback cannot restore rows.
Examples
-- PostgreSQL: rows return because the transaction was not committed.
BEGIN;
TRUNCATE TABLE audit_logs;
ROLLBACK;

-- MySQL/Oracle: TRUNCATE performs implicit DDL commit.
START TRANSACTION;
TRUNCATE TABLE audit_logs;
ROLLBACK; -- does not restore the rows
TRUNCATE vs DELETE
PointDELETETRUNCATE
RowsCan remove selected rows with WHERE.Removes all rows; no WHERE.
Logging/performanceTypically logs row-level deletes; slower for huge tables.Usually deallocates data pages; much faster for clearing a table.
RollbackNormally rolls back in a transaction.Database-specific: check the table above.
Identity/sequenceUsually does not reset identity.Often resets identity/auto-increment, but exact behavior is database-specific.
DELETE triggersUsually fires row-level delete triggers.Typically does not fire delete triggers.
ConstraintsWorks subject to normal foreign-key rules.May be blocked when other tables reference the table through foreign keys.
When to use which

Use DELETE ... WHERE ... when removing specific data, when delete triggers/audit behavior is required, or when you need predictable transaction rollback across databases. Use TRUNCATE only when intentionally clearing a whole staging, temporary, test, or archive table and the database's rollback, identity, trigger, and foreign-key behavior has been confirmed. Production use should be protected by backup, approval, and an explicit operational procedure.

Interview-ready answer

"TRUNCATE rollback is database-dependent. PostgreSQL and SQL Server can roll it back inside an open transaction, while MySQL and Oracle treat it as implicitly committed DDL, so rollback cannot restore the rows. DELETE is row-based, supports WHERE, and is the safer choice when selective removal or portable transaction behavior is needed."

Zipkin is a distributed tracing backend and UI. It stores spans, shows the timeline of one request across services, and helps us find where latency or failure happened.

Spring Cloud Sleuth was the Spring Boot auto-configuration and instrumentation layer for distributed tracing. It automatically created and propagated trace/span context, correlated logs, and sent tracing data to systems like Zipkin.

Why they were used
  • Track one request across gateway, services, database, and downstream calls.
  • Correlate logs with trace IDs for faster debugging.
  • Visualize which hop caused the delay or failure.
  • Reduce manual tracing code by auto-instrumenting common Spring components.
Important modern note

Spring Cloud Sleuth does not work with Spring Boot 3.x onward. Its core moved to Micrometer Tracing, so in new Boot 3+ applications we use Micrometer Tracing plus an exporter/backend such as Zipkin, Jaeger, or Tempo.

Real-world example

If a checkout request is slow, Sleuth-style tracing would show spans for API Gateway, Order Service, Payment Service, and Inventory Service. Zipkin would display the waterfall timeline so we can see which service consumed the most time.

Interview-ready answer

"Zipkin is the tracing backend/UI that stores and displays request traces. Sleuth was the Spring auto-instrumentation layer that created trace IDs, span IDs, and log correlation and sent that data to Zipkin. In Spring Boot 3, Sleuth has been replaced by Micrometer Tracing."

The best choice is structured JSON logging. It makes logs easy to search, parse, filter, and correlate with traceId, spanId, service name, environment, and instance id. In Spring Boot, a common default choice is the Logstash JSON format; if your log platform expects ECS, you can use that instead.

Why JSON is best
  • Works well with ELK, Loki, Splunk, CloudWatch, and most log pipelines.
  • Preserves key/value fields without brittle text parsing.
  • Lets you search by traceId or spanId across services.
  • Makes dashboards and alerts easier to build from logs.
Recommended fields
  • timestamp
  • level
  • service or application
  • env
  • instanceId
  • traceId
  • spanId
  • business ids such as orderId or userId when safe
Spring Boot example
spring:
  application:
    name: order-service

logging:
  structured:
    format:
      console: logstash

With Micrometer Tracing enabled, Spring Boot automatically puts traceId and spanId into the logging context, so they appear in structured logs without manual string concatenation.

Example log line
{
  "@timestamp": "2026-08-09T10:15:00.111+05:30",
  "service": "order-service",
  "env": "prod",
  "instanceId": "order-service-7d87f",
  "traceId": "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736",
  "spanId": "00f067aa0ba902b7",
  "level": "INFO",
  "message": "Order created"
}
When plain text is okay

Plain text logs are fine for local development, but they are harder to query and correlate in production. For microservices, JSON is the safer interview answer because it works much better with distributed tracing and centralized log aggregation.

Interview-ready answer

"The best log format for tracing in microservices is structured JSON, usually Logstash JSON or ECS in Spring Boot. It lets us include traceId, spanId, service name, and environment as searchable fields, so logs can be correlated with distributed traces and centralized logging tools."

Distributed tracing tracks one user request as it moves across multiple services. It shows the full path, timing, and parent-child relationship of each operation so we can find where time was spent or where the request failed.

Core ideas
  • traceId identifies the whole end-to-end request.
  • spanId identifies one operation inside that request.
  • Parent and child spans form a timeline across gateway, service, database, and downstream calls.
Why we need it

In a monolith, one log file may be enough. In microservices, the request can cross gateway, order, payment, inventory, and notification services. Without tracing, it is hard to tell which hop was slow or which service caused the failure.

How it works
Client request
  -> API Gateway
  -> order-service
  -> payment-service
  -> inventory-service

traceId stays the same across the request
spanId changes for each hop or operation

The trace context is propagated through headers such as traceparent. In Spring Boot, we usually use Micrometer Tracing with OpenTelemetry so the trace context moves automatically across HTTP and supported clients.

What we configure
  • Spring Boot Actuator for exposure and management endpoints.
  • Micrometer Tracing or OpenTelemetry instrumentation.
  • Exporter such as OTLP to send traces to Tempo, Jaeger, or Zipkin.
  • Structured logs that include the same traceId and spanId.
  • Feign/HTTP client propagation so downstream calls keep the same trace.
Real-world example

If checkout is slow, tracing can show that the payment-service span took 3 seconds, while the order service and inventory service were fast. Then we can open the same traceId in logs and see the exact timeout or dependency error.

Interview-ready answer

"Distributed tracing follows one request across multiple microservices using traceId and spanId. It helps us find where latency or failure occurred. In Spring Boot, we implement it with Actuator, Micrometer Tracing, OpenTelemetry, and a backend like Jaeger, Zipkin, or Tempo."

OpenTelemetry is an open standard and toolkit for collecting traces, metrics, and logs in a vendor-neutral way. It gives us a common API, SDK, and data model so we can instrument the application once and export telemetry to different backends.

Why it is used
  • One instrumentation standard for many observability backends.
  • Avoids being locked into a single vendor's tracing library.
  • Propagates context across HTTP, messaging, and service boundaries.
  • Makes it easier to switch or add backends like Jaeger, Tempo, Zipkin, Prometheus, or cloud tools.
What it overcomes from older approaches
  • Older tracing often used different agents or APIs per tool, so migration was painful.
  • Logs, metrics, and traces were often disconnected instead of using a shared model.
  • Propagation of trace context was not standardized across frameworks and clients.
  • Teams had to rewrite instrumentation when changing observability vendors.
Real-world example

In a Spring Boot microservice, OpenTelemetry can capture an incoming HTTP request, create child spans for DB and downstream service calls, and export the data through OTLP to Jaeger or Tempo. If the company later changes the backend, the app instrumentation usually stays the same.

How it fits with Spring Boot

Spring Boot commonly uses Micrometer Tracing or OpenTelemetry instrumentation underneath. Actuator exposes management endpoints, OpenTelemetry carries the trace context, and an exporter sends the data to the chosen backend.

Interview-ready answer

"OpenTelemetry is a vendor-neutral standard for traces, metrics, and logs. We use it to instrument once and export to different observability tools. It solves the older problem of tool-specific agents and inconsistent trace propagation across services."

Observability is the ability to understand what is happening inside a system from the data it emits. In practice, it means using metrics, logs, and traces together so we can ask new questions during an incident and still find the answer.

Observability vs monitoring
Monitoring Observability
Checks known metrics and alerts, such as CPU, error rate, and latency. Lets us explore unknown root causes using logs, metrics, and traces together.
Answers "Is something wrong?" Answers "What happened and why?"
Usually rule-based alerting and dashboards. Correlated data for debugging a request across services.

A simple way to remember it: monitoring tells you a symptom exists, while observability helps you investigate the cause.

How we implement it
  • Expose health and metrics from Spring Boot Actuator.
  • Collect metrics with Micrometer and export them to Prometheus.
  • Visualize and alert with Grafana.
  • Write structured logs with shared correlation fields like traceId and spanId.
  • Ship logs to a central system such as Loki or ELK.
  • Propagate distributed traces with Micrometer Tracing and OpenTelemetry.
Real-world example

If checkout latency rises, monitoring tells us p95 is high. Observability lets us open the trace, identify the slow payment call, and then search the payment-service logs using the same traceId to see the exact error.

Interview-ready answer

"Monitoring checks known health signals and raises alerts. Observability goes further and helps us ask new questions about the system by correlating logs, metrics, and traces. In Spring Boot, we implement it with Actuator, Micrometer, Prometheus, Grafana, centralized logs, and distributed tracing with Micrometer Tracing/OpenTelemetry."

End-to-end observability combines metrics, logs, and traces. Metrics answer "is the service unhealthy?"; logs answer "what happened?"; a trace answers "which request path was slow or failed across services?". Health checks and alerts complete the picture.

Roles of the main tools
ToolRoleExample question it answers
Spring Boot ActuatorExposes health, metrics, Prometheus scrape endpoint, and management endpoints.Is this instance alive, ready, or using too many DB connections?
MicrometerMetrics/observation facade; records JVM, HTTP, datasource, and custom meters.What is order API p95 latency and payment failure count?
PrometheusPulls, stores, and queries time-series metrics; evaluates alert rules.Did 5xx rate rise in the last five minutes?
GrafanaDashboards, alert visualization, and correlation across data sources.Can I see latency, logs, and traces for order-service together?
Loki / ELK / SplunkCentral log aggregation, indexing, retention, and search.What did this exact order request log in each service?
Tempo / Jaeger / ZipkinStores and displays distributed traces.Which downstream service made checkout take 4 seconds?
One request across microservices
Client request
  -> API Gateway (traceId: 4bf92f...)
  -> order-service
  -> payment-service
  -> inventory-service

Every service writes structured logs containing traceId and spanId.
Each service emits metrics through Micrometer.
Trace context travels in the HTTP traceparent header.

Metrics: service -> /actuator/prometheus -> Prometheus -> Grafana
Logs:    stdout JSON -> Fluent Bit/Promtail -> Loki or Elasticsearch -> Grafana/Kibana
Traces:  Micrometer Tracing -> OpenTelemetry OTLP -> Tempo/Jaeger -> Grafana
1. Add Spring Boot dependencies
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
  <artifactId>micrometer-registry-prometheus</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
  <artifactId>micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.opentelemetry</groupId>
  <artifactId>opentelemetry-exporter-otlp</artifactId>
</dependency>
2. Configure Actuator, metrics, tracing, and JSON logs
spring:
  application:
    name: order-service

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,metrics,prometheus
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true
  tracing:
    sampling:
      probability: 1.0 # use a lower, deliberate sampling rate in high-volume production
  otlp:
    tracing:
      endpoint: http://otel-collector:4318/v1/traces

logging:
  structured:
    format:
      console: logstash

Actuator exposes /actuator/health, /actuator/metrics, and /actuator/prometheus. Keep management endpoints private or protected; never expose sensitive endpoints publicly just to make monitoring convenient. Containerized services should usually write JSON logs to standard output, not manage local log files.

3. Add business metrics with Micrometer
@Service
class OrderService {
  private final Counter ordersCreated;

  OrderService(MeterRegistry registry) {
    this.ordersCreated = Counter.builder("orders.created")
        .description("Number of successfully created orders")
        .register(registry);
  }

  OrderResponse create(CreateOrderRequest request) {
    OrderResponse response = createOrder(request);
    ordersCreated.increment();
    return response;
  }
}

Use low-cardinality metric tags such as service, endpoint, method, and outcome. Do not use user ID, order ID, email, request ID, or trace ID as metric tags: each unique value creates a costly new time series. Put those identifiers in logs and traces instead.

4. Configure Prometheus and Grafana
# prometheus.yml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: order-service
    metrics_path: /actuator/prometheus
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["order-service:8080"]

In Kubernetes, prefer Prometheus service discovery or a ServiceMonitor rather than static targets. Configure Prometheus as a Grafana data source, import/build dashboards for request rate, error rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, JVM heap/GC, CPU, thread count, Hikari connection pool, Kafka lag, and business counters. Alert on user symptoms: sustained error rate, high p95 latency, unavailable readiness, or exhausted DB connections.

5. Configure centralized log aggregation

A log aggregator collects each container's standard output. In Kubernetes, deploy Fluent Bit, Promtail, or Filebeat as a DaemonSet; it enriches every log with pod, namespace, node, and container metadata, then sends it to Loki, Elasticsearch, Splunk, or a cloud logging platform. Grafana reads Loki; Kibana commonly reads Elasticsearch. Applications should emit structured JSON and must never log passwords, tokens, or full sensitive personal data. 

{
  "timestamp": "2026-08-08T10:15:00Z",
  "service": "order-service",
  "level": "INFO",
  "traceId": "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736",
  "spanId": "00f067aa0ba902b7",
  "orderId": "ORD-101",
  "message": "Order created"
}
6. Distributed tracing and finding one request

A traceId identifies one end-to-end business request. A spanId identifies one operation inside it, such as the order controller, SQL query, or payment HTTP call. Parent/child spans form a waterfall timeline. Micrometer Tracing creates and propagates context; OpenTelemetry exports it through OTLP to Tempo, Jaeger, or Zipkin. The standard traceparent HTTP header carries the context to downstream services. 

Slow checkout investigation
  1. Grafana alert shows p95 POST /orders latency is high.
  2. Open the Tempo/Jaeger trace from the affected request or traceId.
  3. Waterfall shows payment-service span consumed 3.5 seconds.
  4. Click the payment-service logs filtered by the same traceId.
  5. Find a payment-provider timeout and correlate its error count metric.
  6. Fix/scale/timeout-tune the dependency, then confirm metrics recover.
Production checklist

Set service name and environment consistently; propagate trace context through HTTP, messaging, and Feign clients; protect Actuator; define log retention and PII masking; sample traces deliberately; avoid high-cardinality metric labels; create SLO-based alerts; and test dashboards during an incident simulation. Logs, metrics, and traces are complementary: do not try to use one as a replacement for the others.

Interview-ready answer

"In Spring Boot I enable Actuator and Micrometer, expose Prometheus metrics, scrape them with Prometheus, and use Grafana for dashboards and alerts. Services write JSON logs to stdout, and a Fluent Bit/Promtail agent ships them to Loki or ELK. For a request across services, Micrometer Tracing propagates traceId and spanId and exports spans through OpenTelemetry to Tempo or Jaeger. During an incident I start with a metric alert, open the trace to locate the slow service, and use the shared traceId to see its exact logs."

A lambda can throw an exception, but what it may throw is controlled by the abstract method of its target functional interface. An unchecked exception such as IllegalArgumentException or NullPointerException is always allowed. A checked exception such as IOException is allowed only when that functional-interface method declares it with throws.

Unchecked exceptions: allowed
List<String> names = List.of("Ravi", "", "Anu");

names.forEach(name -> {
  if (name.isBlank()) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("Name cannot be blank");
  }
  System.out.println(name);
});

Consumer.accept(...) does not declare checked exceptions, but unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException, so Java permits them. The stream/loop stops and the exception propagates to the caller unless it is caught.

Checked exceptions: why this does not compile
List<Path> files = List.of(Path.of("a.txt"));

files.forEach(path -> Files.readString(path));
// Compile error: Files.readString throws checked IOException,
// but Consumer<Path>.accept does not declare throws IOException.
Option 1: handle it inside the lambda
files.forEach(path -> {
  try {
    String content = Files.readString(path);
    process(content);
  } catch (IOException ex) {
    log.warn("Could not read {}", path, ex);
    // Decide deliberately: skip, collect an error, or stop.
  }
});

Use this when one bad item can be skipped or recorded while the remaining items should continue. Do not silently swallow the error; log, return a result containing failures, or send it to a retry/dead-letter flow according to the business requirement.

Option 2: wrap a checked exception
files.forEach(path -> {
  try {
    process(Files.readString(path));
  } catch (IOException ex) {
    throw new UncheckedIOException("Failed to read " + path, ex);
  }
});

This keeps the stream API clean and fails the whole operation. At a higher application boundary, catch UncheckedIOException and map it to an API error or retry decision. Preserve the original exception as the cause; never discard it.

Option 3: use a custom throwing functional interface
@FunctionalInterface
interface ThrowingFunction<T, R> {
  R apply(T value) throws Exception;
}

static String readFile(Path path) throws IOException {
  return Files.readString(path);
}

ThrowingFunction<Path, String> reader = MyFiles::readFile;
String content = reader.apply(Path.of("a.txt")); // caller must handle Exception

This is useful in your own APIs when checked failure is part of the contract. Standard Java streams use Function, Consumer, and Supplier, which do not declare checked exceptions, so a small adapter is still needed before using this directly in a stream.

Method references follow the same rule

A method reference such as Files::readString is allowed only when the receiving functional interface permits its checked exception. It works with a custom ThrowingFunction but not with Function<Path, String>. This is not a lambda limitation; it is Java's checked-exception type checking.

Spring Boot advice

In a service, convert infrastructure exceptions to meaningful domain/application exceptions at the right layer and handle them with @RestControllerAdvice. For parallel streams, avoid assuming all errors are easy to handle per item; exceptions can be wrapped and processing is not a replacement for a managed executor or resilient message workflow.

Interview-ready answer

"A lambda can always throw unchecked exceptions. It can throw a checked exception only if the target functional interface method declares that exception. Since standard stream interfaces do not declare checked exceptions, I either handle it inside the lambda, wrap it in an appropriate unchecked exception such as UncheckedIOException, or use a custom throwing functional interface when checked failure is part of my own API contract."

No. A constructor cannot be static, final, or abstract. A constructor is used to create an object, so it belongs to an instance-creation flow, not to a class behavior that can be inherited or overridden.

Why not static?

static means class-level and callable without creating an object first. A constructor exists specifically to create the object, so making it static would defeat its purpose.

Why not final?

final prevents overriding, but constructors are never inherited or overridden in the first place. So final is meaningless on a constructor.

Why not abstract?

abstract means "must be implemented by a subclass." A constructor is not inherited and cannot be called polymorphically, so an abstract constructor does not make sense.

Invalid example
class User {
  static User() { }   // compile error
  final User(int id) { } // compile error
  abstract User();    // compile error
}
What you can do instead

Use a private constructor for utility classes or factory methods, and use static factory methods like of() or getInstance() when you want controlled object creation. 

class UserFactory {
  private UserFactory() { }

  static User create() {
    return new User();
  }
}
Interview-ready answer

"No, a constructor cannot be static, final, or abstract. It is only for object creation. Static is for class members, final is for preventing overriding, and abstract is for methods that subclasses must implement."

A private constructor cannot be called from outside the class. That means other classes cannot directly create objects with new. It is usually used for singleton classes, utility classes, or factory-based creation.

What it changes
  • External code cannot instantiate the class directly.
  • The class can still create objects from inside its own methods.
  • Subclasses cannot call that constructor, so inheritance is restricted unless another accessible constructor exists.
Example: utility class
public final class MathUtils {
  private MathUtils() {
    // no instances allowed
  }

  public static int add(int a, int b) {
    return a + b;
  }
}

Here the private constructor prevents someone from writing new MathUtils(). The class is meant to be used only through static methods.

Example: singleton / factory
public class AppConfig {
  private static final AppConfig INSTANCE = new AppConfig();

  private AppConfig() { }

  public static AppConfig getInstance() {
    return INSTANCE;
  }
}

This gives controlled object creation. The constructor is private, but the class exposes a public method to return the one allowed instance.

Interview-ready answer

"A private constructor blocks direct object creation from outside the class. It is used when we want to control instantiation, like in utility classes, singleton patterns, or factory methods."

In normal Java control flow, finally runs after try or catch, even when an exception happens. But there are a few rare cases where it may not execute.

Common cases where it may not run
  • The JVM process exits abruptly, such as System.exit() or Runtime.halt().
  • The JVM crashes, is forcibly terminated, or the machine loses power.
  • The thread is killed in an unsafe external way before the block can complete.
  • A daemon thread may be stopped when the JVM shuts down, so its finally block is not guaranteed to finish.
Example
try {
  System.out.println("Inside try");
  System.exit(0);
} finally {
  System.out.println("This will not print");
}

System.exit(0) terminates the JVM before finally can run. That is why shutdown hooks or explicit cleanup are needed for critical resources.

Interview-ready answer

"Usually finally always runs, but it may not execute if the JVM exits abruptly, crashes, or is forcibly stopped. In normal exception flow it does execute, so I use it for cleanup like closing resources or releasing locks."

Java streams are mostly lazy. Intermediate operations such as map(), filter(), and sorted() do not run immediately. They build a pipeline and wait until a terminal operation like collect(), forEach(), or reduce() starts the execution.

Lazy behavior
Stream<String> stream = List.of("a", "bb", "ccc").stream()
    .filter(s -> {
      System.out.println("filtering " + s);
      return s.length() > 1;
    })
    .map(String::toUpperCase);

System.out.println("Pipeline built");
List<String> result = stream.collect(Collectors.toList());

Nothing runs when the pipeline is created. The work happens only when the terminal operation executes. This is why streams can short-circuit efficiently with findFirst() or anyMatch().

What is eager?

The terminal operation is effectively eager because it consumes the stream and triggers the whole pipeline. Some operations such as sorted() or distinct() may also need to buffer data internally before they can produce results, but the stream API still executes them only when the pipeline is consumed.

Real-world example

Think of an online order filter: you can keep adding conditions on paper lazily, but the real work starts only when you press Search. In code, that means the pipeline is prepared first and executed only at the terminal step.

Interview-ready answer

"Java streams are lazy for intermediate operations and eager at the terminal operation. The pipeline is assembled first, and execution starts only when a terminal operation consumes it."

peek() is mainly used for debugging or observing elements as they flow through a stream pipeline. It lets you look at intermediate values without changing them.

Example
List<String> names = List.of("ravi", "anu", "kiran");

List<String> result = names.stream()
    .filter(name -> name.length() > 3)
    .peek(name -> System.out.println("After filter: " + name))
    .map(String::toUpperCase)
    .peek(name -> System.out.println("After map: " + name))
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

In this example, peek() prints the values passing through each stage, but it does not transform the stream. The actual data change happens only in map().

When to use

Use it for logging, debugging, or tracing a pipeline during development. In production code, avoid using it for business logic because it is meant to be a side-effect helper, not a transformation step.

Important caution

peek() runs only when the stream is consumed by a terminal operation. If there is no terminal operation, nothing happens. Also, do not rely on it for critical side effects in parallel streams because execution order may be surprising.

Interview-ready answer

"peek() is a debugging and inspection method in streams. It helps us observe intermediate values without modifying them, and it should not be used for business logic."

HashMap is not thread-safe. If two threads modify it at the same time, you can get lost updates, inconsistent reads, corrupted internal state, or even an infinite loop in older JVM scenarios while resizing or rehashing.

What can go wrong
  • One thread overwrites the other thread's put/update, so data is lost.
  • A reader may see partially updated or stale data.
  • During resize, concurrent structural changes can corrupt bucket links.
  • Iteration may throw ConcurrentModificationException if the map is structurally changed while iterating.
Example
Map<String, Integer> map = new HashMap<>();

Runnable task = () -> {
  for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
    map.put("count", map.getOrDefault("count", 0) + 1);
  }
};

new Thread(task).start();
new Thread(task).start();

This code is unsafe because the read-modify-write sequence is not atomic. The final value can be smaller than expected, and the map itself is not protected from concurrent structural updates.

How to fix it

Use ConcurrentHashMap for shared access, or synchronize access with a lock if the entire update sequence must be atomic. For counters, prefer AtomicInteger or LongAdder instead of manual get plus put.

Interview-ready answer

"If two threads modify a HashMap concurrently, the result is undefined because HashMap is not thread-safe. You can lose updates, see inconsistent data, or corrupt the map. For shared concurrent access, use ConcurrentHashMap or proper synchronization."

private controls access from other classes, not thread safety. Two threads can still read and write the same private field through the same object, and without synchronization there is no guarantee that one thread will immediately see another thread's update.

Why this happens
  • Visibility: one thread may keep a cached value and not see the latest write.
  • Atomicity: operations like count++ are read, modify, then write, not a single step.
  • Ordering: the JVM and CPU may reorder instructions unless you create a happens-before relationship.
Example
class Counter {
  private int count = 0;

  void increment() {
    count++; // not atomic
  }

  int getCount() {
    return count;
  }
}

Even though count is private, two threads calling increment() can still lose updates because both may read the same old value before either write completes.

How to make it safe

Use synchronized, volatile for visibility only, locks, or atomic classes such as AtomicInteger depending on the problem. For compound updates, volatile alone is not enough because it does not make the operation atomic.

Interview-ready answer

"Private does not mean thread-safe. A private field can still be accessed by multiple threads through the same object, and without synchronization they may see stale values or lose updates because of visibility and atomicity issues."

The full SQL question bank is available as a collapsed section below. It includes joins, aggregates, constraints, ranking, sales analytics, customer/order scenarios, and extra real-world interview cases.

SQL joins are used to combine rows from two or more tables based on related columns. In real projects, joins are used for reports like customers with orders, employees with departments, products with sales, and users with roles.

Sample tables used in examples
customers
---------
customer_id | customer_name
1           | Ravi
2           | Anu
3           | Kiran

orders
------
order_id | customer_id | order_amount
101      | 1           | 500
102      | 1           | 800
103      | 2           | 300
1. INNER JOIN

INNER JOIN returns only matching records from both tables. If a customer has no order, that customer will not appear. 

SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.customer_name,
       o.order_id,
       o.order_amount
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

Real-world use: show customers who have placed orders.

2. LEFT JOIN / LEFT OUTER JOIN

LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table and matching rows from the right table. If no match exists, right-side columns become NULL. 

SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.customer_name,
       o.order_id,
       o.order_amount
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

Real-world use: show all customers, including customers who have not ordered yet.

3. RIGHT JOIN / RIGHT OUTER JOIN

RIGHT JOIN returns all rows from the right table and matching rows from the left table. It is less commonly used because most developers rewrite it as a LEFT JOIN for readability. 

SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.customer_name,
       o.order_id,
       o.order_amount
FROM customers c
RIGHT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

Real-world use: show all orders even if some order has a missing or invalid customer reference.

4. FULL OUTER JOIN

FULL OUTER JOIN returns all matching and non-matching records from both tables. MySQL does not directly support FULL OUTER JOIN, so use LEFT JOIN plus RIGHT JOIN with UNION. 

SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.customer_name,
       o.order_id,
       o.order_amount
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id

UNION

SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.customer_name,
       o.order_id,
       o.order_amount
FROM customers c
RIGHT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

Real-world use: reconciliation reports, where you need all customers and all orders, including unmatched records from either side.

5. CROSS JOIN

CROSS JOIN returns every combination of rows from both tables. If table A has 3 rows and table B has 4 rows, result will have 12 rows. 

SELECT p.product_name,
       s.store_name
FROM products p
CROSS JOIN stores s;

Real-world use: generate all product-store combinations before checking inventory availability.

6. SELF JOIN

SELF JOIN joins a table with itself. It is commonly used for hierarchy data like employee and manager relationships. 

SELECT e.employee_id,
       e.first_name AS employee_name,
       m.first_name AS manager_name
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m
    ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id;

Real-world use: show every employee with their manager name.

7. ANTI JOIN using LEFT JOIN

An anti join finds records in one table that do not have a matching record in another table. 

SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.customer_name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;

Real-world use: find customers who registered but never placed an order.

8. SEMI JOIN using EXISTS

A semi join returns rows from the first table when a match exists in the second table, without duplicating the first table rows. 

SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.customer_name
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM orders o
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
);

Real-world use: find customers who have at least one order without showing each order row.

9. NON-EQUI JOIN

A non-equi join uses conditions other than equality, such as ranges. It is common in salary slabs, tax brackets, discounts, and commission rules. 

SELECT e.employee_id,
       e.first_name,
       e.salary,
       s.grade
FROM employees e
JOIN salary_grades s
    ON e.salary BETWEEN s.min_salary AND s.max_salary;

Real-world use: assign each employee to a salary grade.

10. MULTIPLE JOINS

Real reports often need more than two tables. This example shows orders with customer name, product name, quantity, and item amount. 

SELECT o.order_id,
       c.customer_name,
       p.product_name,
       oi.quantity,
       oi.total_amount
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c
    ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi
    ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
JOIN products p
    ON oi.product_id = p.product_id;

Real-world use: invoice details, order history, sales reports, and product revenue reports.

Join comparison summary
Join type What it returns Real-world use
INNER JOIN Only matching rows from both tables Customers with orders
LEFT JOIN All left rows plus matching right rows All customers with optional orders
RIGHT JOIN All right rows plus matching left rows All orders even if customer is missing
FULL OUTER JOIN All rows from both tables Reconciliation reports
CROSS JOIN Every combination of rows Product-store combinations
SELF JOIN Table joined with itself Employee-manager hierarchy
ANTI JOIN Rows with no matching record Customers without orders
SEMI JOIN Rows where a match exists Customers who have at least one order
NON-EQUI JOIN Rows matched by range or inequality Salary grade or tax slab matching
Important interview points
  • INNER JOIN removes non-matching rows.
  • LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left table.
  • Use LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL to find missing child records.
  • Use EXISTS when you only need to check whether a related row exists.
  • Avoid unnecessary CROSS JOIN because it can create a huge result set.
  • For readability, many teams prefer LEFT JOIN over RIGHT JOIN.

Interview one-liner: joins combine related tables; use INNER JOIN for matching rows, LEFT JOIN for all left-side records, SELF JOIN for hierarchy, and EXISTS or LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL for existence and missing-record checks.

In Java, custom/global exceptions are often extended from RuntimeException, especially in Spring Boot REST APIs, because most application exceptions are not realistically recoverable by the immediate caller.

The core difference is: 

// Checked exception
public class UserNotFoundException extends Exception {
    public UserNotFoundException(String message) {
        super(message);
    }
}

// Unchecked exception
public class UserNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
    public UserNotFoundException(String message) {
        super(message);
    }
}

If you extend Exception, Java forces the caller to handle or declare it: 

public User getUser(Long id) throws UserNotFoundException {
    if (id == null) {
        throw new UserNotFoundException("User not found");
    }
    return repository.findById(id).orElse(null);
}

Then this caller must also deal with it: 

public void processUser() {
    try {
        User user = getUser(10L);
    } catch (UserNotFoundException e) {
        // forced handling
    }
}

Or propagate it: 

public void processUser() throws UserNotFoundException {
    User user = getUser(10L);
}

That can spread through many layers: 

Controller
   -> throws UserNotFoundException
Service
   -> throws UserNotFoundException
Repository

But in a Spring Boot REST API, suppose the user does not exist: 

public User getUser(Long id) {
    return repository.findById(id)
        .orElseThrow(() ->
            new UserNotFoundException("User not found: " + id)
        );
}

Usually, the service caller cannot meaningfully fix that missing user. We want the exception to bubble up to centralized handling: 

public class UserNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {

    public UserNotFoundException(String message) {
        super(message);
    }
}

@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(UserNotFoundException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<String> handleUserNotFound(
            UserNotFoundException ex) {

        return ResponseEntity
                .status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
                .body(ex.getMessage());
    }
}

The flow is: 

HTTP GET /users/100
        ->
Controller
        ->
Service
        ->
repository.findById(100)
        ->
Not found
        ->
throw UserNotFoundException
        ->
No try/catch needed in Service
        ->
No try/catch needed in Controller
        ->
@RestControllerAdvice catches it
        ->
HTTP 404 response

That is why RuntimeException fits very naturally.

Useful rule
Situation Prefer
User not found RuntimeException
Invalid business state RuntimeException
Duplicate email RuntimeException
Insufficient balance Usually RuntimeException
Validation failure RuntimeException
REST API domain error RuntimeException
Caller is expected to recover Checked Exception
Caller must consciously handle failure Checked Exception

For example, a checked exception can make sense when recovery is genuinely expected: 

public void importFile(Path path) throws InvalidImportFileException {
    // caller may ask user to upload another file
}

But even here, many modern Java/Spring applications still choose unchecked exceptions depending on architecture.

Spring transaction rollback behavior

One more important reason in Spring: by default, Spring rolls back transactions for unchecked exceptions such as RuntimeException, but not generally for checked exceptions. 

@Transactional
public void transferMoney() {
    debit();
    credit();

    throw new PaymentFailedException();
}

If: 

class PaymentFailedException extends RuntimeException

Rollback happens by default.

If: 

class PaymentFailedException extends Exception

You may need: 

@Transactional(rollbackFor = PaymentFailedException.class)

So the deeper answer is: we do not extend RuntimeException merely because it is convenient. We use it when the caller is not expected to recover locally and the exception should propagate to a centralized boundary such as @RestControllerAdvice.

Best interview sentence: I use checked exceptions when the caller is expected to explicitly recover from the failure; I use unchecked exceptions for programming errors, invalid state, and domain/API failures that should propagate to centralized exception handling.

What is Jackson?

Jackson is one of the most commonly used JSON processing libraries in Java applications.

Its main responsibility is converting between: 

Java Object
<->


JSON

The two most important operations are: 

Serialization


Deserialization
Serialization

Serialization means converting a Java object into JSON. 

User user = new User(
    101L,
    "Narahari",
    "narahari@example.com"


);

Jackson converts it into: 

{


"id": 101,
"name": "Narahari",
"email": "[narahari@example.com](mailto:narahari@example.com)"
}

Direction: 

Java Object
|
v


Jackson Serializer
|
v
JSON
Deserialization

Deserialization means converting JSON into a Java object. 

{


"id": 101,
"name": "Narahari",
"email": "[narahari@example.com](mailto:narahari@example.com)"
}

Jackson converts it into: 

User user;

Direction: 

JSON
|
v


Jackson Deserializer
|
v
Java Object
Important Jackson modules

Jackson is not just one class or one JAR.

Common modules include:

Module Purpose
jackson-core Low-level streaming JSON parser and generator APIs
jackson-databind ObjectMapper and Java object mapping
jackson-annotations Annotations such as @JsonProperty and @JsonIgnore
jackson-datatype-jsr310 Java 8+ date/time types such as LocalDate and LocalDateTime
jackson-datatype-jdk8 JDK 8 types such as Optional
jackson-module-parameter-names Constructor parameter-name support
Jackson dependency in Spring Boot

In a typical Spring Boot MVC REST application, Jackson support is commonly available through the web starter and Spring MVC JSON message conversion infrastructure. 

<dependency>
<groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
<artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>

Conceptually, the dependency chain provides Spring MVC and Jackson integration.

Therefore, in a normal Spring Boot REST API, we usually do not manually write: 

String json = objectMapper.writeValueAsString(response);

inside every controller method.

Spring performs response conversion automatically.

Simple Spring Boot REST API example
public record UserResponse(
    Long id,
    String name,
    String email


) {
}
@RestController


@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {


@GetMapping("/{id}")
public UserResponse getUser(
        @PathVariable Long id) {

    return new UserResponse(
            id,
            "Narahari",
            "narahari@example.com"
    );
}


}

Client calls: 

GET /api/users/101


Accept: application/json

Controller returns: 

new UserResponse(
101L,
"Narahari",
"narahari@example.com"


)

HTTP response becomes: 

{


"id": 101,
"name": "Narahari",
"email": "[narahari@example.com](mailto:narahari@example.com)"
}

The controller did not manually convert the object into JSON.

How Spring Boot response serialization works internally
Client
|
| GET /api/users/101
v


DispatcherServlet
|
v
HandlerMapping
|
v
Controller Method
|
v
Returns UserResponse object
|
v
Spring MVC return-value processing
|
v
Select HttpMessageConverter
|
v
MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter
|
v
ObjectMapper
|
v
Jackson Serializer
|
v
JSON bytes
|
v
HTTP Response

The key integration component is: 

MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter

It bridges: 

Spring MVC
<->


Jackson ObjectMapper
Why @RestController matters
