@RestController is effectively: 

@Controller


@ResponseBody

Therefore: 

@RestController


class UserController {


@GetMapping("/user")
public UserResponse getUser() {
    return new UserResponse(
            1L,
            "Hari",
            "hari@example.com"
    );
}


}

means the return value should be written to the HTTP response body rather than interpreted as a view name.

How Spring Boot request deserialization works internally

Consider: 

public record CreateUserRequest(
    String name,
    String email


) {
}
@PostMapping


public ResponseEntity createUser(
@RequestBody CreateUserRequest request) {


return ResponseEntity.ok(
        "Created: " + request.name()
);


}

Client sends: 

POST /api/users


Content-Type: application/json
{


"name": "Narahari",
"email": "[narahari@example.com](mailto:narahari@example.com)"
}

Internal flow: 

HTTP Request
|
v


DispatcherServlet
|
v
Controller method selected
|
v
@RequestBody detected
|
v
Spring checks Content-Type
|
v
Select HttpMessageConverter
|
v
MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter
|
v
ObjectMapper
|
v
Jackson Deserializer
|
v
CreateUserRequest object
|
v
Controller method invoked
Very important: @RequestBody is not Jackson

A common interview mistake is saying: 

@RequestBody converts JSON to Java object

More precisely: 

@RequestBody
|
v


Tells Spring MVC to read HTTP request body
|
v
Spring selects an HttpMessageConverter
|
v
Jackson-based converter uses ObjectMapper
|
v
JSON becomes Java object

So: 

@RequestBody


is a Spring annotation

ObjectMapper
is a Jackson class
What is ObjectMapper?

ObjectMapper is the central high-level Jackson databinding API. 

ObjectMapper objectMapper = new ObjectMapper();

It performs operations such as: 

Java Object -> JSON String


JSON String -> Java Object
JSON -> JsonNode tree
JsonNode -> Java Object
Java Object -> Map
Map -> Java Object
Read/write files
Read/write streams
Configure serialization
Configure deserialization
Register modules
Important ObjectMapper methods
Method Purpose
writeValueAsString() Java object to JSON string
writeValueAsBytes() Java object to JSON byte array
writeValue() Write JSON to file, stream, or generator
readValue() JSON to Java object
readTree() JSON to JsonNode tree
treeToValue() JsonNode to Java object
valueToTree() Java object to JsonNode
convertValue() Convert one Java representation to another
createObjectNode() Create mutable JSON object node
createArrayNode() Create mutable JSON array node
readerFor() Create reusable configured ObjectReader
writerFor() Create reusable configured ObjectWriter
registerModule() Register Jackson module
findAndRegisterModules() Discover and register modules available through service loading
configure() Enable or disable a feature
enable() Enable feature
disable() Disable feature
setSerializationInclusion() Control property inclusion such as null values
setPropertyNamingStrategy() Configure property naming strategy
1. writeValueAsString()

Converts a Java object into a JSON string. 

ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper();


User user = new User(
101L,
"Narahari",
"[narahari@example.com](mailto:narahari@example.com)"
);

String json =
mapper.writeValueAsString(user);

System.out.println(json);

Output: 

{


"id": 101,
"name": "Narahari",
"email": "[narahari@example.com](mailto:narahari@example.com)"
}

Conceptually: 

User Object
|
v


writeValueAsString()
|
v
JSON String
2. readValue()

Converts JSON into a Java object. 

String json = """


{
"id": 101,
"name": "Narahari",
"email": "[narahari@example.com](mailto:narahari@example.com)"
}
""";

User user =
mapper.readValue(
json,
User.class
);

Conceptually: 

JSON String
|
v


readValue()
|
v
User Object
readValue() overload examples

From String: 

User user =
    mapper.readValue(
            jsonString,
            User.class
    );

From byte array: 

User user =
    mapper.readValue(
            jsonBytes,
            User.class
    );

From InputStream: 

User user =
    mapper.readValue(
            inputStream,
            User.class
    );

From File: 

User user =
    mapper.readValue(
            file,
            User.class
    );
3. writeValue()

Writes JSON directly to a destination.

Write to file: 

mapper.writeValue(
    new File("user.json"),
    user


);

Write to output stream: 

mapper.writeValue(
    outputStream,
    user


);
4. writeValueAsBytes()
byte[] jsonBytes =
    mapper.writeValueAsBytes(user);

Useful when working with: 

HTTP


Kafka
Files
Network communication
Binary APIs around JSON payloads
5. readTree()

Converts JSON into Jackson's tree model. 

String json = """


{
"id": 101,
"name": "Narahari",
"address": {
"city": "Hyderabad"
}
}
""";

JsonNode root =
mapper.readTree(json);

Access fields: 

long id =
    root.get("id").asLong();


String name =
root.get("name").asText();

String city =
root.path("address")
.path("city")
.asText();
get() vs path() in JsonNode

This is an important interview difference. 

root.get("missingField")

can return: 

null

But: 

root.path("missingField")

returns a missing-node representation instead of Java null.

Therefore chaining is often safer: 

root.path("address")
.path("city")
.asText();
6. treeToValue()

Converts a JsonNode into a Java object. 

JsonNode node =
    mapper.readTree(json);


User user =
mapper.treeToValue(
node,
User.class
);

Flow: 

JSON
->


JsonNode
->
User
7. valueToTree()

Converts a Java object into a JsonNode. 

JsonNode node =
    mapper.valueToTree(user);

Flow: 

User Object
->


JsonNode
8. convertValue()

Converts one Java representation into another using Jackson's mapping rules.

Object to Map: 

Map<String, Object> map =
    mapper.convertValue(
            user,
            new TypeReference<
                    Map<String, Object>
            >() {}
    );

Map to Object: 

User user =
    mapper.convertValue(
            map,
            User.class
    );

DTO to DTO: 

UserResponse response =
    mapper.convertValue(
            entity,
            UserResponse.class
    );

Important:

Although convertValue() is convenient, using it as a universal replacement for explicit domain mapping can hide important business transformations and type mismatches.

9. createObjectNode()
ObjectNode node =
    mapper.createObjectNode();


node.put("id", 101);
node.put("name", "Narahari");
node.put("active", true);

Result: 

{


"id": 101,
"name": "Narahari",
"active": true
}
10. createArrayNode()
ArrayNode array =
    mapper.createArrayNode();


array.add("Java");
array.add("Spring Boot");
array.add("Kafka");

Result: 

[


"Java",
"Spring Boot",
"Kafka"
]
Most important problem: Generic collections and type erasure

Suppose JSON is: 

[


{
"id": 1,
"name": "A"
},
{
"id": 2,
"name": "B"
}
]

This is not sufficient: 

List<User> users =
    mapper.readValue(
            json,
            List.class
    );

Why?

Because at runtime: 

List.class

does not contain: 

User

due to Java generic type erasure.

You may receive: 

List<LinkedHashMap>

rather than: 

List<User>
Solution: TypeReference
List<User> users =
    mapper.readValue(
            json,
            new TypeReference<List<User>>() {}
    );

This preserves generic type information for Jackson.

Nested generic example
Map<String, List<User>> data =
    mapper.readValue(
            json,
            new TypeReference<
                    Map<String, List<User>>
            >() {}
    );
Alternative: JavaType
JavaType type =
    mapper.getTypeFactory()
          .constructCollectionType(
                  List.class,
                  User.class
          );


List users =
mapper.readValue(
json,
type
);

Useful when generic types are constructed dynamically.

ObjectReader and ObjectWriter

Jackson also provides: 

ObjectReader


ObjectWriter

Example: 

ObjectReader reader =
    mapper.readerFor(User.class);


User user =
reader.readValue(json);

Writer: 

ObjectWriter writer =
    mapper.writerFor(User.class);


String json =
writer.writeValueAsString(user);

Pretty writer: 

String json =
    mapper.writerWithDefaultPrettyPrinter()
          .writeValueAsString(user);

ObjectReader and ObjectWriter are useful for reusable, preconfigured read/write operations.

How Jackson discovers properties

Jackson can inspect Java types using metadata and introspection rules involving: 

Fields


Getters
Setters
Constructors
Record components
Annotations
Visibility rules

Example: 

public class User {

private Long id;
private String name;

public Long getId() {
    return id;
}

public String getName() {
    return name;
}


}

Jackson can serialize properties exposed through getters: 

{


"id": 101,
"name": "Narahari"
}
Does Jackson always require a no-argument constructor?

Not always.

This is an important interview point.

A traditional mutable POJO often works with: 

No-args constructor


+
Setters

But Jackson can also deserialize using: 

@JsonCreator constructors


@JsonProperty constructor parameters
Records
Registered modules
Recognized creators

Therefore the statement: 

Jackson always requires default constructor

is incorrect.

@JsonProperty

Changes or explicitly defines the JSON property name. 

public class User {

@JsonProperty("user_name")
private String name;


}

Java: 

name = "Narahari"

JSON: 

{


"user_name": "Narahari"
}
@JsonIgnore

Ignores a property during Jackson processing according to its placement and property configuration. 

public class User {

private Long id;

private String name;

@JsonIgnore
private String password;


}

Java object: 

id       = 101


name     = Narahari
password = secret123

JSON: 

{


"id": 101,
"name": "Narahari"
}

Password is excluded.

@JsonIgnoreProperties

Can ignore selected properties: 

@JsonIgnoreProperties({
    "password",
    "internalCode"


})
public class User {
}

Or ignore unknown JSON fields: 

@JsonIgnoreProperties(
    ignoreUnknown = true


)
public class User {
}
Unknown property problem

Java class: 

public class User {

private Long id;
private String name;


}

Incoming JSON: 

{


"id": 101,
"name": "Narahari",
"age": 30
}

Java class has no: 

age

Depending on configuration, Jackson can fail with: 

UnrecognizedPropertyException

One class-level solution: 

@JsonIgnoreProperties(
    ignoreUnknown = true


)
public class User {
}

Global ObjectMapper configuration: 

mapper.configure(
    DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES,
    false


);
@JsonInclude

Controls which values are included during serialization. 

@JsonInclude(
    JsonInclude.Include.NON_NULL


)
public class User {
}

Java object: 

id    = 101


name  = Narahari
email = null

JSON: 

{


"id": 101,
"name": "Narahari"
}

The null email is excluded.

Common JsonInclude options
Option Meaning
ALWAYS Include values normally, including null according to default handling
NON_NULL Exclude null values
NON_EMPTY Exclude null and empty values according to Jackson emptiness rules
NON_DEFAULT Exclude values considered default
NON_ABSENT Exclude absent reference values such as empty Optional in supported configurations
@JsonFormat

Controls formatting for values such as dates. 

public class OrderResponse {

@JsonFormat(
    pattern = "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss"
)
private LocalDateTime createdAt;


}

JSON: 

{


"createdAt": "2026-07-08 10:30:00"
}
Java time support

Modern Java applications commonly use: 

LocalDate


LocalDateTime
Instant
OffsetDateTime
ZonedDateTime

Jackson support is commonly provided through: 

JavaTimeModule

Manual registration example: 

ObjectMapper mapper =
    new ObjectMapper();


mapper.registerModule(
new JavaTimeModule()
);

In Spring Boot, supported Jackson modules present in the application are commonly auto-configured into the managed mapper, so manually creating a fresh mapper can accidentally lose Boot-provided configuration.

Important mistake: new ObjectMapper() inside application code

Avoid repeatedly doing: 

public void process() {

ObjectMapper mapper =
        new ObjectMapper();

...


}

Problems: 

Repeated configuration


Possible missing modules
Different behavior from Spring MVC
Unnecessary object creation
Date/time configuration mismatch
Naming-strategy mismatch

Prefer injecting Spring's configured mapper: 

@Service


public class JsonService {


private final ObjectMapper objectMapper;

public JsonService(
        ObjectMapper objectMapper) {

    this.objectMapper = objectMapper;
}


}
ObjectMapper thread safety

A commonly used rule is: 

Configure ObjectMapper before concurrent use,


then reuse it.

Reusing a stable configured mapper is preferable to repeatedly creating and mutating mappers during request processing.

For per-operation variations, immutable-style readers and writers are useful: 

ObjectReader reader;


ObjectWriter writer;
@JsonAlias

Allows alternate input property names during deserialization. 

public class UserRequest {

@JsonAlias({
    "user_name",
    "username",
    "full_name"
})
private String name;


}

These inputs can map to the same Java property: 

{


"user_name": "Narahari"
}

or: 

{


"username": "Narahari"
}

or: 

{


"full_name": "Narahari"
}
@JsonCreator

Defines a constructor or factory method Jackson can use to create an object. 

public class User {

private final Long id;
private final String name;

@JsonCreator
public User(
        @JsonProperty("id") Long id,
        @JsonProperty("name") String name) {

    this.id = id;
    this.name = name;
}


}

Useful for immutable classes.

@JsonValue

Defines a single value representation during serialization. 

public enum OrderStatus {

CREATED("created"),
SHIPPED("shipped");

private final String value;

OrderStatus(String value) {
    this.value = value;
}

@JsonValue
public String getValue() {
    return value;
}


}

JSON: 

"created"

instead of: 

"CREATED"
@JsonAnySetter

Captures unknown or dynamic JSON properties. 

public class UserRequest {

private String name;

private Map<String, Object> additional =
        new HashMap<>();

@JsonAnySetter
public void add(
        String key,
        Object value) {

    additional.put(key, value);
}


}

Input: 

{


"name": "Narahari",
"city": "Hyderabad",
"skill": "Java"
}

Dynamic values can be captured: 

city  -> Hyderabad


skill -> Java
@JsonAnyGetter

Exposes map entries as top-level JSON properties. 

@JsonAnyGetter


public Map getAdditional() {
return additional;
}
@JsonGetter and @JsonSetter
@JsonGetter("user_name")


public String getName() {
return name;
}

@JsonSetter("user_name")
public void setName(String name) {
this.name = name;
}

Useful when explicit serialization and deserialization property methods are needed.

@JsonProperty access control

Sometimes a property should only be accepted in requests or only returned in responses.

Write-only: 

@JsonProperty(
access = JsonProperty.Access.WRITE_ONLY


)
private String password;

Incoming request: 

{


"name": "Narahari",
"password": "secret"
}

Password can be deserialized.

But response serialization excludes it.

Read-only: 

@JsonProperty(
access = JsonProperty.Access.READ_ONLY


)
private Long id;

Useful for server-generated values.

Jackson with Java Records
public record UserResponse(
    Long id,
    String name,
    String email


) {
}

Serialization: 

{


"id": 101,
"name": "Narahari",
"email": "[narahari@example.com](mailto:narahari@example.com)"
}

Records are particularly useful for: 

Request DTOs


Response DTOs
Immutable API contracts
Custom Serializer

Suppose we have: 

public class Money {

private BigDecimal amount;
private String currency;


}

Default JSON might be: 

{


"amount": 1000,
"currency": "INR"
}

But requirement is: 

"INR 1000"

Create custom serializer: 

public class MoneySerializer
    extends JsonSerializer<Money> {

@Override
public void serialize(
        Money money,
        JsonGenerator gen,
        SerializerProvider serializers)
        throws IOException {

    gen.writeString(
            money.getCurrency()
            + " "
            + money.getAmount()
    );
}


}

Apply: 

@JsonSerialize(
using = MoneySerializer.class


)
private Money price;
Custom Deserializer

Input: 

"INR 1000"

Desired Java object: 

Money(
amount = 1000,
currency = INR


)

Custom deserializer: 

public class MoneyDeserializer
    extends JsonDeserializer<Money> {

@Override
public Money deserialize(
        JsonParser parser,
        DeserializationContext context)
        throws IOException {

    String value =
            parser.getValueAsString();

    String[] parts =
            value.split(" ");

    return new Money(
            new BigDecimal(parts[1]),
            parts[0]
    );
}


}

Apply: 

@JsonDeserialize(
using = MoneyDeserializer.class


)
private Money price;
Register custom serializer globally with Module
@Configuration


public class JacksonConfig {


@Bean
public Module moneyModule() {

    SimpleModule module =
            new SimpleModule();

    module.addSerializer(
            Money.class,
            new MoneySerializer()
    );

    module.addDeserializer(
            Money.class,
            new MoneyDeserializer()
    );

    return module;
}


}

In a Spring Boot application, exposing Jackson modules as beans is a common way to integrate custom mapping behavior with the managed mapper.

Global Spring Boot Jackson configuration

Example: 

spring.jackson.default-property-inclusion=non_null


spring.jackson.deserialization.fail-on-unknown-properties=false
spring.jackson.serialization.indent-output=true

These properties customize Jackson behavior through Spring Boot configuration.

Customize using Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer
@Configuration


public class JacksonConfig {


@Bean
public Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer
        jacksonCustomizer() {

    return builder -> builder
            .serializationInclusion(
                    JsonInclude.Include.NON_NULL
            )
            .featuresToDisable(
                    SerializationFeature
                            .WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS
            );
}


}

This is often preferable to replacing the entire Spring-managed ObjectMapper.

Custom ObjectMapper bean

It is possible to define your own mapper: 

@Bean


public ObjectMapper objectMapper() {


ObjectMapper mapper =
        new ObjectMapper();

mapper.registerModule(
        new JavaTimeModule()
);

mapper.disable(
        SerializationFeature
                .WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS
);

return mapper;


}

But be careful:

Replacing the auto-configured mapper can require you to preserve modules and settings that Spring Boot would otherwise configure.

Therefore targeted customization is often safer.

Snake case naming strategy

Java: 

private String firstName;


private String lastName;

Desired JSON: 

{


"first_name": "Narahari",
"last_name": "G"
}

Configure: 

mapper.setPropertyNamingStrategy(
    PropertyNamingStrategies
            .SNAKE_CASE


);

Or through supported Spring Boot configuration: 

spring.jackson.property-naming-strategy=SNAKE_CASE
Common serialization error: No serializer found

Example error: 

No serializer found for class ...

Possible causes: 

No visible properties


Unsupported type
Proxy object
Missing module
Visibility configuration
Problematic lazy-loaded entity
Common deserialization error: Cannot construct instance
Cannot construct instance of User

Possible causes: 

No usable creator


Constructor metadata mismatch
Abstract type
Interface type
Missing @JsonCreator
Missing subtype information
Common error: MismatchedInputException

Expected Java object: 

User

But JSON is array: 

[


{
"id": 1
}
]

Jackson may throw: 

MismatchedInputException

because: 

Expected:


Object

Received:
Array
Common error: InvalidFormatException

Java: 

private Integer age;

JSON: 

{


"age": "abc"
}

Jackson cannot convert: 

"abc"


->
Integer

This can produce: 

InvalidFormatException
How Jackson errors appear in Spring Boot REST API

Suppose: 

public record CreateUserRequest(
    Integer age


) {
}

Client sends: 

{


"age": "abc"
}

Flow: 

HTTP Request
|
v


@RequestBody
|
v
MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter
|
v
ObjectMapper.readValue-like databinding
|
v
Cannot convert "abc" to Integer
|
v
Jackson mapping exception
|
v
Spring wraps/translates request read failure
|
v
HttpMessageNotReadableException
|
v
HTTP 400 Bad Request

This distinction is important: 

Low-level/root Jackson problem:


InvalidFormatException

Spring MVC level:
HttpMessageNotReadableException
Handle Jackson request errors globally
@RestControllerAdvice


public class GlobalExceptionHandler {


@ExceptionHandler(
    HttpMessageNotReadableException.class
)
public ResponseEntity<Map<String, Object>>
        handleInvalidJson(
                HttpMessageNotReadableException ex) {

    Map<String, Object> response =
            new LinkedHashMap<>();

    response.put(
            "status",
            HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST.value()
    );

    response.put(
            "message",
            "Invalid JSON request"
    );

    return ResponseEntity
            .badRequest()
            .body(response);
}


}
Jackson vs Bean Validation

Jackson mapping and Jakarta Bean Validation are different responsibilities. 

public record CreateUserRequest(

    @NotBlank
    String name,

    @Email
    String email


) {
}
@PostMapping


public ResponseEntity create(
@Valid
@RequestBody
CreateUserRequest request) {


return ResponseEntity.ok().build();


}

Flow: 

JSON
|
v


Jackson deserialization
|
v
CreateUserRequest object
|
v
Bean Validation
|
v
Controller method

Therefore: 

Jackson:


Can JSON be converted into Java object?

Bean Validation:
Is the converted object valid according to constraints?
Jackson and JPA entities: common production problem

Consider bidirectional relationships: 

@Entity


class Parent {


@OneToMany(mappedBy = "parent")
private List<Child> children;


}
@Entity


class Child {


@ManyToOne
private Parent parent;


}

Serialization can conceptually recurse: 

Parent
->


Children
->
Parent
->
Children
->
Parent
->
...

Possible result: 

Infinite recursion


StackOverflowError
JSON mapping failure
Possible relationship annotations
class Parent {

@JsonManagedReference
private List<Child> children;


}
class Child {

@JsonBackReference
private Parent parent;


}

Another possible option: 

@JsonIgnore


private Parent parent;

However, in REST APIs a strong general design is: 

Do not expose JPA entities directly.


Entity
->
Response DTO
->
JSON
Why DTOs are better than exposing entities directly
JPA Entity
|
+-- Persistence concerns
+-- Lazy relationships
+-- Internal fields
+-- Bidirectional references
+-- Database structure


API DTO
|
+-- Explicit contract
+-- Controlled fields
+-- Stable JSON
+-- Security boundary
+-- Client-focused structure

Example: 

public record UserResponse(
    Long id,
    String name,
    String email


) {
}
Lazy loading problem

Suppose: 

@OneToMany(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)


private List orders;

Returning the entity directly can cause issues such as: 

LazyInitializationException


Unexpected SQL queries
N+1 queries
Huge JSON payloads
Proxy serialization problems

Jackson itself may trigger getter access during serialization, which can interact badly with lazy-loaded persistence associations.

Polymorphic deserialization

Suppose: 

interface Payment {


}

Implementations: 

class CardPayment implements Payment {


}

class UpiPayment implements Payment {
}

JSON: 

{


"type": "upi",
"upiId": "user@bank"
}

Jackson needs type-selection information. 

@JsonTypeInfo(
use = JsonTypeInfo.Id.NAME,
property = "type"


)
@JsonSubTypes({
@JsonSubTypes.Type(
value = CardPayment.class,
name = "card"
),
@JsonSubTypes.Type(
value = UpiPayment.class,
name = "upi"
)
})
interface Payment {
}

Now: 

{


"type": "upi",
"upiId": "user@bank"
}

can become: 

UpiPayment
Security warning about polymorphic typing

Do not casually enable broad default polymorphic typing for untrusted JSON.

Dangerous design: 

Client controls arbitrary Java type information

Safer approach: 

Explicit known subtypes


Strict allow-listing
Minimal accepted type metadata
Streaming API: JsonParser

For very large JSON payloads, tree or full object binding may consume more memory.

Jackson provides a streaming API: 

JsonFactory factory =
    new JsonFactory();


JsonParser parser =
factory.createParser(json);

Process tokens: 

while (parser.nextToken() != null) {

JsonToken token =
        parser.currentToken();

System.out.println(token);


}

Token examples: 

START_OBJECT


FIELD_NAME
VALUE_STRING
VALUE_NUMBER_INT
END_OBJECT
Streaming API: JsonGenerator
JsonFactory factory =
    new JsonFactory();


StringWriter writer =
new StringWriter();

JsonGenerator generator =
factory.createGenerator(writer);

generator.writeStartObject();

generator.writeNumberField(
"id",
101
);

generator.writeStringField(
"name",
"Narahari"
);

generator.writeEndObject();

generator.close();

Result: 

{


"id": 101,
"name": "Narahari"
}

Data Binding ObjectMapper Java object mapping
Tree Model JsonNode Dynamic or partially known JSON
Streaming JsonParser / JsonGenerator Large payloads and low-level control

Common Jackson annotations summary
Annotation Purpose
@JsonProperty Define JSON property name and access behavior
@JsonIgnore Ignore property
@JsonIgnoreProperties Ignore selected or unknown properties
@JsonInclude Control property inclusion
@JsonFormat Control formatting
@JsonAlias Accept alternate input names
@JsonCreator Define object creator
@JsonValue Serialize object as one value
@JsonGetter Explicit serialization getter
@JsonSetter Explicit deserialization setter
@JsonAnyGetter Expose dynamic properties
@JsonAnySetter Capture dynamic properties
@JsonSerialize Specify custom serializer
@JsonDeserialize Specify custom deserializer
@JsonTypeInfo Add polymorphic type information
@JsonSubTypes Declare known polymorphic subtypes
@JsonManagedReference Forward side of managed/back reference relationship
@JsonBackReference Back side omitted to break recursion
Common senior-level interview questions

1. Who converts @RequestBody JSON into Java object? 

Spring MVC selects an HttpMessageConverter.


For JSON, MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter commonly delegates to Jackson ObjectMapper.

2. Does @RequestBody itself perform JSON parsing? 

No.


@RequestBody is Spring MVC metadata.
Actual conversion is performed by a selected HttpMessageConverter.

3. Why use TypeReference? 

To preserve generic type information such as List<User>


that cannot be represented by List.class alone.

4. Why not create new ObjectMapper everywhere? 

It can lose application-wide configuration and modules,


create inconsistent behavior, and add unnecessary repeated setup.

5. Does Jackson always need a default constructor? 

No.


It can use creators, constructor metadata, records,
factory methods, and configured modules.

6. What is the difference between readTree and readValue? 

readTree:


JSON -> JsonNode

readValue:
JSON -> Typed Java object

7. What is the difference between serialization and deserialization? 

Serialization:


Java -> JSON

Deserialization:
JSON -> Java

8. How do Jackson errors become HTTP 400? 

Jackson mapping/parsing failure
->


HttpMessageConverter read failure
->
Spring exception such as HttpMessageNotReadableException
->
400 Bad Request handling

9. Why avoid returning JPA entities directly? 

Lazy loading


Infinite recursion
Proxy serialization
N+1 queries
Data leakage
Tight API/database coupling

10. Is Jackson only for JSON? 

Jackson has a broader data-format ecosystem,


although JSON is its most common use in Spring REST APIs.
Best interview answer

Jackson is the JSON processing and data-binding library commonly integrated with Spring Boot REST APIs. On an incoming request, @RequestBody tells Spring MVC to read the HTTP body. Spring selects an appropriate HttpMessageConverter; for JSON this is commonly MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter, which delegates to a configured Jackson ObjectMapper to deserialize JSON into the controller parameter type. On the response side, @RestController or @ResponseBody causes the returned Java object to be written to the HTTP response body, and the Jackson message converter serializes it into JSON. The main ObjectMapper operations include readValue, writeValueAsString, readTree, treeToValue, valueToTree, and convertValue. For generic types such as List<User>, we use TypeReference or JavaType because of Java type erasure. In production, I prefer reusing Spring Boot's configured mapper, using DTOs instead of exposing JPA entities directly, registering modules for special types, and handling malformed JSON centrally through @RestControllerAdvice.

@Service


public class UserService {


private final UserRepository repository;

public UserService(
        UserRepository repository) {

    this.repository = repository;
}

@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public UserResponse getUser(Long id) {

    User user = repository.findById(id)
            .orElseThrow(() ->
                    new UserNotFoundException(
                            "User not found: " + id
                    )
            );

    return new UserResponse(
            user.getId(),
            user.getName(),
            user.getEmail()
    );
}


}

Phase 4: TCP connection

For HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 over TCP, a TCP connection is established.

What is CyclicBarrier?

CyclicBarrier is a synchronization aid that makes a group of threads wait until all of them reach the same point. Once the last thread arrives, the barrier opens and all waiting threads continue together. It is called cyclic because the same barrier can be reused after it trips.

Why use it?

Use it when multiple worker threads must finish one phase before any of them can move to the next phase, such as parallel data loading, multi-step computation, or test setup where every worker must start together.

Example
int parties = 3;
CyclicBarrier barrier = new CyclicBarrier(parties, () ->
    System.out.println("All workers reached the barrier"));

Runnable task = () -> {
  try {
    System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " loading data");
    barrier.await(); // wait for the other threads
    System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " starts next phase");
  } catch (InterruptedException | BrokenBarrierException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    throw new RuntimeException(e);
  }
};

In this example, each thread finishes the first phase and waits. Only after all 3 threads arrive does the barrier trip, run the optional barrier action, and let everyone continue.

CyclicBarrier vs CountDownLatch
  • CyclicBarrier: reusable; threads wait for each other at a phase boundary.
  • CountDownLatch: one-time; one or more threads wait until a count reaches zero.
Interview-ready answer

"CyclicBarrier is used when a fixed number of threads need to meet at a checkpoint before continuing. It is reusable after it trips, which makes it useful for phased parallel processing. If I only need a one-time wait, I would use CountDownLatch instead."

Custom Filter example
@Component


public class RequestLoggingFilter
extends OncePerRequestFilter {


@Override
protected void doFilterInternal(
        HttpServletRequest request,
        HttpServletResponse response,
        FilterChain filterChain)
        throws ServletException, IOException {

    long start =
            System.currentTimeMillis();

    try {

        System.out.println(
                "Before request: "
                + request.getRequestURI()
        );

        filterChain.doFilter(
                request,
                response
        );

    } finally {

        long time =
                System.currentTimeMillis()
                - start;

        System.out.println(
                "After request: "
                + time
                + " ms"
        );
    }
}


}

The critical line is: 

filterChain.doFilter(
request,
response


);

Without it: 

Request stops in the filter


DispatcherServlet is never reached

Controller is never called
Filter execution behaves like a stack

Suppose: 

Filter A


Filter B
Filter C

Execution: 

A before
|
v


B before
|
v
C before
|
v
Controller
|
v
C after
|
v
B after
|
v
A after

Why?

Because each filter calls the next element: 

filterChain.doFilter(...);

and resumes after the downstream chain returns.

protected void doDispatch(
    HttpServletRequest request,
    HttpServletResponse response) {

HandlerExecutionChain chain =
        getHandler(request);

HandlerAdapter adapter =
        getHandlerAdapter(
                chain.getHandler()
        );

adapter.handle(
        request,
        response,
        chain.getHandler()
);


}

The real implementation is much more detailed, but this is the core mental model.

Interceptor example
@Component


public class AuditInterceptor
implements HandlerInterceptor {


@Override
public boolean preHandle(
        HttpServletRequest request,
        HttpServletResponse response,
        Object handler) {

    System.out.println(
            "Before controller"
    );

    return true;
}

@Override
public void postHandle(
        HttpServletRequest request,
        HttpServletResponse response,
        Object handler,
        ModelAndView modelAndView) {

    System.out.println(
            "After controller"
    );
}

@Override
public void afterCompletion(
        HttpServletRequest request,
        HttpServletResponse response,
        Object handler,
        Exception ex) {

    System.out.println(
            "Request completed"
    );
}


}
Register Interceptor
@Configuration


public class WebConfig
implements WebMvcConfigurer {


private final AuditInterceptor interceptor;

public WebConfig(
        AuditInterceptor interceptor) {

    this.interceptor = interceptor;
}

@Override
public void addInterceptors(
        InterceptorRegistry registry) {

    registry.addInterceptor(interceptor)
            .addPathPatterns("/api/**");
}


}

Top senior-level interview questions

1. Who listens on port 8080? 

The embedded web server, commonly Tomcat,


not the Spring Controller.

2. Does every TCP connection get one permanent Tomcat worker thread? 

No.


With NIO, many connections can exist without one permanently dedicated worker thread per connection.

3. Who finds the Controller method? 

HandlerMapping,


commonly RequestMappingHandlerMapping
for annotated controllers.

4. Who actually invokes the Controller method? 

A compatible HandlerAdapter,


commonly RequestMappingHandlerAdapter.

5. Who resolves @PathVariable? 

Spring MVC method argument resolution infrastructure.

6. Who converts JSON to Java? 

A JSON HttpMessageConverter commonly delegates to Jackson ObjectMapper.

7. Does @RequestBody parse JSON? 

No.


It marks the parameter for request-body resolution.
Message converters perform conversion.

8. Where does Spring Security run? 

Primarily in the Servlet Filter chain,


before DispatcherServlet reaches the Controller.

9. Difference between Filter and Interceptor? 

Filter:


Servlet layer

Interceptor:
Spring MVC handler layer

10. Who handles @Transactional? 

Spring transaction infrastructure,


commonly through AOP proxy/interceptor mechanisms.

11. Why can self-invocation break @Transactional expectations? 

Because an internal this.method() call can bypass


the external Spring proxy that applies transaction advice.

12. Who creates JpaRepository implementation? 

Spring Data creates runtime repository infrastructure/proxies.

13. Does Controller return JSON directly? 

Usually no.


Controller returns a Java object.
A selected HttpMessageConverter serializes it to JSON.

14. What happens to worker thread after response? 

It normally returns to the worker pool


and can process another request.

15. Can request fail before Controller? 

Yes.


Filter
Security
Handler mapping
Argument conversion
Jackson
Validation
Interceptor

can all stop processing before Controller invocation.
Best interview answer

When a client calls a Spring Boot MVC REST API, the request first reaches the server operating system and the embedded Servlet container, commonly Tomcat. Tomcat's Connector and NIO infrastructure manage socket activity, and request processing is assigned to a worker thread. The request enters the Servlet FilterChain, where custom filters and Spring Security filters can perform authentication and authorization. If allowed, it reaches Spring MVC's DispatcherServlet, which acts as the Front Controller. DispatcherServlet asks a HandlerMapping to locate the matching controller handler and receives a HandlerExecutionChain containing the handler and mapped interceptors. After interceptor preHandle methods succeed, a compatible HandlerAdapter invokes the controller method. Before invocation, HandlerMethodArgumentResolvers resolve values such as @PathVariable, @RequestParam, and @RequestHeader. For @RequestBody, Spring selects an HttpMessageConverter; for JSON, a Jackson-based converter commonly delegates to ObjectMapper for deserialization. Bean Validation then runs when @Valid is present. The controller calls the service, which may pass through Spring AOP proxies for concerns such as @Transactional. The repository is commonly a Spring Data-generated proxy that delegates through JPA EntityManager and Hibernate, obtains a connection from the pool, and executes SQL through JDBC. The result returns to the service, is mapped to a DTO, and returns to the controller. Spring MVC then processes the return value, performs content negotiation, selects an HttpMessageConverter, and Jackson serializes the Java response object into JSON. Interceptor completion callbacks run, the Servlet filter chain unwinds, Tomcat writes the HTTP response to the socket, and the worker thread normally returns to the pool for reuse. If an exception occurs, Spring MVC's HandlerExceptionResolver infrastructure can route it to matching @ExceptionHandler or @RestControllerAdvice methods and serialize the resulting error response.

The main confusion

Suppose a Spring Boot application uses embedded Tomcat and receives: 

100,000 connected clients

But Tomcat has approximately: 

200 worker threads

The obvious question is: 

If 100,000 clients are connected,


do we need 100,000 threads?

If only 200 threads exist,
how can Tomcat serve 100,000 connections?

The key answer is: 

Connection
!=


Active Request
!=
Worker Thread

These three concepts must be separated.

First understand: Connection vs Request vs Thread
Concept Meaning
Connection A TCP connection between client and server
Request An HTTP operation such as GET /users/101
Worker Thread A thread actively executing request-processing code

Example: 

Client A
|
+-- TCP Connection Open
|
+-- Currently sending no request

This client has: 

1 open connection


0 active requests

0 permanently dedicated worker threads

This is the foundation of the entire topic.

Old incorrect mental model

Many developers imagine: 

Client 1
->


Thread 1

Client 2
->
Thread 2

Client 3
->
Thread 3

...

Client 100,000
->
Thread 100,000

That would mean: 

100,000 connections
=


100,000 permanently allocated threads

Modern NIO-based servers do not need to work like this.

Better NIO mental model
100,000 TCP Connections
    |
    v


Small number of connection-management threads
|
v
Monitor socket readiness
|
v
Only sockets with useful work become active
|
v
Submit processing work
|
v
Worker Thread Pool
|
v
Spring MVC application code

Therefore: 

100,000 connected sockets


does not mean

100,000 simultaneously executing Java request threads
Real-time example: WhatsApp-like mobile clients

Imagine: 

100,000 mobile clients connected

At a particular millisecond: 

95,000 clients
->


Idle

4,500 clients
->
Keep-alive connection open
->
No current HTTP request

400 clients
->
Request data arriving

100 clients
->
Actively being processed

So: 

Connected Clients:


100,000

Clients currently sending useful data:
400

Requests actively executing:
100

There is no reason to create 100,000 worker threads.

Simple Java NIO Selector example

SocketChannel.open();

selector,
SelectionKey.OP_READ

Then: 

Set<SelectionKey> keys =

Critical distinction: maxConnections vs maxThreads
Setting Controls

maxThreads Maximum request-processing worker threads

These are not interchangeable.

Top senior-level interview questions

1. Can Tomcat have more connections than worker threads? 

Yes.


Connection count and worker-thread count
represent different resources.

2. Does every idle keep-alive connection hold one worker thread? 

No.


Idle connections can be monitored through NIO readiness mechanisms
without permanently occupying one application worker thread each.

3. What does Acceptor do? 

Accepts incoming TCP connections


from the listening server socket.

4. What does Poller do? 

Monitors registered sockets


for I/O readiness and related events.

5. What does Selector do? 

Allows a thread to monitor many channels


and identify channels ready for operations such as read or write.

6. Does Selector execute Controller code? 

No.


Controller code is executed by request-processing workers
in the traditional Spring MVC model.

7. What is maxConnections? 

Configured limit related to concurrent connections


managed by the connector.

8. What is maxThreads? 

Maximum number of worker threads


available for request processing.

9. What is acceptCount? 

Backlog/queue configuration for incoming connections


when connection capacity has been reached,
subject to OS and connector behavior.

10. Is acceptCount an HTTP Controller request queue? 

No.


It should not be understood simply as
"requests waiting for Controller execution."

11. Does Tomcat NIO make JDBC non-blocking? 

No.


Traditional JDBC remains blocking.

12. Why can 200 threads serve thousands of requests per second? 

Because threads are reused.


If each request is short,
one thread can process many requests over time.

13. Why can Redis serve many clients with a small number of threads? 

Because connection handling uses I/O multiplexing


and command execution is typically very short and memory-oriented.

14. What is the danger of a slow Redis command? 

Long-running work can delay other commands


on the main execution path.

15. What happens after Tomcat sends the response? 

Worker returns to the pool.


If keep-alive remains active,
the connection can return to readiness monitoring.
Best interview answer

Tomcat can manage far more TCP connections than worker threads because a connection is not the same as an active request and is not permanently tied to one worker thread. With the NIO connector, incoming connections are accepted by Acceptor logic and represented through non-blocking socket infrastructure. Connections are monitored for I/O readiness by Poller logic using Java NIO Selector-style mechanisms backed by operating-system readiness facilities. Idle keep-alive connections therefore do not need one permanently blocked application worker thread each. When a socket becomes readable because HTTP request data arrives, Tomcat schedules socket-processing work to its executor. An available worker thread then performs request processing through the Servlet FilterChain, Spring Security, DispatcherServlet, Controller, Service, Repository, and downstream systems. After the response completes, the worker thread returns to the pool, while the TCP connection may remain open and return to readiness monitoring for a later request. This is why thousands of connections can coexist with only hundreds of request workers. However, NIO only solves efficient network connection management; it does not make blocking JDBC, database calls, or external HTTP calls non-blocking. If all worker threads are blocked on slow downstream systems, Tomcat can still suffer thread-pool exhaustion. Redis uses a related I/O multiplexing idea but is more event-loop-centered for command processing, which works extremely well because most Redis operations are short, in-memory operations. The core principle in both systems is that a large number of connected clients does not require the same number of dedicated threads.

Now enter Virtual Threads

Virtual Threads are lightweight threads managed primarily by the JVM rather than mapping every application thread permanently to its own operating-system thread.

Example: 

Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> {

System.out.println("Running in virtual thread");


});

Or: 

Thread.ofVirtual()
    .start(() -> {

        System.out.println("Hello");

    });

Or using an executor: 

try (var executor =
    Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {

executor.submit(() -> {
    processRequest();
});


}

Now the critical topic: Pinning

Pinning means a virtual thread cannot be unmounted from its carrier thread during a blocking operation in certain situations.

Conceptually: 

Normal case:


Virtual Thread blocks
|
v
Unmount
|
v
Carrier becomes free

Pinned case: 

Virtual Thread blocks
|
v


Cannot unmount
|
v
Carrier remains occupied

This can reduce scalability.

Classic pinning example with synchronized
public synchronized void process() {

callSlowExternalApi();


}

Or: 

public void process() {

synchronized (lock) {

    callSlowExternalApi();

}


}

Conceptually: 

Virtual Thread V1
    |
    v


Enter synchronized block
|
v
Mounted on Carrier C1
|
v
Call slow blocking operation
|
v
Potential pinning situation
|
v
Carrier C1 remains occupied

If many virtual threads do this: 

V1 pins C1


V2 pins C2

V3 pins C3

V4 pins C4

...

Carrier pool becomes constrained

Important: 

Do not interpret this as:


"Never use synchronized with Virtual Threads"

Short synchronized sections that do not perform long blocking operations may be perfectly reasonable.

The dangerous combination is: 

Long-running blocking I/O


inside

synchronized region
Better approach for long blocking critical sections

Depending on the correctness requirements, a lock such as: 

ReentrantLock

may be considered.

Example: 

private final ReentrantLock lock =
    new ReentrantLock();


public void process() {


lock.lock();

try {

    callSlowExternalApi();

} finally {

    lock.unlock();

}


}

But do not blindly replace every synchronized block. Correctness, contention, JVM version, and actual profiling matter.

ReentrantLock vs ReadWriteLock

This is a very common senior Java interview topic. Both are explicit locking mechanisms from java.util.concurrent.locks, but they solve different concurrency problems.

Lock Best for Key idea
ReentrantLock General exclusive locking Only one thread enters critical section at a time
ReadWriteLock Read-heavy shared data Many readers allowed together, but writers need exclusive access
What is ReentrantLock?

ReentrantLock is an explicit mutual exclusion lock. It works like a stronger and more flexible alternative to synchronized.

Reentrant means the same thread can acquire the same lock again without deadlocking itself. 

private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

public void updateBalance() {
    lock.lock();
    try {
        // critical section
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();
    }
}
Why use ReentrantLock instead of synchronized?
  • Supports tryLock() so thread can avoid waiting forever.
  • Supports timed lock attempts.
  • Supports interruptible lock waiting.
  • Supports fairness mode.
  • Works well when advanced lock control is needed.
if (lock.tryLock()) {
    try {
        processPayment();
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();
    }
} else {
    // skip, retry, or return busy response
}

Real-world example: In a payment service, if one thread is already updating the same wallet, another thread may use tryLock() and return "please retry" instead of waiting too long.

What is ReadWriteLock?

ReadWriteLock gives two different locks:

  • Read lock: multiple threads can hold it together.
  • Write lock: only one writer at a time, and no readers during write.
private final ReadWriteLock rwLock = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();

public String getConfig(String key) {
    rwLock.readLock().lock();
    try {
        return configMap.get(key);
    } finally {
        rwLock.readLock().unlock();
    }
}

public void updateConfig(String key, String value) {
    rwLock.writeLock().lock();
    try {
        configMap.put(key, value);
    } finally {
        rwLock.writeLock().unlock();
    }
}

Real-world example: If thousands of requests read application configuration but only admins update it occasionally, ReadWriteLock can improve concurrency.

Main behavioral difference
ReentrantLock
->
1 reader at a time
1 writer at a time

ReadWriteLock
->
many readers together
but only 1 writer, exclusively
When ReadWriteLock helps
  • Shared data is read very frequently.
  • Writes are much less frequent than reads.
  • Read operation is not trivial enough to ignore contention.

Good example: 

95% reads
5% writes

Example:
- configuration cache
- product catalog lookup
- in-memory metadata registry
When ReadWriteLock is not a good fit
  • Write frequency is high.
  • Critical section is very small.
  • Underlying data structure already has better concurrent implementation.

Real-world example: For counters or high-update maps, ConcurrentHashMap or atomic classes are often better than manually managing ReadWriteLock.

Feature comparison
Feature ReentrantLock ReadWriteLock
Exclusive access Yes Write lock only
Concurrent reads No Yes
Reentrancy Yes Yes, via read/write lock implementations like ReentrantReadWriteLock
tryLock() support Yes Available through underlying read/write locks
Best use case General mutual exclusion Read-heavy shared state
Complexity Lower Higher
Reentrancy example
private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

public void outer() {
    lock.lock();
    try {
        inner();
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();
    }
}

private void inner() {
    lock.lock();
    try {
        // same thread re-enters safely
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();
    }
}

Same thread can acquire the lock again. That is why it is called reentrant.

Important caution
  • Always unlock in finally.
  • Do not hold locks while calling slow external APIs unless necessary.
  • Prefer higher-level concurrent collections if they solve the problem directly.
ReentrantLock vs ReadWriteLock interview answer

I use ReentrantLock when I need one-at-a-time exclusive access with extra features like tryLock, fairness, or interruptible waiting. I use ReadWriteLock when shared data is read much more often than it is written, because it allows multiple readers concurrently while still protecting writes.

Important modern Java nuance about pinning

Pinning behavior has evolved across JDK releases.

Therefore, a senior answer should not blindly memorize: 

synchronized always destroys Virtual Threads

Instead say: 

Pinning behavior depends on the JDK version


and the blocking construct involved.

Long blocking operations while holding monitors
or entering native/foreign code require careful analysis.

This is more accurate than repeating an outdated absolute rule.

Why are wait, notify, and notifyAll in Object?

They belong to Object because every Java object can act as a monitor lock. These methods are not about thread identity; they are about coordinating threads that are waiting on the same shared object.

In Java, a thread calls wait() on the shared condition object, not on the thread itself. That is why the methods live on Object: any object can be the monitor that threads synchronize on.

How they work
  • wait() makes the current thread release the object's monitor and sleep until it is notified.
  • notify() wakes one waiting thread on that same monitor.
  • notifyAll() wakes all waiting threads on that same monitor.

These methods must be called while holding the object's monitor, usually inside a synchronized block or method. Otherwise Java throws IllegalMonitorStateException.

Example
class MessageBox {
  private String message;
  private boolean hasMessage = false;

  public synchronized void put(String msg) throws InterruptedException {
    while (hasMessage) {
      wait();
    }
    message = msg;
    hasMessage = true;
    notifyAll();
  }

  public synchronized String take() throws InterruptedException {
    while (!hasMessage) {
      wait();
    }
    hasMessage = false;
    notifyAll();
    return message;
  }
}

Here, the producer waits when the box is full, and the consumer waits when it is empty. The same object is used as the condition and the lock.

notify vs notifyAll
  • notify() is faster, but wakes only one waiting thread and can be risky if multiple conditions share the same monitor.
  • notifyAll() wakes all waiters so they can re-check the condition; it is safer in most real-world code.
Why not on Thread?

A thread is not the shared condition. The shared object is. The object owns the monitor, and threads coordinate by waiting on or notifying that monitor.

Interview-ready answer

"wait, notify, and notifyAll are in Object because any object can be used as a monitor for thread coordination. A thread waits on a shared object and another thread signals the same object. They must be called inside a synchronized block, and notifyAll is usually safer than notify in real systems."

Virtual Thread vs CompletableFuture

Before Virtual Threads, developers often wrote: 

CompletableFuture<User> userFuture =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(
        () -> userService.getUser()
    );


CompletableFuture ordersFuture =
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(
() -> orderService.getOrders()
);

CompletableFuture.allOf(
userFuture,
ordersFuture
).join();

With Virtual Threads, blocking-style code can remain simpler: 

try (var executor =
    Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {

Future<User> user =
    executor.submit(
        () -> userService.getUser()
    );

Future<Orders> orders =
    executor.submit(
        () -> orderService.getOrders()
    );

return new Response(
    user.get(),
    orders.get()
);


}

The code remains imperative and easier to debug for many teams.

Best interview question: Do Virtual Threads use ForkJoinPool?

A useful high-level answer is:

but you should not confuse Virtual Threads
with ordinary CompletableFuture tasks
submitted to ForkJoinPool.commonPool().

They are different abstractions.

The correct senior answer is:

Modern JDK behavior has improved in this area,
so avoid repeating outdated blanket statements.

Native/foreign calls and other pinning scenarios
still require attention.
