Top senior-level interview questions

1. What is a Virtual Thread? 

A lightweight Java Thread managed by the JVM


that can be scheduled onto carrier platform threads.

2. What is a Carrier Thread? 

A platform thread that executes a mounted Virtual Thread.

3. What is mounting? 

Attaching a Virtual Thread to a carrier


so it can execute.

4. What is unmounting? 

Suspending the Virtual Thread


and freeing the carrier for other work.

5. What is pinning? 

A situation where a Virtual Thread cannot unmount


and remains attached to its carrier during blocking.

6. Are Virtual Threads faster? 

Not necessarily per request.


They improve scalability for high-concurrency,
waiting-heavy workloads.

7. Do Virtual Threads make JDBC non-blocking? 

No.


JDBC remains blocking.

8. Do Virtual Threads remove HikariCP? 

No.


Database connections remain scarce resources.

9. Can ThreadLocal work with Virtual Threads? 

Yes.


But excessive per-thread state can become expensive
when Virtual Thread counts are huge.

10. Does carrier switching break @Transactional? 

No.


The Virtual Thread remains the logical Thread
even if it executes on different carriers over time.

11. Virtual Threads or WebFlux? 

Choose Virtual Threads for simpler imperative code


and blocking ecosystem integration.

Choose WebFlux for end-to-end reactive systems,
streaming, and reactive backpressure.

12. Should Virtual Threads be pooled? 

Generally no.


Use a Virtual Thread per task model.

13. Are Virtual Threads useful for CPU-bound work? 

They do not create more CPU cores


and do not magically improve CPU-bound parallelism.

14. What is the biggest production risk? 

Creating huge concurrency


without protecting downstream scarce resources.
Best interview answer

Platform Threads are expensive OS-backed threads, so traditional Spring MVC applications normally use a bounded worker pool such as a few hundred request-processing threads. The scalability problem appears when these expensive threads spend most of their time waiting for databases, remote APIs, files, or other I/O. Virtual Threads provide a lightweight Java Thread abstraction managed by the JVM. A Virtual Thread executes by mounting onto a carrier Platform Thread. When it reaches a supported blocking operation, it can often suspend and unmount, allowing the carrier to execute another runnable Virtual Thread. Later, when the operation completes, the Virtual Thread becomes runnable and may continue on the same or a different carrier. This allows very large numbers of concurrent waiting tasks without requiring the same number of OS threads. However, Virtual Threads do not make JDBC non-blocking, do not increase CPU cores, do not remove HikariCP limits, and do not make downstream systems infinitely scalable. Pinning and long blocking operations in problematic critical sections must still be understood, with behavior considered against the actual JDK version. ThreadLocal and Spring transaction context can work because the Virtual Thread remains the logical Thread even when carrier threads change, but arbitrary asynchronous task boundaries such as @Async still require separate context-propagation thinking. Compared with WebFlux, Virtual Threads preserve simple imperative programming and integrate naturally with existing blocking ecosystems such as Spring MVC, JPA, Hibernate, and JDBC, while WebFlux uses a small event-loop model with reactive pipelines and requires blocking work to stay away from event-loop threads. The most important production rule is that cheap threads do not mean unlimited capacity: database connections, external API concurrency, CPU, memory, sockets, and downstream services still require explicit limits, timeouts, bulkheads, and backpressure strategies.

@GeneratedValue tells JPA/Hibernate how the primary key value should be generated for an entity. It is commonly used with @Id. 

@Entity
class Employee {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    private String name;
}

JPA provides four main strategies: AUTO, IDENTITY, SEQUENCE, and TABLE.

1. GenerationType.IDENTITY

The database generates the primary key using an auto-increment column. Hibernate inserts the row first and then reads the generated id from the database. 

@Entity
class Product {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    private String name;
}
CREATE TABLE product (
    id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

Use IDENTITY mostly with MySQL, SQL Server, and databases where auto-increment identity columns are common.

2. GenerationType.SEQUENCE

The database sequence generates the id before the insert. Hibernate can ask the sequence for the next value and then use that value while inserting the row. 

@Entity
class OrderEntity {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "order_seq")
    @SequenceGenerator(
        name = "order_seq",
        sequenceName = "order_sequence",
        allocationSize = 1
    )
    private Long id;

    private String orderNumber;
}
CREATE SEQUENCE order_sequence
    START WITH 1
    INCREMENT BY 1;

CREATE TABLE orders (
    id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    order_number VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

Use SEQUENCE mostly with PostgreSQL, Oracle, and databases that support sequences. It is often better for batching than IDENTITY.

3. GenerationType.AUTO

Hibernate chooses the best strategy based on the database dialect. For example, it may choose SEQUENCE for PostgreSQL or a different strategy depending on the database. 

@Entity
class Customer {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.AUTO)
    private Long id;

    private String email;
}

Use AUTO when you want Hibernate to decide. For interview answers and production clarity, many teams prefer explicitly choosing IDENTITY or SEQUENCE.

4. GenerationType.TABLE

Hibernate uses a separate table to store and update id values. This works across databases, but it is usually slower because every id generation needs extra table access. 

@Entity
class Invoice {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.TABLE, generator = "invoice_gen")
    @TableGenerator(
        name = "invoice_gen",
        table = "id_generator",
        pkColumnName = "gen_name",
        valueColumnName = "gen_value",
        pkColumnValue = "invoice_id",
        allocationSize = 1
    )
    private Long id;

    private Double amount;
}
CREATE TABLE id_generator (
    gen_name VARCHAR(100) PRIMARY KEY,
    gen_value BIGINT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE invoice (
    id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    amount DOUBLE
);

Use TABLE rarely. It is mostly useful for legacy databases or databases without identity or sequence support.

Comparison table
Strategy How id is generated Common database When to use
AUTO Hibernate chooses automatically Depends on dialect Simple apps, database-independent code
IDENTITY Auto-increment column MySQL, SQL Server When the database table owns id generation
SEQUENCE Database sequence PostgreSQL, Oracle High-performance inserts and batching
TABLE Separate id generator table Any database Legacy or portable fallback, rarely preferred
Important interview points
  • IDENTITY gets the id from an auto-increment column after insert.
  • SEQUENCE gets the id from a database sequence before insert.
  • SEQUENCE usually works better with Hibernate batch inserts.
  • AUTO lets Hibernate choose, but explicit strategy is clearer.
  • TABLE is portable but slower and rarely used in modern applications.

Interview one-liner: use IDENTITY for MySQL-style auto-increment, use SEQUENCE for PostgreSQL/Oracle sequence-based ids, avoid TABLE unless needed, and use AUTO only when you are comfortable letting Hibernate decide.

We have a list of employees, and each employee has multiple hobbies. The requirement is to return a map where the key is the hobby and the value is the list of employee names who have that hobby. 

class Employee {
    private String name;
    private List<String> hobbies;

    public Employee(String name, List<String> hobbies) {
        this.name = name;
        this.hobbies = hobbies;
    }

    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }

    public List<String> getHobbies() {
        return hobbies;
    }
}
List<Employee> employees = Arrays.asList(
    new Employee("Ravi", Arrays.asList("Cricket", "Music")),
    new Employee("Anu", Arrays.asList("Music", "Reading")),
    new Employee("Kiran", Arrays.asList("Cricket", "Travel"))
);

Expected output: 

{
    Cricket=[Ravi, Kiran],
    Music=[Ravi, Anu],
    Reading=[Anu],
    Travel=[Kiran]
}
Way 1: Using flatMap + groupingBy + mapping
Map<String, List<String>> hobbyToEmployeeNames =
    employees.stream()
        .flatMap(employee ->
            employee.getHobbies().stream()
                .map(hobby ->
                    Map.entry(hobby, employee.getName())
                )
        )
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
            Map.Entry::getKey,
            Collectors.mapping(Map.Entry::getValue, Collectors.toList())
        ));
Methods used
  • stream() converts the employee list into a stream.
  • flatMap() converts one employee into multiple hobby-name pairs.
  • map() creates one pair like Cricket -> Ravi.
  • groupingBy() groups all pairs by hobby.
  • mapping() collects only employee names, not the whole pair object.
  • toList() creates the final list of names for each hobby.

This is the most common interview solution because it shows proper Stream API usage.

Way 2: Using normal for loops
Map<String, List<String>> result = new HashMap<>();

for (Employee employee : employees) {
    for (String hobby : employee.getHobbies()) {
        result
            .computeIfAbsent(hobby, key -> new ArrayList<>())
            .add(employee.getName());
    }
}

computeIfAbsent() checks whether the hobby already exists in the map. If it does not exist, it creates a new ArrayList. Then we add the employee name to that list.

This approach is very readable and is often preferred in production when the stream version feels too dense.

Way 3: Using Map.merge()
Map<String, List<String>> result = new HashMap<>();

for (Employee employee : employees) {
    for (String hobby : employee.getHobbies()) {
        List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
        names.add(employee.getName());

        result.merge(hobby, names, (oldList, newList) -> {
            oldList.addAll(newList);
            return oldList;
        });
    }
}

merge() says: if the hobby is not present, insert the new list. If the hobby is already present, merge the old list and the new list.

Way 4: If duplicate names should be avoided

If an employee has duplicate hobbies, or you want each name only once per hobby, collect into a Set instead of a List. 

Map<String, Set<String>> hobbyToEmployeeNames =
    employees.stream()
        .flatMap(employee ->
            employee.getHobbies().stream()
                .map(hobby ->
                    new AbstractMap.SimpleEntry<>(hobby, employee.getName())
                )
        )
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
            Map.Entry::getKey,
            Collectors.mapping(Map.Entry::getValue, Collectors.toSet())
        ));
Complete runnable example
import java.util.AbstractMap;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public class EmployeeHobbyGrouping {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Employee> employees = Arrays.asList(
            new Employee("Ravi", Arrays.asList("Cricket", "Music")),
            new Employee("Anu", Arrays.asList("Music", "Reading")),
            new Employee("Kiran", Arrays.asList("Cricket", "Travel"))
        );

        Map<String, List<String>> result =
            employees.stream()
                .flatMap(employee ->
                    employee.getHobbies().stream()
                        .map(hobby ->
                            new AbstractMap.SimpleEntry<>(hobby, employee.getName())
                        )
                )
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                    Map.Entry::getKey,
                    Collectors.mapping(Map.Entry::getValue, Collectors.toList())
                ));

        System.out.println(result);
    }
}

Interview one-liner: use flatMap because each employee produces multiple hobby-name pairs, then use groupingBy to group by hobby and mapping to collect only employee names.

@Transactional tells Spring to run a method inside a database transaction. If the method completes successfully, Spring commits the transaction. If it fails with an unchecked exception, Spring rolls back the transaction by default. 

@Service
public class PaymentService {

    @Transactional
    public void transferMoney(Long fromAccountId, Long toAccountId, BigDecimal amount) {
        Account from = accountRepository.findById(fromAccountId).orElseThrow();
        Account to = accountRepository.findById(toAccountId).orElseThrow();

        from.debit(amount);
        to.credit(amount);

        accountRepository.save(from);
        accountRepository.save(to);
    }
}

In the above example, debit and credit should succeed together. If credit fails after debit, the whole transaction should roll back.

Important attributes
Attribute Meaning
propagation Defines how this method joins, creates, or avoids a transaction.
isolation Defines how visible changes from other transactions are.
rollbackFor Forces rollback for checked exceptions.
readOnly Optimizes transaction for read operations.
timeout Sets maximum transaction execution time.
Propagation

Propagation answers this question: if one transactional method calls another transactional method, should the second method use the existing transaction, create a new one, or run without a transaction?

Propagation Behavior Common use
REQUIRED Use existing transaction; create one if none exists. Default for most service methods.
REQUIRES_NEW Suspend existing transaction and start a new one. Audit/log record that must save independently.
NESTED Run inside nested transaction using savepoint. Partial rollback inside a larger transaction.
SUPPORTS Use transaction if present; otherwise run without one. Read methods that can work either way.
NOT_SUPPORTED Suspend transaction and run without transaction. Long external calls that should not hold DB locks.
MANDATORY Must have an existing transaction; otherwise error. Internal method that should never run alone.
NEVER Must not run inside a transaction; error if one exists. Rare cases where transaction is forbidden.
Example: REQUIRED
@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRED)
public void placeOrder(OrderRequest request) {
    orderRepository.save(request.toOrder());
    inventoryService.reduceStock(request.productId(), request.quantity());
}

REQUIRED is the default. If placeOrder() is already called inside another transaction, it joins that transaction. Otherwise, Spring creates a new transaction.

Example: REQUIRES_NEW for audit logs
@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final AuditService auditService;

    public OrderService(AuditService auditService) {
        this.auditService = auditService;
    }

    @Transactional
    public void placeOrder(OrderRequest request) {
        orderRepository.save(request.toOrder());

        auditService.saveAudit("ORDER_CREATED");

        if (request.quantity() <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid quantity");
        }
    }
}

@Service
public class AuditService {

    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void saveAudit(String message) {
        auditRepository.save(new AuditLog(message));
    }
}

If placeOrder() fails, the order transaction rolls back. But saveAudit() uses REQUIRES_NEW, so its audit record can commit independently.

Example: MANDATORY
@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.MANDATORY)
public void reduceStock(Long productId, int quantity) {
    Product product = productRepository.findById(productId).orElseThrow();
    product.reduceStock(quantity);
}

Use MANDATORY when the method must be called only from an existing transaction. If no transaction exists, Spring throws an exception.

Isolation

Isolation answers this question: how much should one transaction be protected from changes made by other concurrent transactions?

Isolation Allows / prevents When to use
READ_UNCOMMITTED Allows dirty reads. Almost never used in business apps.
READ_COMMITTED Prevents dirty reads. Common default in many databases.
REPEATABLE_READ Prevents dirty and non-repeatable reads. When same row must stay stable during transaction.
SERIALIZABLE Strongest isolation; transactions behave one by one. Critical consistency, but lower performance.
DEFAULT Uses database default isolation level. Most common choice.
Read problems
Problem Meaning
Dirty read Transaction reads uncommitted data from another transaction.
Non-repeatable read Same row gives different values when read twice in one transaction.
Phantom read Same query returns new rows because another transaction inserted matching data.
Example: isolation for balance check
@Transactional(isolation = Isolation.REPEATABLE_READ)
public void withdraw(Long accountId, BigDecimal amount) {
    Account account = accountRepository.findById(accountId).orElseThrow();

    if (account.getBalance().compareTo(amount) < 0) {
        throw new InsufficientBalanceException("Insufficient balance");
    }

    account.debit(amount);
}

REPEATABLE_READ helps when the same account row should not unexpectedly change while the transaction is running.

Example: read-only transaction
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public List<AccountStatement> getStatements(Long accountId) {
    return statementRepository.findByAccountId(accountId);
}

readOnly = true is useful for query methods. It tells Spring/Hibernate that the method should not modify data and can be optimized for reads.

Rollback rules
  • Runtime exceptions trigger rollback by default.
  • Checked exceptions do not trigger rollback by default.
  • Use rollbackFor when a checked exception should roll back.
@Transactional(rollbackFor = PaymentFailedException.class)
public void makePayment() throws PaymentFailedException {
    debit();
    credit();
    throw new PaymentFailedException("Payment failed");
}
Who defines isolation - Spring or the database?

Spring lets you request an isolation level through @Transactional(isolation = ...), but the actual enforcement happens at the database/driver level through JDBC. Spring does not invent isolation on its own. It simply translates the request into a transaction setting for the underlying connection.

So the short answer is:

  • Spring exposes the annotation and passes the requested setting.
  • The database decides what that setting really means and whether it can honor it.
  • If the database or driver cannot support the requested isolation, Spring does not emulate it in memory.
What happens if the requested isolation is not supported?

It depends on the database and JDBC driver. In many cases, the driver or transaction manager will either throw an exception or fall back to the nearest supported behavior. Spring itself does not magically guarantee the unsupported level.

Example: if you request SERIALIZABLE on a database that supports it, the database will try to enforce the strictest behavior. If you request a level that the database cannot provide, the transaction may fail to start or the database may map it to a supported level, depending on the vendor.

Default isolation level

In Spring, the default is Isolation.DEFAULT. That means "use the database default isolation level." The actual default depends on the database:

Layer Default
Spring Isolation.DEFAULT
Most databases Commonly READ_COMMITTED
MySQL InnoDB Commonly REPEATABLE_READ
Oracle Commonly READ_COMMITTED
Isolation levels with real-world analogy
Isolation Analogy Meaning
READ_UNCOMMITTED Looking at a whiteboard while someone is still writing on it You may see unfinished changes.
READ_COMMITTED Only reading notes after the writer says "done" You never see uncommitted changes.
REPEATABLE_READ Photographing a page and reading the same snapshot again Same row stays stable inside the transaction.
SERIALIZABLE Only one person is allowed in the room at a time Transactions behave one after another.
Clear-cut example
@Transactional(isolation = Isolation.READ_COMMITTED)
public BigDecimal checkBalance(Long accountId) {
    return accountRepository.findById(accountId)
            .orElseThrow()
            .getBalance();
}
@Transactional(isolation = Isolation.REPEATABLE_READ)
public void readSameBalanceTwice(Long accountId) {
    BigDecimal first = accountRepository.findById(accountId).orElseThrow().getBalance();
    // another transaction may update the row here
    BigDecimal second = accountRepository.findById(accountId).orElseThrow().getBalance();
    // with REPEATABLE_READ, first and second should remain consistent within this transaction
}

A common business example is wallet balance or inventory stock. If two checkout requests run together, lower isolation can allow one request to see changing values, while higher isolation reduces that risk but can reduce throughput.

Quick interview questions on isolation
  • What is the difference between propagation and isolation in @Transactional?
  • Is isolation controlled by Spring or by the database?
  • What is Spring's default isolation level?
  • What are dirty read, non-repeatable read, and phantom read?
  • When would you choose READ_COMMITTED over REPEATABLE_READ?
  • What happens if the requested isolation level is not supported by the database?
  • Why is SERIALIZABLE the safest but usually the slowest?
Common pitfalls
  • @Transactional usually works through Spring proxy, so self-invocation may not apply it.
  • Do not keep transactions open during slow external API calls.
  • Use REQUIRES_NEW carefully because it creates an independent transaction.
  • Higher isolation improves consistency but can reduce performance.
  • Put transaction boundaries mostly on service methods, not controller methods.

Interview one-liner: @Transactional controls commit and rollback; propagation controls how methods join or create transactions, and isolation controls how concurrent transactions see each other's data.

Audit fields are used to track who created or updated a row and when it happened. Common columns are created_by, updated_by, created_date, and updated_date.

There are two common ways to do this in Spring Boot:

  • Using Spring Data JPA auditing annotations like @CreatedBy and @LastModifiedBy.
  • Using a Hibernate interceptor/listener to set audit fields before insert and update.
Way 1: Spring Data JPA auditing annotations

This is the cleanest and most common approach when you are using Spring Data JPA repositories. 

@MappedSuperclass
@EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class)
public abstract class AuditEntity {

    @CreatedBy
    @Column(name = "created_by", updatable = false)
    private String createdBy;

    @LastModifiedBy
    @Column(name = "updated_by")
    private String updatedBy;

    @CreatedDate
    @Column(name = "created_date", updatable = false)
    private LocalDateTime createdDate;

    @LastModifiedDate
    @Column(name = "updated_date")
    private LocalDateTime updatedDate;
}

Any entity can extend this base class: 

@Entity
@Table(name = "orders")
public class Order extends AuditEntity {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    private String orderNumber;
    private BigDecimal amount;
}
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    order_number VARCHAR(100),
    amount DECIMAL(10, 2),
    created_by VARCHAR(100),
    updated_by VARCHAR(100),
    created_date TIMESTAMP,
    updated_date TIMESTAMP
);

Enable JPA auditing in a configuration class: 

@Configuration
@EnableJpaAuditing(auditorAwareRef = "auditorProvider")
public class JpaAuditConfig {

    @Bean
    public AuditorAware<String> auditorProvider() {
        return new SecurityAuditorAware();
    }
}

Get the username from the token stored in Spring Security context: 

public class SecurityAuditorAware implements AuditorAware<String> {

    @Override
    public Optional<String> getCurrentAuditor() {
        Authentication authentication =
                SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();

        if (authentication == null || !authentication.isAuthenticated()) {
            return Optional.of("SYSTEM");
        }

        if (authentication instanceof JwtAuthenticationToken jwtAuth) {
            String username = jwtAuth.getToken().getClaimAsString("preferred_username");

            if (username != null) {
                return Optional.of(username);
            }
        }

        return Optional.of(authentication.getName());
    }
}

Flow: 

JWT token
   -> Spring Security filter validates token
   -> Authentication stored in SecurityContextHolder
   -> AuditorAware reads current username
   -> @CreatedBy / @LastModifiedBy fields are filled automatically
   -> Entity is saved with audit columns
Way 2: Hibernate interceptor approach

A Hibernate interceptor can set audit fields before insert and update. This is useful when you want audit logic at the Hibernate layer, or when some saves do not go through normal repository auditing.

First create a common interface: 

public interface Auditable {
    void setCreatedBy(String createdBy);
    void setUpdatedBy(String updatedBy);
    void setCreatedDate(LocalDateTime createdDate);
    void setUpdatedDate(LocalDateTime updatedDate);
}

Then make your base entity implement it: 

@MappedSuperclass
public abstract class AuditEntity implements Auditable {

    @Column(name = "created_by", updatable = false)
    private String createdBy;

    @Column(name = "updated_by")
    private String updatedBy;

    @Column(name = "created_date", updatable = false)
    private LocalDateTime createdDate;

    @Column(name = "updated_date")
    private LocalDateTime updatedDate;

    public void setCreatedBy(String createdBy) {
        this.createdBy = createdBy;
    }

    public void setUpdatedBy(String updatedBy) {
        this.updatedBy = updatedBy;
    }

    public void setCreatedDate(LocalDateTime createdDate) {
        this.createdDate = createdDate;
    }

    public void setUpdatedDate(LocalDateTime updatedDate) {
        this.updatedDate = updatedDate;
    }
}

Create a helper to read username from the current token: 

@Component
public class CurrentUserProvider {

    public String getUsername() {
        Authentication authentication =
                SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();

        if (authentication == null || !authentication.isAuthenticated()) {
            return "SYSTEM";
        }

        if (authentication instanceof JwtAuthenticationToken jwtAuth) {
            String username = jwtAuth.getToken().getClaimAsString("preferred_username");
            return username != null ? username : jwtAuth.getName();
        }

        return authentication.getName();
    }
}

Create the Hibernate interceptor: 

@Component
public class AuditHibernateInterceptor extends EmptyInterceptor {

    private final CurrentUserProvider currentUserProvider;

    public AuditHibernateInterceptor(CurrentUserProvider currentUserProvider) {
        this.currentUserProvider = currentUserProvider;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean onSave(Object entity, Serializable id, Object[] state,
                          String[] propertyNames, Type[] types) {

        if (entity instanceof Auditable auditable) {
            String username = currentUserProvider.getUsername();
            LocalDateTime now = LocalDateTime.now();

            auditable.setCreatedBy(username);
            auditable.setUpdatedBy(username);
            auditable.setCreatedDate(now);
            auditable.setUpdatedDate(now);

            setValue(state, propertyNames, "createdBy", username);
            setValue(state, propertyNames, "updatedBy", username);
            setValue(state, propertyNames, "createdDate", now);
            setValue(state, propertyNames, "updatedDate", now);

            return true;
        }

        return false;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean onFlushDirty(Object entity, Serializable id, Object[] currentState,
                                Object[] previousState, String[] propertyNames,
                                Type[] types) {

        if (entity instanceof Auditable auditable) {
            String username = currentUserProvider.getUsername();
            LocalDateTime now = LocalDateTime.now();

            auditable.setUpdatedBy(username);
            auditable.setUpdatedDate(now);

            setValue(currentState, propertyNames, "updatedBy", username);
            setValue(currentState, propertyNames, "updatedDate", now);

            return true;
        }

        return false;
    }

    private void setValue(Object[] state, String[] propertyNames,
                          String propertyName, Object value) {
        for (int index = 0; index < propertyNames.length; index++) {
            if (propertyNames[index].equals(propertyName)) {
                state[index] = value;
                return;
            }
        }
    }
}

Register the interceptor with Hibernate: 

@Configuration
public class HibernateAuditConfig {

    @Bean
    public HibernatePropertiesCustomizer hibernatePropertiesCustomizer(
            AuditHibernateInterceptor interceptor) {

        return properties ->
                properties.put("hibernate.session_factory.interceptor", interceptor);
    }
}
Annotation approach vs interceptor approach
Approach Best use Notes
Spring Data JPA auditing Normal Spring Boot JPA applications Simple, readable, recommended for most projects.
Hibernate interceptor Central Hibernate-level audit behavior More control, but more complex and Hibernate-specific.
Database trigger Audit must happen even outside application Strong DB-level guarantee, but logic is outside Java code.
Important points
  • createdBy and createdDate should normally be set only during insert.
  • updatedBy and updatedDate should change on every update.
  • The token should be validated before the username is read from SecurityContextHolder.
  • Use SYSTEM for scheduler jobs, batch jobs, or unauthenticated internal operations.
  • For normal applications, prefer Spring Data auditing; use interceptor only when you need Hibernate-level control.

Interview one-liner: use Spring Data auditing annotations for standard audit columns; implement AuditorAware to read the username from the token, and use a Hibernate interceptor only when audit values must be handled centrally at the Hibernate persistence layer.

Microservices architecture breaks a large application into small, independently deployable services. Each service owns a specific business capability, has its own data responsibility, and communicates with other services using APIs or messages.

Core components
Component Purpose Example
Microservice Small service focused on one business capability. OrderService, PaymentService, UserService
API Gateway Single entry point for clients; handles routing, auth, rate limiting, and aggregation. Spring Cloud Gateway, Kong, NGINX
Service Discovery Finds service instances dynamically instead of hardcoding host and port. Eureka, Consul, Kubernetes Service
Config Server Centralizes service configuration. Spring Cloud Config, Kubernetes ConfigMap
Database per Service Each service owns its own database or schema. Order DB, Payment DB, Inventory DB
Message Broker Enables async communication and event-driven processing. Kafka, RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ
Observability Tracks logs, metrics, traces, and health. ELK, Prometheus, Grafana, Zipkin, Jaeger
Security Protects APIs and service communication. OAuth2, JWT, Keycloak, mTLS
Example flow
Client
   -> API Gateway
   -> Order Service
   -> Payment Service
   -> Inventory Service
   -> Notification Service

In a real order system, the client does not directly call all services. It calls the API Gateway. The gateway routes the request to OrderService. The order service may call payment and inventory, or publish an event to Kafka so other services can react asynchronously.

Spring Boot style example
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/orders")
public class OrderController {

    private final OrderService orderService;

    public OrderController(OrderService orderService) {
        this.orderService = orderService;
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> createOrder(@RequestBody OrderRequest request) {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(orderService.createOrder(request));
    }
}
@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final PaymentClient paymentClient;
    private final InventoryClient inventoryClient;
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, OrderCreatedEvent> kafkaTemplate;

    @Transactional
    public OrderResponse createOrder(OrderRequest request) {
        inventoryClient.reserveStock(request.productId(), request.quantity());
        paymentClient.charge(request.paymentDetails());

        Order order = orderRepository.save(request.toOrder());

        kafkaTemplate.send("order-created", new OrderCreatedEvent(order.getId()));

        return OrderResponse.from(order);
    }
}
Communication styles
Style How it works When to use
Synchronous Service calls another service and waits for response. Immediate response is required.
Asynchronous Service publishes event/message and continues. Loose coupling, background processing, notifications.
Important interview points
  • Each microservice should own one business capability.
  • Each service should be independently deployable.
  • Prefer database per service to avoid tight coupling.
  • Use API Gateway for client-facing routing and cross-cutting concerns.
  • Use observability because debugging distributed systems is harder than monoliths.

Interview one-liner: microservices architecture is made of independently deployable services plus supporting components like API Gateway, service discovery, config server, message broker, security, and observability.

Microservices solve scale and deployment problems, but they introduce distributed-system complexity. The biggest challenges are communication, data consistency, observability, failure handling, deployment, and operational overhead.

Common challenges
  • Service-to-service communication: network calls are slower and less reliable than in-process calls.
  • Data consistency: each service owns its data, so distributed transactions are hard.
  • Failure handling: one slow or failing service can affect others if timeouts and circuit breakers are missing.
  • Observability: logs, metrics, and traces must be correlated across services.
  • Deployment and versioning: backward compatibility and coordinated releases become important.
  • Security: service-to-service authentication and authorization are more complex.
  • Testing: integration, contract, and end-to-end tests are harder than in a monolith.
  • Operations: more services mean more config, more infrastructure, and more monitoring.
Real-world example

In an order flow, the API Gateway calls Order Service, which calls Payment Service and Inventory Service. If Payment Service is slow, the whole checkout can fail unless we use timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, correlation IDs, and fallback behavior carefully.

How we reduce the pain

Use service discovery, API gateway, resilience patterns, centralized logging, tracing, metrics, database per service, contract testing, and strong CI/CD. Keep each service small and align it to a business capability.

Interview-ready answer

"Microservices introduce distributed-system problems: network latency, data consistency, failures, observability, deployment complexity, testing complexity, and security. We manage them with timeouts, circuit breakers, tracing, centralized logs, database-per-service, and strong automation."

For resilient microservices, I combine timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads, and fallback logic. The goal is to stop one failing dependency from taking down the whole system.

What the circuit breaker does
  • Closed: calls flow normally while the dependency is healthy.
  • Open: calls are rejected fast when failures cross the threshold.
  • Half-open: a few trial requests are allowed to see if the dependency recovered.
Why it helps

Without protection, a slow downstream service can create thread exhaustion, connection pool saturation, and cascading failures. A circuit breaker gives the system time to recover instead of endlessly waiting.

Spring Boot + Resilience4j example
@Service
public class PaymentClient {

    @CircuitBreaker(name = "paymentService", fallbackMethod = "paymentFallback")
    @Retry(name = "paymentService")
    public PaymentResponse callPayment(OrderRequest request) {
        return restTemplate.postForObject("/payments", request, PaymentResponse.class);
    }

    private PaymentResponse paymentFallback(OrderRequest request, Throwable ex) {
        return new PaymentResponse("DEGRADED", "Payment service unavailable");
    }
}
Real-world example

In checkout flow, if Payment Service is temporarily slow, the Order Service can fail fast, show a clean message, or queue the request instead of letting every request block threads.

Important design points
  • Set strict timeouts before retries.
  • Retry only idempotent operations.
  • Use bulkheads so one dependency does not consume all worker threads.
  • Track metrics for failure rate, slow calls, and open-state duration.
  • Keep fallbacks safe and business-friendly, not silent failures.
Interview-ready answer

"I design resilient service-to-service communication with timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, and bulkheads. With Resilience4j in Spring Boot, I protect downstream calls using @CircuitBreaker and fallback methods, so a slow dependency fails fast instead of causing cascading outages."

I would make the API stateless, accept data quickly, and push the heavy work to Kafka and downstream consumers. That keeps latency low even when millions of devices send telemetry concurrently.

High-level design
  • Devices call a Spring Boot ingestion API behind a load balancer or API gateway.
  • The API authenticates the device, validates the payload, and publishes the event to Kafka.
  • Partition Kafka topics by deviceId so ordering is preserved per device.
  • Consumer groups process events in parallel and persist them to time-series storage, object storage, or analytics systems.
Why Kafka fits here

Kafka absorbs burst traffic, decouples ingestion from processing, and allows horizontal scaling through partitions and consumer groups. It is a strong fit when telemetry arrives faster than the database can process it directly.

Spring Boot producer example
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/telemetry")
public class TelemetryController {

    private final KafkaTemplate<String, TelemetryEvent> kafkaTemplate;

    public TelemetryController(KafkaTemplate<String, TelemetryEvent> kafkaTemplate) {
        this.kafkaTemplate = kafkaTemplate;
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<Void> ingest(@RequestBody TelemetryEvent event) {
        kafkaTemplate.send("telemetry-events", event.deviceId(), event);
        return ResponseEntity.accepted().build();
    }
}
How I keep it fast and safe
  • Use compression, batching, and idempotent producers for Kafka.
  • Return 202 Accepted quickly instead of blocking on downstream storage.
  • Use rate limiting and backpressure for overloaded devices.
  • Add retries and a dead-letter topic for poison messages.
  • Use schema management such as Avro or Protobuf to keep message contracts stable.
Scaling strategy
  • Scale the API horizontally because it is stateless.
  • Increase Kafka partitions as throughput grows.
  • Scale consumers independently based on lag.
  • Store aggregates in a read-optimized store for dashboards and alerts.
Real-world example

If ten million smart meters send readings every minute, the API should only validate and enqueue the event. Kafka fans the load out to consumers that calculate alerts, persist trends, and trigger alarms without blocking device requests.

Interview-ready answer

"For millions of IoT devices, I would use a stateless Spring Boot ingestion API, publish telemetry to Kafka, partition by deviceId, and scale consumers independently. That gives low latency at the edge, high throughput in the pipeline, and resilient asynchronous processing downstream."

CAP theorem says that in a distributed system, when a network partition happens, we must choose between Consistency and Availability while still keeping Partition Tolerance. In real systems, partitions can happen, so partition tolerance is not optional.

What the letters mean
  • C - Consistency: all nodes see the same latest data.
  • A - Availability: every request gets a response, even if some data may be stale.
  • P - Partition tolerance: the system continues operating when nodes cannot communicate perfectly.
When do we use CAP theorem?

We use it while designing distributed databases, caches, and microservice-backed data stores, especially when deciding what should happen during a network split or node failure. The real question is not "whether CAP exists" but "which tradeoff is acceptable for this business case?"

Typical choices
  • CP: prefer correctness over always responding. Good for banking, inventory, and order state.
  • AP: prefer availability over immediate freshness. Good for feeds, caches, and some shopping experiences.
Real-world example

For a payment ledger, I would usually prefer consistency, even if the system temporarily rejects writes during a partition. For a product recommendation feed, I may prefer availability so users still get a response even if the data is slightly stale.

Important interview point

CAP is mainly about what happens during a partition. In normal healthy operation, systems can often provide both strong consistency and availability, but once communication breaks, the tradeoff becomes real.

Interview-ready answer

"CAP theorem is used when designing distributed systems to decide what to do during a network partition. Since partitions are unavoidable, we must choose between consistency and availability for the business case. I use CP for correctness-critical flows like payments and AP when availability matters more, such as feeds or caches."

In microservices, each service usually owns its own database, so we cannot rely on one big ACID transaction across the whole system. The usual goal is eventual consistency with safe business workflows.

Common approaches
  • Saga pattern: each service completes a local transaction and, if needed, runs a compensating action on failure.
  • Transactional Outbox: save the business data and the event in the same local transaction, then publish it reliably.
  • Idempotent consumers: handle duplicate messages safely so repeated delivery does not corrupt state.
  • Event-driven updates: let other services react to events and build their own read models.
  • Optimistic locking / versioning: prevent lost updates inside a service-owned aggregate.
Real-world example

In an order flow, the Order Service creates the order, the Payment Service charges the card, and the Inventory Service reserves stock. If payment fails after order creation, a Saga can cancel the order. If the service publishes OrderCreated through an outbox table, the event is not lost even if the app crashes after the database commit.

What we avoid

We usually avoid a distributed transaction across all services because it is slow, tightly coupled, and harder to operate at scale. That is why microservices prefer consistency patterns that keep each service independent but coordinate the business process safely.

Interview-ready answer

"In microservices, we usually achieve consistency with eventual consistency patterns such as Saga, Outbox, idempotent consumers, and versioning. Each service commits its own local transaction, and the overall business process is coordinated through events and compensating actions rather than one global transaction."

Microservices patterns solve common distributed-system problems like service communication, failure handling, consistency, deployment, security, and observability.

Important design patterns
Pattern Problem solved Example
API Gateway Clients should not call many services directly. Gateway routes /orders to Order Service.
Database per Service Services should not be tightly coupled through one shared DB. Order DB and Payment DB are separate.
Saga Distributed transaction without 2-phase commit. Order created, payment charged, inventory reserved.
Circuit Breaker Prevent repeated calls to failing service. Stop calling Payment Service after many failures.
Retry Handle temporary network/service failure. Retry payment status check 3 times.
Bulkhead Isolate failures so one slow dependency does not block all threads. Separate thread pool for payment calls.
CQRS Separate write model from read model. Order writes in DB, order search reads from Elasticsearch.
Event Sourcing Store state changes as events. OrderCreated, PaymentCompleted, OrderShipped
Outbox Reliably publish events when DB transaction commits. Save order and outbox event in same transaction.
Strangler Fig Migrate monolith gradually. Move payment module from monolith to Payment Service.
Example: Circuit Breaker
@Service
public class PaymentServiceClient {

    @CircuitBreaker(name = "paymentService", fallbackMethod = "paymentFallback")
    @Retry(name = "paymentService")
    public PaymentResponse charge(PaymentRequest request) {
        return restTemplate.postForObject(
            "http://payment-service/payments",
            request,
            PaymentResponse.class
        );
    }

    public PaymentResponse paymentFallback(PaymentRequest request, Exception exception) {
        return PaymentResponse.failed("Payment service temporarily unavailable");
    }
}

If the payment service is failing repeatedly, the circuit opens and calls go to fallback instead of continuously hitting the failing dependency.

Example: Saga pattern
Order Service:
    create order with status PENDING
    publish OrderCreated event

Payment Service:
    consume OrderCreated
    charge payment
    publish PaymentCompleted or PaymentFailed

Inventory Service:
    consume PaymentCompleted
    reserve stock
    publish StockReserved or StockFailed

Order Service:
    consume final event
    mark order CONFIRMED or CANCELLED

Saga is used when multiple services need to complete a business transaction, but each service owns its own database. If one step fails, compensating actions are triggered. 

@KafkaListener(topics = "payment-failed")
public void handlePaymentFailed(PaymentFailedEvent event) {
    Order order = orderRepository.findById(event.orderId()).orElseThrow();
    order.cancel();
    orderRepository.save(order);
}
Example: Outbox pattern
@Transactional
public void createOrder(OrderRequest request) {
    Order order = orderRepository.save(request.toOrder());

    OutboxEvent event = new OutboxEvent(
        "ORDER_CREATED",
        "{ \"orderId\": " + order.getId() + " }"
    );

    outboxRepository.save(event);
}

The order and outbox event are saved in the same database transaction. A background publisher later reads the outbox table and publishes the event to Kafka.

Pattern selection guide
Situation Use this pattern
Client needs one entry point API Gateway
Service should own its data Database per Service
Need transaction across many services Saga
Dependency is failing Circuit Breaker + Retry
Need reliable event publishing Outbox
Need fast read model CQRS
Migrating monolith slowly Strangler Fig
Important interview points
  • Use patterns to solve real distributed-system problems, not just because the app uses microservices.
  • Saga gives eventual consistency, not immediate strong consistency.
  • Retry should usually be combined with timeout and circuit breaker.
  • Outbox prevents losing events after database commit.
  • API Gateway should not contain heavy business logic.

Interview one-liner: microservices design patterns handle routing, resilience, data ownership, distributed transactions, reliable messaging, and migration from monolith to independent services.

What is CQRS?

CQRS stands for: 

Command Query Responsibility Segregation

The main idea is to separate: 

WRITE operations
    from


READ operations

In a traditional application, the same model, service, repository, and database are often used for both reads and writes.

In CQRS, we separate them into: 

Command Side
-> Changes system state


Query Side
-> Reads system state
Core principle

A Command asks the system to perform an action. 

CreateOrder


CancelOrder
ApprovePayment
UpdateCustomerAddress
ShipOrder

A Query asks the system for information. 

GetOrderById


GetCustomerOrders
SearchOrders
GetOrderDashboard
GetMonthlySalesReport

The fundamental separation is: 

Command
-> changes state


Query
-> returns data
-> should not change state
Simple definition
CQRS separates the write model from the read model


so that each side can be designed, optimized,
scaled, secured, and evolved independently.
Traditional CRUD architecture

Consider an Order Management application. 

Client


|
v
OrderController
|
v
OrderService
|
v
OrderRepository
|
v
Orders Database

The same flow handles: 

POST   /orders


PUT    /orders/{id}
DELETE /orders/{id}
GET    /orders/{id}
GET    /orders/search
GET    /orders/dashboard

One model may be used for everything: 

@Entity


class Order {


@Id
private Long id;

private Long customerId;

private BigDecimal totalAmount;

private String status;

private LocalDateTime createdAt;


}

This same entity may be used for: 

Create Order


Update Order
Cancel Order
Get Order
Search Order
Dashboard
Reports
Analytics

For simple applications, this is completely acceptable.

CQRS should not be introduced automatically into every project.

Why can traditional CRUD become difficult?

Real systems often have very different write and read requirements.

Example: 

WRITE requirement:


Create order
Validate customer
Validate products
Check inventory
Calculate price
Apply coupon
Enforce business rules
Persist transactionally

But read requirements may be: 

Search orders by customer


Filter by status
Filter by city
Filter by date
Dashboard counts
Monthly revenue
Top-selling products
Order timeline
Customer order history

These two workloads are fundamentally different.

CQRS architecture
                         Client
                       |
          +------------+------------+
          |                         |
          v                         v
    Command API                 Query API
          |                         |
          v                         v
   Command Handler              Query Handler
          |                         |
          v                         v
    Write Model                  Read Model
          |                         |
          v                         v
    Write Database              Read Database
          |
          v
     Domain Event
          |
          v
   Message Broker
          |
          v
  Projection Consumer
          |
          v
   Update Read Model

The write side and read side now have different responsibilities.

Command side responsibilities

The command side handles business state changes. 

Validate business rules


Check invariants
Execute domain logic
Create entities
Update entities
Delete or cancel entities
Persist transactional state
Publish domain/integration events

Examples: 

CreateOrderCommand


CancelOrderCommand
ShipOrderCommand
ApproveOrderCommand
Query side responsibilities

The query side is optimized for retrieving data. 

Fast lookup


Search
Filtering
Sorting
Pagination
Dashboard views
Aggregations
Reports
Denormalized responses

Examples: 

GetOrderByIdQuery


SearchOrdersQuery
GetCustomerOrderHistoryQuery
GetSalesDashboardQuery
Real-time example: Order Management System

Suppose we are building an e-commerce Order Service.

Requirements: 

1. Customer creates order


2. Order is validated
3. Order is stored
4. Customer immediately receives order ID
5. Order appears in search screen
6. Dashboard is updated
7. Customer order history is updated

We will implement this using CQRS.

High-level request flow
POST /api/orders
    |
    v


Command Controller
|
v
CreateOrderCommand
|
v
CreateOrderCommandHandler
|
v
Write Database
|
v
OrderCreatedEvent
|
v
Kafka
|
v
Order Projection Consumer
|
v
Read Database
|
v
GET /api/orders/{id}
Step 1: Create the Command

A command represents the intention to change system state. 

public record CreateOrderCommand(
    Long customerId,
    List<OrderItemCommand> items


) {
}

Order item command: 

public record OrderItemCommand(
    Long productId,
    int quantity


) {
}

Notice the naming: 

CreateOrderCommand

It expresses business intent.

Compare: 

Weak:


OrderDTO

Better business intent:
CreateOrderCommand
Step 2: Command Controller
@RestController


@RequestMapping("/api/orders")
public class OrderCommandController {


private final CreateOrderCommandHandler handler;

public OrderCommandController(
        CreateOrderCommandHandler handler) {

    this.handler = handler;
}

@PostMapping
public ResponseEntity<Long> createOrder(
        @RequestBody CreateOrderRequest request) {

    CreateOrderCommand command =
            new CreateOrderCommand(
                    request.customerId(),
                    request.items()
            );

    Long orderId = handler.handle(command);

    return ResponseEntity
            .status(HttpStatus.CREATED)
            .body(orderId);
}


}

The command controller handles write operations. 

POST


PUT
PATCH
DELETE

Conceptually: 

HTTP Request
->


Command
->
Command Handler
Step 3: Write-side Entity

The write model focuses on transactional business state. 

@Entity


@Table(name = "orders")
public class Order {


@Id
@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
private Long id;

private Long customerId;

private BigDecimal totalAmount;

@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
private OrderStatus status;

private LocalDateTime createdAt;

protected Order() {
}

public Order(
        Long customerId,
        BigDecimal totalAmount) {

    this.customerId = customerId;
    this.totalAmount = totalAmount;
    this.status = OrderStatus.CREATED;
    this.createdAt = LocalDateTime.now();
}

public void cancel() {

    if (status == OrderStatus.SHIPPED) {
        throw new IllegalStateException(
                "Shipped order cannot be cancelled"
        );
    }

    this.status = OrderStatus.CANCELLED;
}


}

The write entity protects business rules.

Example: 

A shipped order cannot be cancelled

This is a command-side concern.

Step 4: Write Repository
public interface OrderWriteRepository
    extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {


}

This repository talks to the write database. 

Command Side
->


OrderWriteRepository
->
PostgreSQL / MySQL
Step 5: Command Handler
@Service


public class CreateOrderCommandHandler {


private final OrderWriteRepository repository;
private final ApplicationEventPublisher eventPublisher;

public CreateOrderCommandHandler(
        OrderWriteRepository repository,
        ApplicationEventPublisher eventPublisher) {

    this.repository = repository;
    this.eventPublisher = eventPublisher;
}

@Transactional
public Long handle(CreateOrderCommand command) {

    BigDecimal totalAmount =
            calculateTotal(command.items());

    Order order = new Order(
            command.customerId(),
            totalAmount
    );

    Order savedOrder = repository.save(order);

    eventPublisher.publishEvent(
            new OrderCreatedEvent(
                    savedOrder.getId(),
                    savedOrder.getCustomerId(),
                    savedOrder.getTotalAmount(),
                    savedOrder.getStatus().name(),
                    savedOrder.getCreatedAt()
            )
    );

    return savedOrder.getId();
}

private BigDecimal calculateTotal(
        List<OrderItemCommand> items) {

    // Simplified example
    return BigDecimal.valueOf(1000);
}


}

The command handler: 

Receives command
->


Validates business rules
->
Creates domain entity
->
Persists write state
->
Produces event
->
Returns result
Important design point: Can a Command return data?

A common misconception is: 

Command must always return void

That is not universally required.

A command may return minimal execution information such as: 

Created entity ID


Operation status
Version number
Tracking ID

Example: 

Long orderId = handler.handle(command);

What CQRS discourages is using the command side as a rich read-query mechanism.

Step 6: Domain/Integration Event
public record OrderCreatedEvent(
    Long orderId,
    Long customerId,
    BigDecimal totalAmount,
    String status,
    LocalDateTime createdAt


) {
}

This event means: 

Something already happened:


Order was created

Compare: 

Command:


CreateOrder

Event:
OrderCreated

Commands are usually imperative: 

CreateOrder


CancelOrder
ShipOrder

Events describe completed facts: 

OrderCreated


OrderCancelled
OrderShipped
Command vs Event
Command Event
Request to do something Fact that something happened
CreateOrder OrderCreated
May be rejected Represents completed fact
Usually has intended handler Can have multiple consumers
Imperative naming Past-tense naming
Step 7: Publish event to Kafka

In a distributed CQRS architecture, events may be published through a message broker. 

@Component


public class OrderEventPublisher {


private final KafkaTemplate<String, Object> kafkaTemplate;

public OrderEventPublisher(
        KafkaTemplate<String, Object> kafkaTemplate) {

    this.kafkaTemplate = kafkaTemplate;
}

public void publish(OrderCreatedEvent event) {

    kafkaTemplate.send(
            "order-created-events",
            event.orderId().toString(),
            event
    );
}


}

Flow: 

Write Service
->


OrderCreatedEvent
->
Kafka Topic
->
Projection Consumer
Step 8: Read Model

The read model does not need to look exactly like the write entity.

Write model: 

Order


OrderItem
Customer
Product

Read model may be completely denormalized: 

@Document(indexName = "orders")


public class OrderView {


@Id
private Long orderId;

private Long customerId;

private String customerName;

private BigDecimal totalAmount;

private String status;

private LocalDateTime createdAt;


}

The read model may contain: 

customerName

directly, even if the write model stores only: 

customerId

Why?

Because the read model is optimized for queries.

Normalized write model vs denormalized read model

Write database: 

orders


---

id
customer_id
total_amount
status

## customers

id
name

## order_items

order_id
product_id
quantity

To display an order screen, a traditional query may require: 

SELECT
o.id,
o.total_amount,
o.status,
c.name


FROM orders o
JOIN customers c
ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.id = ?;

But the CQRS read model may store: 

{


"orderId": 101,
"customerId": 5001,
"customerName": "Narahari",
"totalAmount": 2500,
"status": "CREATED",
"createdAt": "2026-07-08T10:30:00"
}

Query becomes conceptually: 

Find document by orderId = 101

No runtime join may be required for that view.

Step 9: Projection Consumer

A projection consumer listens to write-side events and updates the read model. 

@Component


public class OrderProjectionConsumer {


private final OrderReadRepository readRepository;

public OrderProjectionConsumer(
        OrderReadRepository readRepository) {

    this.readRepository = readRepository;
}

@KafkaListener(
        topics = "order-created-events",
        groupId = "order-read-model"
)
public void consume(OrderCreatedEvent event) {

    OrderView view = new OrderView();

    view.setOrderId(event.orderId());
    view.setCustomerId(event.customerId());
    view.setTotalAmount(event.totalAmount());
    view.setStatus(event.status());
    view.setCreatedAt(event.createdAt());

    readRepository.save(view);
}


}

Flow: 

Kafka receives OrderCreatedEvent
    ->


OrderProjectionConsumer
->
Creates OrderView
->
Stores in Read Database
Step 10: Read Repository

Suppose the read side uses Elasticsearch: 

public interface OrderReadRepository
    extends ElasticsearchRepository<OrderView, Long> {


}

Or the read side could use: 

PostgreSQL


MySQL
MongoDB
Elasticsearch
Redis
Cassandra

CQRS does not require a specific database technology.

Step 11: Query object
public record GetOrderByIdQuery(
    Long orderId


) {
}

This query expresses: 

I want order information

It does not modify state.

Step 12: Query Handler
@Service


public class GetOrderByIdQueryHandler {


private final OrderReadRepository repository;

public GetOrderByIdQueryHandler(
        OrderReadRepository repository) {

    this.repository = repository;
}

public OrderView handle(
        GetOrderByIdQuery query) {

    return repository
            .findById(query.orderId())
            .orElseThrow(() ->
                    new OrderNotFoundException(
                            "Order not found: "
                            + query.orderId()
                    )
            );
}


}
Step 13: Query Controller
@RestController


@RequestMapping("/api/orders")
public class OrderQueryController {


private final GetOrderByIdQueryHandler handler;

public OrderQueryController(
        GetOrderByIdQueryHandler handler) {

    this.handler = handler;
}

@GetMapping("/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<OrderView> getOrder(
        @PathVariable Long id) {

    GetOrderByIdQuery query =
            new GetOrderByIdQuery(id);

    return ResponseEntity.ok(
            handler.handle(query)
    );
}


}

The query side performs: 

GET /api/orders/101
    ->


GetOrderByIdQuery
->
Query Handler
->
Read Database
->
OrderView
->
HTTP 200
Complete CQRS flow
1. Client sends:


POST /api/orders


    |
    v


2. Command Controller creates:

CreateOrderCommand


    |
    v


3. Command Handler validates business rules


    |
    v


4. Save Order into Write DB


    |
    v


5. Create:

OrderCreatedEvent


    |
    v


6. Publish event to Kafka


    |
    v


7. Projection Consumer receives event


    |
    v


8. Build OrderView


    |
    v


9. Save OrderView into Read DB


    |
    v


10. Client sends:

GET /api/orders/101


    |
    v


11. Query Handler reads Read DB


    |
    v


12. Return optimized response
Most important CQRS concept: Eventual consistency

Suppose: 

10:00:00.000


POST /orders

Write database is updated: 

10:00:00.020


Order saved successfully

Event reaches Kafka: 

10:00:00.050

Projection consumer updates read database: 

10:00:00.100

There is a short period where: 

Write DB:


Order exists

Read DB:
Order not visible yet

This is called: 

Eventual Consistency
Real user-visible problem

User creates an order: 

POST /orders


Response:
201 Created
Order ID: 101

Immediately the frontend calls: 

GET /orders/101

But the read model has not yet consumed the event.

Possible response: 

404 Not Found

After a short delay: 

GET /orders/101


200 OK

This is one of the most important practical challenges in CQRS.

How can we handle read-after-write problems?

Possible strategies include:

  1. Return enough data from the command response for immediate UI display.
  2. Temporarily read from the write model for critical read-after-write flows.
  3. Use polling with retry and backoff.
  4. Use WebSocket or Server-Sent Events when the projection becomes available.
  5. Track projection versions or event offsets.
  6. Use synchronous projection updates when strict consistency is truly required.

There is no universal solution. The correct choice depends on business requirements.

Critical problem: Database save succeeds but Kafka publish fails

Consider this code: 

@Transactional


public Long createOrder(CreateOrderCommand command) {


Order order = repository.save(...);

kafkaTemplate.send(
        "order-created-events",
        new OrderCreatedEvent(...)
);

return order.getId();


}

Dangerous failure scenario: 

1. Order saved in DB


2. DB transaction commits
3. Kafka unavailable
4. Event not published

Result: 

Write DB:


Order 101 exists

Read DB:
Order 101 never appears

The read model becomes inconsistent.

This is the classic: 

Dual Write Problem
Why @Transactional alone does not solve DB + Kafka consistency

A normal database transaction controls database resources. 

@Transactional

does not magically make: 

Database write


+
Kafka publish

one universal atomic operation.

Therefore this assumption is dangerous: 

If method is @Transactional,


DB and Kafka are automatically atomic

They are separate systems and require an explicit reliability strategy.

Recommended solution: Transactional Outbox Pattern

Instead of directly writing to the database and independently publishing to Kafka: 

Order DB Write


+
Kafka Publish

write both the business record and an outbox record in the same local database transaction. 

BEGIN TRANSACTION


Insert Order

Insert Outbox Event

COMMIT TRANSACTION

Because both writes happen in the same database transaction: 

Either both commit


or
both rollback
Outbox table
CREATE TABLE outbox_events (
id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
aggregate_type VARCHAR(100),
aggregate_id VARCHAR(100),
event_type VARCHAR(100),
payload TEXT,
status VARCHAR(30),
created_at TIMESTAMP


);

Example row: 

id             : 9001


aggregate_type : Order
aggregate_id   : 101
event_type     : OrderCreated
payload        : {...}
status         : NEW
Command handler with Outbox
@Transactional


public Long handle(CreateOrderCommand command) {


Order order = new Order(
        command.customerId(),
        calculateTotal(command.items())
);

Order savedOrder =
        orderRepository.save(order);

OrderCreatedEvent event =
        new OrderCreatedEvent(
                savedOrder.getId(),
                savedOrder.getCustomerId(),
                savedOrder.getTotalAmount(),
                savedOrder.getStatus().name(),
                savedOrder.getCreatedAt()
        );

OutboxEvent outboxEvent =
        OutboxEvent.create(
                "Order",
                savedOrder.getId().toString(),
                "OrderCreated",
                serialize(event)
        );

outboxRepository.save(outboxEvent);

return savedOrder.getId();


}

Transaction: 

Save Order
+


Save Outbox Event
|
v
Same DB Transaction
Outbox Publisher
@Scheduled(fixedDelay = 1000)


public void publishEvents() {


List<OutboxEvent> events =
        outboxRepository.findByStatus("NEW");

for (OutboxEvent event : events) {

    kafkaTemplate.send(
            "order-events",
            event.getAggregateId(),
            event.getPayload()
    );

    event.markPublished();

    outboxRepository.save(event);
}


}

Flow: 

Database Transaction
|
+-- Save Order
|
+-- Save Outbox Event
        |
        v
  Outbox Publisher
        |
        v
      Kafka
        |
        v
Projection Consumer
        |
        v
   Read Database

In production, outbox publishing can also be implemented using CDC tools rather than polling.

Important problem: Duplicate event delivery

Message brokers and retry mechanisms can cause the same event to be delivered more than once. 

OrderCreatedEvent


eventId = EVT-1001

Delivered once
|
Consumer processes it
|
Consumer crashes before offset acknowledgement
|
Broker redelivers
|
Same event arrives again

If the consumer blindly inserts again: 

Duplicate read model


Duplicate notification
Duplicate payment
Duplicate side effect
Solution: Idempotent Consumer

Every event should have a unique event ID. 

public record OrderCreatedEvent(
    UUID eventId,
    Long orderId,
    Long customerId,
    BigDecimal totalAmount


) {
}

Consumer: 

@Transactional


@KafkaListener(topics = "order-events")
public void consume(OrderCreatedEvent event) {


if (processedEventRepository
        .existsById(event.eventId())) {

    return;
}

updateReadModel(event);

processedEventRepository.save(
        new ProcessedEvent(event.eventId())
);


}

Flow: 

Receive Event
|
v


Already processed?
|
+-- Yes -> Ignore
|
+-- No
|
v
Process Event
|
v
Save Event ID
CQRS does not mean separate databases are mandatory

This is a very important interview point.

CQRS fundamentally means: 

Separate command responsibility


from
query responsibility

You can implement CQRS with: 

Same database


Different services/repositories/models

Example: 

Command Service
->


OrderWriteRepository
->
PostgreSQL

Query Service
->
OrderReadRepository
->
Same PostgreSQL

This is still a form of CQRS because responsibilities are separated.

CQRS maturity levels
Level Command Side Query Side Database
Simple CQRS Separate methods Separate methods Same DB
Model-separated CQRS Write model Read model Same DB
Store-separated CQRS Write DB Read DB Separate stores
Distributed CQRS Command service Query service Separate + events
CQRS vs Event Sourcing

CQRS and Event Sourcing are not the same thing.

CQRS Event Sourcing
Separates reads and writes Stores state changes as events
Can use normal relational tables Uses event history as source of truth
Does not require event store Requires durable event stream/store
Can exist without Event Sourcing Often combined with CQRS

Normal CQRS write database: 

orders


---

id = 101
status = SHIPPED

Event Sourcing: 

OrderCreated
|


OrderPaid
|
OrderPacked
|
OrderShipped

Current state is reconstructed from events.

Can CQRS work without Kafka?

Yes.

CQRS does not require Kafka.

Possible implementations: 

CQRS + same DB


CQRS + synchronous projection
CQRS + application events
CQRS + Kafka
CQRS + RabbitMQ
CQRS + cloud messaging
CQRS + CDC

Kafka is an infrastructure choice, not a CQRS requirement.

Yes.

Advantages of CQRS
Advantage Explanation
Independent scaling Read and write workloads can scale separately
Optimized read model Queries can use denormalized projections
Optimized write model Domain rules can remain focused on consistency
Different databases Each side can use a suitable storage technology
Clear responsibilities Commands and queries have different models and handlers
Better complex domains Write-side domain logic is not distorted by reporting needs
Flexible projections Multiple read models can be built from events
Disadvantages of CQRS
Disadvantage Explanation
More complexity More models, handlers, events, and infrastructure
Eventual consistency Read model may temporarily lag
Operational complexity Broker, consumers, retries, DLQ, monitoring
Duplicate events Consumers should be idempotent
Event ordering Out-of-order events can corrupt projections
Schema evolution Event contracts must evolve safely
Debugging complexity One request may cross several asynchronous components
When should we use CQRS?

CQRS can be useful when: 

Read traffic is much higher than write traffic


Read and write models are significantly different

Complex business rules exist on command side

Many dashboards and search views exist

Independent scaling is required

Multiple projections are needed

Event-driven architecture already exists

Different storage technologies provide real value

Examples: 

Banking platforms


Large e-commerce systems
Trading systems
Order management
Logistics platforms
Reservation systems
Complex SaaS platforms
When should we NOT use CQRS?

Avoid CQRS when: 

Application is simple CRUD


Small team

Low traffic

Read and write models are almost identical

Strong immediate consistency is required everywhere

Operational complexity is not justified

Example: 

Simple Employee CRUD


Create Employee
Update Employee
Delete Employee
Get Employee

Introducing: 

Kafka


Separate DB
Projection Consumer
Outbox
Idempotency Store
DLQ

may be unnecessary overengineering.

Important interview question: Is CQRS only for microservices?

No.

CQRS is an architectural pattern and can be used in: 

Monolith


Modular Monolith
Microservices

No.

CQRS requires responsibility separation, not necessarily physical database separation. 

Same DB:


Possible

Separate DB:
Possible

Different DB technologies:
Possible

This depends on the architecture.

Possible approaches: 

Replay durable events


Re-read source-of-truth write tables

Run a projection rebuild job

Use CDC history if available

If using Event Sourcing: 

Replay events
->


Rebuild projection

If not using Event Sourcing, you need another reliable rebuild source.

Important interview question: What happens if events arrive out of order?

Suppose: 

Expected:


1. OrderCreated
2. OrderPaid
3. OrderShipped

But consumer receives: 

1. OrderCreated

4. OrderShipped
5. OrderPaid

The read model may become incorrect.

Common solutions: 

Partition by aggregate ID

Use aggregate version
Store event sequence number
Reject stale events
Buffer missing versions
Design idempotent projections

With Kafka, using: 

orderId.toString()

as the message key helps route events for the same order to the same partition, where partition ordering can be preserved.

Important interview question: What if projection consumer fails?

Typical production strategy: 

Consume event
|
v


Processing fails
|
v
Retry
|
v
Retry again
|
v
Still fails
|
v
Dead Letter Topic / DLQ
|
v
Alert + investigation + replay

A mature CQRS implementation needs: 

Retries


Backoff
DLQ
Metrics
Tracing
Consumer lag monitoring
Replay strategy
Production-grade architecture
                       CLIENT
                      |
        +-------------+-------------+
        |                           |
        v                           v
  COMMAND API                   QUERY API
        |                           |
        v                           v
Command Handler               Query Handler
        |                           |
        v                           v
  Domain Model                  Read Model
        |                           |
        v                           v
   WRITE DB                    READ DB
        |
        +-- Same Transaction --+
        |                      |
        v                      v
   Business Data          Outbox Table
                               |
                               v
                       Outbox Publisher
                               |
                               v
                            Kafka
                               |
                +--------------+--------------+
                |                             |
                v                             v
        Projection Consumer          Other Consumers
                |                             |
                v                             v
           READ DB                  Notification/Analytics
                |
                v
           QUERY API
Best interview answer

CQRS stands for Command Query Responsibility Segregation. It separates operations that change system state from operations that read system state. The command side is optimized for business rules, transactional consistency, and domain invariants, while the query side is optimized for fast reads, search, filtering, dashboards, and denormalized views. In a distributed implementation, a command updates the write model and produces an event; a projection consumer processes that event and updates the read model. This allows independent scaling and different data models or databases, but introduces eventual consistency, duplicate delivery, ordering, replay, and operational complexity. In production, I would address reliable event publication using the Transactional Outbox Pattern and make consumers idempotent. CQRS does not require Kafka, separate databases, microservices, or Event Sourcing; those are optional architectural choices.

Given an integer array, separate all 0s to the end and keep all non-zero values at the beginning. The important condition is: do it in the same array, without creating another array. 

Input:  [0, 1, 0, 3, 12]
Output: [1, 3, 12, 0, 0]

If the array contains only 0s and 1s, the same idea becomes: 

Input:  [0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0]
Output: [1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0]
Way 1: Stable two-pointer approach

This keeps the relative order of non-zero elements the same. 

public static void moveZerosToEnd(int[] nums) {
    int insertPosition = 0;

    for (int index = 0; index < nums.length; index++) {
        if (nums[index] != 0) {
            nums[insertPosition] = nums[index];
            insertPosition++;
        }
    }

    while (insertPosition < nums.length) {
        nums[insertPosition] = 0;
        insertPosition++;
    }
}

Explanation:

  • insertPosition points to where the next non-zero number should be placed.
  • The first loop copies all non-zero values to the front of the same array.
  • The second loop fills the remaining positions with 0.
  • No extra array is used; only one variable is used.
Dry run
Array: [0, 1, 0, 3, 12]

index = 0, value = 0  -> skip
index = 1, value = 1  -> nums[0] = 1
index = 2, value = 0  -> skip
index = 3, value = 3  -> nums[1] = 3
index = 4, value = 12 -> nums[2] = 12

Now fill remaining positions with 0:
[1, 3, 12, 0, 0]
Complete example
import java.util.Arrays;

public class MoveZeros {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] nums = {0, 1, 0, 3, 12};

        moveZerosToEnd(nums);

        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(nums));
    }

    public static void moveZerosToEnd(int[] nums) {
        int insertPosition = 0;

        for (int index = 0; index < nums.length; index++) {
            if (nums[index] != 0) {
                nums[insertPosition] = nums[index];
                insertPosition++;
            }
        }

        while (insertPosition < nums.length) {
            nums[insertPosition] = 0;
            insertPosition++;
        }
    }
}
Way 2: Swap-based two-pointer approach

This also works in-place. It swaps every non-zero element with the position where the next non-zero value should go. 

public static void moveZerosToEndUsingSwap(int[] nums) {
    int nonZeroPosition = 0;

    for (int index = 0; index < nums.length; index++) {
        if (nums[index] != 0) {
            int temp = nums[index];
            nums[index] = nums[nonZeroPosition];
            nums[nonZeroPosition] = temp;

            nonZeroPosition++;
        }
    }
}

This is useful when you want to perform fewer writes in some cases. It still uses the same array and does not create another array.

If array contains only 0s and 1s

If the question specifically means separate 1s first and 0s last, use this two-pointer version. It swaps values in the same array and does not use an extra array. 

public static void separateOnesAndZeros(int[] nums) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = nums.length - 1;

    while (left < right) {
        while (left < right && nums[left] == 1) {
            left++;
        }

        while (left < right && nums[right] == 0) {
            right--;
        }

        if (left < right) {
            int temp = nums[left];
            nums[left] = nums[right];
            nums[right] = temp;
            left++;
            right--;
        }
    }
}
Input:  [0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0]
Output: [1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0]
Complexity
  • Time complexity: O(n)
  • Space complexity: O(1)
  • Same array is modified in-place.

Interview one-liner: use a two-pointer approach; keep one pointer for the next non-zero position, move non-zero values to the front, and fill the remaining positions with zero.
