This section collects SQL scenario-based interview questions from filtering, joins, constraints, aggregation, subqueries, ranking, sales analytics, and real-world business cases. The examples use MySQL style syntax like LIMIT, DATE_FORMAT, and INTERVAL.

Note: The provided screenshots contain questions 1-40 and 46-53. Questions 41-45 were not present in the shared images, so extra real-world interview cases are added at the end.

1. Find employees whose salary is greater than 50,000
SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 50000;

Use WHERE to filter rows before results are returned.

2. Identify duplicate email addresses in customers
SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS email_count
FROM customers
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

GROUP BY groups same emails, and HAVING filters grouped results.

3. Correct wrong data inserted into a table
UPDATE table_name
SET column_name = 'correct_value'
WHERE condition;

Always use a proper WHERE condition with UPDATE to avoid modifying all rows.

4. Retrieve rows where phone number is missing
SELECT *
FROM table_name
WHERE phone_number IS NULL;

Use IS NULL, not = NULL, because null means unknown value.

5. Display employees sorted by highest salary first
SELECT *
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC;

ORDER BY DESC sorts from highest to lowest.

6. Retrieve customers along with their orders
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.customer_name,
       o.order_id,
       o.order_date
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

INNER JOIN returns only customers who have matching orders.

7. Find customers who have not placed any orders
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.customer_name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;

Use LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL to find missing related records.

8. Find total sales made by each employee
SELECT employee_id,
       SUM(sales_amount) AS total_sales
FROM sales
GROUP BY employee_id;

SUM calculates total amount per employee.

9. Count how many employees work in each department
SELECT department_id,
       COUNT(*) AS employee_count
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id;

COUNT(*) counts rows in each department group.

10. Show departments with more than 10 employees
SELECT department_id,
       COUNT(*) AS employee_count
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 10;

Use HAVING when filtering aggregate results.

11. Fetch only the first 5 records from a table
SELECT *
FROM table_name
LIMIT 5;

LIMIT restricts the number of returned rows.

12. Update one employee's department
UPDATE employees
SET department_id = 5
WHERE employee_id = 101;

The WHERE clause ensures only employee 101 is updated.

13. Remove all records but keep table structure
TRUNCATE TABLE table_name;

TRUNCATE removes rows quickly but keeps the table definition.

14. Prevent duplicate employee IDs
ALTER TABLE employees
ADD CONSTRAINT pk_employee_id
PRIMARY KEY (employee_id);

A primary key enforces uniqueness and prevents null values for the key column.

15. Ensure salary values cannot be null
ALTER TABLE employees
MODIFY salary DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL;

NOT NULL ensures every employee must have a salary value.

16. Combine results from two same-structure tables and remove duplicates
SELECT column1, column2, column3
FROM table1
UNION
SELECT column1, column2, column3
FROM table2;

UNION removes duplicates. Use UNION ALL when duplicates should remain.

17. Ensure usernames are unique in a login system
ALTER TABLE users
ADD CONSTRAINT username_unique
UNIQUE (username);

A unique constraint prevents duplicate usernames.

18. Search customers whose names start with A
SELECT *
FROM customers
WHERE customer_name LIKE 'A%';

LIKE 'A%' matches names starting with A.

19. Find the second highest salary
SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest_salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary < (
    SELECT MAX(salary)
    FROM employees
);

This finds the highest salary that is less than the maximum salary.

20. Improve search performance on employee_id
CREATE INDEX idx_employee_id
ON employees (employee_id);

An index improves lookup speed for frequently searched columns.

21. List departments that do not have employees
SELECT d.department_id,
       d.department_name
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e
    ON d.department_id = e.department_id
WHERE e.employee_id IS NULL;

This is another common LEFT JOIN missing-child-record scenario.

22. Count employees hired in each year
SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM hire_date) AS hire_year,
       COUNT(*) AS employee_count
FROM employees
GROUP BY EXTRACT(YEAR FROM hire_date)
ORDER BY hire_year;

Use date extraction functions to group records by year.

23. Find employees earning more than their department average salary
SELECT employee_id,
       first_name,
       salary,
       department_id
FROM employees e
WHERE salary > (
    SELECT AVG(salary)
    FROM employees e2
    WHERE e2.department_id = e.department_id
);

This uses a correlated subquery because the inner query depends on the outer employee's department.

24. List every employee with their manager name
SELECT e.employee_id,
       e.first_name,
       e.last_name,
       m.first_name AS manager_first_name,
       m.last_name AS manager_last_name
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m
    ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id;

This is a self join because the employee and manager are in the same table.

25. Find top 3 highest paid employees in each department
SELECT department_id,
       employee_id,
       first_name,
       salary
FROM (
    SELECT e.*,
           RANK() OVER (
               PARTITION BY department_id
               ORDER BY salary DESC
           ) AS rnk
    FROM employees e
) t
WHERE rnk <= 3
ORDER BY department_id, salary DESC;

RANK() gives the same rank to ties. Use ROW_NUMBER() for exactly 3 rows.

26. Find total orders placed by each customer
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;

Basic aggregation by customer.

27. Find average order amount for each customer
SELECT customer_id,
       AVG(order_amount) AS avg_order_amount
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;

AVG calculates average order value per customer.

28. Find customers who placed more than 5 orders
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

Use HAVING to filter customers after counting orders.

29. Find total revenue generated each month
SELECT DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '%Y-%m') AS order_month,
       SUM(order_amount) AS total_revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '%Y-%m')
ORDER BY order_month;

This groups revenue by month.

30. Find the most recent order date for each customer
SELECT customer_id,
       MAX(order_date) AS last_order_date
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;

MAX returns the latest order date per customer.

31. List all products that are out of stock
SELECT product_id,
       product_name
FROM products
WHERE stock_quantity = 0;

Inventory checks often use simple filtering.

32. Find the number of active customers
SELECT COUNT(*) AS active_customer_count
FROM customers
WHERE status = 'Active';

This counts customers with active status.

33. Find customers registered in the last 30 days
SELECT customer_id,
       customer_name,
       register_date
FROM customers
WHERE register_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL 30 DAY;

Useful for recently joined users, onboarding reports, and growth dashboards.

34. List orders with customer names
SELECT o.order_id,
       o.order_date,
       c.customer_name
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN customers c
    ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;

Join order rows to customer details for readable reports.

35. Find top 5 best-selling products by quantity sold
SELECT product_id,
       product_name,
       SUM(quantity) AS total_quantity_sold
FROM order_items
GROUP BY product_id, product_name
ORDER BY total_quantity_sold DESC
LIMIT 5;

This is a common product analytics query.

36. Find total quantity sold for each product each month
SELECT product_id,
       DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '%Y-%m') AS order_month,
       SUM(quantity) AS total_quantity_sold
FROM order_items
GROUP BY product_id, DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '%Y-%m')
ORDER BY product_id, order_month;

Monthly product movement is useful for demand forecasting.

37. Find average rating of each product
SELECT product_id,
       AVG(rating) AS average_rating
FROM product_reviews
GROUP BY product_id
ORDER BY average_rating DESC;

Ratings are commonly aggregated for product ranking.

38. Find products that have never been ordered
SELECT p.product_id,
       p.product_name
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi
    ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE oi.product_id IS NULL;

This finds products with no matching row in order_items.

39. Find customers who spent more than 1000 in total
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.customer_name,
       SUM(o.total_amount) AS total_spent
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.customer_name
HAVING SUM(o.total_amount) > 1000
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;

Use HAVING for aggregate spend filters.

40. Find the category with the highest total sales
SELECT p.category_id,
       c.category_name,
       SUM(oi.total_quantity) AS total_sales
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products p
    ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN categories c
    ON p.category_id = c.category_id
GROUP BY p.category_id, c.category_name
ORDER BY total_sales DESC
LIMIT 1;

This combines joins, grouping, ordering, and limiting.

46. Find the customer who placed the most orders
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.customer_name,
       COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.customer_name
ORDER BY order_count DESC
LIMIT 1;

LEFT JOIN keeps customers even if they have zero orders, but the top result will usually have orders.

47. Find the month with the highest number of employees hired
SELECT DATE_FORMAT(hire_date, '%Y-%m') AS hire_month,
       COUNT(*) AS hire_count
FROM employees
GROUP BY DATE_FORMAT(hire_date, '%Y-%m')
ORDER BY hire_count DESC
LIMIT 1;

This is useful for hiring trend analytics.

48. Find total employees in each department including departments with no employees
SELECT d.department_id,
       d.department_name,
       COUNT(e.employee_id) AS employee_count
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e
    ON d.department_id = e.department_id
GROUP BY d.department_id, d.department_name
ORDER BY d.department_name;

Count a nullable child column like e.employee_id so empty departments return 0.

49. List top 5 customers who spent the most
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.customer_name,
       SUM(o.total_amount) AS total_spent
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.customer_name
ORDER BY total_spent DESC
LIMIT 5;

This is a common high-value customer report.

50. Find departments with more than 5 employees and average salary above 60000
SELECT d.department_id,
       d.department_name,
       COUNT(e.employee_id) AS employee_count,
       AVG(e.salary) AS avg_salary
FROM departments d
JOIN employees e
    ON d.department_id = e.department_id
GROUP BY d.department_id, d.department_name
HAVING COUNT(e.employee_id) > 5
   AND AVG(e.salary) > 60000
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC;

This combines multiple aggregate conditions in HAVING.

51. Find the second highest order amount
SELECT MAX(order_amount) AS second_highest_amount
FROM orders
WHERE order_amount < (
    SELECT MAX(order_amount)
    FROM orders
);

This returns the second distinct highest order amount.

52. Find customers who have not placed any orders yet
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.customer_name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;

Same pattern as inactive relationship lookup: LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL.

53. Find lifetime value of each customer including zero-spend customers
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.customer_name,
       COALESCE(SUM(o.total_amount), 0) AS lifetime_value
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.customer_name
ORDER BY lifetime_value DESC;

COALESCE converts null totals into 0 for customers with no orders.

Extra real-world SQL interview cases
54. Delete duplicate customers but keep the latest record
DELETE c1
FROM customers c1
JOIN customers c2
    ON c1.email = c2.email
   AND c1.customer_id < c2.customer_id;

This keeps the row with the greater customer_id. In production, first run a SELECT preview.

55. Find running total revenue by order date
SELECT order_date,
       order_amount,
       SUM(order_amount) OVER (
           ORDER BY order_date
       ) AS running_revenue
FROM orders
ORDER BY order_date;

Window functions calculate analytics without collapsing rows like GROUP BY.

56. Find customers inactive for the last 90 days
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.customer_name,
       MAX(o.order_date) AS last_order_date
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.customer_name
HAVING MAX(o.order_date) < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL 90 DAY
    OR MAX(o.order_date) IS NULL;

This is useful for churn, retention, and reactivation campaigns.

57. Find each customer's first order
SELECT *
FROM (
    SELECT o.*,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY customer_id
               ORDER BY order_date
           ) AS rn
    FROM orders o
) t
WHERE rn = 1;

ROW_NUMBER is best when you want exactly one first row per group.

58. Find products whose stock is below reorder level
SELECT product_id,
       product_name,
       stock_quantity,
       reorder_level
FROM products
WHERE stock_quantity <= reorder_level;

This is a common inventory alert query.

59. Find month-over-month revenue growth
WITH monthly_revenue AS (
    SELECT DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '%Y-%m') AS order_month,
           SUM(order_amount) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '%Y-%m')
)
SELECT order_month,
       revenue,
       LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_month) AS previous_month_revenue,
       revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_month) AS revenue_growth
FROM monthly_revenue
ORDER BY order_month;

LAG compares current row values with previous row values.

60. Find employees whose salary is in the top 10 percent
SELECT employee_id,
       first_name,
       salary
FROM (
    SELECT e.*,
           PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS salary_percent_rank
    FROM employees e
) t
WHERE salary_percent_rank >= 0.90
ORDER BY salary DESC;

This is useful for compensation analytics and advanced window-function interviews.

If the child overridden method declares Exception, the compiler gives an error because Exception is a broader checked exception than the parent contract allows.

The rule is simple:

  • A child method cannot introduce a broader checked exception than the parent method declares.
  • A child method may throw the same exception or a narrower checked exception.
  • A child method may throw any unchecked exception, even if the parent throws none.
class Parent {
    void calculate() throws RuntimeException {
        System.out.println("Parent");
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    @Override
    void calculate() throws Exception {   // Compile-time error
        System.out.println("Child");
    }
}

This also fails: 

class Parent {
    void calculate() throws ArithmeticException {
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    @Override
    void calculate() throws Exception {  // Compile-time error
    }
}

But these are allowed: 

class Parent {
    void calculate() throws RuntimeException {
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    @Override
    void calculate() throws ArithmeticException {
    }
}
class Parent {
    void calculate() {
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    @Override
    void calculate() throws ArithmeticException {
    }
}

The vice versa cases follow the same inheritance rule:

Parent method Child method Result
throws Exception throws IOException Allowed
throws IOException throws Exception Compile-time error
throws RuntimeException throws Exception Compile-time error
throws RuntimeException throws ArithmeticException Allowed
No throws throws RuntimeException Allowed
No throws throws IOException Compile-time error

Interview one-liner: a child method can narrow checked exceptions, but it cannot widen them; unchecked exceptions are always allowed in overriding.

Relational mapping means mapping Java entities to database tables and mapping object relationships to foreign keys or join tables in the database.

In Spring Boot, JPA/Hibernate handles this using annotations like @Entity, @Id, @OneToOne, @OneToMany, @ManyToOne, @ManyToMany, @JoinColumn, and @JoinTable.

1. One-to-One example

Example: one user has one profile. 

@Entity
class User {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    private String name;

    @OneToOne(cascade = CascadeType.ALL)
    @JoinColumn(name = "profile_id")
    private UserProfile profile;
}

@Entity
class UserProfile {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    private String bio;
}
CREATE TABLE user_profile (
    id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    bio VARCHAR(255)
);

CREATE TABLE users (
    id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    profile_id BIGINT UNIQUE,
    CONSTRAINT fk_user_profile
        FOREIGN KEY (profile_id) REFERENCES user_profile(id)
);
2. One-to-Many and Many-to-One example

Example: one department has many employees. 

@Entity
class Department {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    private String name;

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "department", cascade = CascadeType.ALL)
    private List<Employee> employees;
}

@Entity
class Employee {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    private String name;

    @ManyToOne
    @JoinColumn(name = "department_id")
    private Department department;
}
CREATE TABLE department (
    id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE employee (
    id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    department_id BIGINT,
    CONSTRAINT fk_employee_department
        FOREIGN KEY (department_id) REFERENCES department(id)
);

In this relationship, the many side owns the foreign key. The @ManyToOne side is usually the owning side, and mappedBy is used on the parent collection side.

Important mapping points
Relation Typical annotation Database shape
One-to-One @OneToOne Foreign key + unique constraint
One-to-Many @OneToMany Foreign key on many-side table
Many-to-One @ManyToOne Foreign key on current table
Many-to-Many @ManyToMany Join table with two foreign keys

In real projects, keep the owning side clear, use cascade carefully, and prefer FetchType.LAZY for collection relationships unless eager loading is truly required.

For Many-to-Many, the mapping is usually handled through a separate join table, which is covered in the next question.

A Many-to-Many relation means many rows in one table can match many rows in another table. In relational databases, this is not stored directly in the two tables. Instead, Hibernate creates a join table.

Example: one student can join many courses, and one course can have many students. 

@Entity
class Student {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    private String name;

    @ManyToMany
    @JoinTable(
        name = "student_course",
        joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "student_id"),
        inverseJoinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "course_id")
    )
    private Set<Course> courses;
}

@Entity
class Course {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    private String title;

    @ManyToMany(mappedBy = "courses")
    private Set<Student> students;
}
CREATE TABLE student (
    id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE course (
    id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    title VARCHAR(150) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE student_course (
    student_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    course_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id),
    CONSTRAINT fk_sc_student
        FOREIGN KEY (student_id) REFERENCES student(id),
    CONSTRAINT fk_sc_course
        FOREIGN KEY (course_id) REFERENCES course(id)
);

Here, student_course is the join table. It stores only the relationship, not extra business data.

When to avoid direct Many-to-Many
  • If the join table needs extra columns like enrolled_at, status, or grade, use a separate entity instead of plain @ManyToMany.
  • In that case, model it as two @ManyToOne relationships through an intermediate entity such as Enrollment.
  • Be careful with cascade and fetch type because many-to-many graphs can grow quickly.

Interview one-liner: Many-to-Many in JPA is backed by a join table, and if the association has extra attributes, an intermediate entity is usually the better design.

Annotations are metadata attached to Java code. They do not change program logic by themselves, but they give instructions to the compiler, runtime, or frameworks about how to treat that code.

Before Java 5, metadata lived in external XML or comments. Annotations moved that metadata into the source code itself, making it type-safe, discoverable, and easier to maintain. 

@Override
public String toString() {
    return "User{id=1}";
}

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/users")
public class UserController {

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public User getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.findById(id);
    }
}
Why we use annotations
Reason What it solves Real-time example
Reduce boilerplate No repeated XML/config for every class @Entity instead of manual Hibernate mapping XML
Declarative programming Describe what you want, not how to wire it @Transactional starts/commits DB transaction automatically
Framework integration Tools scan code and apply behavior Spring creates beans from @Service, @Repository
Compile-time safety Catch mistakes early @Override fails if method signature does not match parent
Cross-cutting concerns Logging, security, caching in one place @PreAuthorize, @Cacheable
Documentation Self-describing API contracts @Deprecated, @NotNull

Annotations are processed in three phases: 

Source Code
   + @Annotation
        |
        v
Compile Time  -> Compiler checks (@Override, @FunctionalInterface)
        |
        v
Runtime       -> Reflection / Spring scans (@Component, @Autowired)
        |
        v
Framework     -> AOP, JPA, Validation, Security applied automatically

Best interview sentence: Annotations are metadata markers that let frameworks and tools inspect code and apply behavior declaratively, instead of forcing developers to write repetitive wiring code manually.

Built-in annotations (java.lang)
Annotation Purpose Example
@Override Compiler verifies method override Prevents typo in method name during inheritance
@Deprecated Marks API as obsolete Warn developers not to use old REST endpoint
@SuppressWarnings Suppress compiler warnings @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") on legacy generic code
@FunctionalInterface Single abstract method interface Lambdas: () -> System.out.println("hi")
@SafeVarargs Suppress varargs generic warnings Utility methods with generic varargs 
class Parent {
    void print() {
        System.out.println("Parent");
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    @Override
    void print() {          // OK
        System.out.println("Child");
    }

    // @Override
    // void prnt() {       // Compile error — typo caught by @Override
    // }
}
Meta-annotations (annotations on annotations)

Meta-annotations define rules for custom annotations.

Meta-annotation Meaning
@Target Where annotation can be applied (class, method, field, parameter, etc.)
@Retention How long annotation survives: SOURCE, CLASS, or RUNTIME
@Documented Include in generated Javadoc
@Inherited Subclass inherits annotation from parent class
@Repeatable Same annotation can appear multiple times on one element 
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Documented
public @interface AuditLog {
    String action();
}

Real-time: Spring's @RestController is itself meta-annotated with @Controller + @ResponseBody. When you write @RestController, Spring understands both behaviors without you repeating them.

1. Marker annotation (no elements)

Pure tag with no attributes. Framework checks only presence. 

@FunctionalInterface
public interface PaymentProcessor {
    void process();
}

@Entity   // JPA marker — tells Hibernate this class maps to a table
public class Order {
    @Id
    private Long id;
}
2. Single-value annotation

One element named value(). You can omit the element name when using it. 

@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface RolesAllowed {
    String value();   // single element
}

// Usage — "value=" is optional
@RolesAllowed("ADMIN")
public void deleteUser() { }
3. Normal / multi-value annotation

Multiple named elements. 

@Table(name = "employees", schema = "hr")
public class Employee { }

@RequestMapping(value = "/api/users", method = RequestMethod.GET)
public List<User> getUsers() { }
4. Meta-annotation

Annotation applied to another annotation definition. 

@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@SpringBootApplication   // meta-annotated with @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, @ComponentScan
public class Application {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args);
    }
}
5. Repeatable annotation
@Repeatable(Schedules.class)
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface Schedule {
    String cron();
}

public @interface Schedules {
    Schedule[] value();
}

@Schedule(cron = "0 0 8 * * *")
@Schedule(cron = "0 0 20 * * *")
public void sendReport() { }

Real-time: Bean Validation uses multi-value annotations like @Size(min = 2, max = 50, message = "Name too long") on DTO fields in REST APIs.

Creating a custom annotation has four steps: define it, set meta-annotations, use it, and process it (via reflection, AOP, or annotation processor).

Step 1 — Define the annotation
import java.lang.annotation.*;

@Target({ElementType.METHOD, ElementType.TYPE})
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Documented
public @interface RateLimited {
    int requests() default 100;      // max requests
    int perSeconds() default 60;     // time window
    String key() default "";         // optional custom key
}
Step 2 — Use the annotation
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/payments")
public class PaymentController {

    @RateLimited(requests = 10, perSeconds = 60)
    @PostMapping("/pay")
    public ResponseEntity<String> pay(@RequestBody PaymentRequest req) {
        paymentService.process(req);
        return ResponseEntity.ok("Payment success");
    }
}
Step 3 — Process at runtime with Aspect (Spring AOP)
@Aspect
@Component
public class RateLimitAspect {

    private final Map<String, AtomicInteger> counters = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    @Around("@annotation(rateLimited)")
    public Object enforce(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp, RateLimited rateLimited) throws Throwable {
        String key = rateLimited.key().isBlank()
                ? pjp.getSignature().toShortString()
                : rateLimited.key();

        AtomicInteger count = counters.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new AtomicInteger(0));
        if (count.incrementAndGet() > rateLimited.requests()) {
            throw new TooManyRequestsException("Rate limit exceeded for " + key);
        }

        return pjp.proceed();
    }
}
Step 4 — Read annotation via reflection (without AOP)
Method method = PaymentController.class
        .getMethod("pay", PaymentRequest.class);

if (method.isAnnotationPresent(RateLimited.class)) {
    RateLimited rl = method.getAnnotation(RateLimited.class);
    System.out.println("Limit: " + rl.requests() + " per " + rl.perSeconds() + " sec");
}

Annotation elements must be compile-time constants: primitives, String, Class, enum, other annotations, or arrays of those types. You cannot use arbitrary objects. 

public @interface ValidExample {
    int count() default 1;
    String message() default "invalid";
    Class<?> validator() default String.class;
    Severity level() default Severity.ERROR;
}

enum Severity { ERROR, WARN }

Real-time use case: Teams build @AuditLog, @Retry, or @FeatureFlag annotations so business code stays clean and cross-cutting logic lives in one aspect or interceptor.

@Retention — how long annotation lives
Policy Available at Typical use
SOURCE Source file only; stripped by compiler @Override, Lombok @Getter
CLASS Bytecode; not visible via reflection at runtime Bytecode tools, default if @Retention omitted
RUNTIME Bytecode + reflection at runtime Spring, JPA, Jackson, Bean Validation 
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.SOURCE)
public @interface GeneratedCode { }

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface JsonField {
    String name();
}

If Spring cannot see your custom annotation at runtime, you almost certainly forgot @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME).

@Target — where annotation can be placed
@Target(ElementType.FIELD)
public @interface Encrypted { }

@Target(ElementType.PARAMETER)
public @interface CurrentUser { }

@Target({ElementType.METHOD, ElementType.TYPE})
public @interface Secured {
    String[] roles();
}
ElementType Real-time example
TYPE @Entity, @Service, @RestController
METHOD @GetMapping, @Transactional, @Scheduled
FIELD @Autowired, @Column, @JsonProperty
PARAMETER @PathVariable, @RequestBody, @Valid
CONSTRUCTOR @Autowired on constructor injection (recommended in Spring) 
// Compile error if @Target(ElementType.METHOD) only:
@Encrypted
private String creditCardNumber;   // needs ElementType.FIELD

@GetMapping("/{id}")
public User get(@PathVariable Long id) { }  // PARAMETER + METHOD targets

Interview one-liner: @Target controls where you can write the annotation; @Retention(RUNTIME) is required for Spring, Hibernate, and any reflection-based framework. 

                    COMPILE TIME                    RUNTIME
                         |                              |
              Annotation Processor                 Reflection / Spring
              (javax.annotation.processing)        (Class.getAnnotations)
                         |                              |
              Generates code at build               Applies behavior when app runs
              e.g. Lombok, MapStruct                e.g. @Autowired, @Transactional
Compile-time processing

Annotation processors run during javac and can generate source files or validate code. 

// Lombok @Getter generates getName() at compile time — you never write it
@Getter
public class User {
    private String name;
}

// MapStruct generates mapper implementation at compile time
@Mapper
public interface UserMapper {
    UserDto toDto(User user);
}
Runtime processing

Framework scans classpath, reads annotations via reflection, and wires behavior. 

@SpringBootApplication
public class App { }

// At startup Spring does roughly:
// 1. Scan packages for @Component, @Service, @Repository
// 2. Create beans and inject @Autowired dependencies
// 3. Register @RestController mappings
// 4. Enable @Transactional proxy for @Service methods
Comparison table
Aspect Compile-time Runtime
When it runs During build (mvn compile) When application starts / method invoked
Performance No runtime cost after generation Reflection + proxy overhead (usually small)
Examples Lombok, MapStruct, Immutables Spring, JPA, Jackson, Validation
Retention needed SOURCE or CLASS RUNTIME

Real-time: In a microservice, MapStruct generates DTO mappers at compile time (fast, type-safe), while Spring reads @KafkaListener at runtime to subscribe to topics when the app boots.

Most backend Java developers use annotations daily through Spring Boot. Each annotation triggers framework behavior without manual wiring.

REST API layer
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/orders")
@Validated
public class OrderController {

    private final OrderService orderService;

    public OrderController(OrderService orderService) {
        this.orderService = orderService;   // constructor injection
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> create(
            @Valid @RequestBody CreateOrderRequest request) {
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED)
                .body(orderService.create(request));
    }

    @GetMapping("/{orderId}")
    public OrderResponse get(@PathVariable Long orderId) {
        return orderService.getById(orderId);
    }
}
Service + transaction + caching
@Service
public class OrderService {

    @Cacheable(value = "orders", key = "#orderId")
    public OrderResponse getById(Long orderId) {
        return orderRepository.findById(orderId)
                .map(this::toResponse)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new OrderNotFoundException(orderId));
    }

    @Transactional
    @CacheEvict(value = "orders", allEntries = true)
    public OrderResponse create(CreateOrderRequest request) {
        Order order = orderRepository.save(toEntity(request));
        eventPublisher.publish(new OrderCreatedEvent(order.getId()));
        return toResponse(order);
    }
}
JPA entity mapping
@Entity
@Table(name = "orders")
public class Order {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private BigDecimal amount;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    @JoinColumn(name = "customer_id")
    private Customer customer;

    @CreatedDate
    private Instant createdAt;
}
Validation on DTO
public class CreateOrderRequest {

    @NotNull
    private Long customerId;

    @DecimalMin(value = "0.01", message = "Amount must be positive")
    private BigDecimal amount;

    @Size(max = 200)
    private String notes;
}
Security
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
@DeleteMapping("/{orderId}")
public void delete(@PathVariable Long orderId) {
    orderService.delete(orderId);
}
Annotation What Spring/framework does
@RestController Registers HTTP endpoints, serializes response to JSON
@Transactional Opens/commits/rolls back DB transaction via AOP proxy
@Cacheable Stores method result in Redis/Caffeine cache
@Entity Maps class to database table via Hibernate
@Valid Triggers Bean Validation on request body
@Scheduled Runs method on cron expression
@KafkaListener Subscribes to Kafka topic at startup

Without annotations, the same app would need hundreds of lines of XML or manual bean registration.

A common real-time pattern: create a custom annotation for audit logging so every sensitive operation is tracked consistently without copy-pasting log statements.

1. Define annotation
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface AuditLog {
    String action();
    String module() default "GENERAL";
    boolean logArgs() default false;
}
2. Use on business methods
@Service
public class AccountService {

    @AuditLog(action = "TRANSFER_MONEY", module = "PAYMENTS", logArgs = true)
    @Transactional
    public void transfer(Long from, Long to, BigDecimal amount) {
        debit(from, amount);
        credit(to, amount);
    }

    @AuditLog(action = "BLOCK_ACCOUNT", module = "COMPLIANCE")
    public void blockAccount(Long accountId) {
        accountRepository.updateStatus(accountId, Status.BLOCKED);
    }
}
3. Aspect to process annotation
@Aspect
@Component
@Slf4j
public class AuditLogAspect {

    private final AuditRepository auditRepository;

    public AuditLogAspect(AuditRepository auditRepository) {
        this.auditRepository = auditRepository;
    }

    @Around("@annotation(auditLog)")
    public Object logAudit(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp, AuditLog auditLog) throws Throwable {
        String user = SecurityContextHolder.getContext()
                .getAuthentication().getName();

        long start = System.currentTimeMillis();
        try {
            Object result = pjp.proceed();
            saveAudit(user, auditLog, pjp, "SUCCESS", System.currentTimeMillis() - start);
            return result;
        } catch (Exception ex) {
            saveAudit(user, auditLog, pjp, "FAILED", System.currentTimeMillis() - start);
            throw ex;
        }
    }

    private void saveAudit(String user, AuditLog auditLog,
                           ProceedingJoinPoint pjp, String status, long durationMs) {
        auditRepository.save(new AuditEntry(
                user,
                auditLog.module(),
                auditLog.action(),
                pjp.getSignature().toShortString(),
                status,
                durationMs
        ));
    }
}
4. Optional — compose with meta-annotations
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@AuditLog(action = "DEFAULT", module = "PAYMENTS")
public @interface PaymentAudit {
    String value();   // overrides action
}

// Usage
@PaymentAudit("REFUND")
public void refund(Long orderId) { }

This pattern is used in banking, healthcare, and e-commerce for compliance (who did what, when, and whether it succeeded). The business method stays focused on domain logic; the annotation + aspect handle cross-cutting audit concerns.

Best interview sentence: Custom annotations shine when you need reusable, declarative metadata that frameworks or AOP can interpret — logging, retries, feature flags, rate limits, and audit trails are all common production examples.

@Inherited behavior

By default, annotations on a parent class are not inherited by subclasses. @Inherited changes that for class-level annotations only. 

@Inherited
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
public @interface SecureService { }

@SecureService
public class BasePaymentService { }

public class RazorpayPaymentService extends BasePaymentService {
    // inherits @SecureService because of @Inherited
}

public interface PaymentGateway { }

@SecureService
public abstract class AbstractGateway implements PaymentGateway { }

public class StripeGateway extends AbstractGateway { }
// @SecureService is visible on StripeGateway.class

Note: method-level annotations are never inherited, even with @Inherited.

Common pitfalls
Mistake Problem Fix
Missing @Retention(RUNTIME) Reflection returns null at runtime Add @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
Wrong @Target Compile error when placing annotation Allow METHOD, FIELD, PARAMETER as needed
Expecting annotations to execute code Annotation alone does nothing Need processor: Spring, AOP, or annotation processor
@Transactional on private method Proxy cannot intercept — no transaction Put on public service method; use self-injection if needed
Non-constant default values Compile error Only constants, Class, enum, annotation allowed 
// WRONG — annotation elements must be compile-time constants
public @interface Bad {
    // List<String> tags();   // not allowed
    String createdAt() default LocalDateTime.now().toString();  // not allowed
}

// CORRECT
public @interface Good {
    String[] tags() default {};
    Class<?> handler() default Void.class;
}
Quick revision — annotation lifecycle
1. Define  -> @interface MyAnno { String value(); }
2. Meta    -> @Target + @Retention + optional @Inherited/@Documented
3. Apply   -> @MyAnno("demo") on class/method/field
4. Process -> Compiler / Annotation Processor / Reflection / AOP

Interview one-liner: Annotations are metadata; they become powerful only when a compiler, framework, or aspect knows how to read and act on them.

In real projects, migration is rarely only code movement. It usually includes framework upgrades, infrastructure changes, database changes, security changes, CI/CD changes, and production traffic cutover.

Common migration issues
Area Issue faced How to handle
Java/Spring upgrade Deprecated APIs, dependency conflicts, javax to jakarta migration Upgrade in small steps, run regression tests, fix imports and library versions
Database Schema mismatch, slow migration scripts, data inconsistency Use Flyway/Liquibase, dry-run scripts, backups, rollback scripts
Configuration Wrong environment variables, missing secrets, profile mismatch Externalize config and validate startup properties
Performance New version has different memory, connection pool, or query behavior Load test before go-live, tune JVM, HikariCP, indexes, cache
Security Old auth filters break, CORS/CSRF behavior changes Test login, token refresh, role checks, API gateway rules
Deployment Docker image works locally but fails in Kubernetes Check env vars, health probes, config maps, secrets, resource limits
Production cutover Downtime, DNS/cache delay, partial traffic issues Use blue-green/canary deployment and rollback plan
Example interview answer

In one migration, we moved a Spring Boot service to a newer Java/Spring version and containerized it. The main issues were dependency conflicts, changed security configuration, database script ordering, and memory tuning in Docker. We handled it by creating a migration checklist, running automated tests, doing data backup, using canary deployment, monitoring logs/metrics, and keeping rollback images ready.

Cloud deployment means running applications on platforms like AWS, Azure, or GCP instead of only using our own office data center, local servers, or private network. In interviews, the best answer is not "cloud is always better", but cloud gives faster scaling, managed services, and global reach, while on-prem gives more direct control.

What is the main difference?
Area Cloud Own network / on-prem
Infrastructure setup Provision in minutes Need to buy, rack, configure servers
Scaling Fast autoscaling Capacity expansion is slower and manual
Cost model Pay as you use High upfront capital expense
Managed services DB, cache, storage, queue, monitoring managed by provider Team must manage most things directly
Availability Multi-AZ / multi-region options Need to build HA and DR yourself
Operations effort Less hardware work More hardware, patching, network, backup work
Control Less low-level control More direct control over infra and network
Why should we use cloud for deployment?
  • Faster provisioning: create servers, databases, load balancers, and storage quickly.
  • Easy scaling: scale up during high traffic and scale down later.
  • Managed services: use RDS, S3, Redis, Kafka, secret stores, monitoring, CDN, etc.
  • High availability: deploy across zones/regions with lower effort.
  • Disaster recovery: snapshots, backups, cross-region replication, and automated restore options.
  • Global access: serve users closer to their region using CDN and regional deployment.
  • Automation: infra-as-code, auto-healing, autoscaling, CI/CD integration.
  • Faster team productivity: developers focus more on application work than hardware setup.
Real-world example

Suppose an e-commerce app has normal traffic on regular days but 10x traffic during a sale. In cloud, we can autoscale app pods, use managed database replicas, store images in object storage, and use CDN for static assets. On our own network, we would need to buy extra servers in advance even if they stay idle most of the year.

Benefits over our own network / on-premises
Benefit Why it matters Example
Elastic scaling Match traffic without permanent over-provisioning Scale API from 3 pods to 20 pods during campaign traffic
Lower initial cost No need to buy hardware at day one Startup deploys with small monthly bill
Managed DB/cache/storage Less ops burden and faster delivery Use RDS + Redis + S3 instead of self-managing all servers
Better release speed CI/CD, container registry, infra APIs are easier to automate Deploy using Jenkins/GitHub Actions to EKS/AKS/GKE
Better reliability options Built-in HA patterns reduce downtime risk Run app in multiple availability zones
Observability Cloud monitoring/logging tools are easy to integrate CloudWatch, Azure Monitor, GCP Monitoring
Disadvantages of cloud
  • Recurring cost: pay every month; bad architecture can make bills high.
  • Vendor lock-in: deep use of one cloud provider can make migration harder.
  • Internet dependency: public access and remote operations depend on good connectivity.
  • Less low-level control: some infra/network behavior is abstracted by provider.
  • Security misconfiguration risk: wrong IAM, security groups, or public buckets can expose data.
  • Cost surprises: autoscaling, data transfer, and managed services can increase cost unexpectedly.
  • Compliance limits: some industries or clients require strict local/private hosting.
Disadvantages of only using our own network / on-prem
  • Need large upfront hardware investment.
  • Scaling is slow because hardware procurement takes time.
  • Ops team must manage servers, patching, power, cooling, network, firewall, backups, and DR.
  • Multi-region or high availability setup is harder and more expensive.
  • Idle infrastructure wastes money when traffic is low.
When cloud is the better choice
  • Traffic is variable or growing.
  • We want faster release cycles and easier automation.
  • We need CDN, object storage, managed DB, queue, cache, monitoring, and autoscaling.
  • We are building SaaS, APIs, mobile backends, or microservices.
  • We want lower time-to-market.
When on-prem / private network may be better
  • Strict compliance or data residency requires private hosting.
  • Very stable long-term workload where owned infra may be cheaper.
  • Low-latency dependency on internal systems inside the same private network.
  • Organization already has strong internal data center investment and ops team.
Hybrid approach

Many enterprises use hybrid architecture. Sensitive systems may stay on-prem, while public APIs, web apps, analytics, batch jobs, backups, and disaster recovery move to cloud.

Interview-ready answer

We use cloud for deployment because it gives faster provisioning, easier autoscaling, managed services, better availability options, and quicker delivery than running everything only on our own network. On-prem gives more control, but cloud usually reduces operational overhead and improves agility. The right choice depends on traffic pattern, compliance, latency, and cost model.

Scaling means increasing the system capacity so it can handle more users, requests, data, or background jobs without breaking SLA.

Horizontal vs vertical scaling
Type Meaning Example Best for
Vertical scaling Increase CPU/RAM of the same machine or pod 2 CPU/4 GB to 8 CPU/16 GB Database, memory-heavy jobs, quick capacity increase
Horizontal scaling Add more instances/pods/nodes Run 2 app pods to 10 app pods Stateless APIs, web apps, workers, microservices
What can be scaled?
  • Web layer: replicate UI/static web servers behind CDN or load balancer.
  • Application layer: run multiple stateless Spring Boot replicas behind load balancer.
  • Database read layer: add read replicas for SELECT-heavy traffic.
  • Database write layer: shard/partition data, optimize indexes, batch writes.
  • Cache layer: Redis cluster, local cache, CDN cache.
  • Queue/worker layer: scale consumers based on queue depth.
  • Infrastructure layer: add Kubernetes worker nodes through cluster autoscaler.
Load balancer algorithms
Algorithm How it works Use case
Round robin Sends requests one by one to each server Similar app instances with similar capacity
Least connections Sends request to server with fewest active connections Long-running requests or uneven request duration
Weighted round robin More traffic to powerful servers Mixed capacity servers
IP hash Same client IP goes to same backend Sticky session requirement
Latency based Routes to fastest/nearest healthy backend Multi-region systems
Important rule

For application horizontal scaling, keep the service stateless. Store session in Redis/JWT/database, store files in object storage like S3, and never depend on local container memory or disk for shared state.

Kubernetes is used to run containers at scale. The most common building blocks are cluster, node, pod, deployment, service, and ingress.

Term Meaning Example
Cluster Group of machines managed by Kubernetes Production EKS/AKS/GKE cluster
Node Worker machine where containers run EC2 VM with CPU/RAM
Pod Smallest deployable unit; wraps one or more containers One Spring Boot container inside one pod
Deployment Manages desired number of pod replicas and rollout Keep 3 app pods running
Service Stable internal network endpoint for pods user-service:8080
Ingress External HTTP routing into services api.company.com/users 
Cluster
  Node 1
    Pod: app-1
    Pod: app-2
  Node 2
    Pod: app-3
    Pod: worker-1

Interview one-liner: A cluster is the full Kubernetes environment, nodes are machines inside it, and pods are the smallest units where our containers actually run.

Autoscaling automatically increases or decreases resources based on load. In Kubernetes, the common mechanisms are HPA, VPA, and Cluster Autoscaler.

Autoscaler Scales what? Trigger examples
HPA - Horizontal Pod Autoscaler Number of pods CPU, memory, RPS, queue length, custom metrics
VPA - Vertical Pod Autoscaler CPU/memory requests of pods Pod consistently needs more/less memory or CPU
Cluster Autoscaler Number of worker nodes Pods are pending because cluster has no capacity
HPA example
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: user-service-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: user-service
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
When to autoscale
  • Traffic changes by time, campaign, sale, or seasonal load.
  • Queue processing needs more consumers when backlog increases.
  • CPU or memory crosses a defined threshold for a sustained time.
  • Pods are stateless and can safely run in multiple replicas.
When to be careful
  • Do not blindly autoscale database writers; first optimize queries, indexes, pooling, and locking.
  • Use cooldown/stabilization windows to avoid scaling up/down continuously.
  • Set proper resource requests and limits; HPA decisions depend on them.

File handling can be done as simple multipart upload, streaming upload/download, chunk upload, or direct object-storage upload using pre-signed URLs.

What is multipart?

multipart/form-data is an HTTP request format where text fields and files are sent as separate parts in one request. In Spring Boot, a file part is commonly received as MultipartFile.

Default Spring Boot upload size

Spring Boot's default multipart limits are commonly 1MB per file and 10MB per request. Increase them in configuration when your use case needs larger files. 

spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size=100MB
spring.servlet.multipart.max-request-size=100MB
spring.servlet.multipart.file-size-threshold=2MB
Approach 1 - Simple multipart upload
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/files")
public class FileController {

    private final Path root = Paths.get("uploads");

    @PostMapping("/upload")
    public ResponseEntity<String> upload(@RequestParam("file") MultipartFile file) throws IOException {
        if (file.isEmpty()) {
            return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body("File is empty");
        }

        Files.createDirectories(root);
        String safeName = Paths.get(file.getOriginalFilename()).getFileName().toString();
        Path target = root.resolve(UUID.randomUUID() + "-" + safeName);

        try (InputStream inputStream = file.getInputStream()) {
            Files.copy(inputStream, target, StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);
        }

        return ResponseEntity.ok("Uploaded: " + target.getFileName());
    }
}
Approach 2 - Stream download
@GetMapping("/download/{fileName}")
public ResponseEntity<StreamingResponseBody> download(@PathVariable String fileName) throws IOException {
    Path file = Paths.get("uploads").resolve(fileName).normalize();
    if (!Files.exists(file)) {
        return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
    }

    StreamingResponseBody body = outputStream -> {
        try (InputStream inputStream = Files.newInputStream(file)) {
            inputStream.transferTo(outputStream);
        }
    };

    return ResponseEntity.ok()
            .header(HttpHeaders.CONTENT_DISPOSITION, "attachment; filename=\"" + file.getFileName() + "\"")
            .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM)
            .body(body);
}
Approach 3 - Chunk upload business logic

Chunk upload means the client splits a large file into smaller parts and sends each part with metadata like upload id, chunk number, total chunks, and file name. The server stores chunks temporarily and merges them after all parts arrive. 

@PostMapping("/upload-chunk")
public ResponseEntity<String> uploadChunk(
        @RequestParam String uploadId,
        @RequestParam int chunkNumber,
        @RequestParam int totalChunks,
        @RequestParam String fileName,
        @RequestParam("chunk") MultipartFile chunk) throws IOException {

    Path tempDir = Paths.get("uploads", "tmp", uploadId);
    Files.createDirectories(tempDir);

    Path chunkPath = tempDir.resolve(String.valueOf(chunkNumber));
    try (InputStream in = chunk.getInputStream()) {
        Files.copy(in, chunkPath, StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);
    }

    long uploadedChunks = Files.list(tempDir).count();
    if (uploadedChunks == totalChunks) {
        Path finalFile = Paths.get("uploads").resolve(fileName).normalize();
        try (OutputStream out = Files.newOutputStream(finalFile, StandardOpenOption.CREATE,
                StandardOpenOption.TRUNCATE_EXISTING)) {
            for (int i = 1; i <= totalChunks; i++) {
                Files.copy(tempDir.resolve(String.valueOf(i)), out);
            }
        }
        return ResponseEntity.ok("Upload completed: " + finalFile.getFileName());
    }

    return ResponseEntity.ok("Chunk " + chunkNumber + " uploaded");
}
What is resumable upload?

Resumable upload allows retrying only missing chunks instead of uploading the full file again. Store metadata in DB/Redis: uploadId, file name, total chunks, uploaded chunk numbers, checksum, status, and expiry time. 

@GetMapping("/upload-status/{uploadId}")
public ResponseEntity<Set<Integer>> uploadedChunks(@PathVariable String uploadId) {
    Set<Integer> chunks = uploadSessionService.findUploadedChunkNumbers(uploadId);
    return ResponseEntity.ok(chunks);
}
Different approaches
Approach Use when
Multipart upload to app server Small/medium files and simple business validation
Streaming Large downloads/uploads where memory usage must stay low
Chunk upload Large files, flaky networks, resumable behavior
Pre-signed URL to S3/Azure Blob/GCS Very large files; avoid routing bytes through app server

Point RDBMS NoSQL
Data model Tables, rows, joins Document, key-value, column, graph
Schema Fixed schema Flexible schema
Transaction Strong ACID support Varies by database; often optimized for scale/flexibility
Query style SQL, joins, relational queries Access-pattern based queries
Examples MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle MongoDB, Cassandra, DynamoDB, Redis, Neo4j
Choose RDBMS when
  • You need strong transactions, joins, constraints, reporting, and relational integrity.
  • Examples: banking, order management, payments, inventory, ERP.
Choose NoSQL when
  • You need flexible schema, very high read/write scale, low latency, or document-style data.
  • Examples: product catalog, user preferences, logs, events, session store, IoT data.

Interview one-liner: I choose RDBMS for relational consistency and transactions; I choose NoSQL when access patterns, scale, flexibility, or low latency matter more than complex joins.

Improving Spring Boot performance is not one single change. We improve it by finding the bottleneck first and then tuning the correct layer: database, API design, caching, thread pools, JVM, logging, serialization, external calls, and infrastructure.

1. First identify the bottleneck
  • Check response time, throughput, CPU, memory, GC, DB query time, and external API latency.
  • Use APM and metrics before changing code randomly.
  • Measure p95/p99 latency, not only average latency.

Real-world example: Sometimes the app looks slow, but the real issue is a slow SQL query or external API.

2. Database optimization gives the biggest win in many projects
  • Write efficient queries and avoid unnecessary joins.
  • Add correct indexes for frequently filtered and joined columns.
  • Avoid N+1 query issues in Hibernate/JPA.
  • Use pagination instead of loading huge result sets.
  • Use projections/DTO queries when full entity is not needed.
  • Tune connection pool size properly.
@Query("""
select new com.example.dto.UserSummary(u.id, u.name, u.email)
from User u
where u.status = :status
""")
Page<UserSummary> findActiveUsers(@Param("status") String status, Pageable pageable);

Real-world example: Instead of loading full user entity with relationships, return only fields needed for list screen.

3. Use caching for repeated reads
  • Cache frequently used, rarely changing data.
  • Use Redis or local cache depending on deployment model.
  • Choose proper TTL and invalidation strategy.
@Cacheable(value = "products", key = "#productId")
public ProductDto getProduct(Long productId) {
    return productRepository.findById(productId)
            .map(ProductDto::from)
            .orElseThrow();
}

Real-world example: Product details or configuration tables are good cache candidates.

4. Keep APIs efficient
  • Avoid very large request/response payloads.
  • Use compression when useful.
  • Return DTOs instead of large nested object graphs.
  • Use streaming for large file download/upload.

Real-world example: Returning 10,000 records in one response increases memory, serialization time, and network latency.

5. Reduce blocking and use async where it makes sense
  • Do not block request thread for email, audit, report generation, or slow external work.
  • Use async processing, queues, or background workers for non-immediate tasks.
  • Use timeouts for external API calls.
@Async
public CompletableFuture<Void> sendWelcomeMail(String email) {
    emailService.send(email);
    return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(null);
}

Real-world example: Order placement should not wait for promotional email sending.

6. Tune thread pools and server settings
  • Use proper Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow thread configuration.
  • Use dedicated executor pools for async jobs instead of one shared default pool.
  • Avoid too many threads because context switching also hurts performance.
server.tomcat.threads.max=200
server.tomcat.accept-count=100
server.compression.enabled=true
server.compression.mime-types=application/json,text/html,text/plain

Real-world example: If external calls are slow, a badly sized thread pool can cause request queue buildup.

7. Tune connection pools

HikariCP is the default in Spring Boot and usually performs very well, but wrong pool sizes can still hurt. 

spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=20
spring.datasource.hikari.minimum-idle=5
spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=30000
spring.datasource.hikari.idle-timeout=600000
  • Too small pool causes waiting.
  • Too large pool can overload database.
8. JVM and garbage collection tuning
  • Set proper heap size for workload.
  • Choose a suitable GC like G1 for general workloads.
  • Watch GC pause time, allocation rate, and memory leaks.
java -Xms1g -Xmx1g -XX:+UseG1GC -jar app.jar

Real-world example: High latency spikes may come from GC pauses, not from business logic.

9. Avoid unnecessary object creation and heavy serialization
  • Do not create large temporary objects in hot paths.
  • Prefer lightweight DTOs.
  • Be careful with deep JSON nesting and very large collections.

Real-world example: Huge nested response payloads increase CPU time in Jackson serialization.

10. Improve external API interaction
  • Use connection pooling HTTP clients.
  • Set connect/read timeouts.
  • Use retry carefully, only for retry-safe flows.
  • Use circuit breaker for failing downstream services.
@Bean
RestTemplate restTemplate(RestTemplateBuilder builder) {
    return builder
            .setConnectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
            .setReadTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
            .build();
}

Real-world example: One slow payment gateway can make the whole API look slow if timeout is not configured.

11. Logging should be useful, not expensive
  • Avoid excessive debug logs in hot code paths in production.
  • Avoid logging huge objects and full payloads repeatedly.
  • Use async logging if needed in high-throughput systems.

Real-world example: Logging every DB record or full request body can increase CPU and I/O cost significantly.

12. Use proper architecture patterns
  • Make service stateless for easier scaling.
  • Offload heavy jobs to Kafka/RabbitMQ/workers.
  • Use CDN/object storage for static files instead of serving everything from app server.

Real-world example: Large file uploads should go to S3 using pre-signed URLs instead of always going through Spring Boot server.

13. Monitor continuously
  • Use Actuator, Micrometer, Prometheus, Grafana, ELK, or APM tools.
  • Track CPU, memory, GC, thread count, DB pool usage, API latency, error rate, and cache hit ratio.

Interview point: Performance tuning without observability is mostly guessing.

14. Common interview answer structure
1. Find bottleneck first
2. Optimize DB queries and indexes
3. Add caching where repeated reads happen
4. Use async/queue for slow non-critical work
5. Tune thread pools, connection pools, and JVM
6. Reduce payload size and serialization cost
7. Monitor and load test again
Interview-ready answer

To improve a Spring Boot application's performance, I first identify the actual bottleneck using metrics and profiling. Then I optimize database queries and indexes, add caching for repeated reads, reduce unnecessary payload and object creation, tune thread pools, connection pools, and JVM settings, move non-critical work to async/background processing, and monitor the system again after load testing.

Vulnerability management is the process of continuously finding, prioritizing, fixing, and verifying security weaknesses in code, dependencies, containers, infrastructure, and runtime configuration.

Typical flow
Scan -> Triage -> Prioritize -> Fix -> Test -> Deploy -> Rescan -> Monitor
Common tools
  • SCA/dependency scan: Snyk, OWASP Dependency-Check, Dependabot, GitHub Advanced Security.
  • SAST/code scan: SonarQube, Checkmarx, Fortify, Semgrep.
  • Container scan: Trivy, Grype, Docker Scout, ECR image scanning.
  • DAST/runtime scan: OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite.
How to fix
Vulnerability type Fix
Dependency CVE Upgrade direct dependency or override vulnerable transitive dependency
Container base image CVE Use patched base image, smaller runtime image, rebuild regularly
SQL injection Use prepared statements/JPA parameters, never string-concatenate SQL
XSS Escape output, sanitize input, use CSP headers
Secret leakage Remove secret, rotate it, move to vault/secret manager
Misconfiguration Disable debug endpoints, enforce TLS, least privilege IAM/RBAC 
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId>
    <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
    <version>2.17.2</version>
</dependency>

Nexus Repository Manager is an artifact repository. It stores build artifacts and proxies external repositories like Maven Central, npm registry, Docker registry, and PyPI.

Why use Nexus?
  • Store internal company libraries and application artifacts.
  • Cache Maven Central dependencies to make builds faster and more reliable.
  • Control which dependencies are allowed in enterprise builds.
  • Publish Docker images, npm packages, jar files, and release artifacts.
Maven example
<distributionManagement>
    <repository>
        <id>nexus-releases</id>
        <url>http://nexus.company.com/repository/maven-releases/</url>
    </repository>
    <snapshotRepository>
        <id>nexus-snapshots</id>
        <url>http://nexus.company.com/repository/maven-snapshots/</url>
    </snapshotRepository>
</distributionManagement>
# Build and publish jar to Nexus
mvn clean deploy
Docker image flow
docker build -t nexus.company.com:5000/user-service:1.0 .
docker login nexus.company.com:5000
docker push nexus.company.com:5000/user-service:1.0

JFrog is a company/platform, and its best-known product is Artifactory. Like Nexus, Artifactory is an artifact repository used to store, proxy, and distribute build artifacts and packages.

What it is used for
  • Host Maven, Gradle, npm, Docker, PyPI, and other artifacts.
  • Proxy external repositories and cache dependencies.
  • Store release, snapshot, and internal build outputs.
  • Support enterprise artifact promotion and release flows.
Nexus vs JFrog Artifactory
Nexus JFrog Artifactory
Sonatype product focused on artifact repository and repository proxying. JFrog product with artifact repository plus a broader platform around releases and DevOps tooling.
Often used to store Maven, Docker, npm, and other build artifacts. Also stores Maven, Docker, npm, and more, with strong enterprise workflow support.
Common choice for dependency caching and internal artifact hosting. Common choice for enterprise artifact management and release pipelines.

In interview terms, both solve the same core problem: a controlled internal place to store and fetch artifacts instead of downloading everything directly from public repositories each time.

Interview-ready answer

"Nexus and JFrog Artifactory are both artifact repositories. Nexus is Sonatype's product, and JFrog's main artifact repository product is Artifactory. We use both to proxy external repos, cache dependencies, and host internal build artifacts like jars, Docker images, and npm packages."

A good interview answer should show that you use AI as an engineering assistant, but you still own design, correctness, security, testing, and production responsibility.

  • Understanding legacy code faster by asking for flow summaries and risk areas.
  • Generating first drafts of boilerplate code, unit tests, DTOs, mappings, and documentation.
  • Debugging errors by sharing stack traces and asking for likely root causes.
  • Improving SQL queries, API contracts, log messages, and code readability.
  • Writing test cases for edge cases that I may miss manually.
  • Creating Jenkins/Kubernetes/Docker templates faster and then reviewing them carefully.
Important boundaries
  • I do not paste secrets, credentials, customer PII, or proprietary data into public AI tools.
  • I review every AI-generated code change before using it.
  • I run tests, static analysis, and security scans instead of trusting generated code blindly.

Interview one-liner: AI helps me reduce repetitive work and explore options faster, but I treat its output like a junior developer's draft that must be reviewed, tested, and secured.

Agile is an iterative delivery approach where teams deliver small increments frequently, get feedback, and adapt. Scrum is one common Agile framework.

Scrum events
  • Sprint planning: decide sprint goal and stories.
  • Daily standup: discuss progress, blockers, and plan for the day.
  • Backlog refinement: clarify upcoming stories and acceptance criteria.
  • Sprint review/demo: show completed work to stakeholders.
  • Retrospective: discuss what went well and what to improve.
Common terms
Term Meaning
User story Requirement written from user's perspective
Acceptance criteria Conditions that define when story is complete
Story points Relative estimation of complexity and effort
Definition of Done Code complete, reviewed, tested, documented, deployable

Peer review means another developer reviews your code before it is merged. The goal is to catch bugs, improve maintainability, share knowledge, and maintain team standards.

Typical review process
  • Developer creates feature branch and commits changes.
  • Developer opens pull request with description, screenshots/logs if needed, and test evidence.
  • CI runs build, unit tests, static analysis, and security scans.
  • One or two peers review correctness, edge cases, readability, performance, and security.
  • Developer fixes comments and gets approval.
  • Code is merged using squash/merge/rebase based on team policy.
Reviewer checklist
  • Does it meet acceptance criteria?
  • Are there missing validations, null checks, or error handling?
  • Are tests added for important flows and edge cases?
  • Are logs meaningful without exposing secrets?
  • Does it follow existing project patterns?

Yes, you can create a global variable using let if it is declared at the top level of a script. But unlike var, top-level let does not become a property of the window object in browsers. 

var a = 10;
let b = 20;

console.log(window.a); // 10
console.log(window.b); // undefined
console.log(b);        // 20
In modules

In ES modules and most React files, top-level variables are module-scoped, not true browser globals. 

// userStore.js
let currentUser = null;

export function setCurrentUser(user) {
    currentUser = user;
}

export function getCurrentUser() {
    return currentUser;
}

Interview one-liner: let can be global in a normal script, but it does not attach to window; in modules/React it is module-scoped.

Plain JavaScript does not have interfaces. TypeScript has interface and type. React applications commonly use TypeScript interfaces/types for props, API objects, and state shape.

Use interface/type for data shape
interface User {
    id: number;
    name: string;
    email: string;
}

function UserCard({ user }: { user: User }) {
    return <div>{user.name}</div>;
}
Use class when you need behavior
class Money {
    constructor(private amount: number, private currency: string) {}

    format() {
        return `${this.currency} ${this.amount}`;
    }
}
Practical rule
  • Use interface or type for props, DTOs, API responses, and plain objects.
  • Use class only when you need methods, encapsulation, inheritance, or object instances.
  • In modern React, prefer functional components with typed props over class components.

It depends on project size, compliance, environments, and deployment strategy. For a typical Spring Boot microservice, I prefer separate pipelines or stages for CI, image build, security scan, and environment deployments.

Common pipeline structure
  • CI pipeline: compile, unit test, code quality, package jar.
  • Docker pipeline: build image, scan image, push image to registry.
  • Dev deploy pipeline: auto-deploy to dev after merge.
  • QA/UAT pipeline: deploy with approvals and run integration/regression tests.
  • Prod pipeline: manual approval, canary/blue-green deployment, smoke tests, rollback.

For a small project, this can be one Jenkinsfile with multiple stages. For enterprise projects, teams often separate build and deployment pipelines for better control and approvals.

A Jenkins deployment task takes a tested artifact or Docker image and releases it to an environment like dev, QA, staging, or production.

Typical deployment tasks
  • Checkout code and read version/commit id.
  • Build jar using Maven/Gradle.
  • Run unit tests and publish reports.
  • Run SonarQube/security/dependency scans.
  • Build Docker image and tag with build number or git commit.
  • Push image to Nexus/ECR/Docker Hub.
  • Update Kubernetes manifest or Helm values with new image tag.
  • Deploy using kubectl apply or helm upgrade.
  • Run smoke tests and verify rollout.
  • Rollback if rollout or health check fails.
kubectl set image deployment/user-service \
  user-service=nexus.company.com:5000/user-service:${BUILD_NUMBER} \
  -n dev

kubectl rollout status deployment/user-service -n dev

Dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
WORKDIR /app
COPY target/*.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
Kubernetes deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: user-service
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: user-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: user-service
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: user-service
          image: nexus.company.com:5000/user-service:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:

              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 20
            periodSeconds: 10

Kubernetes service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: user-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: user-service
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
Jenkinsfile
pipeline {
    agent any

    environment {
        APP_NAME = "user-service"
        REGISTRY = "nexus.company.com:5000"
        IMAGE = "${REGISTRY}/${APP_NAME}"
        K8S_NAMESPACE = "dev"
    }

    stages {
        stage("Checkout") {
            steps {
                checkout scm
            }
        }

        stage("Build and Unit Test") {
            steps {
                sh "mvn clean package"
            }
            post {
                always {
                    junit "target/surefire-reports/*.xml"
                }
            }
        }

        stage("Code Quality") {
            steps {
                sh "mvn sonar:sonar -Dsonar.projectKey=${APP_NAME}"
            }
        }

        stage("Build Docker Image") {
            steps {
                sh "docker build -t ${IMAGE}:${BUILD_NUMBER} ."
                sh "docker tag ${IMAGE}:${BUILD_NUMBER} ${IMAGE}:latest"
            }
        }

        stage("Push Docker Image") {
            steps {
                withCredentials([usernamePassword(credentialsId: "nexus-docker-creds",
                        usernameVariable: "DOCKER_USER",
                        passwordVariable: "DOCKER_PASS")]) {
                    sh "echo ${DOCKER_PASS} | docker login ${REGISTRY} -u ${DOCKER_USER} --password-stdin"
                    sh "docker push ${IMAGE}:${BUILD_NUMBER}"
                    sh "docker push ${IMAGE}:latest"
                }
            }
        }

        stage("Deploy to Kubernetes") {
            steps {
                withKubeConfig([credentialsId: "dev-kubeconfig"]) {
                    sh "kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml -n ${K8S_NAMESPACE}"
                    sh "kubectl apply -f k8s/service.yaml -n ${K8S_NAMESPACE}"
                    sh "kubectl set image deployment/${APP_NAME} ${APP_NAME}=${IMAGE}:${BUILD_NUMBER} -n ${K8S_NAMESPACE}"
                    sh "kubectl rollout status deployment/${APP_NAME} -n ${K8S_NAMESPACE} --timeout=120s"
                }
            }
        }

        stage("Smoke Test") {
            steps {
                sh "curl -f http://user-service.dev.company.com/actuator/health"
            }
        }
    }

    post {
        failure {
            withKubeConfig([credentialsId: "dev-kubeconfig"]) {
                sh "kubectl rollout undo deployment/${APP_NAME} -n ${K8S_NAMESPACE} || true"
            }
        }
        always {
            cleanWs()
        }
    }
}
Pipeline explanation
  • mvn clean package creates the Spring Boot jar and runs tests.
  • Docker image is tagged with Jenkins BUILD_NUMBER for traceability.
  • Image is pushed to Nexus Docker registry.
  • Kubernetes deployment is updated with the new image tag.
  • kubectl rollout status verifies that the new pods became healthy.
  • On failure, Jenkins tries kubectl rollout undo.
Production improvements
  • Add manual approval before production deployment.
  • Use Helm/Kustomize instead of editing raw YAML in large projects.
  • Add Trivy/Snyk image scan before pushing or deploying.
  • Use blue-green/canary rollout with Argo Rollouts or service mesh.
  • Store credentials in Jenkins Credentials, Vault, or cloud secret manager.

First I would stop the bad rollout, identify the missing or incorrect environment variable, and compare the running config with the expected config from the deployment manifest, Helm values, ConfigMap, Secret, or pipeline variables. Then I would either fix the variable and redeploy or roll back immediately if production is impacted.

Immediate steps
  • Check pod logs and startup failure messages for the exact missing variable name.
  • Inspect the deployed ConfigMap, Secret, Helm values, or CI/CD environment settings.
  • Confirm whether the issue is a missing value, wrong spelling, wrong profile, or wrong secret reference.
  • Rollback the deployment if the new version is already serving bad traffic.
  • Redeploy only after the corrected config is validated in lower environments.
How to prevent this next time
  • Fail fast on startup with clear validation for required properties.
  • Use @ConfigurationProperties with validation annotations for required config.
  • Keep environment-specific config in ConfigMaps/Secrets and validate it in CI/CD.
  • Use canary or blue-green deployment so a bad config affects fewer users.
Real-world example

If PAYMENT_URL is missing in production, the service may start failing before it becomes ready. In that case, I would check the Kubernetes manifest or Helm chart, fix the value in the secret or values file, and then redeploy. If the release is already live, I would roll back first to restore service, then ship the corrected config.

Interview-ready answer

"If a new microservice version fails because of an environment variable, I verify the deployed config, identify the bad or missing value, and either fix and redeploy or roll back immediately if production is affected. I would also add startup validation and deployment checks so required variables fail fast before traffic reaches the service."

The 3xx series tells the client: "the request was understood, but you need to take another step — usually follow a different URL." These are redirection responses. 

Client  --GET /old-page-->  Server
Client  <--301 Location: /new-page--  Server
Client  --GET /new-page-->  Server
Client  <--200 OK--  Server
Complete 3xx status code reference
Code Name Meaning Real-time use case
300 Multiple Choices Server offers multiple options; client chooses one Content negotiation — same resource in JSON or XML format
301 Moved Permanently Resource permanently moved to new URL Old API /v1/users permanently moved to /v2/users; SEO redirects
302 Found (Temporary Redirect) Resource temporarily at different URL Maintenance page redirect, legacy temporary migration
303 See Other After POST, redirect client to GET another URL Form submit → redirect to success page (PRG pattern)
304 Not Modified Cached version is still valid; no body returned Browser/CDN cache — send If-None-Match ETag header
307 Temporary Redirect Like 302 but method must not change (POST stays POST) Load balancer temporary routing during deployment
308 Permanent Redirect Like 301 but method must not change Permanent API URL change where POST must remain POST
301 vs 302 vs 307 vs 308
Code Permanent? Method preserved? When to use
301 Yes May change POST → GET (browser behavior) Deprecated URL, SEO permanent move
302 No May change method Short-term redirect
307 No Yes — POST stays POST Temporary redirect for APIs/forms
308 Yes Yes — POST stays POST Permanent API migration
Spring Boot examples
@RestController
public class RedirectController {

    // 301 — permanent redirect
    @GetMapping("/old-users")
    public ResponseEntity<Void> oldUsers() {
        return ResponseEntity
