                .status(HttpStatus.MOVED_PERMANENTLY)   // 301
                .location(URI.create("/api/v2/users"))
                .build();
    }

    // 302 — temporary redirect
    @GetMapping("/maintenance")
    public ResponseEntity<Void> maintenance() {
        return ResponseEntity
                .status(HttpStatus.FOUND)               // 302
                .location(URI.create("/status/maintenance"))
                .build();
    }

    // 303 — Post/Redirect/Get after form submission
    @PostMapping("/orders")
    public ResponseEntity<Void> createOrder(@RequestBody OrderRequest req) {
        Long orderId = orderService.create(req);
        return ResponseEntity
                .status(HttpStatus.SEE_OTHER)           // 303
                .location(URI.create("/orders/" + orderId))
                .build();
    }
}
304 Not Modified — caching in REST APIs
@GetMapping("/products/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<Product> getProduct(
        @PathVariable Long id,
        @RequestHeader(value = "If-None-Match", required = false) String etag) {

    Product product = productService.findById(id);
    String currentEtag = "\"" + product.getVersion() + "\"";

    if (currentEtag.equals(etag)) {
        return ResponseEntity
                .status(HttpStatus.NOT_MODIFIED)        // 304 — no body
                .eTag(currentEtag)
                .build();
    }

    return ResponseEntity.ok()
            .eTag(currentEtag)
            .body(product);
}

Real-time: CDNs (CloudFront, Akamai) and browsers rely heavily on 304 to avoid re-downloading unchanged assets. API gateways use 301/308 when deprecating old endpoint paths.

Best interview sentence: 3xx codes redirect the client to another resource; use 301/308 for permanent moves, 302/307 for temporary ones, and 304 for cache validation without sending the body again.

The 4xx series means the client sent a bad or unauthorized request. The server understood the request but refuses to process it (or cannot find what was asked). These are client errors. 

Client  --POST /api/users (invalid JSON)-->  Server
Client  <--400 Bad Request--  Server

Client  --GET /api/users/999 (no token)-->  Server
Client  <--401 Unauthorized--  Server

Client  --DELETE /api/admin (user role=USER)-->  Server
Client  <--403 Forbidden--  Server
Complete 4xx status code reference
Code Name Meaning Real-time use case
400 Bad Request Malformed syntax, invalid JSON, missing required field Broken JSON body, invalid query param format
401 Unauthorized Authentication missing or invalid No JWT token, expired login session
403 Forbidden Authenticated but not allowed to access resource User logged in but lacks ADMIN role
404 Not Found Resource or endpoint does not exist User ID 999 not in database, wrong URL path
405 Method Not Allowed HTTP method not supported on this URL POST sent to GET-only endpoint
406 Not Acceptable Server cannot produce response in requested format Client asks for Accept: application/xml but API returns JSON only
408 Request Timeout Client took too long to send complete request Slow upload, idle connection on API gateway
409 Conflict Request conflicts with current server state Duplicate email registration, optimistic lock version mismatch
410 Gone Resource permanently removed (stronger than 404) Deprecated account deleted forever, old promo link expired
413 Payload Too Large Request body exceeds server limit File upload > 10 MB limit, huge JSON payload
415 Unsupported Media Type Content-Type not supported Send text/plain to endpoint expecting application/json
422 Unprocessable Entity Syntax valid but semantic/business validation failed Valid JSON but email format wrong, age negative, insufficient balance
429 Too Many Requests Rate limit exceeded API gateway throttling, login brute-force protection
400 vs 422 — most asked interview question
Aspect 400 Bad Request 422 Unprocessable Entity
Request syntax Invalid — broken JSON, wrong data type in raw payload Valid JSON/XML — structure parses correctly
Problem type Malformed request Semantic / business rule violation
Example { "age": "twenty" } — age must be number { "age": -5 } — age must be positive
Spring default HttpMessageNotReadableException MethodArgumentNotValidException (often mapped to 400 or 422)
Who uses 422 Less common for validation Rails, Laravel, many REST APIs, OpenAPI specs 
// 400 — malformed JSON (Spring returns automatically)
POST /api/users
Content-Type: application/json
{ "email": "not-closed-quote }

// 422 — valid JSON but validation fails
POST /api/users
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "email": "invalid-email",
  "age": -1,
  "password": "12"
}
// Response: field-level errors for @Email, @Min, @Size
401 vs 403
401 Unauthorized  = "Who are you?"     → missing/invalid token
403 Forbidden     = "I know you, but no" → valid token, insufficient permission

// Example
GET /api/reports/salary
Authorization: Bearer <valid-user-token>   → 403 (user is not HR/ADMIN)

GET /api/reports/salary
(no Authorization header)                  → 401
404 vs 410
404 Not Found  → resource may never have existed OR ID wrong
410 Gone       → resource existed but is permanently deleted

// E-commerce: product was removed and will never come back
GET /api/products/deleted-promo-2023  → 410 Gone

422 Unprocessable Entity (WebDAV RFC 4918, widely adopted in REST APIs) means: the server understood the request format, but the content failed validation or business rules.

Use 422 when:

  • JSON/XML is syntactically correct
  • Bean Validation (@NotNull, @Email, @Size) fails
  • Business rules fail (e.g., order amount exceeds credit limit)
  • Domain constraints violated (duplicate SKU, invalid state transition)

Use 400 when the request itself is broken (malformed JSON, wrong Content-Type).

DTO with validation annotations
public class CreateUserRequest {

    @NotBlank(message = "Name is required")
    @Size(min = 2, max = 100, message = "Name must be 2-100 characters")
    private String name;

    @NotBlank(message = "Email is required")
    @Email(message = "Email format is invalid")
    private String email;

    @NotNull(message = "Age is required")
    @Min(value = 18, message = "User must be at least 18 years old")
    private Integer age;

    @Size(min = 8, message = "Password must be at least 8 characters")
    private String password;
}
Controller
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<UserResponse> createUser(
            @Valid @RequestBody CreateUserRequest request) {
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED)
                .body(userService.create(request));
    }
}
Global exception handler — return 422 with field errors
@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    // 422 — validation failed on valid JSON
    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ErrorResponse> handleValidation(
            MethodArgumentNotValidException ex) {

        Map<String, String> fieldErrors = ex.getBindingResult()
                .getFieldErrors()
                .stream()
                .collect(Collectors.toMap(
                        FieldError::getField,
                        FieldError::getDefaultMessage,
                        (a, b) -> a
                ));

        ErrorResponse body = new ErrorResponse(
                "VALIDATION_FAILED",
                "Request body is valid JSON but failed validation",
                fieldErrors
        );

        return ResponseEntity
                .status(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY)   // 422
                .body(body);
    }

    // 400 — malformed JSON
    @ExceptionHandler(HttpMessageNotReadableException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ErrorResponse> handleBadJson(
            HttpMessageNotReadableException ex) {

        ErrorResponse body = new ErrorResponse(
                "BAD_REQUEST",
                "Malformed JSON or invalid request body",
                Map.of()
        );

        return ResponseEntity
                .status(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST)            // 400
                .body(body);
    }

    // 409 — duplicate resource
    @ExceptionHandler(DuplicateEmailException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ErrorResponse> handleDuplicate(
            DuplicateEmailException ex) {

        return ResponseEntity
                .status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT)               // 409
                .body(new ErrorResponse("DUPLICATE_EMAIL", ex.getMessage(), Map.of()));
    }
}
Sample 422 response body
HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Entity
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "code": "VALIDATION_FAILED",
  "message": "Request body is valid JSON but failed validation",
  "errors": {
    "email": "Email format is invalid",
    "age": "User must be at least 18 years old",
    "password": "Password must be at least 8 characters"
  }
}
Other 4xx — Spring Boot quick examples
// 401 — Spring Security handles automatically when unauthenticated

// 403 — method security
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
@DeleteMapping("/{id}")
public void deleteUser(@PathVariable Long id) { }

// 404 — resource not found
return repository.findById(id)
    .orElseThrow(() -> new UserNotFoundException(id));

@ExceptionHandler(UserNotFoundException.class)
public ResponseEntity<ErrorResponse> notFound(UserNotFoundException ex) {
    return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND).body(...);  // 404
}

// 429 — rate limit
@ExceptionHandler(TooManyRequestsException.class)
public ResponseEntity<ErrorResponse> rateLimit() {
    return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.TOO_MANY_REQUESTS).body(...);  // 429
}
Decision flow for REST APIs
Incoming Request
      |
      v
Is JSON/body parseable? ----NO----> 400 Bad Request
      |
     YES
      v
Is user authenticated? ----NO----> 401 Unauthorized
      |
     YES
      v
Has permission? ----------NO----> 403 Forbidden
      |
     YES
      v
Resource exists? ---------NO----> 404 Not Found
      |
     YES
      v
Validation / business rules pass? --NO--> 422 Unprocessable Entity
      |
     YES
      v
State conflict (duplicate)? --YES--> 409 Conflict
      |
     NO
      v
200 / 201 Success

Real-time: Payment APIs return 422 when card details are well-formed but fail Luhn check or expiry validation. E-commerce returns 409 when two users checkout the last item simultaneously. API gateways return 429 when a client exceeds rate limits.

Best interview sentence: Use 400 for malformed requests, 401 for missing auth, 403 for insufficient permissions, 404 for missing resources, 409 for state conflicts, and 422 when the payload is syntactically valid but fails validation or business rules.

Trap: If a key object's hash code changes after insertion, the entry becomes unreachable in the bucket — get() returns null even though the entry still exists in memory. 

class MutableKey {
    private int id;

    MutableKey(int id) { this.id = id; }

    void setId(int id) { this.id = id; }   // mutating field used in hashCode

    @Override
    public int hashCode() { return id; }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof MutableKey mk && mk.id == this.id;
    }
}

Map<MutableKey, String> map = new HashMap<>();
MutableKey key = new MutableKey(1);
map.put(key, "Order-100");

System.out.println(map.get(key));        // Order-100

key.setId(99);                           // hash bucket is now wrong!
System.out.println(map.get(key));        // null  ← entry lost
System.out.println(map.size());          // 1     ← ghost entry still inside

Why: HashMap stores entry in bucket hash(key) % capacity. After mutation, hash changes but entry stays in old bucket. Lookup searches new bucket → miss.

Senior dev rule
  • Keys must be immutable (String, Integer, record with final fields).
  • Never use mutable entity as key unless ID is set once and never changed.
  • Real-time bug: JPA entity with lazy-loaded fields changing hashCode after persist.
// Safe pattern — use immutable ID as key
Map<Long, Order> orders = new HashMap<>();
orders.put(order.getId(), order);   // Long is immutable

Thrown when a collection is structurally modified while being iterated (except via iterator's own remove()). 

List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of("A", "B", "C"));

// FAIL — for-each uses Iterator internally
for (String s : list) {
    if (s.equals("B")) {
        list.remove(s);   // ConcurrentModificationException
    }
}

// FAIL — stream + external mutation
list.stream()
    .filter(s -> s.equals("B"))
    .forEach(s -> list.remove(s));   // CME or unpredictable
Safe fixes
// 1. Iterator.remove()
Iterator<String> it = list.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) {
    if (it.next().equals("B")) {
        it.remove();   // safe
    }
}

// 2. removeIf (Java 8+)
list.removeIf(s -> s.equals("B"));

// 3. Collect to new list (functional style)
list = list.stream()
        .filter(s -> !s.equals("B"))
        .collect(Collectors.toList());

// 4. CopyOnWriteArrayList for heavy concurrent reads + rare writes
List<String> cow = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(list);
SubList trap (very common in interviews)
List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5));
List<Integer> sub = nums.subList(1, 4);   // [2, 3, 4]

sub.clear();                               // modifies parent too!
System.out.println(nums);                // [1, 5]

nums.add(99);                              // structural change on parent
sub.get(0);                              // ConcurrentModificationException

Real-time: Batch jobs that filter-and-remove from in-memory lists during ETL often hit CME. Use removeIf or stream-to-new-collection instead.

API Mutable? Null allowed? Backed by array? Trap
Arrays.asList(a, b) Fixed size — no add/remove Yes Yes — changes reflect in array list.add() throws; set() mutates source array
List.of(a, b) Immutable No — NPE if null element No set() or add() throws
new ArrayList<>() Fully mutable Yes No None — safe default for business logic 
String[] arr = {"A", "B"};
List<String> list1 = Arrays.asList(arr);
list1.set(0, "Z");
System.out.println(arr[0]);              // Z — array changed!

List<String> list2 = List.of("A", "B");
list2.set(0, "Z");                       // UnsupportedOperationException

List<String> list3 = new ArrayList<>(List.of("A", "B"));
list3.add("C");                          // OK
// Interview trap — varargs + Arrays.asList
List<Integer> nums = Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3);
nums.sort(Comparator.naturalOrder());    // OK — set is allowed

nums.add(4);                             // UnsupportedOperationException

Best interview sentence: Use List.of for immutable constants, new ArrayList<>(List.of(...)) when you need to modify, and avoid Arrays.asList unless you intentionally share backing array.

`ArrayList` and `Set` look simple from the outside, but internally they use very different storage and lookup strategies. That is why they behave differently for duplicates, ordering, memory usage, and search performance.

1. ArrayList internals
  • Backed by a resizable array called elementData.
  • Insertion at the end is usually fast because the array grows amortized.
  • When capacity is full, Java allocates a bigger array and copies the old elements.
  • Random access by index is fast because it reads directly from the array.
  • Middle insert/remove is expensive because elements must shift left or right.
Operation Typical cost
get(index) O(1)
add(value) at end Amortized O(1)
add(index, value) O(n)
remove(index) O(n)
contains(value) O(n) 
List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add("A");
list.add("B");
list.add("C");

System.out.println(list.get(1));   // B
list.add(1, "X");                  // shifts B, C to the right
System.out.println(list);          // [A, X, B, C]

In interviews, remember the growth behavior too: ArrayList starts with a small internal array and grows when needed, which reduces frequent reallocation but can still cause occasional copy overhead.

2. Set internals

`Set` is an interface. Its internal implementation depends on the concrete class you choose.

Implementation Internal structure Ordering How duplicates are handled
HashSet Backed by HashMap No guaranteed order Uses hashCode() + equals()
LinkedHashSet Backed by LinkedHashMap Insertion order preserved Uses hashCode() + equals()
TreeSet Backed by TreeMap / Red-Black Tree Sorted order Uses compareTo() or Comparator
HashSet example
Set<String> set = new HashSet<>();
set.add("A");
set.add("B");
set.add("A");   // duplicate ignored

System.out.println(set); // order not guaranteed
TreeSet example
Set<Integer> sorted = new TreeSet<>();
sorted.add(20);
sorted.add(10);
sorted.add(30);

System.out.println(sorted); // [10, 20, 30]
When to use which
  • Use ArrayList when you need fast index access and frequent reads.
  • Use HashSet when you need uniqueness and fast membership checks.
  • Use LinkedHashSet when insertion order matters.
  • Use TreeSet when you need sorted unique values.

Interview one-liner: ArrayList is a resizable array with fast indexed access, while Set implementations are built on hash-based or tree-based structures to enforce uniqueness and, in some cases, ordering.

ArrayList is backed by a resizable array. When it reaches capacity, Java allocates a new larger array, copies the old elements into it, and then continues writing into the new array.

How growth works
  • On the first real addition, ArrayList allocates an internal array if needed.
  • When the array is full, it grows by roughly 1.5x in modern JDKs.
  • All existing elements are copied to the new array.
  • The old array becomes eligible for garbage collection if nothing else references it.
Why this matters for performance

Most add() calls are fast, but resizing is expensive because it copies the whole array. That is why repeated growth causes occasional O(n) spikes even though the average append cost is amortized O(1).

Example
List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
    list.add(i);
}

As the list grows, it may resize several times. If you know the expected size in advance, use new ArrayList<>(expectedSize) to reduce copying.

Real-world example

If you are collecting thousands of log records or API results into a list, pre-sizing the list can save time and memory churn because the JVM does fewer reallocations and array copies.

Interview-ready answer

"ArrayList uses a backing array. When it becomes full, Java allocates a larger array and copies the old elements over, which makes that particular add expensive. The average append cost is still amortized O(1), but resizing causes temporary O(n) work, so pre-sizing helps when the final size is known."

TreeSet uses compareTo() (or Comparator), not equals(). If compareTo returns 0 but equals is false, both objects can exist — breaking Set contract. 

class Employee {
    int id;
    String name;

    Employee(int id, String name) {
        this.id = id;
        this.name = name;
    }

    @Override
    public int compareTo(Employee other) {
        return this.name.compareTo(other.name);   // sort by name only
    }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof Employee e && e.id == this.id;
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() { return id; }
}

Set<Employee> set = new TreeSet<>();
set.add(new Employee(1, "Alice"));
set.add(new Employee(2, "Alice"));   // same name, different id

System.out.println(set.size());      // 1 — compareTo returns 0, second rejected

// But with broken compareTo:
class BrokenEmployee {
    int id;
    String name;
    // compareTo NOT implemented, only equals/hashCode by id
}

Set<BrokenEmployee> tree = new TreeSet<>(
    Comparator.comparing(e -> e.name));   // only name

tree.add(new BrokenEmployee(1, "Alice"));
tree.add(new BrokenEmployee(2, "Alice"));
System.out.println(tree.size());     // 1

// HashSet uses equals/hashCode — different behavior:
Set<BrokenEmployee> hash = new HashSet<>();
hash.add(new BrokenEmployee(1, "Alice"));
hash.add(new BrokenEmployee(2, "Alice"));
System.out.println(hash.size());     // 2 — different ids
Golden rule for Comparable
// compareTo consistent with equals:
// if compareTo(a,b)==0 then a.equals(b) should be true

// TreeMap null key trap:
TreeMap<String, String> map = new TreeMap<>();
map.put(null, "x");   // NullPointerException — natural order cannot compare null

Real-time: Sorting DTOs in memory for reports — inconsistent compareTo vs equals causes duplicate rows in TreeSet-based dedup logic. 

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"));

System.out.println("--- Start ---");

names.stream()
    .peek(n -> System.out.println("Peek: " + n))
    .filter(n -> {
        System.out.println("Filter: " + n);
        return n.startsWith("A");
    })
    .findFirst();

System.out.println("--- End ---");

Output:

--- Start ---
Peek: Alice
Filter: Alice
--- End ---

Why: Streams are lazy. Intermediate ops run only when terminal op needs next element. findFirst() stops after first match — Bob and Charlie never processed.

More traps
// Trap 1 — stream can be used only once
Stream<String> stream = names.stream();
stream.forEach(System.out::println);
stream.count();   // IllegalStateException: stream already operated upon

// Trap 2 — no terminal op = nothing runs
names.stream()
    .peek(System.out::println);   // prints NOTHING

// Trap 3 — short-circuit skips rest
names.stream()
    .map(n -> { System.out.println("Map: " + n); return n; })
    .anyMatch(n -> n.equals("Alice"));   // only Alice mapped if ordered

Real-time: Logging inside map() in a pipeline with findFirst() or limit() gives incomplete logs — misleading during production debugging. 

record Employee(int id, String dept, double salary) {}

List<Employee> employees = List.of(
    new Employee(1, "IT", 80000),
    new Employee(2, "IT", 90000),
    new Employee(3, "HR", 70000)
);

// BOOM — duplicate key "IT"
Map<String, Employee> map = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(Employee::dept, e -> e));
// IllegalStateException: Duplicate key IT
Fixes senior devs must know
// 1. Merge function — keep higher salary
Map<String, Employee> highestPaid = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(
        Employee::dept,
        e -> e,
        (e1, e2) -> e1.salary() >= e2.salary() ? e1 : e2
    ));

// 2. groupingBy — list per department
Map<String, List<Employee>> byDept = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::dept));

// 3. groupingBy with downstream — count
Map<String, Long> count = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::dept, Collectors.counting()));
groupingBy + null value NPE trap
List<Employee> withNull = List.of(
    new Employee(1, "IT", 80000),
    new Employee(2, null, 60000)
);

// NPE — HashMap does not allow null values in groupingBy by default
employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::dept));   // fails if dept is null

// Fix — use mapping with Optional or filter nulls first
employees.stream()
    .filter(e -> e.dept() != null)
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::dept));
toMap vs groupingBy quick rule
Need Use
One value per key toMap(key, val, mergeFn)
Multiple values per key groupingBy
Aggregate (sum, max, count) groupingBy(key, counting/summing/summarizing) 

Optional<User> user = userRepository.findById(1L);   // empty

// BAD — expensive default ALWAYS computed
User result = user.orElse(buildDefaultUserFromDb());  // DB call even when present!

// GOOD — supplier called only when empty
User result = user.orElseGet(() -> buildDefaultUserFromDb());
// More Optional traps

Optional<String> opt = Optional.ofNullable(getName());

opt.get();                    // NoSuchElementException if empty — avoid in prod

opt.orElse(null);             // OK but defeats purpose

Optional.of(null);            // NPE immediately

Optional.ofNullable(null);    // Optional.empty() — safe

// Anti-pattern — Optional as field or method param everywhere
public void save(Optional<User> user) { }   // prefer @Nullable or overloads
flatMap chain for nested Optional
// Nested: user -> address -> zipCode
String zip = userRepository.findById(1L)
    .flatMap(User::getAddress)
    .flatMap(Address::getZipCode)
    .orElse("000000");

// Without flatMap — ugly
Optional<User> u = userRepository.findById(1L);
String zip2 = "000000";
if (u.isPresent() && u.get().getAddress().isPresent()) {
    zip2 = u.get().getAddress().get().getZipCode().orElse("000000");
}

Real-time: Service layer using orElse(heavyQuery()) adds unnecessary DB load on every cache hit path. 

// DANGEROUS — shared mutable state
List<Integer> result = new ArrayList<>();
IntStream.range(0, 1000)
    .parallel()
    .forEach(result::add);   // race condition — size < 1000, corrupted data

// SAFE — use collector
List<Integer> safe = IntStream.range(0, 1000)
    .parallel()
    .boxed()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// DANGEROUS — non-thread-safe HashMap in parallel collect
Map<Integer, Long> freq = new HashMap<>();
list.parallelStream()
    .forEach(i -> freq.merge(i, 1L, Long::sum));   // corrupt map

// SAFE
Map<Integer, Long> safeFreq = list.parallelStream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(i -> i, Collectors.counting()));
When parallel stream helps vs hurts
Scenario Parallel? Reason
Large list (100k+), CPU-heavy map/filter Maybe yes ForkJoinPool can utilize cores
Small list (< 10k) No Split/merge overhead > benefit
IO-bound (DB/HTTP inside stream) No Blocks common pool — starves other parallel streams
Ordered terminal (forEachOrdered) Caution May lose parallel benefit
LinkedList / slow spliterator No ArrayList/IntStream split better 
// Common ForkJoinPool — parallelStream shares one pool
ForkJoinPool.commonPool().getParallelism();   // usually CPU cores - 1

// Custom pool for isolation (advanced)
ForkJoinPool customPool = new ForkJoinPool(4);
try {
    customPool.submit(() ->
        list.parallelStream().map(this::heavyCpuWork).collect(Collectors.toList())
    ).get();
} finally {
    customPool.shutdown();
}

No. ConcurrentHashMap does not allow null keys or null values. If you try to put one, it throws NullPointerException.

Why null is not allowed
  • null would make get() ambiguous: is the key missing, or is the stored value actually null?
  • Concurrent APIs like computeIfAbsent() and merge() need a clear "present vs absent" signal.
  • Allowing nulls would complicate atomic operations and race handling under concurrent updates.
Example
Map<String, String> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

map.put(null, "A");      // NullPointerException
map.put("key", null);    // NullPointerException

With HashMap, get() can return null for both "missing key" and "present but null value." In a concurrent map, that ambiguity is dangerous because the result can change while another thread is updating the map.

Interview-ready answer

"ConcurrentHashMap does not allow null keys or null values. Null would make it impossible to distinguish between 'not present' and 'present with null value', which breaks the clarity needed for safe concurrent operations." 

Map<String, String> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

map.computeIfAbsent("A", key -> {
    map.computeIfAbsent("B", k -> "valueB");   // DEADLOCK in CHM (Java 8)
    return "valueA";
});

In Java 8, ConcurrentHashMap locks the bucket during computeIfAbsent. Nested compute on same map → deadlock. Fixed/improved in later JDKs but still risky pattern.

putIfAbsent vs computeIfAbsent
// putIfAbsent — only puts if key missing, returns existing
map.putIfAbsent("key", expensiveObject);   // may still create object twice in race

// computeIfAbsent — atomic, but mapping function must be fast and side-effect free
map.computeIfAbsent("key", k -> loadFromDb(k));   // DB call — keep short

// Anti-pattern — long IO inside compute
cache.computeIfAbsent(id, k -> {
    return restTemplate.getForObject("/users/" + k, User.class);  // blocks bucket
});
groupingBy concurrent collector
// Thread-safe grouping in parallel stream
Map<String, List<Employee>> map = employees.parallelStream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingByConcurrent(Employee::dept));
// Uses ConcurrentHashMap internally — safe for parallel

Real-time: In-memory caches using computeIfAbsent for lazy load must avoid calling back into same map or doing slow network I/O while holding internal locks.

Classic senior question: total revenue per product across all orders. 

record LineItem(String product, int qty, double price) {}
record Order(String id, List<LineItem> items) {}

List<Order> orders = List.of(
    new Order("O1", List.of(
        new LineItem("Laptop", 1, 50000),
        new LineItem("Mouse", 2, 500)
    )),
    new Order("O2", List.of(
        new LineItem("Laptop", 2, 48000),
        new LineItem("Keyboard", 1, 1500)
    ))
);

// Total qty sold per product
Map<String, Integer> qtyByProduct = orders.stream()
    .flatMap(order -> order.items().stream())   // Order -> Stream<LineItem>
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        LineItem::product,
        Collectors.summingInt(LineItem::qty)
    ));
// {Laptop=3, Mouse=2, Keyboard=1}

// Total revenue per product
Map<String, Double> revenue = orders.stream()
    .flatMap(order -> order.items().stream())
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        LineItem::product,
        Collectors.summingDouble(item -> item.qty() * item.price())
    ));
map vs flatMap
orders.stream()
    .map(order -> order.items())      // Stream<List<LineItem>> — nested!

orders.stream()
    .flatMap(order -> order.items().stream())  // Stream<LineItem> — flat
Tricky — find top product by revenue
String topProduct = orders.stream()
    .flatMap(o -> o.items().stream())
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        LineItem::product,
        Collectors.summingDouble(i -> i.qty() * i.price())
    ))
    .entrySet().stream()
    .max(Map.Entry.comparingByValue())
    .map(Map.Entry::getKey)
    .orElse("NONE");   // Laptop

Real-time: E-commerce dashboards flatten order → line items exactly this way for analytics without nested loops. 

// Broken — equals overridden, hashCode NOT
class BadUser {
    Long id;
    String email;

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof BadUser u && Objects.equals(id, u.id);
    }
    // hashCode missing — Object.hashCode (identity based)
}

Set<BadUser> set = new HashSet<>();
BadUser u1 = new BadUser(); u1.id = 1L;
BadUser u2 = new BadUser(); u2.id = 1L;

set.add(u1);
set.add(u2);
System.out.println(set.size());        // 2 — should be 1! duplicates allowed

Map<BadUser, String> map = new HashMap<>();
map.put(u1, "A");
System.out.println(map.get(u2));       // null — equals says same, hashCode says different bucket
Contract rules
  • If a.equals(b) then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()
  • Consistent: same object → same hashCode unless fields used in hash change
  • Use Objects.hash(id, email) or Lombok @EqualsAndHashCode
// Lombok record — auto correct equals/hashCode
record User(Long id, String email) {}

// JPA entity trap — lazy collections in equals/hashCode cause bugs
// Never use @Data on entity with lazy fields — use id-only equals
IdentityHashMap — uses == not equals
Map<String, String> identity = new IdentityHashMap<>();
String a = new String("Java");
String b = new String("Java");

Map<String, String> hash = new HashMap<>();
hash.put(a, "1");
hash.put(b, "2");
System.out.println(hash.size());       // 1 — equal strings

IdentityHashMap<String, String> idMap = new IdentityHashMap<>();
idMap.put(a, "1");
idMap.put(b, "2");
System.out.println(idMap.size());      // 2 — different object identity

Real-time: Deduplicating webhook events by DTO without proper hashCode causes duplicate processing in HashSet-based idempotency checks.

== checks reference equality for objects and value equality for primitives. So for object references, it answers "are these two variables pointing to the same object?" For primitives and literals, it compares the actual stored value.

Primitive vs object reference
int a = 10;
int b = 10;
System.out.println(a == b); // true — primitive value comparison

String s1 = new String("Java");
String s2 = new String("Java");
System.out.println(s1 == s2); // false — different objects
System.out.println(s1.equals(s2)); // true — same content
Literal vs literal
String x = "Java";
String y = "Java";
System.out.println(x == y); // true — both point to the same string pool object

String literals are usually interned in the string pool, so two identical literals often refer to the same object. That is why == may return true for two string literals, but that is about object identity, not content comparison.

Object vs Object
Object o1 = new Object();
Object o2 = new Object();
Object o3 = o1;

System.out.println(o1 == o2); // false
System.out.println(o1 == o3); // true

Two separate new Object() calls create different objects, so == is false. If two references point to the same object, == is true.

Wrapper caution
Integer p = 100;
Integer q = 100;
Integer r = 200;
Integer s = 200;

System.out.println(p == q); // true — cached range
System.out.println(r == s); // false — different wrapper objects

Wrapper caching can make == look "correct" sometimes, but it is still unsafe for value comparison. Use equals() for objects when you care about content.

Interview-ready answer

"== compares primitive values directly, but for objects it compares references. Two string literals may be equal with == because of string pooling, while two separately created objects are usually not equal by == even if their contents match. For content comparison, use equals()." 

List<Integer> nums = Arrays.asList(1, 2, null, 4);

// NPE — unboxing null Integer
int sum = nums.stream()
    .mapToInt(i -> i)          // null -> NPE
    .sum();

// Safe — filter nulls
int safeSum = nums.stream()
    .filter(Objects::nonNull)
    .mapToInt(Integer::intValue)
    .sum();

// reduce with identity — trap when identity wrong
int product = List.of(0, 1, 2, 3).stream()
    .reduce(1, (a, b) -> a * b);   // 0 — multiply identity 1 OK
// but sum with identity 1 is wrong: use 0
Overflow trap
List<Integer> big = List.of(Integer.MAX_VALUE, 1);

int wrong = big.stream().mapToInt(i -> i).sum();   // overflow -> Integer.MIN_VALUE

long correct = big.stream()
    .mapToLong(Integer::longValue)
    .sum();   // 2147483648
Collectors.summingInt vs mapToInt().sum()
// groupingBy + summingInt — null-safe if filtered
Map<String, Integer> totalQty = orders.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        Order::dept,
        Collectors.summingInt(Order::qty)
    ));

Real-time: Billing systems summing line amounts must use long or BigDecimal, not chained int streams, to avoid overflow on large invoices.

HashMap stores entries in buckets using hash(key) % capacity. Java 8 improved worst case by converting buckets from LinkedList → Red-Black Tree when size > 8. This improves worst-case lookup from O(n) → O(log n).

✔ Stack → Stores method frames, local variables, references. ✔ Heap → Stores objects, arrays. ✔ Stack is faster & thread-private. ✔ Heap is shared across threads, managed by Garbage Collector.

ThreadPoolExecutor lifecycle: 1. task submitted 2. if worker < corePoolSize → create new thread 3. else task goes to queue 4. if queue full → new thread until maxPoolSize 5. else → RejectionHandler

✔ supplyAsync → Run async task ✔ thenApply → Transform result ✔ thenCompose → Chain async calls ✔ thenCombine → Combine two Futures Used for building async pipelines & microservice orchestration.

Idempotent API returns same output no matter how many times you hit it. Payments use Idempotency-Key header to avoid duplicate transactions.

Protects service from cascading failures. States → CLOSED → OPEN → HALF-OPEN. Used in Netflix Hystrix, Resilience4j.

Spring Bean Lifecycle: Instantiation → DI → postProcessBeforeInit → init() → postProcessAfterInit → Ready → destroy().

Use @Cacheable, @CachePut, @CacheEvict. Real-time: Product Catalogue, Currency Rates, User Profile caching.

The best cache strategy depends on whether your system reads more than it writes, how fresh the data must be, and whether the cache is local, distributed, or edge-based.

Common cache strategies
Strategy How it works Best use case
Cache-aside App checks cache first, then loads from DB and puts value in cache. Most common pattern for Spring apps, product catalog, user profile, reference data.
Read-through App asks cache, and cache loader fetches data from DB if missing. Simple lookup-heavy systems where cache library supports a loader.
Write-through Writes go to cache and DB together before the call returns. When read freshness matters and you want cache and DB to stay in sync immediately.
Write-behind / write-back Write lands in cache first, and DB is updated asynchronously later. High-write systems that can tolerate eventual consistency, like analytics or counters.
Refresh-ahead Cache refreshes hot keys before they expire. Very hot data such as rates, configs, and dashboards that should stay warm.
Near cache A small local cache sits in front of a distributed cache. Ultra-low latency reads in clustered systems.
CDN / edge cache Content is cached near users at the network edge. Images, CSS, JS, static files, and public API responses.
When I would use each one
  • Cache-aside: best default for most business services because it is simple and flexible.
  • Read-through: use when you want cache abstraction to hide DB loading logic.
  • Write-through: use when stale reads are risky, such as user settings or inventory-like data.
  • Write-behind: use when write speed matters more than immediate persistence.
  • Refresh-ahead: use when popular keys must stay warm and latency spikes are unacceptable.
  • Near cache: use in high-throughput clusters where network hops to Redis are still too expensive.
  • CDN cache: use for frontend assets or publicly cacheable responses.
Spring Cache-aside example
@Service
public class ProductService {

    @Cacheable(cacheNames = "products", key = "#productId")
    public ProductDto getProduct(Long productId) {
        return repository.findById(productId)
                .map(this::toDto)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new ProductNotFoundException(productId));
    }

    @CachePut(cacheNames = "products", key = "#result.id")
    public ProductDto updateProduct(ProductDto request) {
        Product saved = repository.save(toEntity(request));
        return toDto(saved);
    }

    @CacheEvict(cacheNames = "products", key = "#productId")
    public void deleteProduct(Long productId) {
        repository.deleteById(productId);
    }
}
Real-world examples
  • Product catalog: cache-aside works well because reads are frequent and updates are less frequent.
  • Currency exchange rates: refresh-ahead or short TTL avoids stale values.
  • User session: Redis cache or session store works well because reads must be fast.
  • Leaderboard or counters: write-behind can help if immediate persistence is not critical.
  • Static assets: CDN cache gives the biggest win for global users.
Practical rule of thumb

If the data is read-heavy and can tolerate slightly stale values, use cache-aside with TTL. If fresh reads are critical, use write-through. If writes are very heavy and eventual consistency is okay, use write-behind. If latency is the top priority, add a near cache or CDN where appropriate.

Interview-ready answer

"The most common strategy is cache-aside, where the app checks cache first and loads from the DB on a miss. I use write-through when freshness matters, write-behind when write throughput matters, and refresh-ahead or near cache for very hot data. For static content, CDN caching is the best fit."

The biggest jump from Java 8 to Java 17 is not just language syntax. The real work is dealing with strong encapsulation, dependency compatibility, removed APIs, and framework upgrades.

Main migration challenges
  • Strong encapsulation: reflective access to JDK internals can fail with InaccessibleObjectException.
  • Internal API usage: old code may depend on sun.* or jdk.internal.* classes.
  • Removed components: Java EE modules, CORBA, Nashorn, Pack200, and some legacy APIs are no longer available.
  • Framework compatibility: Spring, Hibernate, Mockito, ByteBuddy, JAXB, and Jackson versions may need upgrades.
  • Build/tooling changes: Maven/Gradle plugins, test runners, and bytecode libraries often need newer versions.
  • GC and runtime behavior: defaults changed over time, so memory and startup behavior may differ from Java 8.
Why failures happen

Java 9 introduced the module system and later releases tightened access to JDK internals. Code that used reflection to touch private JDK fields or methods may work on Java 8 but break on Java 17 unless we refactor it or temporarily open packages. 

Field valueField = String.class.getDeclaredField("value");
valueField.setAccessible(true); // may fail on Java 17 without --add-opens
How I approach the migration
  • Run jdeps to find deprecated or internal JDK dependencies.
  • Upgrade third-party libraries before changing the runtime in production.
  • Fix reflective access instead of relying only on --add-opens as a permanent solution.
  • Move from old APIs such as JAX-B bundled in the JDK to explicit dependencies where needed.
  • Test startup, unit tests, integration tests, and production-like workloads before rollout.
Real-world example

A legacy Spring Boot 1.x app on Java 8 may use JAXB, old Hibernate, and reflective serializers. On Java 17, that app can fail during startup until the framework and library versions are upgraded and the illegal reflection paths are removed.

Interview-ready answer

"Java 8 to 17 migration usually breaks because of strong encapsulation, removed JDK modules, and library incompatibilities. I first scan with jdeps, upgrade frameworks and plugins, fix reflection on JDK internals, and use --add-opens only as a temporary bridge during the migration."

The Class Loader Subsystem is the JVM part responsible for loading .class files into memory. It loads classes only when needed, verifies them, prepares them, resolves references, and initializes them before execution.

1. Why do we need Class Loaders?
  • Java code is compiled into bytecode, not native machine code.
  • JVM must bring class definitions into memory before methods can run.
  • Classes are loaded lazily, so startup can stay efficient.

Real-world analogy: Class Loader is like a librarian who brings the required books only when someone asks for them.

2. Main responsibilities of Class Loader Subsystem
1. Loading
2. Linking
   - Verification
   - Preparation
   - Resolution
3. Initialization
3. Loading phase

JVM finds the class bytecode and creates an internal runtime representation of that class.

Example: When your application uses UserService for the first time, JVM loads UserService.class.

4. Linking phase
  • Verification: checks whether bytecode is valid and safe.
  • Preparation: allocates memory for static fields and gives default values.
  • Resolution: converts symbolic references into direct references.
5. Initialization phase

JVM runs static blocks and assigns actual values to static variables. 

class Demo {
    static int x = 100;

    static {
        System.out.println("Class initialized");
    }
}

When this class is initialized, JVM assigns x = 100 and runs the static block.

6. Types of Class Loaders
Class Loader What it loads Example
Bootstrap ClassLoader Core Java classes from JDK runtime java.lang.String, java.lang.Object, java.util.*
Platform ClassLoader Platform/JDK library classes above core base modules SQL, XML, management, and other platform modules
Application ClassLoader Application classes from classpath/module path Your Spring Boot controllers, services, entities
7. Bootstrap ClassLoader

This is the root loader. It loads the most fundamental Java classes needed for Java execution to even begin.

  • java.lang.Object
  • java.lang.Class
  • java.lang.String
  • java.lang.System
  • java.lang.Thread
  • other core runtime classes

Important point: The OS/JVM launcher starts the JVM process first, and then Bootstrap ClassLoader loads the core Java runtime classes needed to kick-start Java-side execution.

8. Platform ClassLoader

It loads standard platform libraries that are not part of the minimal bootstrap base.

Example: JDBC, XML processing, management-related JDK modules may be loaded here depending on module usage.

9. Application ClassLoader

This loads your own project classes from classpath or module path.

Real-world example: In a Spring Boot app, your main class, controllers, services, repositories, and DTOs are loaded by the Application ClassLoader.

10. Which classes get loaded first to kick-start Java?
OS/Java launcher starts JVM process
   ↓
Bootstrap ClassLoader loads core runtime classes
   ↓
JVM finds and loads your main application class
   ↓
Application ClassLoader loads your app classes
   ↓
Program execution starts from main()

Interview-safe answer: Bootstrap ClassLoader first loads essential core classes, and then the Application ClassLoader loads the user application's main class and other project classes.

11. Parent Delegation Model

Class loaders usually follow parent delegation. A child loader first asks its parent to load the class. If parent cannot load it, then the child tries. 

Application ClassLoader
   asks Platform ClassLoader
       asks Bootstrap ClassLoader

Why useful:

  • Prevents duplicate loading of core classes
  • Improves security
  • Makes sure app cannot easily replace trusted core Java classes
12. Why can’t my app override java.lang.String?

Because parent delegation ensures core classes are loaded by Bootstrap ClassLoader first, so your custom fake java.lang.String will not replace the real one.

13. How class loading happens in Spring Boot

In a Spring Boot fat jar, JVM loads the main application class, then Spring starts scanning configuration, controllers, services, repositories, and framework classes as they are needed.

Real-world example: When app starts, classes like SpringApplication, your @SpringBootApplication class, and auto-configuration classes begin loading first.

14. Lazy class loading

JVM does not load every class at once. It usually loads classes when they are first actively used.

Real-world example: A report generation class may not load until report API is actually called.

15. Common errors related to class loading
Error Meaning
ClassNotFoundException JVM cannot find class at runtime when explicitly asked to load it
NoClassDefFoundError Class was available at compile time but missing/failed during runtime loading
UnsupportedClassVersionError Class compiled with newer Java version than current JVM supports
16. Real-world interview answer

The Class Loader Subsystem loads Java classes into memory in three broad stages: loading, linking, and initialization. The main loaders are Bootstrap, Platform, and Application ClassLoader. Bootstrap loads core JDK classes first to kick-start Java runtime, and then the Application ClassLoader loads our main class and project classes. Parent delegation ensures core Java classes are loaded safely and consistently.

17. Short one-liner

Class Loader Subsystem is the JVM part that loads core Java classes first, then application classes, and prepares them for execution using loading, linking, and initialization.

JVM decides whether an object stays on stack or heap. If object does not escape method → stack allocation = faster.

REST → JSON, slower, human-readable. gRPC → Protocol Buffers, binary, streaming support, fast → great for inter-service communication.

S → Single Responsibility O → Open/Closed L → Liskov I → Interface Segregation D → Dependency Inversion

@Component → generic bean @Service → business logic @Repository → persistence + exception translation

Optimistic → Versioning, retries, high performance Pessimistic → DB locks row physically Used in banking, inventory systems.

Achieved by: ✔ Idempotent producers ✔ Transactions API ✔ Consumer offset management

Backpressure prevents producer from overwhelming consumer. Used in WebFlux, Reactive Streams, Kafka, messaging systems.

Monolith → single deployable Microservices → distributed system Modular Monolith → one deployable but well-modularized (best of both worlds)

CAP: Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance In distributed systems, you can pick only 2. Example: Cassandra → AP, Mongo → CP.

GC uses: ✔ Mark & Sweep ✔ Young/Old generations ✔ Minor/Major GC ✔ G1, ZGC for low-latency environments.

REQUIRED → join existing or create new REQUIRES_NEW → always new MANDATORY → must have existing NEVER → fail if transaction exists

Distributed cache stores data across nodes. Offers replication, eviction policies, TTL, high availability.

Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Sliding Window. Used in API gateways like Kong, NGINX, AWS.

@Async uses AOP proxies + TaskExecutor thread pool Runs method asynchronously in background.

LAZY → load on demand EAGER → load immediately Lazy preferred for performance; Eager causes N+1 problems.

API Gateway handles routing, authentication, rate limiting, versioning. Example: Kong, Zuul, Spring Cloud Gateway.

Horizontal → more machines Vertical → increase machine power Cloud-native prefers horizontal scaling.

MQ decouples systems, improves reliability and async communication. Kafka → high throughput RabbitMQ → routing-based messaging

Apache Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform. We use it when we need to move large volumes of events reliably between services with high throughput, durability, and replay capability.

Why we use Kafka
  • Decouple services so producers do not call consumers directly.
  • Handle high-volume events like orders, payments, clicks, logs, and notifications.
  • Keep events for a retention period so consumers can replay them later.
  • Scale consumers horizontally using partitions and consumer groups.
  • Build event-driven systems, audit trails, outbox pipelines, and streaming analytics.
Kafka vs traditional JMS
Aspect Kafka Traditional JMS
Model Distributed commit log / event stream Message queue / broker API
Storage Messages are retained on disk for time/size based retention Messages are usually consumed and removed from the queue
Replay Consumers can replay old messages by resetting offsets Replay is not a core design goal
Throughput Very high throughput, partitioned and append-only Good for enterprise messaging, but typically lower throughput
Scaling Horizontal scaling with partitions and consumer groups Depends on broker/queue setup, often more queue-oriented
Ordering Guaranteed within a partition Usually queue-based ordering per destination
Best fit Event streaming, logs, audit, analytics, microservices integration Classic enterprise messaging, command/message routing, request-reply use cases

JMS is a Java messaging API specification. Kafka is a distributed platform and ecosystem. JMS is a programming model, while Kafka is a concrete event streaming system. They solve overlapping problems but are not the same thing.

Real-world analogy

JMS is like sending a package to a mailbox and expecting it to be picked up. Kafka is like publishing a durable newspaper edition that multiple readers can subscribe to, read later, and even reread.

Core Kafka terms
Term Meaning
Broker Kafka server that stores and serves messages
Topic Named stream of events
Partition Parallel shard of a topic
Producer Publishes events to Kafka
Consumer Reads events from Kafka
Consumer Group Multiple consumers sharing work from partitions
Offset Position of a record inside a partition
Getting started with Spring Boot

The usual Spring Boot setup is simple: add the Kafka starter, configure the bootstrap server, create a producer, and create a @KafkaListener consumer. 

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.kafka</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-kafka</artifactId>
</dependency>
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: localhost:9092
    consumer:
      group-id: order-service
      auto-offset-reset: earliest
    producer:
      key-serializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
      value-serializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonSerializer
@Configuration
public class KafkaConfig {

    @Bean
    public NewTopic orderTopic() {
        return TopicBuilder.name("orders")
                .partitions(3)
                .replicas(1)
                .build();
    }
}
@Service
public class OrderEventPublisher {

    private final KafkaTemplate<String, OrderCreatedEvent> kafkaTemplate;

    public OrderEventPublisher(KafkaTemplate<String, OrderCreatedEvent> kafkaTemplate) {
        this.kafkaTemplate = kafkaTemplate;
    }

    public void publish(OrderCreatedEvent event) {
        kafkaTemplate.send("orders", event.orderId().toString(), event);
    }
}
@Component
public class OrderEventConsumer {

    @KafkaListener(topics = "orders", groupId = "order-service")
    public void consume(OrderCreatedEvent event) {
        System.out.println("Consumed order event: " + event);
    }
}
Producer and consumer flow
REST API
  -> Spring Boot service
  -> KafkaTemplate.send()
  -> Topic partition
  -> Consumer group
  -> @KafkaListener processes message
  -> Offset committed after processing
When Kafka is a better fit
  • Need to replay events for rebuilding read models or analytics.
  • Many services must consume the same event independently.
  • Need durable buffering between spikes in traffic.
  • Need event-driven architecture with auditability.
When JMS may be enough
  • Simple enterprise queueing with one producer and one consumer.
  • Traditional Java EE or Spring JMS integration already exists.
  • Routing, selectors, or request-reply patterns are the main need.
Important interview notes
  • Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition, not across the whole topic.
  • More partitions can increase parallelism, but too many partitions also add overhead.
  • Exactly-once processing needs idempotent producers, transactions, and careful consumer handling.
  • Kafka is not just a queue; it is also a durable event log.

Interview one-liner: Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform used for high-throughput, durable, replayable communication between services, while JMS is a messaging API/specification commonly used for classic queue-based enterprise messaging.

Apache ZooKeeper is a distributed coordination service. It is not mainly used to store business data like orders or users. Instead, it helps distributed systems coordinate around shared state such as configuration, service membership, leader election, locks, and naming.

What problem does ZooKeeper solve?

In distributed systems, many nodes run in parallel. They need a trusted way to answer questions like:

  • Which node is the leader?
  • Which services are alive right now?
  • What is the current shared configuration?
  • How do we ensure only one node performs a critical task?

Doing this manually is hard and error-prone because distributed systems can suffer from race conditions, split-brain issues, and partial failures.

Simple definition

ZooKeeper is a centralized but replicated coordination system used by distributed applications for naming, configuration management, synchronization, and group services.

Real-world analogy

Think of ZooKeeper like a control room in a large office building. It does not do the employees' work, but it keeps track of which teams are active, who is the shift lead, and what the current building-wide rules/configuration are.

Core concepts
Concept Meaning
ZNode Data node in ZooKeeper namespace, similar to a file-system node
Persistent ZNode Stays until explicitly deleted
Ephemeral ZNode Removed automatically when client session ends
Watch Notification mechanism when data/node changes
Ensemble Group of ZooKeeper servers working together
Quorum Majority needed for consistency and leader decisions
Why do we use ZooKeeper?
  • Leader election: decide one active leader among many nodes.
  • Service discovery: know which instances are alive.
  • Configuration management: share config centrally.
  • Distributed locking: allow only one node to perform a critical task.
  • Cluster membership: track which nodes joined or left.
  • Coordination: keep distributed components consistent.
Where is ZooKeeper used?
  • Historically with Kafka for broker metadata, controller election, and partition leadership.
  • In distributed systems like Hadoop/HBase ecosystems.
  • In microservices for leader election, distributed locks, service registration, and config coordination.

Important modern point: In new Kafka deployments, ZooKeeper is generally not recommended anymore because Kafka's newer KRaft mode handles metadata without ZooKeeper. ZooKeeper is still important historically and can still exist in older Kafka clusters or migration scenarios.

Example 1: Leader election

Suppose three scheduler instances are running, but only one should generate month-end invoices. 

Instance A creates ephemeral znode /leader
Instance B tries -> fails
Instance C tries -> fails

Result:
Instance A becomes leader

If Instance A crashes:
/leader disappears
Another instance becomes leader

Real-world use: only one node should run a critical batch job to avoid duplicate processing.

Example 2: Service discovery
/services/payment-service/instance-1
/services/payment-service/instance-2
/services/payment-service/instance-3

Each service instance registers itself as an ephemeral node. If an instance dies, its node disappears, so clients know it is no longer available.

Example 3: Shared configuration
/config/payment-service/retry-count = 3
/config/payment-service/timeout-ms = 2000

Services can watch these nodes and react when config changes.

How does ZooKeeper help in microservices?

Microservices are distributed by nature, so coordination problems appear often. ZooKeeper can help with:

  • choosing one leader among many service instances
  • keeping track of active nodes
  • sharing dynamic config
  • coordinating distributed jobs
  • implementing distributed locks

Real-world example: If five notification-service instances are running, only one instance may need to refresh global templates from an external system. ZooKeeper can coordinate that leader selection.

How ZooKeeper stores data

ZooKeeper stores small coordination data in a hierarchical namespace, like a lightweight in-memory file tree with persistence and replication. 

/
  config
    payment-service
  services
    order-service
    payment-service
  leader
  locks
Does ZooKeeper scale?

Yes, but with an important limitation. ZooKeeper is designed to scale for coordination, not for storing large application data or running heavy write workloads like a database.

  • Reads: scale relatively well.
  • Writes: require coordination/quorum, so they do not scale like a distributed database.
  • It is best for small metadata and coordination workloads.

Interview-safe answer: ZooKeeper scales for distributed coordination, but it is not meant to be a general-purpose high-write data store.

How is ZooKeeper deployed?

ZooKeeper usually runs as an ensemble of 3 or 5 servers.

  • 3 nodes -> can survive 1 node failure
  • 5 nodes -> can survive 2 node failures

Because it uses quorum, you should use an odd number of nodes.

Basic ZooKeeper configuration
tickTime=2000
dataDir=/var/lib/zookeeper
clientPort=2181
initLimit=10
syncLimit=5

server.1=zk1:2888:3888
server.2=zk2:2888:3888
server.3=zk3:2888:3888
  • clientPort -> port for applications/clients
  • dataDir -> data storage location
  • server.1, server.2, server.3 -> ensemble members
How do applications connect?
ZooKeeper zooKeeper = new ZooKeeper(
        "zk1:2181,zk2:2181,zk3:2181",
        3000,
        event -> System.out.println("Watcher event: " + event)
);

In production Java apps, teams often use Apache Curator because it gives easier APIs for leader election, distributed locks, and retries.

Curator example for leader election
CuratorFramework client = CuratorFrameworkFactory.newClient(
        "zk1:2181,zk2:2181,zk3:2181",
        new ExponentialBackoffRetry(1000, 3)
);
client.start();

LeaderSelector leaderSelector = new LeaderSelector(
        client,
        "/leaders/payment-job",
        new LeaderSelectorListenerAdapter() {
            @Override
            public void takeLeadership(CuratorFramework client) throws Exception {
                System.out.println("This instance is now the leader");
                Thread.sleep(10000);
            }
        }
);

leaderSelector.autoRequeue();
leaderSelector.start();
How it historically helped Kafka

In older Kafka architecture, ZooKeeper was used to coordinate broker metadata, cluster membership, controller election, and partition leader information. 

Kafka Broker starts
  ->
Registers in ZooKeeper
  ->
ZooKeeper tracks active brokers
  ->
One broker becomes controller
  ->
Partition leader/follower metadata coordinated

Modern note: Kafka's newer KRaft mode replaces this metadata dependency for new clusters.

Advantages of ZooKeeper
  • Very strong coordination model
  • Reliable for leader election and service membership
  • Ordered updates
  • Watches make coordination reactive
  • Battle-tested in distributed systems
Limitations of ZooKeeper
  • Not for large business data storage
  • Write-heavy workloads are not its strength
  • Operational complexity if you do not actually need strong coordination
  • Many modern platforms now prefer built-in alternatives depending on architecture
When would I use ZooKeeper in microservices?
  • Need robust leader election
  • Need distributed locks
  • Need shared coordination state
  • Working with older Kafka/Hadoop ecosystems

But if you are on Kubernetes, Eureka, Consul, or a managed cloud setup, some discovery/coordination use cases may be handled by those systems instead.

Interview-ready answer

ZooKeeper is a distributed coordination service used for leader election, configuration management, service discovery, distributed locking, and cluster membership. It is not a general business database. It scales well for coordination reads and metadata, but not like a large write-heavy data store. It was historically important in Kafka and still appears in older clusters, while in microservices it helps coordinate shared distributed behavior such as leader election and locks.

Kafka is usually faster for very high-throughput event streaming because it is built like an append-only distributed log, while RabbitMQ is designed more like a traditional message broker with richer routing and queue semantics.

Why Kafka is often faster
  • Kafka appends records sequentially to disk instead of doing a lot of per-message queue movement.
  • Kafka batches records efficiently, which reduces network and disk overhead.
  • Kafka keeps messages on disk for retention, so consumers control their own offset progress.
  • Kafka partitions topics, so many consumers can read in parallel.
  • Kafka avoids expensive broker-side routing logic for every message in many common use cases.
  • Kafka uses zero-copy and other storage optimizations in its architecture.
Why RabbitMQ can feel slower at very high scale
  • RabbitMQ performs more broker-side queue and routing work per message.
  • It is excellent for flexible routing, but that flexibility can add overhead.
  • It is usually better for command delivery, task queues, and complex message patterns than raw streaming throughput.
Important nuance

Faster does not always mean better. RabbitMQ may be the better fit when you need routing keys, priorities, dead-lettering, per-message acknowledgements, or classic work queues. Kafka is generally faster for append-heavy streaming and replayable event pipelines.

Simple analogy

Kafka is like writing entries into a long ledger book and letting multiple readers keep their own page number. RabbitMQ is more like a package sorting desk that routes each item to a destination box.

Example use cases
System Better fit
Clickstream analytics Kafka
Order events for microservices Kafka
Background job queue RabbitMQ
Complex routing between consumers RabbitMQ

Interview one-liner: Kafka is usually faster because it is an append-only distributed log optimized for batching, partitioning, and replay, while RabbitMQ spends more work on per-message routing and queue management.

What is a topic?

A topic is a named stream of records in Kafka. Producers publish events to a topic, and consumers read from that topic. 

orders
payments
user-events
audit-logs
What is a partition?

A partition is a shard of a topic. Kafka stores records inside partitions in append-only order, and each record inside a partition gets a unique offset. 

Topic: orders
Partition 0 -> offsets 0,1,2,3
Partition 1 -> offsets 0,1,2,3
Partition 2 -> offsets 0,1,2,3
Why partitions?
  • Partitions allow parallel write and read throughput.
  • More partitions mean more consumers can process in parallel.
  • Partitions help distribute load across brokers and disks.
  • Ordering is preserved inside a partition, so you can keep related events together.
Does Kafka guarantee message order?

Kafka guarantees order only within a single partition. It does not guarantee global order across the entire topic when multiple partitions are involved.

How do you maintain ordering?
  • Use the same message key for related records, such as the same order id or customer id.
  • Kafka routes records with the same key to the same partition.
  • Keep the number of consumers in a group less than or equal to the number of partitions if you want each partition processed by a single consumer at a time.
  • Do not split one business entity across multiple partitions if strict ordering is required.
kafkaTemplate.send("orders", orderId.toString(), event);
What is a consumer group?

A consumer group is a set of consumers working together to process a topic. Kafka assigns partitions so that each partition is consumed by only one consumer within the same group at a time. 

Topic with 3 partitions
Consumer Group with 3 consumers

P0 -> C1
P1 -> C2
P2 -> C3
What happens if one consumer dies?

Kafka detects that the consumer has stopped heartbeating. Then the group coordinator triggers a rebalance and reassigns that consumer's partitions to the remaining consumers in the group. 

Before failure
P0 -> C1
P1 -> C2
P2 -> C3

C2 dies

After rebalance
P0 -> C1
P1 -> C3
P2 -> C3

If offsets were already committed, the new consumer continues from the last committed offset. If the old consumer died after processing but before committing, duplicate processing can happen, so consumer logic should be idempotent.

Small Spring Boot example
@Service
public class OrderPublisher {
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, OrderCreatedEvent> kafkaTemplate;

    public OrderPublisher(KafkaTemplate<String, OrderCreatedEvent> kafkaTemplate) {
        this.kafkaTemplate = kafkaTemplate;
    }

    public void publish(OrderCreatedEvent event) {
        kafkaTemplate.send("orders", event.orderId().toString(), event);
    }
}
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders", groupId = "order-service")
public void consume(OrderCreatedEvent event) {
    // idempotent processing is important here
}
Quick interview answers
  • Topic: logical stream of events.
  • Partition: ordered shard of a topic.
  • Why partitions: scale and parallelism.
  • Ordering: guaranteed only within a partition.
  • Consumer group: multiple consumers sharing partitions.
  • Consumer dies: rebalance and reassignment of partitions.

Interview one-liner: Kafka stores events in topics, splits topics into partitions for scale, preserves order only within a partition, and uses consumer groups so partitions can be rebalanced automatically when a consumer fails.

What is an offset?

An offset is the position number of a record inside a Kafka partition. It is like a line number in a log file. Each partition has its own offset sequence. 

orders-topic
Partition 0:
  offset 0 -> order-101
  offset 1 -> order-102
  offset 2 -> order-103
Where are offsets stored?

Consumer group offsets are stored in Kafka itself, in the internal topic called __consumer_offsets. Kafka uses that to remember what each consumer group has already processed.

Auto commit vs manual commit
Mode How it works Risk / use case
Auto commit Kafka commits offsets automatically at intervals Simple, but you can lose records or commit before processing finishes
Manual commit Your code commits the offset after successful processing Safer for business logic because you control when a message is marked done 
spring:
  kafka:
    consumer:
      enable-auto-commit: false
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders", groupId = "order-service")
public void consume(OrderCreatedEvent event, Acknowledgment ack) {
    process(event);
    ack.acknowledge(); // manual commit after successful processing
}
At most once, at least once, exactly once
Guarantee Meaning Tradeoff
At most once Message is processed zero or one time May lose messages, but no duplicates
At least once Message is processed one or more times Can create duplicates, so consumer should be idempotent
Exactly once Message is processed exactly one time from the business point of view Hardest to implement; needs transactions/idempotence carefully
What is an idempotent producer?

An idempotent producer ensures that retries do not create duplicate records in Kafka when the same send is attempted again. Kafka can detect duplicate producer attempts using producer id and sequence numbers. 

spring:
  kafka:
    producer:
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true
What are ACKs?

ACKs define when Kafka considers a producer send successful.

ACK level Meaning
acks=0 Producer does not wait for broker response; fastest, least safe
acks=1 Leader broker confirms write; faster but replicas may not yet have it
acks=all or -1 Leader waits for all in-sync replicas; safest, slower than acks=1
What happens if producer crashes?

If the producer crashes before Kafka receives the record, the message is lost unless the client retries. If the producer crashes after Kafka already accepted the record, the message may already be stored. With retries and idempotence disabled, duplicate sends can happen. With idempotence enabled, Kafka can avoid many duplicate writes caused by retries. 

Producer sends record
  -> network issue
  -> producer retries
  -> if idempotence is OFF, duplicate can happen
  -> if idempotence is ON, Kafka can deduplicate retry attempts
Clear delivery rule of thumb
  • At most once: commit before processing.
  • At least once: process first, commit later.
  • Exactly once: combine idempotent producer, proper commit strategy, and business idempotency.
Simple Spring Boot producer example
@Service
public class PaymentPublisher {

    private final KafkaTemplate<String, PaymentEvent> kafkaTemplate;

    public PaymentPublisher(KafkaTemplate<String, PaymentEvent> kafkaTemplate) {
        this.kafkaTemplate = kafkaTemplate;
    }

    public void publish(PaymentEvent event) {
        kafkaTemplate.send("payments", event.paymentId().toString(), event);
    }
}
Quick interview answers
  • Offset: position of a record in a partition.
  • Stored where: Kafka internal topic __consumer_offsets.
  • Auto commit: Kafka commits automatically.
  • Manual commit: app commits after processing.
  • At most once: no duplicates, possible loss.
  • At least once: no loss, possible duplicates.
  • Exactly once: no duplicates from business perspective, hardest to achieve.
  • Idempotent producer: retry-safe producer behavior.
  • ACKs: when producer gets confirmation from broker.

Interview one-liner: Offsets track progress inside partitions, Kafka stores consumer offsets in __consumer_offsets, auto commit is simpler but less safe, manual commit gives control, ACKs control producer durability, and idempotence helps avoid duplicate writes during retries.

Leader and follower replicas

Each Kafka partition can have multiple replicas across brokers. One replica is elected as the leader. Producers write to the leader, and consumers usually read from the leader. The other replicas are followers that copy data from the leader. 

Partition 0
Broker 1 -> Leader
Broker 2 -> Follower
Broker 3 -> Follower
Replication factor

Replication factor is the total number of copies of a partition. If the replication factor is 3, each partition has one leader and two followers across three brokers.

What is ISR?

ISR means In-Sync Replicas. These are replicas that are sufficiently caught up with the leader. Kafka prefers to keep replicas in ISR so data is safe and failover can happen cleanly.

  • If a follower lags too much, it can fall out of ISR.
  • If a follower catches up again, it can rejoin ISR.
  • Kafka uses ISR to decide which replicas are safe enough for acknowledgements and leader election.
What happens if the leader crashes?

Kafka elects a new leader from the ISR replicas for that partition. If at least one in-sync follower is available, the partition can keep serving traffic with minimal disruption. 

Leader broker fails
Kafka controller elects new leader from ISR
Partition continues serving reads/writes

If no ISR replica is available, the partition may become unavailable until Kafka can recover a suitable replica.

Why replication matters
  • Provides fault tolerance if a broker goes down.
  • Improves availability during maintenance or hardware failure.
  • Helps protect data durability when combined with proper acknowledgements.
What is rebalancing?

Rebalancing is the process of redistributing partitions among consumers in a consumer group when consumers join, leave, or change membership.

It also happens when partitions are added, consumer group settings change, or a consumer stops heartbeating.

Problems during rebalance
  • Temporary pause in consumption while partitions are reassigned.
  • Duplicate processing if offsets were not committed before rebalance.
  • In-flight messages may be processed twice after reassignment.
  • In large clusters, frequent rebalances can create instability and latency spikes.
Sticky assignor

Sticky assignor tries to keep the same partition-to-consumer assignment as much as possible during rebalances. That reduces movement, reduces cache loss, and makes rebalances less disruptive.

Cooperative rebalancing

Cooperative rebalancing is a more gradual rebalance strategy. Instead of revoking all partitions at once, Kafka moves partitions incrementally, which reduces stop-the-world style pauses.

Can multiple consumers read the same partition?

In the same consumer group, one partition is assigned to only one consumer at a time. But multiple consumer groups can read the same partition independently. So:

  • Same group: no, not at the same time.
  • Different groups: yes, each group can read the same partition separately.
What happens if partitions are more than consumers?

If there are more partitions than consumers in a group, some consumers will be assigned more than one partition. That is normal. Kafka tries to balance the partitions as evenly as possible. 

6 partitions
2 consumers

C1 -> P0, P1, P2
C2 -> P3, P4, P5

This improves parallelism, but one consumer may become a hotspot if it gets too many busy partitions.

Simple real-world analogy

Think of partitions as lanes on a highway. The leader is the active lane controller, followers are backup lanes ready to take over, ISR are the healthy backups, rebalancing is reassigning lanes to drivers, and sticky/cooperative strategies try to avoid unnecessary lane changes.

Spring Boot example with replicas and consumer group
spring:
  kafka:
    consumer:
      group-id: billing-service
      auto-offset-reset: earliest
    producer:
      acks: all
@KafkaListener(topics = "payments", groupId = "billing-service")
public void consume(PaymentEvent event) {
    // one partition is processed by one consumer in this group at a time
}
Quick interview answers
  • Leader: handles reads/writes for a partition.
  • Follower: replica that copies data from the leader.
  • ISR: replicas in sync with the leader.
  • Replication factor: number of copies of a partition.
  • Rebalance: repartitioning work across consumers.
  • Sticky assignor: keeps assignments stable when possible.
  • Cooperative rebalance: incremental rebalance with fewer pauses.
  • More partitions than consumers: some consumers get multiple partitions.

Interview one-liner: Kafka uses leader-follower replication with ISR for fault tolerance, and consumer-group rebalancing to spread partitions across consumers; sticky and cooperative strategies reduce rebalance disruption.

Retention vs log compaction
Concept Meaning Use case
Retention Delete records after time or size limit Event streams, audit logs, clickstream, replay for a limited time
Log compaction Keep latest record for each key, older duplicates can be removed Reference data, current state, user profile cache, key-value style topics 
spring:
  kafka:
    topics:
      orders:
        retention-ms: 604800000
      user-profile:
        cleanup-policy: compact
Schema Registry and message versioning

Schema Registry stores and manages Avro/Protobuf/JSON Schema definitions so producers and consumers can evolve message formats safely over time.

  • Add new optional fields instead of breaking old consumers.
  • Keep backward or forward compatibility rules in place.
  • Version messages intentionally instead of changing payloads randomly.

A schema registry is especially useful when many services share the same events.

Kafka transactions and exactly-once

Kafka transactions allow a producer to write to multiple partitions and commit offsets atomically for a consume-transform-produce pipeline. This is one of the building blocks for exactly-once semantics. 

@Transactional
public void processAndPublish() {
    // read from Kafka
    // write result
    // publish output
    // commit offsets in the same transactional flow
}
Kafka Streams

Kafka Streams is a Java library for building stream-processing applications on top of Kafka. Use it when you need transformations, joins, aggregations, or windowing over Kafka data.

  • Great for stream processing inside your Spring/Java ecosystem.
  • Supports stateless and stateful processing.
  • Useful for enrich, group, aggregate, window, and join pipelines.
Kafka Connect and CDC

Kafka Connect is used to move data between Kafka and external systems like databases, object storage, and search engines. CDC tools like Debezium can capture database changes and publish them to Kafka. 

MySQL/Postgres
   -> Debezium CDC
   -> Kafka topic
   -> Consumers / search index / analytics
When to use what
Need Use
Keep all events for a while Retention
Keep latest state per key Log compaction
Safe schema evolution Schema Registry
Atomic consume-process-publish Kafka transactions
Stream transformations Kafka Streams
Database-to-Kafka sync Kafka Connect / CDC

Interview one-liner: retention keeps event history, compaction keeps latest state per key, Schema Registry manages payload evolution, transactions help exactly-once workflows, Kafka Streams handles stream processing, and Kafka Connect/CDC move data between Kafka and external systems.

Retries and poison messages

A poison message is a record that keeps failing because of bad data or a bug in consumer logic. If you keep retrying forever, the consumer can get stuck. Production systems usually use bounded retries and then move the message to a Dead Letter Topic.

Dead Letter Topic (DLT)
