Real-world example: Order-service looks healthy, but Prometheus shows Kafka lag rising sharply in notification-service consumer group. That means async processing is falling behind.

11. Alerting is part of monitoring

Monitoring is incomplete without alerts.

  • High 5xx rate
  • p95 latency crossing SLA
  • DB pool almost exhausted
  • Kafka lag too high
  • Too many pod restarts
  • Disk/memory nearing limit

Common tools: Prometheus Alertmanager, Grafana alerts, CloudWatch alarms, Datadog monitors, Splunk alerts.

12. Dashboards we usually create
  • Service health dashboard
  • Latency and throughput dashboard
  • Error dashboard
  • JVM dashboard
  • Database pool dashboard
  • Kafka lag / queue depth dashboard
  • Business KPI dashboard
13. End-to-end troubleshooting example
Alert: p95 latency of /api/orders increased
  ->
Open Grafana dashboard
  ->
See order-service latency spike
  ->
Open trace in Jaeger/Tempo
  ->
Find payment-service span is slow
  ->
Open centralized logs using traceId
  ->
See payment gateway timeout
  ->
Root cause found
14. Best practices
  • Use common tags like serviceName, env, instanceId, traceId.
  • Define SLI/SLO/SLA for important APIs.
  • Monitor both technical and business metrics.
  • Use health probes for Kubernetes.
  • Use centralized logs and distributed tracing together.
  • Alert on symptoms that matter to users, not only on low-level metrics.
  • Keep dashboards simple and actionable.
Interview-ready answer

In a microservices system, I monitor services end to end using metrics, logs, traces, health checks, and alerts together. In Spring Boot, I usually enable Actuator and Micrometer, expose Prometheus metrics, visualize them in Grafana, centralize logs in ELK/Loki/CloudWatch, and enable tracing with OpenTelemetry or Micrometer Tracing to Jaeger/Tempo/Zipkin. I also configure Kubernetes readiness and liveness probes, monitor DB pools, Kafka lag, JVM metrics, and business KPIs, then create alerts for latency, errors, and failure spikes so production issues can be found quickly.

In microservices, logs are generated by many services, many pods, many servers, and many environments. A log aggregator collects logs from all these places into one centralized searchable system.

Why do we need a log aggregator in microservices?
  • One user request may travel through API Gateway, auth-service, order-service, payment-service, and notification-service.
  • If each service keeps logs locally, troubleshooting becomes very hard.
  • Pods/containers can restart, so local log files may disappear.
  • Centralized logs make search, debugging, alerting, auditing, and troubleshooting much easier.

Real-world example: A payment failed in production. Without centralized logs, you must check logs in 5 different services manually. With a log aggregator, you search by requestId or orderId and trace the full flow in one place.

Simple definition

A log aggregator is a centralized logging solution that collects, stores, indexes, and makes logs searchable across multiple services and machines.

Common tools
Tool Purpose
ELK / Elastic Stack Elasticsearch + Logstash + Kibana for centralized logging
EFK Elasticsearch + Fluent Bit/Fluentd + Kibana, common in Kubernetes
Grafana Loki Label-based log storage integrated with Grafana
Splunk Enterprise log analytics and search
CloudWatch AWS-native centralized logging
Azure Monitor / Log Analytics Azure-native centralized logging
GCP Logging Google Cloud-native centralized logging
Typical logging architecture in microservices
Microservice logs
  ->
stdout / log file
  ->
log collector agent (Fluent Bit / Fluentd / Filebeat / Vector)
  ->
log processor or pipeline (optional)
  ->
central log store (Elasticsearch / Loki / Splunk / CloudWatch)
  ->
search / dashboard / alerting
End-to-end example flow
User places order
  ->
API Gateway logs request
  ->
Order Service logs order creation
  ->
Payment Service logs payment failure
  ->
Notification Service logs retry event
  ->
All logs shipped to ELK
  ->
Search by requestId = 12345
  ->
See full distributed flow in one place
How do we achieve log aggregation?
  • Print structured logs, usually JSON.
  • Include correlation fields like requestId, traceId, serviceName, instanceId.
  • Ship logs using collector agents such as Fluent Bit, Fluentd, Filebeat, or cloud-native log agents.
  • Store logs in a central searchable system like Elasticsearch, Loki, Splunk, or CloudWatch.
  • Create dashboards and alerts on errors, exceptions, latency, and business failures.
Most important logging fields in microservices
Field Why it matters
@timestamp When the event happened
level INFO, WARN, ERROR, DEBUG
serviceName Which microservice logged it
instanceId Which pod/container/node produced it
requestId / traceId Trace same request across services
path / method Which API was called
status HTTP result or business state
durationMs Performance insight
errorCode / exception Failure analysis
businessId Order id, user id, payment id, etc.
How do we find which microservice generated a log?

We usually identify the source microservice using fields like serviceName, applicationName, instanceId, podName, containerName, and sometimes logger_name. 

{
  "@timestamp": "2026-08-06T11:12:13.456+05:30",
  "serviceName": "payment-service",
  "applicationName": "payment-service",
  "instanceId": "payment-service-7d87f",
  "podName": "payment-service-7d87f-abc12",
  "containerName": "payment-service",
  "requestId": "req-12345",
  "message": "payment_failed"
}

From this log, we immediately know the log came from payment-service, and even which exact instance or pod produced it.

What is app id / application name / service name?

This is the identity of the microservice that produced the log.

  • applicationName or serviceName usually means the microservice itself, such as order-service or payment-service.
  • instanceId usually means the specific running instance or pod of that service.

Real-world example: 

serviceName = payment-service
instanceId  = payment-service-7d87f-abc12

Meaning: the log came from the payment-service microservice, specifically from one running pod/container instance.

What is traceId?

traceId represents the entire end-to-end request journey across multiple services.

If one user request goes through 5 services, all those logs should ideally share the same traceId. 

Client request
  ->
API Gateway
  ->
Order Service
  ->
Payment Service
  ->
Inventory Service

Same traceId in all logs

Real-world example: If an order creation request fails in payment-service, we search by traceId and see the full path from gateway to payment.

What is spanId?

spanId represents a single step or single operation inside the larger trace.

One trace has multiple spans. 

traceId = whole request

span 1 = API Gateway receives request
span 2 = Order Service validates order
span 3 = Payment Service charges payment
span 4 = Inventory Service reserves stock

So:

  • traceId: full journey
  • spanId: one step in that journey
Simple analogy for trace and span

Think of traceId like a full courier shipment tracking number, and each spanId like one stop in the shipment journey: pickup, sorting center, transit hub, delivery.

How traceId and spanId look in logs
{
  "@timestamp": "2026-08-06T11:12:13.456+05:30",
  "serviceName": "payment-service",
  "instanceId": "payment-service-7d87f",
  "traceId": "8b7f2d13c44a9e1d9ac42c010f100111",
  "spanId": "39af1200bb9911aa",
  "requestId": "req-12345",
  "message": "payment_failed"
}
requestId vs traceId
Field Meaning
requestId Custom request correlation id, often generated by API gateway or app
traceId Distributed tracing id for full request flow across services
spanId One operation inside that trace

In many systems, requestId and traceId may be mapped together or one may be reused, but conceptually they are not exactly the same.

How do we search logs in practice?
  • Search by traceId to see the whole cross-service journey.
  • Search by serviceName to see only one microservice's logs.
  • Search by instanceId if one specific pod is misbehaving.
  • Search by orderId, userId, or paymentId for business debugging.
Structured JSON logs are strongly preferred

Plain text logs are hard to search reliably in distributed systems. JSON logs let log aggregation tools index and query fields directly. 

{
  "@timestamp": "2026-08-06T11:12:13.456+05:30",
  "level": "ERROR",
  "serviceName": "payment-service",
  "instanceId": "payment-service-7d87f",
  "requestId": "req-12345",
  "orderId": "ORD-1001",
  "path": "/api/payments",
  "status": 500,
  "durationMs": 92,
  "message": "payment_failed",
  "exception": "TimeoutException"
}
Spring Boot logging configuration idea

In Spring Boot, we usually use Logback with JSON encoder and MDC. 

<dependency>
    <groupId>net.logstash.logback</groupId>
    <artifactId>logstash-logback-encoder</artifactId>
    <version>7.4</version>
</dependency>
<configuration>
    <appender name="JSON_CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder"/>
    </appender>

    <root level="INFO">
        <appender-ref ref="JSON_CONSOLE"/>
    </root>
</configuration>

In containers and Kubernetes, printing JSON to stdout is often the cleanest approach. The platform log collector then ships those logs centrally.

Use correlation ID / trace ID

This is one of the most important parts in microservices logging. Every service should log the same request id or trace id for the same business flow. 

Gateway adds X-Request-Id
  ->
Order Service logs it
  ->
Payment Service logs same id
  ->
Inventory Service logs same id
  ->
Search one id in Kibana / Splunk / Loki
Spring Boot MDC example
MDC.put("requestId", requestId);
MDC.put("serviceName", "order-service");
MDC.put("orderId", orderId);

log.info("order_created");

MDC.clear();
Log collectors commonly used
Collector Where used Notes
Fluent Bit Kubernetes / containers Lightweight, very common
Fluentd Kubernetes / VMs Flexible routing and parsing
Filebeat VMs / containers Common with Elastic stack
Vector Modern log pipelines Fast and efficient
ELK / EFK example architecture
Spring Boot services
  ->
JSON logs to stdout
  ->
Fluent Bit DaemonSet on Kubernetes
  ->
Elasticsearch
  ->
Kibana dashboard and search
Loki example architecture
Spring Boot services
  ->
stdout logs
  ->
Promtail / Fluent Bit
  ->
Grafana Loki
  ->
Grafana dashboards
Cloud-native example
Spring Boot services on EKS/ECS
  ->
stdout logs
  ->
CloudWatch Agent / Fluent Bit
  ->
CloudWatch Logs
  ->
Metric filters / alarms / dashboards
How to configure in Kubernetes
  • Print application logs to stdout instead of maintaining local log files inside container.
  • Deploy Fluent Bit / Fluentd / Promtail as DaemonSet or sidecar depending on architecture.
  • Tag logs with namespace, pod name, container name, and app labels.
  • Send to Elasticsearch, Loki, or cloud log service.

Real-world example: Each node in the cluster runs a Fluent Bit agent that reads pod container logs and ships them centrally.

Best practices
  • Use structured JSON logs.
  • Always include request/correlation id.
  • Include service name and instance id.
  • Do not log passwords, tokens, OTPs, card numbers, or sensitive PII.
  • Use INFO for business milestones, WARN for recoverable issues, ERROR for failures.
  • Mask sensitive fields before shipping logs.
  • Set retention policy because logs can become expensive.
  • Use alerts on repeated exceptions, 5xx spikes, and unusual patterns.
  • Combine logs with metrics and tracing for full observability.
Challenges in log aggregation
  • Huge log volume can increase storage cost.
  • Noisy logs make troubleshooting harder.
  • Missing correlation id breaks request tracing.
  • Sensitive data leakage is a serious risk.
  • Clock/timezone mismatch can confuse investigations if timestamps are inconsistent.
Logs vs Metrics vs Traces
Signal Used for
Logs Detailed events and debugging
Metrics CPU, latency, throughput, error rate, dashboards
Traces Request path across microservices

Interview point: A log aggregator solves centralized log collection, but true observability usually needs logs + metrics + distributed tracing together.

Interview-ready answer

In microservices, a log aggregator is a centralized logging system that collects logs from multiple services and instances into one searchable place such as ELK, Loki, Splunk, or CloudWatch. We achieve it by printing structured JSON logs, adding correlation ids with MDC, shipping logs through agents like Fluent Bit or Filebeat, and storing them in a central index or log store. This helps us trace requests across services, debug failures faster, and build alerts and dashboards for production support.

In production, logs should be structured JSON so tools like ELK, Splunk, Datadog, CloudWatch, or Grafana Loki can search by fields like requestId, method, path, status, durationMs, applicationName, and instanceId.

Expected JSON logs
{
  "@timestamp": "2026-07-07T10:15:30.150+05:30",
  "level": "INFO",
  "logger_name": "com.example.demo.logging.RequestLoggingFilter",
  "message": "request_end",
  "applicationName": "order-service",
  "instanceId": "order-service-7f9d85b6c8-abc12",
  "requestId": "6ce50a6d-4af8-4f71-b7c4-d6aa09afdd1b",
  "method": "POST",
  "path": "/api/orders",
  "query": "source=mobile",
  "status": "201",
  "durationMs": "84",
  "clientIp": "10.20.30.40"
}
1. Maven dependency

Spring Boot uses Logback by default. Add logstash-logback-encoder to print logs as JSON. 

<dependency>
    <groupId>net.logstash.logback</groupId>
    <artifactId>logstash-logback-encoder</artifactId>
    <version>7.4</version>
</dependency>
2. application.yml
spring:
  application:
    name: order-service

server:
  port: 8080

app:
  instance-id: ${HOSTNAME:${spring.application.name}-local}

logging:
  level:
    root: INFO
    com.example.demo: INFO
3. logback-spring.xml

This config prints every log line as JSON and includes MDC fields added by our request filter. 

<configuration>
    <springProperty scope="context" name="appName" source="spring.application.name"/>

    <appender name="JSON_CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder">
            <customFields>{"applicationName":"${appName}"}</customFields>
        </encoder>
    </appender>

    <root level="INFO">
        <appender-ref ref="JSON_CONSOLE"/>
    </root>
</configuration>
4. Request logging filter

Use OncePerRequestFilter so each HTTP request gets exactly one start log and one end log. MDC adds searchable fields to all logs printed during the same request thread. 

package com.example.demo.logging;

import jakarta.servlet.FilterChain;
import jakarta.servlet.ServletException;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.slf4j.MDC;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.web.filter.OncePerRequestFilter;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.UUID;

@Component
public class RequestLoggingFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(RequestLoggingFilter.class);

    @Value("${spring.application.name}")
    private String applicationName;

    @Value("${app.instance-id:${spring.application.name}-local}")
    private String instanceId;

    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest request,
                                    HttpServletResponse response,
                                    FilterChain filterChain)
            throws ServletException, IOException {

        long startNanos = System.nanoTime();
        Instant startTime = Instant.now();

        String requestId = Optional.ofNullable(request.getHeader("X-Request-Id"))
                .filter(id -> !id.isBlank())
                .orElse(UUID.randomUUID().toString());

        response.setHeader("X-Request-Id", requestId);

        MDC.put("applicationName", applicationName);
        MDC.put("instanceId", instanceId);
        MDC.put("requestId", requestId);
        MDC.put("method", request.getMethod());
        MDC.put("path", request.getRequestURI());
        MDC.put("query", Optional.ofNullable(request.getQueryString()).orElse(""));
        MDC.put("clientIp", getClientIp(request));
        MDC.put("startTime", startTime.toString());

        log.info("request_start");

        try {
            filterChain.doFilter(request, response);
        } catch (Exception ex) {
            MDC.put("exception", ex.getClass().getSimpleName());
            log.error("request_failed", ex);
            throw ex;
        } finally {
            long durationMs = (System.nanoTime() - startNanos) / 1_000_000;

            MDC.put("endTime", Instant.now().toString());
            MDC.put("durationMs", String.valueOf(durationMs));
            MDC.put("status", String.valueOf(response.getStatus()));

            log.info("request_end");
            MDC.clear();
        }
    }

    private String getClientIp(HttpServletRequest request) {
        String forwardedFor = request.getHeader("X-Forwarded-For");
        if (forwardedFor != null && !forwardedFor.isBlank()) {
            return forwardedFor.split(",")[0].trim();
        }
        return request.getRemoteAddr();
    }
}
5. Application startup and shutdown logs

This logs application lifecycle events with application name, instance id, start time, ready time, and shutdown time. 

package com.example.demo.logging;

import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.slf4j.MDC;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.boot.context.event.ApplicationReadyEvent;
import org.springframework.context.event.EventListener;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

import jakarta.annotation.PreDestroy;
import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory;
import java.time.Instant;

@Component
public class ApplicationLifecycleLogger {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(ApplicationLifecycleLogger.class);

    @Value("${spring.application.name}")
    private String applicationName;

    @Value("${app.instance-id:${spring.application.name}-local}")
    private String instanceId;

    private final Instant appStartTime =
            Instant.ofEpochMilli(ManagementFactory.getRuntimeMXBean().getStartTime());

    @EventListener(ApplicationReadyEvent.class)
    public void onApplicationReady() {
        MDC.put("applicationName", applicationName);
        MDC.put("instanceId", instanceId);
        MDC.put("appStartTime", appStartTime.toString());
        MDC.put("appReadyTime", Instant.now().toString());

        log.info("application_ready");
        MDC.clear();
    }

    @PreDestroy
    public void onShutdown() {
        MDC.put("applicationName", applicationName);
        MDC.put("instanceId", instanceId);
        MDC.put("shutdownTime", Instant.now().toString());

        log.info("application_shutdown");
        MDC.clear();
    }
}
6. Example controller logs

Any log inside the request automatically carries the same MDC fields like requestId, method, path, applicationName, and instanceId. 

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/orders")
public class OrderController {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(OrderController.class);
    private final OrderService orderService;

    public OrderController(OrderService orderService) {
        this.orderService = orderService;
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> createOrder(@RequestBody OrderRequest request) {
        log.info("creating_order");

        OrderResponse response = orderService.create(request);

        log.info("order_created");
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).body(response);
    }
}
Production best practices
  • Always log in JSON in container/Kubernetes environments.
  • Use a correlation id such as X-Request-Id or trace id from OpenTelemetry/Sleuth/Micrometer tracing.
  • Do not log passwords, tokens, OTPs, card numbers, or full request bodies with PII.
  • Log request metadata, status, duration, and business identifiers like order id or user id only when safe.
  • Use INFO for start/end/business events, WARN for recoverable problems, and ERROR for failures.
  • Set log retention and masking rules in ELK/Splunk/CloudWatch.
  • For async execution, copy MDC context to async threads using a TaskDecorator.

Interview one-liner: In production Spring Boot apps, I use JSON logs with MDC fields and a OncePerRequestFilter to log request start, request end, method, path, status, duration, request id, application name, and instance id so every request can be traced end to end.
